text:
Livia went to the art gallery with Papa. She saw a big red circle on the wall. "Red," said Livia. Then she saw a big blue square. "Blue," said Livia. Papa smiled. There was a yellow star too. "Yellow!" said Livia. Her feet made a little noise on the shiny floor.

In the corner was a paint table for kids. Livia wanted to paint a sky. She stirred red and yellow together. Now she had orange! But her sky was dark blue. Too dark. Livia made a sad face. A boy next to her had white paint. "You can use some," he said. "Thank you," said Livia.

Livia dripped white into her blue. She stirred it round and round. Her dark blue got lighter. Now it looked like a soft morning sky. Livia held it up high. "Look, Papa! My sky!" she said. Papa clapped his hands, and the boy clapped too.

Scarlett was playing in the yard. She wanted to find a pretty stone for her pocket. She looked by the flowers. She looked under the bench. Then she saw something small and yellow. It was a lighter. It had rolled under the swing.

Scarlett bent down low. She looked at it. She did not pick it up. She knew it was not a toy.

"Mom!" she called. Mom came out slow and calm. "That is for grown-ups only," said Mom. Mom picked it up and put it high on a shelf. "Good job telling me," she said.

Scarlett went back to looking. She looked by the flowers again. At last she found a round white stone. It was warm from the sun. She put it in her pocket.

Later Scarlett felt tired. She took her stone to bed. She held it until her eyes closed.

Miles went to the library with his dad. They rode the bus. The bus was big, and Miles held his dad's hand. At the library, Miles saw the tablets on a low table.

"I want to draw," said Miles. He pushed the round button. The screen lit up. Miles tapped the drawing app. A dog appeared! He tapped blue, and the dog turned blue. He tapped red, and the sky turned red. "My taps make it change," said Miles.

Then the tablet went dark. "Why did it stop?" Miles asked. "It needs power," said Dad. Miles found the charger on the shelf. It was heavy. He carried it to his dad, who plugged it into the wall. Miles waited. The screen lit up again. He drew one more blue dog, then put the tablet back on the table, all by himself.

"Hungry?" asked Dad, hanging up his coat. Miles smiled and said, "Yes, and I want the bus home."

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. Her bowl was full of warm soup. "I don't want soup," she said. "It smells too strong." Her nose knew it. Her nose did not like it.

Mom sat down beside her. "Take a little sip," said Mom. "You are lucky. It is mild today." Aubrey looked at the soup with her eyes. She heard it go plop, plop in the bowl. She touched her spoon with her fingers. "One, two, three," she counted the carrots.

Aubrey had an idea. She held her nose closed. She sipped the soup. It tasted plain, like warm water. "Oh!" she said. She let go of her nose. She sipped again. Now it tasted strong again. Aubrey giggled. She held her nose. She let go. She held it again. "Pass the bread, please," she said. Mom passed the bread. Aubrey dipped it in the soup. Then she ate the whole bowl, spoon by spoon. "More soup, please," said Aubrey.

Nora saw the snow out the window. Big brother Sam was going to the bus stop. Nora wanted to go too. She ran to the door with no coat.

Mom opened the door a tiny bit. Cold air came in. It went right down Nora's neck. "Brr!" said Nora. Her arms got little bumps. The wind was loud outside. Nora stepped back. "I need my coat," she said.

Her red coat was on the hook. Nora pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The zipper was tricky. Up, up it went, all by itself. "I did it!" said Nora. Mom smiled. "My warm little sheep," said Mom. Nora pretended to be a sheep. She said, "Baa!" Then she held Sam's hand. They walked out into the snow, warm all over.

Cooper built a big tower of blocks. He made a long track for his cars too. Then he heard the rain stop. He ran to the window. The wet street was shiny in the sun.

"I want to go out," said Cooper. He started to run to the door. Dad held his hand. "The cars need a home first," said Dad. Cooper looked back. The blocks were all over the rug. The cars were everywhere.

Cooper went back. He put one block in the basket. Then another. He slid a car onto the shelf. His socks would slip on the rug, so he walked slow and careful. Soon the rug was clear. The room looked big and calm.

"Now we can go," said Dad. Cooper clapped his hands and held the door.

Thomas stood in the bathroom. He wanted his bath now. He saw the big faucet. He reached up his hand.

Daddy caught his hand. "Not that tap," said Daddy. "That water is hot." Daddy turned the small tap instead. Cool water came out. Thomas put his fingers in. "Cold!" he said. Then Daddy added warm water, slow and careful. Thomas touched it. Warm now, like soup.

Thomas got in the tub. He splashed and played with his yellow duck. The duck went under. Then it popped up. Thomas laughed. Daddy washed his hair. The water ran down, drip drip.

Bath time was done. Daddy lifted Thomas out. The towel was soft on one side. The other side felt rough. The rough side dried his toes fast. Thomas got his pajamas on. Then he saw his cookie on the sink. He took a big bite. "Yum," he said.

Then Thomas heard a bell outside. His friend Mia was on her bike. Thomas ran for the door. He did not stop. He almost forgot something. Daddy held up the red helmet. Thomas ran back. Daddy put it on his head. It clicked under his chin. Thomas ran outside to his trike.

Mia rang her bell again. Thomas pushed his pedals. Off he went, helmet shining in the sun.

Amelia went to the library with her mother. She wanted a book about a big red dog. She looked and looked. She found one at last.

She opened the book. The dog was on the first page. She turned the pages one by one. The story went on and on. Then she was at the last page. "It ended!" she said. "I read all the way to the end."

"Now you can take it home," said her mother. "But first we sign a card." Her mother wrote Amelia on the card. Amelia looked at it. The letters were A, m, e, l, i, a. Then she looked at her little red bag. Her name was on that too. A, m, e, l, i, a. Same letters. Same order. She put her finger on the card. She put her finger on the bag. "It's me, two times!" she said.

The librarian laughed. "Two Amelias," she said. Amelia gave the dog book a little wave. "Come on, book," she said. "Home time."

Sara went to the library with Dad. She wanted the big bear book. She ran to the shelf.

A boy was there first. He held the bear book. Sara stomped her foot. She felt angry. She wanted to yell.

Then she saw the boy's face. A tear ran down. He looked sad. "I feel sad," the boy told the librarian. "The dog book is gone."

The librarian smiled. "Let's look together," she said. She found the dog book on a cart. The boy hugged it. He was happy now.

Sara felt excited. She waited for her turn. The boy gave her the bear book. "Thank you," she said.

On the way home, Sara told Dad, "I feel happy." Dad gave her a big hug. The bear book felt warm in her arms.

Charlie stood on her stool by the counter. Mama put warm toast on her plate. The toast smelled so good.

"I want to do it myself," said Charlie. Mama gave her a dull knife with some soft butter on it. Charlie poked the toast with the pointy tip. The toast tore. Little bits fell off. "Oh no," said Charlie. "Why did it tear?"

She looked at the knife. It had a flat side too. What would the flat side do? Charlie turned the knife over. She pushed the flat side across the bread. The butter spread out thin and smooth. One push, two pushes, three pushes. The whole toast turned shiny.

"Now the milk," said Mama. Charlie took the small cup and the little pitcher. She poured very slowly. Drip, drip, drip. Would it spill? The milk went up, up, up. Not one drop fell.

Charlie took a bite of her toast. "I made it myself," she said. She looked at the flower on her cup. "Can I do it again tomorrow, Mama?"

Maria put on her new hat. She ran to the backyard. Grandma was at the little grill with a pot. The pot went puff, puff, puff. Little white clouds rose up. Maria wanted to see the bubbles in the pot. "Come see," said Grandma. "Stand here by me."

Maria stood next to Grandma. The pot went puff, puff, puff again. Maria stepped back one step. The white clouds touched the air above her head. They did not touch Maria. Grandma stirred the pot. Round bubbles went blub, blub, blub.

"I see them!" said Maria. She watched from her spot by Grandma. Then she wiped the little table with a cloth. She set out cups, one, two, three. Grandma carried the pot over, slow and careful. They sat in the shade. "Hot tea for me," said Grandma. "Cold water for you." Maria drank her cold water. Her new hat kept the sun off. The pot sat far away, going puff, puff, puff.

Alice went to the store with her brother. He was hungry for apples. "We need five apples," he said.

Alice held up her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said.

The apple bins had big signs. One sign had a 5 on it. Alice looked at the 5. Then she looked at her five fingers. "It is the same," she said. The 5 meant five apples!

Alice put apples in the bag. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. Her brother counted too.

At home, Mom washed the apples. Alice tried a small bite. It was sweet and crunchy. Her brother smiled and held up one apple. "One left for you," he said.

Madeline sat on a big chair at Grandma's house. Today was a party. It was Sam's birthday. Sam was turning five. Grandma brought out a chocolate cake. It smelled sweet like cocoa.

"Look at the candles," said Mom. Madeline looked. She pointed at them. She counted out loud. "One, two, three, four." Then she stopped. She looked at Sam. Sam held up his hand. His fingers were spread wide.

"There are four candles," said Madeline. Mom looked at the cake. Mom looked at Sam. Then Mom got another candle from the box. She pushed it gently into the frosting. Now Madeline counted again. "One, two, three, four, five." Five candles for five years.

The room felt warm and full of voices. Grandpa lit the candles with a long match. The little flames wiggled. Madeline stood far back and watched. The cake sat in the middle of the table, glowing. Everyone sang to Sam. Then Sam took a big breath.

"Make a wish," said Madeline. Sam blew out all five candles at once. Grandma cut the cake with a safe knife, far from small hands. She gave Madeline a cool slice on a blue plate. Madeline clapped and took a big bite.

Declan is at daycare. He paints a big sun. The paint is red and warm looking. It smells like paint, a little bit like crayons.

"My paint will not stick," says Declan. He tries to stick the paper on the wall. It falls down.

"That is the problem," says Miss Amy. "The paint is wet now. It will dry later. You can take your sun home tomorrow."

"Where does today go when I sleep?" asks Declan.

"It gets a new name," says Miss Amy. "Tomorrow we will call it yesterday."

Declan sleeps in his bed. The moon is out. In the morning the sun is out again.

At daycare, Miss Amy holds up his painting. It is dry now. The red sun looks different, shiny and smooth.

"You made this yesterday," she says.

"Yesterday I made the sun," says Declan. He hugs the paper to his chest.

Lydia went to the big stadium with Mom and Dad. The green field was far away. The crowd was loud. Lydia held her bunny tight.

The red team ran and ran. The blue team ran and ran too. "The red team ran the most," said Lydia. "Red wins!" Dad smiled. "Let's look at the board," he said. Lydia looked up high. The board said: red team, one point. Blue team, two points. "Blue has more points," said Lydia. "Blue wins!" The whistle blew. The blue team jumped and hugged. "They ran less, but they got more points," said Lydia.

Lydia skipped in a little circle. Her tummy felt giggly. Mom laughed. The blue fans waved their scarves. One fan, two fans, lots of fans. "Same team, same scarves," said Lydia. She waved her little blue scarf too. Dad lifted her up high. Lydia shouted with the crowd, "We won! We won!"

Emilia went to the store with Mama. She wanted to pick a present for Grandma. There was a big basket of apples near the door. Emilia ran to see it. She bumped into a boy. His apple fell down and rolled under the shelf. The boy made a sad face. Emilia said, "Sorry." She got down on her knees. She reached into the deep, dark space under the shelf. Her hand came back with the apple. The boy smiled.

Then it was their turn at the apple basket. The man in front took one apple and stepped away. Emilia waited. She took one apple and put it in Mama's bag. The boy waited too. He took one apple. They each had one apple. It was fair.

At the toy shelf, Emilia found a soft red scarf. It would keep Grandma warm. She held it up to show Mama. The boy waved bye from the door. Emilia waved back and hugged the scarf tight.

Chloe sat at the kitchen table. Mom put a plate in front of her. On it were a cracker, a lemon, and a soft bit of bread.

"Let's play a game," said Mom. "Find your five senses."

"Easy!" said Chloe. She pointed at her eyes. "I see with these. I see the cracker."

"Yes," said Mom. "What about the lemon?"

Chloe sniffed the lemon. Her nose wiggled. "I smell with my nose! It smells sour."

She bit the cracker. Crunch, crunch. "I hear it! My ears hear it. And my mouth tastes it."

"Now the bread," said Mom.

Chloe squeezed it. It was squishy. "I feel it with my hand!"

"With your skin," said Mom. "Your fingertips feel it."

Chloe touched the plate, the lemon, the bread again. Each one felt different. "My fingers know so much!"

She touched Mom's nose. "Your nose feels squishy too!"

Mom laughed. "Stop that, silly girl!"

Chloe sat back and held up her hand. "Five senses. I found them all!"

Then she touched her own nose. "Boop," said Chloe.

Andrew was at the lake with Dad. The lake had a little pool by the shore. Andrew wanted to swim in it. He held Dad's hand. He went down the steps, one step at a time. The water felt cool. "Kick, kick," said Dad. Andrew kicked. His feet made splashes. A shy fish swam away fast. Andrew laughed. "Again," he said. He kicked again and again. He was tired now. He wanted to get out.

Andrew pulled on the pool edge. It was too tall. He slipped back into the water. He tried again. Still too tall. Dad stood close by. "Look, Andrew," said Dad. "There are more steps." Andrew saw the steps. He held the rail. He went up, one step at a time. It was easy. He sat on the warm grass. "I did it," said Andrew. Dad clapped. Then Andrew yawned. "Nap time," said Dad. Andrew lay on the towel. His eyes closed. The water went pop, pop against the steps.

Emilia sat in the big chair at the clinic. Today she would get a shot. Her tummy felt funny and her arms felt weak.

"Will it hurt a lot?" she asked Grandpa.

"Just a tiny pinch," Grandpa said. "Now smell this." He held up his jacket. It smelled like cookies. Emilia took one slow, deep smell. Then Grandpa counted, and she let the air out slow, like a birthday candle going out. Her tummy felt better. They did it again. And again.

The nurse came in with a little line of medicine in the tiny needle. Emilia took a slow, deep breath. She smelled the cookie smell. She blew it out slow. Then the nurse said, "All done!"

"That was it?" Emilia asked. She looked at her arm and smiled. "Can I have a sticker now?"

"You sure can," said the nurse, and she picked out a shiny gold star.

Chloe wanted toast with butter, all by herself. Daddy made the toast. The toast was hot, so Daddy put it on her plate. Chloe held the little knife. She spread the butter. The butter made a mark on the toast. She pushed more, and the butter slid. Slip, slip, slip. Now the toast was all yellow. Daddy laughed. "Good spreading, Chloe!"

Next came the milk. Chloe held the cup with one hand. She poured slowly with the other hand. The milk went in the cup. Not one drop spilled. "I did it!" said Chloe. Then she ran to show Mama. On the way back, she saw the milk jug. It sat by the wall, far from the fridge. The milk needed to be cold. Chloe picked up the jug. She pushed the fridge door. She put the milk inside. The door shut with a little bump.

Outside the window the sky looked stormy and gray. "Rain soon," said Daddy. Chloe drank her milk. It was nice and cold. She took a big bite of toast. "Butter face!" said Daddy. Chloe giggled. There was butter on her nose.

Hayden ran to the big library playroom. He wanted the red ball, but it rolled far under the shelf. He got down on his knees. The ball was too far back. He could not reach it.

Then he saw a girl named Mia. She had a loose tooth that wiggled when she smiled. She was filling the toy box. "Blocks," she said, dropping them in. "Dolls," she said, and they went in too. Hayden watched. Then he had an idea. He found a long stuffed elephant. The elephant had a big gray trunk. He pushed the trunk under the shelf. He wiggled it like a magic wand. Out rolled the red ball!

"Good trick," said Mia. She clapped her hands. Hayden hugged the elephant and threw the ball high. It bounced, bounce, bounce, all the way to the story rug. "Again!" said Mia. Hayden ran after it.

Henry ran to the park with his teddy bear. The sun was warm on his face. He heard kids laugh and shout. The swings went squeak, squeak!

Henry saw a big tunnel to crawl through. He held teddy tight. But inside the tunnel, it got dark. Henry could not see! He dropped teddy. Teddy was gone in the dark.

"Dad!" Henry called. "I can't see teddy!" Dad came fast. He took out his phone and made a light. Dad shone the light into the tunnel. Now Henry could see! There was teddy, right by his knee. Henry grabbed him and hugged him tight.

Then Henry smelled something smelly. "Pee-yew!" he said. It was his own shoe, full of sandbox sand. Dad laughed. "Let's talk about it at home," he said. "We can wash your feet."

On the walk home, they got an ice pop. Henry tasted the sweet orange ice. "Yum!" he said. He touched teddy's soft ear. Dad said, "See the big blue sky? It looks like the ocean!" Henry waved his hand at the sky. Then he took one more happy lick of his ice pop.

Lincoln wore his blue coat to the corner store with Dad. On the counter sat a plate of little cookies. Ten cookies! Lincoln pointed at them one by one. "One, two, three," he said. He counted all the way to ten.

"I want two," said Lincoln. Dad said he could have two. Lincoln took one cookie and ate it. Crunch! He counted again. Nine cookies. He took another one. Munch, munch. Now eight cookies sat on the plate. "The plate has fewer now," Lincoln said. The man behind the counter smiled. "How many now?" he asked.

They counted together as the cookies went home with other people. Seven, then six, then five. Lincoln watched and waited. At last the plate was empty. "Where did the cookies go?" he asked. "How many are left?" Dad held up the plate. "Zero," said Lincoln. "Zero cookies. Zero means none!" The shy little store cat came out then. Lincoln laughed and held out his empty hand. "Zero cookies for you too, cat."

Henry went to the library today. Yesterday it had rained, so he could not go. Today the sun was out. "Can I play with the blocks?" Henry asked. The librarian smiled. "You can play later," she said. "First we will sing songs now."

Henry sat on the soft red rug. He clapped his hands. He sang about a little duck. The songs were fun, but he kept looking at the blocks. "Is it later yet?" he asked Mom. "Not yet," said Mom. "Sing one more song first."

Henry sang the last song. The singing stopped. Now his hands were quiet. Now the room was quiet. "Is it later now?" he asked. Mom nodded. "Yes. Now it is later."

Henry ran to the blocks. He stacked them up, up, up. He made a tall red tower. Then he pushed one block at the bottom. The whole tower fell down. All the blocks went bump on the rug. Henry laughed. "The little block made them all fall!" he said.

At home, Mom gave Henry a small cake. He got to lick the frosting off his fingers. "Can we go to the library again?" he asked. "Tomorrow," said Mom. Henry smiled. "Tomorrow is after today."

Joshua sat at the big table in the hall. It was cloudy outside. His tummy made a little growl. "Soon," said Grandma. "First we say our blessing."

Grandma folded her hands. "Thank you for this food," she said. Everyone said it together. Then Joshua thought of something. "Who made the bread?" he asked.

"The baker did," said Grandma. "And a farmer grew the wheat."

Joshua put his hands together again. "Thank you, baker!" he said. "Thank you, farmer too!" The man at the desk by the door laughed a kind laugh. A dog outside went bark, bark, as if it wanted to say thank you too.

"Again, again!" said Joshua. So everyone said it one more time. Then the bread basket came around, and Joshua took the biggest piece. "I said two thank-yous," he whispered to Grandma. "So I get the big one." Grandma smiled and gave him a bit more.

Blake walked on the nature trail with her mom. She wanted to learn her five senses. "Each one uses a body part," Mom said. Blake wanted to say them all by herself.

A big truck rumbled by. It was so loud. Blake put her hands over her ears. The sound got quieter. "That is neat!" she said. "My ears hear the truck. My hands make it quiet."

Mom smiled. "Yes, ears are for hearing." Blake looked around. "My eyes see that green leaf," she said. "My nose smells rain coming." She touched a smooth rock. "My hands feel this." Then she said, "My tongue tastes my snack!" They sat on a bench and Blake poured juice from her little cup. She sipped it and grinned. "Five senses, all by me," she said. "Now let's hear the birds."

Michael ran up the steps to Grandma's house. The door swung open fast. "Happy day!" Grandma called. Inside, the house was full of people. Aunts, uncles, and cousins were everywhere.

Michael wanted to find his cousin Ben. He had not seen Ben in a long, long time. But the room was too crowded. Michael looked behind the big chair. No Ben. He looked by the table of food. No Ben. Then he heard a giggle from the hallway. Michael peeked around the corner. There was Ben, hugging a soft pet rabbit!

"Ben!" Michael shouted. Ben jumped up and they hugged tight. "Come see the candles," Ben said. The two boys sat with Grandma. Grandma lit the candles, one by one. Michael watched each little flame grow tall.

Later, Michael got sleepy on Grandma's lap. Ben leaned on his mom's shoulder. "Same time next holiday," Auntie whispered. Michael smiled. He closed his eyes and dreamed of rabbits.

Grandma was coming to stay for a whole week. Violet waited in the kitchen. She tapped her toes on the floor. Then a car pulled up, and Grandma came in with a big bag. Grandma hugged Violet tight.

Violet had a worry. "Grandma," she said, "are you my mom's friend?" Mom was mixing cake batter at the counter. Grandma laughed a funny laugh. "Come and see," she said. She pointed at Mom. Then she pointed at herself. "I am Mom's mom." Violet looked at Mom. Mom nodded and smiled. Violet's eyes got big. Grandma was Mom's mom! So Grandma was a grandma to her.

"Can I paint you a picture?" Violet asked. Grandma sat down at the table. Violet painted a sheep with wiggly legs. Mom put the cake in the oven. Violet and Grandma waited side by side. "Warm cake for my girl," said Grandma, "and for my girl's girl too."

William went to a big festival with his friend Sam. There was a playground with a red slide. William ran to it. He went down fast. His hat began to fall off. He caught it just in time.

Then it was time to eat. Sam's family sat at a long table. They all held hands. Sam's mom asked, "Would you like to say grace, William?"

William did not know what that meant. Sam whispered, "You say thank you for the food." William thought hard. He held hands tight, so no food would fall off the table.

"Thank you for the yummy bread," William said. Everyone smiled. Sam's dad cut the bread with a sharp knife. He gave William the first big piece.

"Can I say it again next time?" William asked.

"You sure can," said Sam.

Axel ran to the block corner at school. He wanted to build a big tower today. His friend Mia was already there. She was stacking blocks and counting them out loud.

"One, two, four," said Mia.

"Wait," said Axel. "Where did three go?"

Mia counted again. "One, two, four." The tower wobbled. Mia frowned. She wanted to count all ten blocks before the tower got too tall.

Axel thought hard. He sang the counting song in his head. He knew how it went. The numbers always came out the same way. "Try it like this," he said. "One, two, three. Then four comes after three!"

Mia nodded. She touched each block. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Then she stopped and laughed. "Eight! I almost forgot eight."

"Then nine," said Axel, bouncing on his toes. "And ten is last."

Together they counted the whole tower. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" The tower stood tall and thick like a wall of snow. It did not fall down.

"Ten blocks!" shouted Mia.

Ms. Rios clapped from across the room. Axel put one more block on top. The tower swayed. Then it came down with a crash. Blocks rolled everywhere. The two friends fell into giggles and began to count them again.

Bennett jumped into the car seat. "We're going to Grandma's!" he called. Dad started the car. The big truck next to them rumbled away, fast. Their car went slow in the line.

Bennett looked out the window. The sun made his arm feel hot. Dad turned on the air. Now cool air blew on his face. "Better?" Dad asked. "Better!" said Bennett.

Then came the problem. Baby sister Mia began to cry. Her cry was loud. Very, very loud. Bennett wanted her to sleep. Grandma had a yummy cake waiting, and a plate with his name on it. But Mia would not close her eyes.

Bennett had an idea. He clapped his hands, loud, loud, loud. Mia cried louder. That did not work! So Bennett tried a tiny pat on his knee. Tap. Tap. Tap. It was so quiet. Mia blinked. Her cry got small. Then it got quiet too. Her eyes closed.

"She's sleeping," Bennett whispered. Dad smiled and drove on, down the big road, past the small houses, all the way to Grandma's cake.

Anna ran to the playground. The sun made the slide shine like gold. A big lion spring toy waited there. It had a dark mane and a long tail. Anna wanted to ride it very much.

But a little boy sat on the lion already. He bounced up and down. He bounced very fast. Anna waved at him. The boy did not wave back. He jumped off and hid behind his grandma.

Anna thought and thought. "How can he be my friend?" she asked herself. "I can say hello." So Anna took one step. Then one more step. She peeked around the grandma's coat. "Hello," said Anna, in a small kind voice.

The boy peeked out. He looked at Anna. Then he smiled. "Hello," he said back. He came out from behind the coat. "Want to bounce too?" he asked. "Yes, please," said Anna.

They bounced on the lion together. Anna bounced so high she bumped the boy's arm. "Sorry," said Anna. The boy rubbed his arm. "It is okay," he said. Then Anna wanted to sit in front. "Can you help me?" she asked. The grandma lifted her up. "Thank you," said Anna. The two friends bounced and bounced, all the way to the pretend moon. "Roar," said the lion, in their big pretend voices.

Blake went to the library with her dad. She found a new book about a duck on a lake. She wanted to take it home.

There was a line at the desk. Blake ran right to the front. A boy was already standing there. He held his book tight. "You have to wait," the boy said. Blake looked back. Three people stood behind him.

"Where is my spot?" Blake asked her dad. "At the end, by me," he said. Blake walked to the back of the line. She held her book. She waited.

The boy got his stamp and smiled. The next person went. Then the next. Soon it was Blake's turn. The librarian stamped her duck book. "You waited so nicely," she said.

On the way out, Blake waved to the boy. He waved back. "Can we read it tonight?" Blake asked. "Yes," said her dad. He took her hand, and they walked out into the sun.

Iris wants her red shoe. She cannot find it. She looked for it yesterday. She looked for it today. Now it is bedtime.

"Daddy, where is my red shoe?" she asks.

Daddy says, "Look in the morning. Now it is night."

Iris peeks out the window. The sky is dark. She sees the moon. "Night," she whispers.

She remembers her day. The sun came up. That was morning. Then she ate lunch. That was afternoon. Then Grandma came. That was evening. Then the sky went dark. That was night.

"Now I sleep," says Iris. "Later, the sun comes back. Then it is morning again."

She gets into bed. Daddy tucks her in. Her blanket is soft. It tickles her toes.

"Tomorrow you can look for your shoe," says Daddy.

"Tomorrow," says Iris. She closes her eyes.

In the morning, the sun peeks in. Iris lifts her blanket. She looks under the bed. There is her red shoe! A sticky candy wrapper is stuck to it.

Iris laughs. "Good morning, shoe," she says. She puts it on her foot.

Aiden ran to the park with his red truck. The sun did shine on the swings. Aiden felt happy. He pushed his truck up the ramp. The truck went far down the slide. That made Aiden laugh and feel excited.

Then Aiden heard a small sound. A girl sat by the sand box. Tears ran down her face. She was crying. Aiden felt sad just looking at her. He held his truck tight. He did not want to give it up. His tummy felt tight and a little angry too.

But the girl kept crying. Aiden walked over slowly. "Do you want my truck?" he asked. She wiped her eyes. She nodded. Aiden put the truck in her hands. She pushed it in the sand. Her tears stopped. She smiled a big smile.

Aiden felt warm inside. He sat down next to her. They made a road together. The truck went far, then came back. "Vroom," said the girl. "Vroom," said Aiden.

Andrew ran to the big red slide. The sun felt warm on his face. The slide was warm too, from sitting in the sun all morning. He touched it with one finger first, then slid down fast. "Wheee!"

Next to the slide stood a bouncy pig. It was a pig on a spring. Andrew bounced on the pig. His boots went up and down. Near the pig, he saw a shiny bottle on the snowy ground. The snow crunched under his feet. He reached for it, but a big kid said, "Don't touch that. Ask a grown-up." Andrew put his hands in his pockets instead.

Then Mom said, "Let's get warm cocoa at the park store." Inside, Andrew looked at a wall of cookies. He turned around. Mom was not there. His tummy felt funny. He walked to the lady at the checkout. "I can't find my grown-up," he said. The lady smiled and called out, "Is a mom looking for Andrew?" Mom came around the shelf right away. She held his hand tight. The lady gave him a cocoa cup to hold with both hands. It was warm, not hot. Andrew took a little sip and smiled.

Brielle stood by the little red chair. The reading corner had soft mats and a long shelf of books. She held her new library card in both hands.

"I want to take this one home," she said. It was a book about a sleepy bear.

But first she saw a boy by the rug. He stood at the edge of the storytime circle. He did not sit down. His toe tapped the mat, tap, tap.

The librarian sat down on her low chair. She held up a book with a pig on it. She opened it wide and read the first page in a big, happy voice. "This little pig found a big mud puddle!"

The boy laughed. Then he sat down on the rug with the other kids. Brielle sat down too, right next to him. The librarian read on. Her voice went high, then low. The pig got very muddy.

When storytime ended, the librarian helped Brielle scan her card. Beep! Then she scanned the bear book. Beep!

"You did it," the librarian said.

Brielle put the card in her pocket. She hugged the book all the way to the door.

Oliver was at summer camp. It was paint day. He sat at a big table with paper and brushes. He painted a lion. The lion had a yellow mane and a red tail.

After painting, the other kids rinsed their brushes in the water cups. Oliver wanted to paint more. He stuck his brush in the red paint cup. Then he ran outside to play.

The next day, camp was paint day again. Oliver grabbed his brush. He tried to paint a sun. The brush would not bend. It was hard like a stick.

"Is it broken?" Oliver asked.

"No," said his teacher, Maya. "Touch it. What does it feel like?"

Oliver touched it. It felt stiff and dry. The paint had dried on it.

Maya held out a new brush. "Here, you can share mine," she said.

Oliver painted a big blue sun. Maya helped him hold the brush flat. At the end, Oliver carried his brush to the sink. He rinsed it all by himself. The water turned pink. Then he shut off the faucet and set the brush on a paper towel.

The next morning, the brush was soft and bendy. Oliver smiled and painted a green lion with a purple mane.

One morning Beatrice went to Grandpa's house. She saw a big black case on the chair. "What is inside?" she asked. Grandpa smiled. "Open it and see." Inside was a little violin.

Grandpa gave her a stick with hairs on it. "This is the bow," he said. Beatrice took the bow. She poked the violin with the tip. The violin made a squeak. Beatrice laughed. Then she poked it again. Squeak, squeak, squeak. "That sounds funny," she said.

Grandpa sat close to her. He showed her how to hold the bow. Then he helped her pull it across the strings. The violin sang. It sang a long, sweet song. One pull, one song. Two pulls, two songs. Beatrice pulled the bow again and again. The music flew around the sleepy room like a bird.

Grandpa played too. He played fast, then slow. Beatrice moved her bow with him. "Can I make it soft?" she asked. "Pull it slow and soft," said Grandpa. So she did. The violin hummed like a small cat. Grandpa clapped his hands, and Beatrice took a little bow.

Henri woke up very awake. Today was his first day of school. He put on his red shirt. He ate his toast. Then his tummy felt funny. It felt like small wings were flapping inside.

"Mom, my tummy is fluttery," said Henri. Mom knelt down beside him. "My tummy felt that way on my first day too," she said. "It is okay to feel like that." Henri held her hand all the way to school.

At the classroom door, a boy was chasing a ball. The ball rolled right to Henri's feet. Henri picked it up and threw it back. The boy laughed. Henri's tummy stopped fluttering. Inside, the teacher held up a green triangle made of paper. Henri sat down on the small blue chair and smiled.

Lily sat at Grandma's big table. She wanted to write her name all by herself. Grandma put a pencil in her hand. Lily grabbed it in her whole fist. She pushed the pencil onto the paper. The letters came out wobbly and fat. They did not look like L I L Y at all.

"Hmm," said Lily. "Why is my L so big and bumpy?" Grandma sat next to her. Grandma picked up her own pencil. She pinched it with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil rested on her middle finger. Grandma wrote her name, and every letter stood neat and small.

Lily looked hard at Grandma's hand. "Can I try that way?" Lily pinched the pencil with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil rested on her middle finger. She drew a line down. Then a little curve. It was an L! Lily made another L, and a tall stick, and a curl. "Lily!" she read out loud. Grandma clapped. On the empty page, Lily wrote her name three more times.

Matteo loved daycare days. Today Miss Ana said, "We will play hide and seek!" Matteo ran outside to the little hill. The grass felt soft under his hands. He touched it with his fingers.

"Where should I hide?" he asked himself. "Behind the short bush!" He could smell the flowers there. He could hear his friend Sam counting. He could see Sam's red shoes.

Then Matteo had an idea. He covered his eyes with his hands. Now he could not see the bush. He could not see Sam. He could not see anything at all. "Sam can't see me either!" he thought.

But Sam found him fast. "I saw you!" Sam laughed. "Your tummy was showing!"

Matteo tried again. He hid behind the hill. He kept his eyes open this time. He watched Sam look and look. Sam could not find him. Matteo waited and waited. The sun felt warm on his face. "The sun can burn your nose," Miss Ana had said, so he sat in the shade.

At snack time, Matteo ate a sweet apple. "Yum," he said. "My tongue likes this!"

"Matteo, where were you?" asked Sam.

"Behind the hill," said Matteo. "My eyes were open. That is why you could not find me!"

Sara planted seeds at the farm. She put carrot seeds in one row. She put tomato seeds in another row. Then she watered them all. "Grow, little seeds," she said. "Grow, grow."

The next day, Sara forgot something. Which row had the tomatoes? She looked and looked. The soil all looked the same. "Oh no," she said. "I can't remember!"

Grandpa had an idea. They cut card into little signs. Sara drew a carrot on one. She drew a tomato on another. Grandpa pushed the signs into the soil. "Now the labels show what is in each spot," said Grandpa. Sara clapped her hands.

Every day Sara checked her garden. Tiny green leaves came up. She looked at the tomato label first. Then she found the baby tomatoes right there. "It worked!" she said. "It worked, it worked!"

Soon there were fat red tomatoes and long orange carrots. Sara washed one carrot with the hose. Her dog Buddy wagged his tail and dropped a bone at her feet, hoping for a share. Grandpa laughed. Sara bit her carrot and smiled. "Tomorrow we pick the tomatoes," she said.

Victor wanted apple juice at snack time. He saw the big jug on the table. He grabbed at it. "Give me juice!" he said. Miss Ana held the jug away. "Try again," she said. Victor felt his face go hot. He looked at his friend Sam. Sam said, "Juice, please." Miss Ana poured the juice right away. Sam got a full cup.

Victor took a big breath. He tried again. "Juice, please," he said. Miss Ana smiled. She poured. Victor got a full cup too. The juice was cold and sweet. He heard the little plink of Sam's cup on the table.

Then Victor bumped Sam's arm. Some juice spilled. "Sorry," said Victor. "It's okay," said Sam. "You can help me wipe it." They wiped the spill together with a paper towel.

After story time, Victor felt sleepy. His eyes blinked slow. "Miss Ana, can you help me find my coat, please?" he asked. Miss Ana handed him his red coat. "Thank you," said Victor. He put it on all by himself. "See you tomorrow," said Miss Ana.

Josephine went to the park with Grandma. She wanted to find a red leaf. Grandma said, "Stay close to me." So Josephine stayed close. "Look, don't touch," Grandma said at the big fire pit. A man was making a fire to cook. Sparks flew up. The fire was hot. The bench in the shade was cold. Hot fire, cold bench. How did one feel so different? Josephine liked wondering about that.

Then they sat at a picnic table for a snack. Josephine saw something shiny on the ground. It was a little bottle. Inside were little red and yellow balls. They looked just like candy. Josephine wanted to pick them up. Her hand came close. Then she remembered her rule. Look, don't touch.

"Grandma!" she called. "I see candy on the ground." Grandma came right over. She looked in the bottle. "These are not candy," Grandma said. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine." Grandma picked up the bottle with a tissue and put it in her pocket. "Good girl," said a kind man with a dog. His dog began to beg for a piece of Josephine's apple.

Josephine gave the dog nothing. Grown-ups give the treats too. She sat by Grandma and ate her apple, all the way to the seeds.

Brooklyn went to the bookshop with her dad. She saw books everywhere. Some were big. Some were small. "Can I look?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "I will sit right here."

Brooklyn found a book with letters in it. The first letter was A. "A," she said. "A says ah, ah, ah!" She turned the page. B came next. "B says buh," she said. She kept turning the pages. C, D, E, F. Each letter made its own sound. "How many letters are there?" she wondered.

She turned more pages. G, H, I. Then J, K, L, M, N, O, P. She stopped at P. "The letters stop here," she thought. "P is the last one." She closed the book. But then she heard a friendly voice singing. It was the bookshop lady. She was singing the letter song. Brooklyn listened.

The song went on and on. Q, R, S, T, U, V. Brooklyn opened the book again. W, X, Y. The song was not done yet! Then the lady sang, "Z!" Brooklyn looked at the last page. Z was there. The letter Z! The alphabet did not stop at P. It went all the way to Z. "Wow," said Brooklyn. "Z says zzz, like a bee!"

Brooklyn ran to Dad. "The alphabet starts at A," she said. "And it ends at Z!" Dad smiled. "Can we sing it?" asked Brooklyn. "After dinner," said Dad. "But we can look now." They looked at the letters together. Brooklyn pointed at Z and said, "Zzz!"

Harrison had three pots on the balcony. One pot, two pots, three pots. In the pots lived lettuce, a carrot, and a tomato plant. Dad stood by the door and watched.

One morning the sun was very hot. Harrison looked at his plants. The carrot stood tall. The tomato stood tall. But the lettuce was drooping. Its leaves hung down like sad little arms.

"The lettuce looks tired," said Harrison.

"Give it a drink," said Dad.

Harrison took his watering can. He poured the water on the soil. The smooth leaves got wet and shiny.

Harrison counted the drops. One drop, two drops, three drops, four.

Later he came back to look. The lettuce was standing up again. The leaves pointed up to the sun.

Harrison ran to Dad. "Come see!" he said. He pointed at the pot. "My lettuce woke up!"

Dad smiled. "It sure did," he said.

After lunch, Harrison got the mail with Dad. There was a letter for Harrison from Grandma. Inside was a sticker of a big red tomato.

Harrison held the sticker up to his pot. "Look, tomato," he said. "Someday you will be big too."

Then Dad gave Harrison a cookie. They sat in the shade and watched the little garden grow.

Joshua was in his bed. The room was dark. His blanket was soft and warm.

Then Joshua heard a sound. Tap, tap, tap. It came from the window. Joshua felt scared. His tummy felt tight. He pulled the blanket up to his chin.

He remembered what Grandpa said one day. "You can tell me anything." So Joshua called out, "Mom! I hear a sound!"

Mom came fast. She turned on the little light. "Let's look together," she said. They stood by the window. Tap, tap, tap. Mom pushed the curtain aside.

A branch was tapping on the glass. The wind made it move. Joshua laughed. "It's just a tree!"

"Want to sleep with the curtain open a little?" Mom asked. "Then you can see it."

Joshua nodded. He felt happy now. Outside, the neighbor's dog began to bark. "Rufus is awake too," Joshua said.

Mom kissed his head. His pillow felt cool on his cheek. Joshua closed his eyes and listened to the soft tap, tap, tap.

Claare wanted to make soup for Grandma. She found a big pot in the toy box. She put in a pinecone, two leaves, and a small stone. "Stir, stir, stir," she said. The soup smelled like nothing at all. That was just fine.

Claare picked up the spoon. She held it to her mouth. She wanted a taste. Grandma sat close by in her soft chair. "Wait," said Grandma. "Pretend soup is for pretending." Claire looked at her pot. Then she made a big slurping sound. "Slurp! Mmm!" she said. Nothing went in her mouth. Grandma laughed and clapped. "That is the best soup I never ate," she said.

Claare fed her teddy bear next. "One bite, teddy," she said. She held the spoon to his fuzzy mouth. Teddy "ate" it all up. Outside, a bird began a song. Claire sang along. It was her last song before lunch. Then Grandma called, "Real soup is ready!" Claire ran to the table. Her bowl was warm, and Grandma held her hand.

Isaac climbed into the family car. He wanted his little blue dinosaur. It was his favorite toy. But where did it go?

"Did you lose Rex?" asked Mom. Isaac looked under his seat. It was too dark in there. He could not see a thing.

Mom reached into her bag. "Here, try this." She clicked on a flashlight. Isaac took it and pointed it down. The light made the dark spot bright. And there was Rex, lying under the seat!

"Rex!" Isaac grabbed him and hugged him tight. "He was hiding in the dark!" Mom laughed. "The light helped us find him."

Isaac held the flashlight up. He made the light go on the ceiling. He made it go on his shoes. "This is the best car day ever!" he said. Rex sat on his lap. Isaac clicked the light off, then on again. The seat went dark, then bright. "We will never lose you again, Rex," said Isaac. Mom started the car. "Home we go, with Rex and the flashlight too." Isaac waved the light at the window. "Bye bye, dark!" he said.

Margot sat at the little table at school. A dark tablet lay in front of her. She wanted to draw a cat on it.

She tapped the dark screen. Nothing happened. She tapped it again and again. The screen stayed dark. "Why won't it wake up?" she asked.

Miss Ada came over. She did not say much. She took Margot's finger and put it on a small button at the side. She helped Margot press it down. The screen lit up. Margot's eyes got big. A press had made it work!

Margot pressed the button by herself next time. On came the screen. She found the drawing app and drew a big orange cat with a fat tail. It was winter outside, and the cat had a scarf.

When she finished, she did not leave the tablet on the table. She pressed the button again and turned it off. The screen went dark, just like before. She put the tablet back in the basket where it belonged.

"You did it all by yourself," said Miss Ada.

Margot smiled and drew a tiny sun in the air with her finger.

Wesley was a small boy. He walked in the forest with his teddy bear. He wanted to play shop, but he had no one to sell to.

Wesley found a flat stump. He set it up like a little counter. He put three pinecones on it. "Shop is open," he said. He waited.

Then his big sister came down the path. "Hello," she said. "I am the shopper. You be the shopkeeper."

Wesley held out a pinecone. But his sister did not take it yet. She looked and looked. Wesley had to wait while she chose.

At last she pointed. "I want this one, please."

Wesley gave it to her. He carried the other pinecones home in his pockets, one for teddy and one for himself.

"Come back tomorrow," said Wesley.

"I will," said his sister, and she hugged him.

Gabriella sat on the small rug at Miss Jo's music studio. Miss Jo played "Mary Had a Little Lamb" on the piano. "Clap with me," said Miss Jo. Gabriella wanted to clap just right. But her claps went faster and faster. They ran away from the song. The song stopped and Gabriella frowned.

"Let's try something," said Miss Jo. She stood up. "March with me." Gabriella marched around the room. March, march, march. Her footsteps went even and kept going. She saw her feet stay steady. Then she clapped the same way her feet went. Clap, clap, clap. The claps stayed with the song now. "You did it!" said Miss Jo.

"Can I sing too?" asked Gabriella. She sang, "Mary had a little sheep." Well, she sang "lamb," but close. Miss Jo played and Gabriella clapped and sang all together. Miss Jo gave her a big smile and a sticker shaped like a star.

Hazel went to the library with Mama. She wanted a book about a chicken. The shelves were big. She could not see the top.

Hazel walked fast. Her elbow hit a boy's tower of blocks. Crash! The blocks fell down. The boy made a sad face. Hazel said, "Sorry." He said, "That's okay." They put the blocks up again. The tower stood tall. The boy smiled.

Then Hazel asked the librarian, "Please, where is the chicken book?" The librarian pointed. There it was! "Thank you," said Hazel. The book was fresh from the shelf. It smelled like paper. On the way home, her bag swung by her side. Mama read the book at bedtime. The chicken said, "Cluck, cluck!"

Natalie had a big yellow bag. The bag was full of toys. She could not see inside it. "Guess a toy!" said Dad.

Natalie put her hand in. Her fingers found something round. "A ball!" she said. She squeezed it. Yes, it was a ball. "It is a red ball!" she said.

She pulled it out. Oh! The ball was blue, not red. Natalie laughed. Her fingers told her it was a ball. But her fingers did not tell her the color. She had to look with her eyes.

She put the ball back in. Then she found something soft. It felt like a little bear. What color was it? She could not tell yet. Out it came. The bear was green! Natalie clapped her hands.

Then she felt something small and bumpy. Maybe a car? She pulled it out. Yes! A little red car. "I looked fast that time," she said. Dad laughed too. "One more?" he asked. Natalie's tummy felt hungry, but she said, "Just one more!" Her hand went in. Her nose came close to the bag. She felt a smooth, flat block. Out came a yellow block. Four toys on the rug, four colors to see. "My turn to fill the bag, Dad," she said.

Logan held his grandma's hand at the library door. He wanted a card of his own. His friend Mia had one. She could take books home.

Logan walked to the big desk. He stood on his toes, but he was too small. "I want a card," he said. The librarian smiled. "A grown-up helps a child sign up," she said. Grandma sat down on a soft chair. She patted her knee. Logan climbed onto her lap. Grandma wrote on the paper. Logan wrote his own name, slow and wobbly. His L came out a little loose at the bottom. "Good try," said Grandma.

Then the librarian handed Logan a small blue card. It had his name on it. He picked out a book about trucks. He held the card out. Beep! The book was his to take home. "I will thank the trucks," Logan said. Grandma laughed. Logan put the card in his pocket, nice and safe.

Dylan woke up in his bed. He could hear Mum in the kitchen. He ran to find her. "Can we go to the park today?" he asked.

"Soon," said Mum. "First, porridge." Mum put the pot on the stove. Dylan saw steam rise up. "The pot is hot," said Mum. Dylan did not touch. He sat at the table. He ate his crunchy toast instead.

After breakfast, Dylan put on his shoes. Then he looked out the window. He could see the park across the road. He could see the swings. He wanted to run straight there. But the road had cars. The cars went fast. Dylan stopped at the front step. He waited. "Mum, hand please," he said.

Mum smiled and took his hand. They looked left. They looked right. No cars came. They walked across together. At the park, Dylan held the gate for a little girl. "Thank you," she said. Dylan ran to the swings. Mum sat on the bench and waved. "Watch me go high!" Dylan called. "I'm watching!" said Mum.

Emily was at Grandpa's house. She wanted a cookie. She could smell them baking.

Grandpa's kitchen had lots of boxes. Each box had little marks on it. Emily pointed at the marks. "What is that?" she asked. Grandpa smiled. "Those are words," he said. "Words tell us things."

Grandpa held up a box. "This box says OATS," he said. He held up another. "This one says SUGAR." Emily looked and looked. The words were everywhere. They were on the big jar. They were on the little tin.

Grandpa's cat came in. The cat rubbed her soft neck on Emily's leg. The dog pushed his slimy nose into Emily's hand. Emily giggled. Then she pointed at a big book on the table. "Does that have words too?" she asked.

"It does," said Grandpa. "We read the front page first. Then we turn each page." Grandpa opened the book. He read to Emily while the cookies cooled.

Emily leaned on his arm. "Read the words again," she said.

Stella stood by the blocks at school. Two kids were rocking baby dolls. One stirred a pretend pot on the toy table. Stella wanted to play too. But she did not know how to start.

She walked closer. She stood and watched. The kids did not look up. Stella asked herself a question. What would make them see her game? Then she had an idea.

"Let's pretend I am the dog," she said. She got down on her hands. She gave a little scratch behind her ear. The girl with the doll laughed. "Dogs need a basket!" she said. She tipped a basket over and put a small blanket in it. The boy patted the basket. "Here, dog, here," he called.

Stella crawled in and curled up. The baby doll was tucked in beside her. "Lucky dog," said the girl. "You get to stay home with the baby."

Stella wagged her pretend tail and barked once, very softly.

Sienna stood at the school playground gate. Her new backpack sat on her back. It was very full. She had packed her bear, three cars, and a big book. The backpack was so heavy that she fell over on the soft grass. "Oh no," said Sienna. A boy named Tom ran to her. "Your bag is too full," he said. Sienna sat up and opened it. She took out the cars. She took out the big book. Now the bag was thin and light. She felt the cool air on her back. Sienna stood up and marched to the slide. Her bear rode on her back. "I did it!" she called. "Slide with me!" said Tom. Down they went, whoosh, into the sand.

Zoey stood in the garage with her dad. A little guitar sat on a wood bench. It was hers, and she wanted to play a song.

She plucked the strings. The sound was funny. It went boing and blurp. Zoey made a mean face at the strings. "You sound silly," she said. She plucked again. Boing, blurp.

Dad knelt down next to her. "Let me try something," he said. He turned the little pegs on the guitar. Zoey watched. He turned one peg a tiny bit. Then he plucked a string. The note sounded clear and sweet.

"Again!" said Zoey. She plucked the string herself. It sang out nicely now. She plucked the next string. That one still went blurp. Dad turned its peg too.

Zoey tapped her foot and played. Boing went one string. She pointed at it. Dad turned that peg. Then Zoey played all the strings, one by one. Each note came out right.

She played her first song in the garage. Dad clapped. Zoey hugged the guitar against her chest. "Play it again," said Dad. So she did.

Georgia sat on Grandpa's big soft chair. Grandma sat beside her. Uncle Ben sat on the floor. Everyone was watching the game on TV.

Georgia was wearing her striped pajamas. The players ran fast. Everyone yelled, "Go, go, go!" Georgia clapped her hands. "Go, go, go!" she said too.

Then the whistle blew. The game stopped. Uncle Ben said, "Two for the red team. Two for the blue team." Georgia pointed at the TV. "Who won?" she asked. Grandpa said, "The same score. The same. It is a tie." Georgia frowned. "Nobody won?" she asked. Grandma smiled. "Nobody won. A tie."

Georgia waited. The players came back out. They ran some more. Georgia clapped again. "Go, go, go!"

The whistle blew one more time. Grandpa held up his hands. "Four for red. Four for blue. A tie again!" Georgia stood up on the chair. "A tie again!" she said. Uncle Ben laughed. Grandma gave her a kiss on her head. Outside, the night was dark and quiet. Georgia waved at the TV. "Bye bye, tie," she said. "Bye bye, game."

Rehmat ran to the backyard. Her water cup sat on the little table. The sun was hot on her head. She saw the shiny table shining in the light. Then she heard her grandma call, "Rehmat, come get some ice!"

Rehmat looked in the bowl. The ice cubes looked like tiny mountains. She picked one up with her fingers. "Ooh!" It felt so cold. She dropped it fast. Plip! It fell into her cup. She touched the cup. The cup was cold now too. She put her nose near it. She smelled nothing at all. Then she took a tiny sip. The cold water tasted good on the hot day.

A bee buzzed by her ear. Rehmat heard its buzz. She stood very still and watched it fly away. Grandma came out with a hat. "Here, so the sun stays off your face." Rehmat touched the soft hat and smiled. "Thank you, Grandma," she said, and drank her cold water.

Adam made a tower at school. It had ten blocks. He wanted to write ten on paper. Miss Kim gave him a fresh sheet and a fat crayon. Adam sang the counting song to himself. One, two, three, all the way to ten. Then he wrote the numbers. He wrote 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Then he stopped. Ten needed more room. Adam asked, "Where do I put ten?" Miss Kim said, "Right after nine." Adam looked at her paper. Ten was not one number. It was a 1 and then a 0, side by side. Adam copied it. "One and zero," he said. "That makes ten." He taped the paper on his tower.

Outside, Maya dropped her leaf. The wind pushed it away. Adam picked it up and gave it back. Maya smiled. Adam took a big bite of his apple at snack time. Then he counted his crackers. "One, two, three," he said. Maya had none left. Adam gave her one. "Now you have one," he said. Maya laughed and held up her cracker. "Ten blocks, one cracker," she said. Adam pointed at his paper in his pocket. "Ten is one and zero," he said. "That one goes first."

Leo ran to the big slide at the park. Mama held his hand on the way. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Leo stayed close.

At the slide, a girl named Mia climbed to the top. She lay down with her head pointing down. Leo watched. Mia's tummy rubbed on the slide. "Ouch," she said. The slide felt rough that way. She sat up and turned around. Then she went down with her feet first. She landed soft in the sand. "That was fun!" she said.

Leo climbed the steps. He wanted to go down, too. He started to lie down with his head first. Then he stopped. He sat up tall. He turned around. He went down with his feet first. Whee! He landed soft in the sand. Leo kicked his feet and laughed.

Mama waved from the bench. Leo ran back to her. "Stay close," said Mama. Leo held her hand. Then they went to the slide again, feet first.

Colton went to the grocery store with Mama. He held his little red car in his hand. "Stay with me," said Mama. Colton walked by the cart.

Then Colton saw the big apples. He let go of the car to touch one apple. The apple was cold and round. "Apples," he said.

When Colton looked down, his car was gone. "Oh no," he said. "My car!" He looked by the apples. No car. He looked by the cart. No car.

A kind worker came over. Her name tag had a big smile on it. "Can I help you look?" she asked. "Yes," said Colton. "My red car rolled away." They looked under the shelf. It was low like a couch at home. And there it was! The car had rolled under the shelf, just like toys rolled under his bed at home. The worker had thick gloves on. She reached way down and pulled the car out.

"Thank you," said Colton. He gave her a big smile. Later, at home, Colton took his crayons to draw the nice worker. He drew her smile too. "There," he said. "That is my helper."

Peyton sat at the big table in math club. "Today we count shells," said Ms. Rosa. She put down two piles. "Which pile has more?"

Peyton looked and looked. She wanted to say the right one. She counted the first pile. "One, two, three, four." Then she forgot. "Oh no," she said. "I lost my number!"

Her friend Leo giggled. "Numbers are sneaky," he said. Peyton laughed too. Then she had an idea. She held up her hands. She touched one finger for each shell. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven fingers stood up tall. They stayed up. They would not sneak away.

She counted the second pile. "One, two, three, four, five." Five fingers. "Seven is more than five!" she said. Ms. Rosa smiled and gave Peyton a sweet cookie. Peyton picked the big piece. "Seven fingers," she said, wiggling them all, "are very hungry fingers."

Brielle sat in the nursery room. Sun came in the little window. The baby was in the crib. He was her new baby brother. He was so cute.

Brielle wanted the baby to look at her. She clapped her hands. The baby did not look. She made a soft face. "Hello, baby," she said. The baby still did not look.

Then Mommy said, "Try your finger, Brielle." Brielle put one finger near the baby's little hand. The baby's fingers closed around it. He held on tight! Brielle giggled. "He has my finger!" she said. She counted his little fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." The baby held on and on. Brielle smiled and waited. Mommy sat in the sun by the crib. "My finger, my finger," said Brielle softly. The baby held tight, and the room was quiet and warm.

Amira was at school. Today the class would bake cookies for her family. The cookies would be little sheep. Amira wanted them to be nice.

First came the sugar. Amira picked up the bag. She tipped it over the bowl. Sugar poured out fast. Too much sugar! A big white hill sat in the bowl.

Her teacher came over. She did not look mad. She showed Amira a small cup. Amira spooned sugar into the cup. She filled it up. Then she tipped it into the bowl. Just the right amount!

Amira looked at the cup. Now she knew what it could do. She used it for the flour too. Then the little spoons for the butter.

Her teacher put the sheep cookies in the oven. Amira watched from her chair.

Soon the cookies came out. They were warm and bumpy like sheep. Amira carried them home in a box.

"Cookies!" said her baby brother. He reached out one small hand. Amira gave him the biggest sheep of all.

Bennett ran into the backyard. The sun made the water table warm. "Splash time!" he said.

He wanted to fill a big bucket. The hose sat by the tall fence. Bennett knew to stay close to Grandma. He ran back to her chair. "Can I turn on the water?" he asked.

Grandma came with him. She turned the tap. Bennett put his hand under the water. "Ow! Hot!" he said. He pulled his hand back fast.

"The sun made the hose hot," said Grandma. She let the water run. She put her own hand in it first. "Now it is warm," she said.

Bennett touched the water. It felt nice, not hot. He filled the bucket all the way. Then he splashed his little boat. "The water is just right," he said.

Grandma sat in her chair by the light of the evening. Bennett stayed near her. "Do it again tomorrow?" he asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "We will always check the water together."

Jules sat at the dinner table. He was scared of the big pot. It went hiss, hiss on the stove. Dad lifted the pot with two big mitts. "Dad, does the pot scare you too?" Jules asked. "Yes," said Dad. "So I use the mitts. Then I am not scared."

Jules felt happy. He banged his spoon. "Yay, noodles!" he said. Then his fork went clatter on the floor. His lip went down, down. He felt sad. Mom picked up the fork. She gave him a clean one near his plate. His sad face went away.

Dad took one bite. Steam came up. "Ow, hot!" said Dad. His face turned red. He looked angry at the noodles. "Dad, you have feelings too?" asked Jules. Dad laughed. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups." Jules clapped. "Even me!" he said. Then he took a tiny bite. The noodles went slurp. "Excited for more!" said Jules. Dad smiled and filled his bowl again.

Sebastian sat at the big table in the library. Miss Jo put out paper and paint. The paint felt smooth and cool on his fingers.

Sebastian wanted to make a butterfly. He painted one wing on one half of his paper. He painted it red. "One wing," he said. "Only one."

Then his elbow bumped the paper. It folded in half on the wet paint. "Oh no," said Sebastian.

He opened the paper slowly. There was the red wing. And there was another wing beside it! Two wings, the same size. "Miss Jo, look!" he said.

"That is a fine butterfly," said Miss Jo.

Sebastian painted a yellow wing on a new paper. He counted, "One wing, two dots." Then he folded the paper. He pressed it with his flat hand. He opened it again. Two yellow wings, and four dots.

"I want more colors," said Sebastian. He dug into the paint cups for blue. He painted a blue wing on one half of the paper. Fold, press, open. Blue wings, matching like twins.

At home in the kitchen that evening, Sebastian hung his butterflies on the fridge. "Red one, yellow one, blue one," he said. His mother clapped.

Sebastian smiled at the blue wings. "Fold it again," he whispered to the paper.

Sadie stood in the school hallway. It was her first day. She held her new lunchbox with two hands.

At lunch time, Sadie sat down. A boy sat next to her. He had a lunchbox just like hers. It was red with a boat on it. So was hers.

"Hey, that is mine," said the boy. "No, that is mine," said Sadie. They both looked sad. Then the teacher came over. She opened one lid. "S-A-D-I-E," she read out loud. "This one says Sadie."

Sadie smiled big. The other lunchbox had the boy's name inside. He was called Tom. Sadie gave Tom his lunchbox. Tom gave Sadie hers. After lunch, they went to the art table. They used a big brush to stir the paint. Tom painted a boat. Sadie painted her name.

Noah stood at the train station. He held his papa's hand tight. The big train puffed in. The doors opened. Out stepped Grandpa with a red bag.

"Grandpa!" Noah ran to him. Grandpa picked him up high.

"I will stay for one whole week," said Grandpa.

At home, Mom hung up the paper calendar. Noah got his crayon. He drew one big dot on Monday. "Grandpa came today," he said.

Each day, Noah drew one dot. Tuesday. Wednesday. Thursday. Friday. Saturday. Grandpa helped him make pancakes. Mom stirred the bowl. Noah watched the eggs sink into the flour.

On Sunday, Noah counted his dots. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." He jumped up and down. "Seven days! That is a week!"

"You counted it right," said Grandpa.

The next morning, they went back to the train station. Grandpa waved from the window. The train puffed away.

Noah looked at his dots. "Come back soon, Grandpa," he said.

Levi stood at the paint table. He wanted to paint a big pumpkin. But there was no orange paint. The pots said red, yellow, blue. "Red, yellow, blue," Levi said. He counted them. "One, two, three." No orange at all.

Levi looked at his pumpkin. He looked at the pots. He dipped his brush in red. Then he dipped it in yellow. He stirred them on his paper. The red and yellow swirled like a thin ribbon. Then, like magic, they turned orange! Levi opened his mouth. "Orange!" he said. His pumpkin could be orange now.

Levi painted the pumpkin round and bright. It looked like a giant orange egg sitting in a green field. He painted a thin stem on top. The teacher came to see. "What a big pumpkin," she said. Levi smiled. "I made the orange myself," he said. He held up his brush. On it was one drop of red and one drop of yellow.

Everett ran to the swings at the playground. The sky was cloudy, but the swings still shined like magic ships. He wanted the red swing most of all. But a girl was already on it.

"My turn soon," said Everett.

"Okay," said the girl. "One, two, three, then you."

She counted, and she hopped off. Everett got on. He flew so high he almost touched a cloud.

Then Everett saw a boy by the tree. The boy had no shovel for the sand. Everett had three shovels in his bucket. All three.

Everett looked at the shovels. He looked at the boy. The boy was digging with just his hand.

"You can use this one," said Everett. He held out the red shovel.

"Thank you," said the boy.

Now they dug together. They made a giant sand cake under the tree. "Let's pretend to cook it," said the boy. They patted the sand and counted, "One, two, three!"

The girl came over too. "I want to cook," she said. Everett gave her the blue shovel. She added leaves on top.

"Best cake ever," said Everett.

"Best cake ever," said the boy.

"Best cake ever," said the girl, and she put one more leaf on top.

Margot sat at the dinner table. She had five toy monkeys with her. She wanted to sing her monkey song before she ate.

"Five little monkeys jumping on the bed," she sang. "One fell off and bumped his head!" She put one monkey under her chair. How many were left now? She counted them. One, two, three, four.

Papa put her warm bowl of soup down. "Sing it again," he said.

"Four little monkeys jumping on the bed. One fell off and bumped his head!" Margot put another monkey under her chair. She counted again. One, two, three. Each time she sang, one more monkey went away.

"Two monkeys left," said Margot. "Then one. Then zero monkeys!" She peeked under her chair. All five monkeys sat together. They were not scary at all. They looked like a little owl family sitting in a tree, all in a row.

"Time to eat," said Papa. Margot picked up her spoon. "Pretend the soup is monkey stew," she said. Papa laughed. "Eat it slow," he said, "one spoon, two spoons, three."

James was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. James wanted to play in the snow.

"Put on your coat," said Grandma. James tried to put it on by himself. He pushed his arms in. He got one sleeve stuck. Grandma helped him find the other arm. Then James pulled the zipper up, little by little. It went all the way to the top!

James ran outside. He made snowballs. Soon one mitten fell off in the snow. James looked and looked. He found it under the sled.

Then James saw his coat pocket. He opened it. It was big enough for two mittens. James put both mittens inside. He zipped the pocket shut.

"I did it!" said James. "My mittens have a home now."

"You are thirsty from all that play," said Grandma. "Come in for warm milk and a sandwich."

"Thank you, Grandma," said James. He patted his pocket. The mittens stayed safe and warm inside.

Matthew went to the farmers' market with Dad. There were big tents and lots of apples. A farmer had a basket of carrots. The carrots were orange and long. They still had dirt on them.

"We can make carrot soup," said Dad. Matthew held the carrots all the way home. He saw dirt on his hands. "Yuck," said Matthew. "The carrots are dirty."

At home, Dad filled the sink with water. Matthew put the carrots in. He rubbed them with his fingers. The water turned brown. Matthew scrubbed and scrubbed. Soon the carrots were shiny and clean.

"Look, Dad!" said Matthew. "The dirt came off!" Dad smiled. Mom came in to help cook. She used the big knife to cut the carrots. Matthew watched from his chair.

Mom put the pot on the stove. Matthew could not touch the hot stove. He sat on his stool and waited. Soon the soup was ready. Matthew wore his bib like a big cook. "I made this soup!" he said. Everyone ate the warm soup. "The dirt came off, and now we eat clean carrots," said Matthew. Dad gave him a hug and a shiny spoon.

Chloe woke up early. She looked out the window. Snow! The backyard was all white.

"Snow day!" said Mom. Chloe put on her boots. She put on her mittens. They were red and fuzzy.

Chloe ran outside. The snow was cold and soft. She made a snowball. She patted and patted. Her mittens got very wet. Snow went into her boots too. Her socks felt squishy and cold.

"I want to slide!" said Chloe. She slid down the little hill. She laughed and laughed. Then her mittens dripped. Drip, drip, drip.

Mom called her inside for warm cocoa. Chloe pulled off her wet boots. "My mittens are all soggy," she said.

"Let's hang them up," said Mom. They hung the red mittens on a low hook. They set the boots by the door, toes out.

"I want to go back out," said Chloe. She touched her mittens. Still wet! She waited. She looked out the window. She sipped her cocoa.

At last she touched them again. Dry and warm! Chloe put them on. She wiggled her fingers. "My mittens are ready!" she shouted. And she ran back out to the snow.

Avery sat in her car seat. The seat belt clicked. "Mommy, is today library day?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Today is now. We are in the car now."

Avery looked out the window. A dog ran by. Now there was a dog. Now the dog was gone. "Where did it go?" she asked.

"It ran away. It will run more later," said Mom. "Later is after now."

Avery put her hand near her ear. She could hear the wheels. Hum, hum, hum. "The wheels make a sound," she said. "The car goes, and then the sound comes."

"That's right," said Mom. "The wheels do that."

Avery saw a thin bird on a wire. The bird was thin and small. "Yesterday we saw a bird too," said Avery.

"Yes, we did," said Mom. "Yesterday is all done. Today we will get books."

"Then tomorrow?" asked Avery.

"Tomorrow we can read them," said Mom.

The car stopped. The library was here, today, right now. Avery held Mom's hand. The doors opened by themselves. "The doors move!" said Avery. "How do they know?"

Mom smiled. "Let's go find out."

Wyatt wanted warm milk for his teddy bear. He carried teddy out to the backyard. The grass was wet with morning dew. Teddy got a little wet too.

"I will make you warm milk," Wyatt said. Inside, Dad stood by the stove. The pot sat on top. The stove did not look hot. There were no flames at all. Wyatt stepped near and reached out his hand.

"Stop," Dad said. "Let me check." Dad held his hand high above the pot. "Still hot," he said. "Only I touch the stove." Wyatt stayed close to Dad. He watched and waited.

Soon the milk was warm. Dad poured a little cup. Wyatt took a small taste. It was warm and sweet. He gave teddy a sip from his own cup. "Only grown-ups touch the stove," Wyatt said to teddy. Then they sat down on the dry step together.

Nova went to the park today. Her mom held her hand. Nova saw a boy by the swing.

"I was here tomorrow!" the boy said. Then he stopped. He thought hard. "No. I was here yesterday. Today is now."

Nova looked at the swing. "Can I swing now?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "But later we will eat lunch. Then later we go home. Tomorrow we can come back."

Nova climbed on the swing. Mom pushed. Up, up went Nova. Down came the swing. Up again. Each push made the swing go higher. That was funny to Nova. She laughed and laughed.

A dog ran by with a bag in its mouth. The bag fell out. A biscuit fell on the grass. The dog stopped. Then it ate the biscuit.

"Mommy! The bag fell, and the biscuit fell too!" said Nova.

Mom kissed Nova's head. "That's right. And now it is lunch time."

Nova slid down from the swing. She held Mom's hand. "Yesterday I was little," said Nova. "Today I am big."

Mom smiled. "Yesterday was the day before today," said Mom. "But you are big now."

They walked to the picnic table. Later, Nova waved at the park. "Bye, park! See you tomorrow!"

Raphael was at Grandma's house. He was painting a big sun. The sun was yellow and round. Grandma gave him red paint too. He painted a red bird next to the sun.

"I want to show Dad!" said Raphael. Dad was in the kitchen. Raphael ran to get him. He touched the sun with his finger. Oh no! The yellow smeared. The sun had a big smudge now.

Raphael looked at his finger. The paint felt squishy and wet. "The paint is still wet," he said. Grandma nodded. "Let's put it in the sun by the window," she said. Raphael set the paper down carefully. He did not touch it.

They ate apple slices and waited. Raphael peeked at the painting. He poked the sun very softly. The paint felt dry now. It did not smear! "Dad, come see!" Raphael called. Dad came in and smiled. "A red bird and a big sun," said Dad. "I love it!" Raphael hugged his paper. "Thank you, Grandma," he said. "Can we paint one more?"

Elias sat on the big paper bed. The nurse came in with a small tray. On the wall there was a red box.

"What is that box for?" Elias asked.

"You will see," said the nurse. She cleaned his arm with a soft cotton ball.

The nurse held up a tiny needle. Elias took a big breath. The needle went in, quick as that. "All done," said the nurse.

Then the nurse dropped the used needle into the red box. It went click, into the hard box and shut.

"Does the needle come back out?" Elias asked.

"No," said the nurse. "It stays in there. The box is hard so nobody gets poked."

Elias looked at the red box. So that is what it was for. The needle went in and stayed in.

Then Dad picked him up. "Ice cream time," said Dad.

At the ice cream shop, Elias got a small cone with pink strawberry. He held it with his good arm. "Look, Dad," he said. He pointed at the trash can. "My napkin goes in there and stays there too."

"That's right," said Dad. He took a big bite and began to smile.

Elias licked his cone. "Can I push the trash lever?"

"You can push it," said Dad. Elias pushed the lever with one finger. The napkin dropped down, and the little door swung shut.

"Bye bye, napkin," said Elias.

Anthony ran into the restaurant with his papa. A big screen glowed on the wall. Everyone was loud and happy. "The big game starts soon," said Papa.

Anthony looked around. Everyone wore green shirts. Green hats too. Green cups! Anthony looked down at his own shirt. His shirt was red. He felt sad. "Papa, I want green," he said.

Papa smiled. He sent Uncle Ben to the car. Uncle Ben came back fast. He held up a small green shirt. "This is yours," he said. Papa helped Anthony put it on. Now Anthony was green like everyone else!

A man at the next table pointed at Anthony. "You cheer for our team too," he said. Anthony nodded big. The game began. The crowd made a happy noise. Anthony clapped and clapped. The team ran fast on the big screen. Anthony jumped up. "Go, go, go!" he yelled. All the green shirts cheered with him. Anthony waved his arms high. The server brought a big plate of fries. Papa gave Anthony a fry. Anthony pointed at the screen and shouted, "We are winning!"

Willow's class had a big job. They had to sort the play market. "Put the fruits on this shelf," said Miss Pam. "Put the foods on that shelf."

Willow picked up a red apple. She put it with the fruits. Ben pulled it back. "It is a food," he said. "I eat it at lunch." Willow pulled it too. "It is a fruit," she said. "It grows on a tree."

The apple went back and forth. Then it fell and rolled under the table. Willow got down on her knees. She reached far. She pulled the apple out.

"Watch," said Miss Pam. She put the apple on a small box. The box sat between both shelves. "Now it is with the fruits and the foods at the same time."

Willow clapped her hands. "One apple, two groups!" said Ben.

Willow ran to get more things for the box. A banana went in. A little cheese went on the food side. Her toy bunny stayed with the toys, and the soft duck too.

At play time, Willow told her mom all about it. "My apple had two homes," she said. "I learned a thing at school today." She held up her snack. "Same apple. Still yummy."

Myles went to Mama's office. He saw a tablet on her desk. "Can I draw?" he asked. Mama turned it on for him. The screen lit up bright.

Myles tapped the screen. He slid his finger across it. A blue line followed his finger! He slid again. Another line came. Myles laughed. He made a big squiggle. "It looks like a snake," he said. He added two dots for eyes. "Hello, snake," he whispered. Mama looked over and smiled.

Soon Myles was tired of drawing. "All done," he said. He pressed the button the way Mama showed him. The screen went dark. He folded his arms over the tablet to carry it. He set it in the drawer, nice and flat. "Bye, snake," he said. Then he waved at the window, and a bus went by on the street below.

Rose sat high in the big stadium. Her mom and dad sat beside her. Her friend Ben sat next to her too. The crowd was loud, like a storm of voices. Rose held her spotted ball, a gift from her grandpa.

Below, the players ran fast. One player threw the ball up. It went right through the hoop. The crowd cheered and cheered. "I want to do that," Rose said.

After the game, Dad took her to a small court. There was a hoop, just her size. Rose planted her feet on the floor. She threw her spotted ball up. It missed. She threw again. The ball went through the hoop. It dropped down, down, down. Ben clapped his hands. "You did it, Rose!"

Sofia wanted to make her own breakfast. Mama put warm toast on a low plate. Sofia held the butter knife with the flat side down. She pushed the soft butter across the toast.
