The butter left little yellow trails. "Look, Mama! My toast has yellow roads on it." The bread got shiny and wet where the butter went.

Next came the milk. Sofia set her cup on the table. She poured and poured. The milk went up and up. It stopped right at the top edge of the cup. "Full to the top!" she said. Sofia picked up the cup. She took one step. The milk wobbled. Then a white wave slid over the edge and onto her toes. Milk made a puddle on the floor.

Mama gave her a towel. Sofia wiped her toes. Was the cup too full? She looked at the milk, then at the puddle. Maybe she could try again. Sofia poured a new cup. This time she stopped pouring before the cup was full to the top. She left some room up there. She walked across the kitchen. The milk wobbled a little bit. But it stayed inside the cup. Not one drop fell.

Sofia took a bite of her buttery toast. The butter tasted real and creamy. She paid attention to the cup as she drank. "Mama, I can carry it all by myself now. Want to see me do it again?"

Max got on the school bus. It was his first day of school. He found a seat by the window. The bus went bump, bump, bump.

A boy sat down next to Max. The boy looked at his shoes. He did not say a word. Max wanted a friend. He thought and thought.

"My name is Max," said Max. "What is your name?" The boy looked up. "I am Sam," he said. Then Sam smiled a big smile. "Want to see my sweet toy car?" asked Sam. "Yes!" said Max.

The bus stopped at school. Max and Sam jumped off together. They ran to the playground, side by side. "Let's play," said Sam. "Okay, friend," said Max.

Anthony woke up and jumped out of bed. The window was full of white. "Snow!" he shouted. "No school today!"

Mom smiled. "It is a snow day," she said. "A surprise snow day."

Anthony ran outside in his red boots. He made a big snowball. It was round and cold. He loved it so much.

"I will keep you forever," Anthony said. He put the snowball in his red bucket. He carried it to his room. He set it on the rug. "Sit there, snowball. One snowball, my best snowball."

Then Anthony went to draw. He drew a dark blue sky. He drew one sun. He drew two trees.

After lunch, he ran back to his room. "Hello, snowball!" he said.

But the bucket was empty. The snowball was gone! There was only a puddle on the rug. Water, water, and more water.

"Oh no," said Anthony. "My snowball ran away."

Mom came in. She looked at the puddle. She looked at Anthony. "Do you want to try again?" she asked.

Anthony got a new snowball from outside. He put it on the big table in the warm kitchen. He sat down. He watched it. He did not look away.

Drip. Drip. Drip. The snowball got small. Then it got smaller. Then it was a puddle too.

"So that is where you go," Anthony said. He carried the puddle outside in his bucket. He poured it on the snow. "Goodbye, water. Come back as snow."

Then he jumped in a big pile with both boots, one, two, and Mom said, "You are my little snowman now!"

Matteo wanted to read his book. It was bedtime. He sat on the big bed next to Dad.

He opened the book. But the dog looked funny. The dog's feet were up. His ears hung down. Matteo laughed. "Silly dog!"

Matteo looked at the book. Then he looked at Dad's book. Dad's book was the other way. The words on Dad's page sat flat and neat.

Matteo had a problem. He turned his book around. Pop, the dog was right side up! The dog's ears stood up. His tail wagged in the picture.

"Dad, I fixed it!" said Matteo. Dad smiled. Matteo turned one page. Then he turned the next page. He saw the cat. Then he saw the bird.

Mom came in with a fresh blanket. It was soft and warm. "My turn," she said. She sat down too. Matteo leaned on her arm and looked at the pictures, all standing up the right way.

"Read to the end," said Matteo. Mom started at the front. Matteo pointed at the words. "That says dog," he said.

"Yes," said Mom. "Those letters say dog."

Matteo looked at the letters. He looked at the dog. The letters and the dog went together. He turned the last page. "The moon," said Matteo. "Goodnight, moon."

Logan looked out the big window. Snow was falling. White flakes danced down, down, down.

"Snowy day!" said Logan. He pulled on his warm coat. He put on his red mittens. Mama helped with his boots. Outside, the wind blew. It was windy too! Logan's hat almost flew away. He grabbed it and laughed.

Logan made a snowball. It was round and cold. He wanted to keep it. He hid it in his pocket. "I will show Daddy later," he said.

Inside, the house was warm. Logan took off his wet boots. He forgot about his pocket. Then he heard it. Drip. Drip. Drip.

There was water on the floor! Logan looked in his pocket. His snowball was gone. There was only a little puddle. "Oh no!" said Logan. The snow had melted. Warm house, melted snow.

Logan got a towel and wiped the water up. Then he ran to Daddy. "Daddy! Come see!"

They opened the door together. Brrr, the cold air rushed in. "Let's make a new snowball," said Logan. "A big one!" Daddy put on his scarf. Logan grabbed his mittens. Out they went, into the white, white snow.

Gabriel ran to the playground. He ran fast. The big kids ran fast too. The little kids went slow.

Gabriel wanted his water bottle. It was in Mom's bag. Mom opened the bag. Gabriel drank. Then Mom closed the bag.

"Look," said Mom. She pointed to the water fountain. Gabriel pressed the handle. The water went up. He let go. The water stopped. Open made it splash. Closed made it quiet.

Gabriel tried it again and again. Open, splash, splash. Closed, quiet and still.

"Hot day," said Mom. She gave him a cold juice box from the cooler. Gabriel held it. Cold felt good.

Then Mom spilled some water on the bench. She wiped it with a towel. Gabriel helped. Big wipe, small wipe.

At home, Gabriel opened the fridge. He got his apple. But he left the door open.

"Gabriel," said Mom. "Is it open or closed?"

Gabriel looked. He pushed the door. "Closed!" he said. He grinned. "Open. Closed. I can do both!"

Sienna went to the store with Mama. "Let's buy apples," said Mama. Sienna put apples in the bag. "One, two, three," said Sienna. Mama added more. "Four, five," said Sienna. At the deli, a man was slicing cheese. "Six, seven, eight," the man counted out loud. Sienna waited and watched. Waiting was nice here.

Then a song played on the speaker. "Nine, ten," sang the song. Sienna liked that song. She did a little dance by the cart. Mama smiled.

At the checkout, a man said, "Hello! How old are you?" Sienna held up three fingers. The man waited. He looked at her fingers. Then Sienna said, "I am three!"

"You get a sticker," said the man. He put a shiny star on her hand. Sienna held up her fingers again. "I am three," she said. "I am three!" Mama laughed and pushed the cart to the car.

Juliette was at the big pool. Her swim team had a game day. Coach Sam gave them a soft ball. There were two little nets in the grass by the pool. "Kick the ball into the net," said Coach Sam. "That is how we score."

Juliette ran to the ball. She gave it a big kick. The ball rolled away. It rolled to the wrong net! Her friend Milo waved his arms. "Not that one, Juliette! That one is the other team's net!"

Juliette looked at the ball. Then she looked at the tall coach. She ran around the ball. She turned herself the other way. She kicked again. The ball rolled and rolled. It went right into the other team's net. "Goal!" shouted Milo. The team jumped up and down.

After the game, they all sat by the pool. Juliette put her toes in the cool water. "Same time next week," said Coach Sam. Juliette smiled and kicked her feet. "I can kick the ball to the right net now," she said. Milo laughed and splashed his toes next to hers.

Brooklyn waited at the bus stop with her dad. Her coat lay on the ground by her feet. The wind blew. Her coat slid away down the sidewalk. "My coat!" said Brooklyn. Dad picked it up. He hung it on the little hook by the bench. The coat stayed right there. It did not touch the ground. Brooklyn hung her hat there too. One, two, three, she counted the hooks. Then Brooklyn tried to zip her coat all by herself. The zipper went up. Then it stopped. She tried again. Up, up, up it went. "I did it!" said Brooklyn. Dad said, "We can dream of carrots on the bus." Brooklyn patted her furry pocket. The bus came around the corner. Brooklyn picked up her coat from the hook and held it tight. "Zipped and ready," she said.

Audrey had been sick with a cold. Today Mom said, "Let's go to the pharmacy." Audrey held Mom's hand in the store. The floor was slippery, so she walked slowly. The pharmacist gave Mom some medicine. It was in a small white box.

At home, Audrey still felt tired. Mom made her favorite soup. Audrey took one bite. Then she took another. "I only want a little," she said. Mom smiled. "That's okay. When you are sick, you might not feel like eating much. Your tummy will want more soon."

After dinner, they called Grandma on the phone. Audrey ate a triangle of toast while they talked. She nibbled it, bit by bit. The next morning, Audrey's tummy made a big growl. "I'm hungry!" she said. Mom laughed and hugged her tight.

Mia was four today. She wore her party dress to the park. The sky was cloudy, but that was okay. Grandma had a big cake. It had four little candles.

Mia grabbed a match box from the picnic basket. "I will light them!" she said.

Dad took the box gently. "Lighting is a grown-up job," he said. "You get the wish."

Dad lit the candles one by one. The flames stood up tall. Mia made a wish, big and quiet. Then she blew hard. All four flames went out. The smoke curled up like little ribbons.

Everyone clapped. Sam, the small twin, rubbed his eyes. He needed a nap. Mom locked the cake safely in the cooler so the ants would not find it. Then Dad handed Mia the first big slice. "Happy birthday, Mia," he said.

"Make a wish too, Daddy," said Mia.

Dylan sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse said, "Time for your checkup, Dylan!"

Dylan jumped up. "Can I get a sticker after?" he asked.

"Yes," said the nurse. "First we look at your hands."

She held his hands up. Dylan saw little black dots on them. Dirt! He had played in the sand outside.

"Want to see something fun?" asked the nurse. "Come with me."

They went to the little sink. The nurse put soap on Dylan's hands. "Now we rub," she said. "We can sing while we rub."

They sang a happy song. They rubbed and rubbed. Bubbles grew big and white.

Then the water washed the bubbles away. Dylan looked at his hands. The black dots were gone!

"Where did the dirt go?" Dylan asked.

"Down the drain," said the nurse. "All gone."

Dylan smiled so big. His hands were clean and pink.

"Now you are ready for snack time," said the nurse. She put two crackers in his hand.

Dylan looked at his crackers. Then he looked at his hands. Clean hands, then crackers. He clapped and said, "Clean hands first!"

The nurse laughed. "Here is your sticker," she said.

Dylan stuck it right on his shirt and ran to show Mom.

It was a rainy day. Asher went to the store with his dad. The store sold crayons in a big box.

Asher saw a red crayon. He saw a yellow one too. He picked up a green crayon. "Green like grass," he said.

Then he held two crayons. One looked like the sky. One looked like the night. "This one is not blue," said a girl next to him. "It is too dark."

Asher put the two crayons side by side on the floor. He found more blues in the box. He lined them up. The first was light, like the sky. The last was dark, like night.

"They are all blue," said the girl.

"Light blue and dark blue," said Asher. Dad smiled and picked him up. "Let's get the box with all the blues," said Dad.

Naomi stood in the reading corner. Today she would get her very first library card. It was new and shiny, with her name on it.

"Pick any book you like," said Miss Ana, the librarian.

Naomi picked a book about a red bird. She sat down on a soft cushion. She opened the book to the first page. In her pocket, she had a fat blue crayon. She loved to draw circles. She pulled out the crayon. She held it near the page.

Then she saw the page. It had a small fold on the corner. Another child had read this book before her. Another child would read it after her, too. The book was for everyone to share.

Naomi put the crayon back in her pocket. "Can I have some paper?" she asked Miss Ana.

Miss Ana gave her a big white sheet. Naomi drew circle after circle. She drew a red bird in a circle too.

At the desk, Miss Ana scanned the book. "It is yours for now," she said. "Bring it back soon."

Naomi hugged the book and her paper. "I will take good care of it," she said.

Charlie ran to soccer practice. He saw the big orange ball. It had a white star on it. Charlie wanted to kick it first.

But Maya got to the ball first. "My turn," she said. Charlie reached out his hand. He wanted to grab it. Then he stopped. Coach Ben blew his whistle. "Maya kicks first," he said.

Charlie stood still. Waiting felt very long. His feet wanted to wiggle. Then he saw the cones nearby. They looked like little hats. Charlie picked up three cones. He stacked them up tall. He put one small ball on top. It looked like a friendly snowman.

"Charlie, your turn!" said Coach Ben. Charlie looked up. His tower was done. Maya sent the orange ball rolling to him. Charlie kicked it far. "Nice kick!" Maya said. "Your snowman is silly," she said, and laughed. Charlie laughed too. "Next time I will build a dog," he said.

Paisley sat in her car seat. Today they were driving to Grandma's house. "Are we there now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "We will get there later."

Paisley looked out the window. A cow stood by a fence. The cow mooed. Paisley laughed. Then the cow was gone. The car had moved past it.

"Grandma has a wild cat," said Mama. "And tomorrow we will look for eggs in her hen house." "What is tomorrow?" asked Paisley. "Tomorrow comes after today," said Mama. "Yesterday we packed your bag. Today we drive. Tomorrow we find eggs."

Paisley held up one hand. She counted her fingers. "Yesterday, today, tomorrow," she said. One, two, three. Then four, five. Then her fingers ran out. "Mama! My hand is too small!"

Mama laughed. "A week is seven days. You need more fingers." Paisley looked at her other hand. She counted on. Six, seven. All done!

The car stopped. "We are here now!" said Mama. Paisley looked out the window. Grandma stood by the door. Beside Grandma sat a wild cat, and on the cat's head sat one small egg. "Look, Mama!" said Paisley. "The cat found the first egg!"

Layla wanted to help Mom make bread. Mom gave her a bowl. It was heavy, but Layla held it with two hands.

Layla poured in the flour. White dust went up, up, up. She saw it float in the sun. She heard the spoon go tap, tap, tap on the bowl. The dough felt soft and squishy under her fingers.

Then Mom said, "Smell this. The bread is baking." Layla sniffed with her nose. "Mmm," she said. "I smell it with my nose."

After that, Mom held up a little mirror. Layla looked at her own face. She saw her nose had two little holes. She sniffed again. Both holes pulled the smell in.

"What are those called?" Layla asked.

"Nostrils," said Mom. "Your nose has two."

Layla sniffed once more. Then she waited by the oven, watching the bread get big.

At last Mom cut a warm slice. "A gift for my helper," she said. Layla took a bite. "I taste it with my tongue!" she said, and she jumped up and down.

Mom laughed and took another slice too.

Audrey was in the playroom with her brother Tom. They were playing the picture game. Mom sat on the soft rug nearby. The game had four red cards and one gold star. "The star goes to the winner," Tom said.

They took turns. Tom went first. Then Audrey went. "One turn for you, one turn for me," they said together. Audrey picked a card. It had a slow turtle on it. Tom picked a card. It had a fast bunny. Tom laughed and laughed.

Then Tom put the star in his own pocket. "I made a new rule," he said. "The star is mine now." Audrey stopped playing. She put her cards down. Tom waited, but no one played with him. The game was very quiet.

Tom took the star out of his pocket. He put it back on the rug. "Let's use the real rules," he said. Audrey smiled. They played again. One turn, then one turn. They said each card's name out loud. "Turtle!" "Bunny!" "Fish!" Audrey even got to spill nothing at all, because Mom brought two cups of juice with careful hands.

At the end, Tom won the game. But Tom gave the star to Audrey for one minute. Then Audrey gave it back. Mom clapped her hands. "Time for a snack," she said. Audrey held Tom's hand all the way to the kitchen.

Milo had big news. His tooth was loose. He wanted to tell Grandma right away.

Grandma was on the phone. She was talking to Aunt Jo.

"Grandma! Grandma!" said Milo.

Grandma held up one finger. She kept talking. Milo tapped his tooth. He waited. It felt long.

Grandma said, "Goodbye, Jo." She put the phone down. Then she looked at Milo.

"Now I can listen," she said.

"My tooth is loose!" said Milo. "Look!"

Grandma looked. She smiled a big smile. "May I touch it?" she asked.

"Please do," said Milo.

Grandma touched it, soft and slow. "It will fall out soon," she said.

"Thank you," said Milo.

At bedtime, Milo sat on his bed. He licked his tooth, shiny and wet.

Tomorrow he would tell Dad. Dad would talk first. Then Milo would wait. Then Milo would talk.

Iris sat at the dinner table. Her bowl was empty. She wanted the yellow pudding in the fridge.

"Is it pudding time now?" she asked.

"Not now," said Mom. "Pudding is for later. Eat your soup first."

Iris puffed her cheeks. She was a little mad. She scratched the table with her spoon. Scratch, scratch, scratch.

Mom pointed at the clock on the kitchen door. "Look at the clock," she said. "The clock shows what time it is. When the big hand goes all the way around, it will be later."

Iris watched the clock. Tick, tick, tick. She ate one spoon of soup. She looked up. The big hand moved a little. She ate another spoon. Tick, tick, tick. The big hand moved some more.

"Yesterday I had pudding," said Iris. "Today I have soup first. Then pudding later!"

"That's right," said Mom.

The big hand went all the way around. Mom set the yellow pudding down. Iris clapped her hands.

"Now is pudding time!" she said.

James sat at the big art table. He was making a card for Grandma. He wanted to paint her favorite flower. The flower was pink. James looked in his paint cups. He had red. He had blue. He had yellow. He had green. He had white. But there was no pink. James frowned at his paper.

He tried the red paint first. He made a red flower. "Too dark," said James. He wanted pink. He tapped his brush and thought. He waited a long time. Then he looked at the white cup. He put his brush in the white. He stirred it into the red paint. Round and round the brush went. Slowly, the red turned pink. Soft, light pink!

James painted a new flower. It was pink, just like Grandma's favorite. Then he painted green leaves beside it. Then he painted a blue pond below it, and a yellow sun up high. Miss Amy leaned over his table. "What a pretty flower," she said. "How did you get that color?"

James held up his red cup. Inside, one last bit of pink was hiding at the bottom. He smiled. "I found it," he said.

Lily stood in the big restaurant kitchen. The cook, Mia, had made warm toast. "You can help," Mia said. Lily wanted to spread the butter all by herself.

Lily took the little knife. Mia held the toast steady. Lily pushed the butter. It slid across the toast. "I did it!" said Lily.

"Now the milk," said Mia. She set a cup on the low table. There was a map of the kitchen on the wall, up high. Lily looked at the cup. She poured fast. Milk splashed out! It ran onto the table.

"Oh no," said Lily. Mia wiped the table. "Try again," she said. Lily picked up the jug. This time she poured slowly. The milk went into the cup. Not one drop came out.

"Look, Mia!" said Lily. Mia smiled. "That will be a good cup of milk," she said. Lily carried it to the table, step by step.

Ella went to the pet store with Dad. She held a little bag of cat food. The store had a bell that would ring when the door opened. Ring, ring, it went.

Ella looked at all the pets. She saw a small gray kitten. "This one," she said. Dad put the kitten in a soft carrier. The carrier had a strong handle. Ella helped carry it to the car.

At home, Ella set out a bowl of food. But the kitten ran under the bed. Ella could not see it at all. "Where did it go?" she asked. She sat down on the floor. She sat very still and very quiet. She waited and waited.

Then two little eyes peeked out. The kitten took one small step. Then another. It came all the way out and sniffed Ella's shoe.

"Hello, kitten," Ella whispered. The kitten rubbed against her hand.

Ayla stood in the band room. Her drum sat on the floor. She patted it. Boom, boom, boom. Her friend Milo patted his drum too. Boomboomboom, so fast! Their sounds bumped into each other. It was a mess.

"Can we make it sound nice?" Ayla asked. "Yes, let's try my way," said Milo. Milo patted his knees. Pat, pat, pat. He went slow and even. Ayla watched him. Then she patted too. Pat, pat, pat. Their hands went up and down together, straight like a line. Boom, boom, boom. The drums sounded like one big drum!

Ayla unzipped the zipper on her drum bag. She put her drumsticks inside. "Tomorrow we play more?" she asked. "Tomorrow," said Milo. They waved and walked out the door.

Romy wanted her teddy. He sat up on the big shelf. She was too small to reach.

"I want Bear," said Romy. She stomped her foot. She felt mad.

Dad came in. "I can help," he said. Dad lifted Bear down. Now Bear was down low with Romy.

"Let's play slide," said Dad. "I will teach you a game." The little slide stood by the wall. Romy put Bear at the bottom. Then she carried him up, up, up the steps. She set him down at the top. Bear went down, down, down. Fast!

The small toy mouse went up too. He came down slow. Romy laughed. "Bear is fast. Mouse is slow."

Mom came in with a drink. "This cocoa is hot," she said. "Here is cold juice for you." Romy drank the cold juice. It was good.

Romy made a sign with Dad. It had a big arrow. The arrow pointed up the steps. She taped it on the slide.

Then something came down the slide. It was not Bear. It was the puppy! The puppy slid down and landed on a soft pillow.

"Again," said Romy. Up went the puppy, and down he came.

Sienna sat at the dinner table. Her plate was almost empty. She wanted more rice.

"Mama, may I have more rice, please?" she asked.

"Yes! What nice words," said Mama. She scooped the rice onto the plate.

Sienna slid her fork toward the rice. She took one bite. Then two bites. Then three bites. Yum.

Then her fork slipped. Clang! It fell on the floor.

"Sorry, Mama," said Sienna.

"That is okay," said Mama. She got a new fork.

"Papa, can you help me cut the chicken, please?" asked Sienna.

Papa cut it into little pieces. "There you go."

"Thank you," said Sienna.

Papa smiled big. "You know what my friend Marco says at the playground? He says gracias. That is his word for thank you."

"Gracias," said Sienna. She said it once. She said it twice. She said it three times.

"Grass-ee-ahs," she said slowly.

"Perfect!" said Papa.

Sienna looked at her empty plate. She held it up high.

"Gracias, Mama!"

Mama laughed and clapped. "One more little scoop for you."

Camille sat at the dinner table. Grandma set down a bowl of peas. Then Grandma gave Camille a shiny red spoon. It was just for Camille. New and bright and hers.

Camille ate her peas fast. She wanted to try the corn too. "Can I have some corn?" she asked. Daddy scooped corn onto her plate. Camille dug in her spoon right away. Then she stopped. Wait. Grandma gave her the spoon. Daddy gave her the corn. Nobody had gotten a "thank you" yet.

Camille looked at the shiny spoon. What would happen if she said it? She took a big breath. "Thank you, Grandma, for my spoon." Grandma's face went all warm and smiley. "Thank you, Daddy, for the corn." Daddy smiled too, and gave Mommy the corn next, so it was fair.

Then Camille saw a little bug on the window. "Look!" she said. "A bug at dinner!" Mommy laughed. "He is smelly, maybe," said Camille, and everyone giggled. Daddy used a cup to carry the bug outside. Camille waved at the door. "Bye, bug," she said. "Thank you for visiting us."

Jaxson wanted to help in the kitchen. His grandma was making soup on the stove. The pot went bubble, bubble. Steam rose up from the pot. Grandma said, "Stay back, Jaxson. The pot is hot." Jaxson stayed close to her legs. He touched the cold fridge instead. It felt smooth and cool.

Grandma gave him a job. He could put spoons on the counter. He carried them one by one. His tummy felt happy. He was a good helper.

Then Jaxson saw something on the wall. It was a small hole with little slots. It was down low, near the floor. He put down his spoon. He did not touch the hole. He did not put his fingers in it. "Grandma, come look," he said. Grandma came right over. "Good boy," she said. "We never touch that. I will cover it up." She plugged in a safe cover. It clicked into place. Jaxson smiled and picked up his spoon again.

Benjamin was playing soccer in his backyard. His team wore red shirts. The sun was hot up in the sky. A butterfly flew by the goal.

Benjamin ran and kicked the ball. He ran some more. His legs felt slow. His mouth felt dry. "I need a drink," he said.

But his water bottle was inside the house. Benjamin sat down on the grass. He watched a ladybug crawl on his shoe. Then Daddy came out with a big cup. "Here is some cold water," Daddy said. Benjamin drank it all up. It was juicy cold and good.

Then he ran back to the game. He kicked the ball into the goal. "Hooray!" said his team. Daddy held up the cup and smiled.

Rosalie sat down at the dinner table. She was very hungry and a little thirsty too. Mama set out a big plate of apples, cheese and grapes. Next to the food, Rosalie saw her toy box was open. Her toy cars had rolled out onto the table!

"Look, Mama, look!" said Rosalie. She pointed at the cars. There was a red car, a blue car, a green car. And there, behind them, something yellow. It was long and curved. It was a banana!

"A banana does not belong with the cars," said Rosalie. She picked it up. It felt smooth and cool. It smelled sweet like a snack. The banana was the odd one out!

"Good spotting," said Mama. "That banana is a gift for you. Put it with the food."

Rosalie placed the banana with the apples and grapes. Now the cars were all cars. The food was all food. Everything was in its right group. Rosalie clapped her hands. "Dinner time!" she said, and took a big happy bite.

Jaxon was at his friend Mia's house. Mia had a little drum. She hit it. Boom, boom, boom. "It goes steady," said Jaxon. "Like walking feet."

Mia sang a song. "Pat-a-cake, pat-a-cake." Jaxon clapped along. Clap, clap, clap. Then his hands got tired. They hurt a little bit. He stopped.

What could he do now? He looked down at his shoes. Could feet keep the beat too? Jaxon stamped the floor. Stomp, stomp, stomp. Yes! His feet went steady, just like the drum. Boom went the drum. Stomp went his feet. One, two, one, two.

Mia stamped too. They sang the song together. "Bake me a cake as fast as you can." Jaxon sang the words all by himself. He did not forget any. After the song, Mia drew a rainbow on paper. It had red, yellow and blue. "Sing it again," said Jaxon. He tapped his knees this time. Pat, pat, pat. The beat went on and on.

Bennett woke up in his bedroom. The sun was up. "Is it today now?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "Yesterday we went to the park. Today we stay home."

Bennett wanted a story. "Read now, please," he said. "Not now," said Mama. "The story is later, after breakfast." Bennett sighed. "Now means right this minute," he said to his teddy. "Later means not yet."

Bennett ate his eggs. He drank his milk. Then he pulled the round knob on his curtain. The curtain slid shut. The room went dark. He pulled it back open. The room went sunny again. He laughed. "Look, teddy! I close it, it is dark. I open it, it is light!"

"After breakfast is now," said Mama. "Story time!" Bennett jumped on his soft rug. He did not miss one page. Yesterday they had gone on the swing. Today was story day. Tomorrow, Mama said, they would swing again.

"When is tomorrow?" asked Bennett.

"Not today," said Mama. "Tomorrow comes after sleep."

Bennett hugged his teddy. "Story now," he whispered. "Swing tomorrow."

Wyatt sat at the art table. He wanted to make a paper sailboat. The boat needed two triangles for sails. He looked in the paper tray. He found only one square. No triangles at all. Wyatt felt upset.

"I need triangles," he said.

Miss Ana came over. "Bring your square," she said. "Let's ask Mr. Cole to help." Mr. Cole used the scissors. He cut from one corner to the opposite corner. The square fell apart. Two triangles! Wyatt clapped his hands.

"Again!" he said. Mr. Cole gave him another square. Mr. Cole cut it the same way. Two more triangles!

Wyatt taped two triangles on his boat. He taped a circle for the sun. He drew a square house. He planted a little paper flag on top.

Miss Ana held up his boat. "Look at that," she said.

"My boat can sail to the cat," Wyatt said. The class cat was sleeping by the door. It opened one eye and yawned.

Hazel loved the dress-up corner at school. There was a box of hats and coats and shiny shoes. But today Ben grabbed the big red hat first. Hazel wanted that hat so much. "My turn soon?" she asked. "Soon," said Ben.

Ben put on the big red hat. He stood up very tall. "I am a firefighter!" he yelled, in a happy way. He picked up a toy baby and rocked it slow and gentle. "The baby is safe now," he said. Hazel watched. The hat had made Ben into someone new. It was like magic.

Soon it was Hazel's turn. She put the big red hat on her head. It slid down over her eyes. She pushed it back up. Now she was a firefighter too! She marched to the toy kitchen. She found the toy dog in the middle of the floor. "Don't worry, little dog," she said. She tucked the dog under a soft blanket. Then she stirred a pretend pot of soup.

Ben sat down next to her. "Firefighters eat soup too," he said. "Yes," said Hazel. "The best soup in town." She held out the wooden spoon to him. "Want a taste?"

Grandma came on the big blue bus. She let Ali carry her small red bag. "You can be my helper," she said. Ali puffed up his chest. He was a very good helper.

In the kitchen, Dad made pancakes. Ali sat on his stool and watched. Grandma sat next to him. "Dad," said Ali, "were you ever little?" Dad laughed. "Yes, silly. Long ago." Ali shook his head. "No. Dads are big. Like a bus."

Grandma leaned close. "I will tell you a secret," she said. "Your dad was little like you. He had a small bike. It was green." Ali's eyes went wide. "Dad had a bike?" "And he fell in a puddle," said Grandma. "Splash! Mud on his nose." Ali laughed so hard his stool wobbled.

After breakfast, Ali ran to the garage. He found Dad's old bike bell. Ding, ding! "Dad, you rang this when you were little?" Dad's face turned pink. "Yes. And Grandma has more stories." Ali clapped his hands. "Every day you are here, tell one!" Grandma smiled. "Deal. Tomorrow, the tale of the runaway hat." Ali hugged the bell tight. Ding, ding, ding!

Luka went to the library with his dad. He wanted the big red book about trucks. But a girl named Mia had it first.

Mia held the book tight. Luka grabbed the edge. "It's mine!" he shouted. His face felt hot. His hands made tight fists. He was angry.

Luka stomped to a soft chair. He sat down hard. Dad sat next to him. "Let's try slow breaths," Dad said. Dad breathed in slowly. Luka watched. He breathed in slowly too. Then he let it out, slow and long. They did it again, like a sleepy bear waking up.

Luka's hands went soft. His tummy felt calm. He walked back to Mia. "Can we look at it together?" he asked. Mia smiled a sweet smile. "Yes," she said.

They turned the pages side by side. Luka pointed at a blue truck in the water. "Big wheels!" said Mia. Luka laughed. "Best library day ever," he said.

Clara put on her red team hat. Her shoes had little white laces. The baseball diamond was bright and green. The dirt smelled like warm dust.

"Play now!" said Clara. She ran to home plate. Coach Mia shook her head and smiled. "First we warm up," she said. "Everyone runs to the fence and back." Clara wanted to swing the bat. But she got in the line anyway.

The team ran to the fence. Clara's feet went pat, pat, pat on the dirt. Then they stretched. Clara touched her toes. She reached up high like a tall tree. Her arms felt loose and good.

Then the game began. Clara ran to first base. Her legs felt fast and springy. She caught a ball with her mitt. Thump! It landed right in the soft pocket.

After the game, Dad gave Clara a piggyback ride to the car. The field was quiet now. "Again tomorrow?" asked Clara. "Yes," said Dad. "First we run, then we play." Clara smiled and hugged her mitt all the way home.

Emily wanted to dress up like a queen. She found a red scarf in the toy box. She put it on. It dragged on the floor. It went trip, trip, trip behind her feet. "This scarf is too long," said Emily.

Her brother Sam came in. He had a blue scarf. His scarf stopped at his knees. It was short. Emily's scarf was long. "Look," said Sam. "Yours is long. Mine is short." Emily looked and looked. How funny, she thought.

Then Emily had an idea. She wrapped the long scarf around her neck two times. Now it was short! She marched like a queen around the kitchen. Daddy was stirring a big pot on the stove. The pot was hot, so Emily stood back. She waved from far away. Steam went up, up, up. Was it true that steam could swim in the air? It looked like a little cloud dancing. "Our queen is here," said Daddy with a bow.

"Snack time!" called Miss Ana. It was summer, and a stormy sky sat outside the window. Sienna ran to the table.

Two bowls waited there. One bowl had crackers. One bowl had apple slices.

"How many crackers?" asked Miss Ana.

Sienna pointed. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." She looked up. "Seven!"

"Yay! And the apples?"

"One, two, three, four, five." Sienna clapped. "Five!"

"Now, which bowl has more?"

Sienna looked at the crackers. She looked at the apples. The cracker bowl looked fuller.

"The crackers!" she cried. "Seven is more than five!"

Miss Ana gave her a cracker from the big bowl. Sienna munched it and grinned.

"More counting after snack," said Miss Ana.

"Yes!" said Sienna. "I love counting!"

Parker stood by the little backyard pool. The water was warm. His green float looked like a turtle.

Dad got in first. "Kick your legs," said Dad. Parker held the edge. He kicked and kicked. The water made waves. The waves pushed the turtle float. It moved away from him.

"I can't reach it!" said Parker.

Dad pointed. "Look who can help."

Nina the lifeguard sat up in her tall chair. She blew her whistle, one small toot. Then she pointed at the turtle too. From up high, she could see the whole pool. She saw Dad reach out and catch it.

After swimming, Parker sat on the towel for lunch. He watched Nina watch the water.

"Can I chase you to the door?" said Dad.

"Only if you count to ten!" said Parker.

"Ready," said Dad. "One, two, three..."

Milo went to the farmers' market with Dad. They stopped at a seed stand. Milo picked a little bag of carrot seeds. "I want to grow carrots," he said. Dad paid for the seeds.

At home, Milo planted them near the fence. He patted the soil down. Then he waited. Each day he looked at the dirt. No carrots came up. "Maybe they are lost," Milo said. Dad said, "Let's wait a little more."

Milo checked again and again. On a warm morning, he saw something tiny and green. It poked up out of the soil. Milo ran to Dad. "A sprout! There is a sprout!" he shouted. Dad smiled. A bird flew by with twigs for its nest. Milo stood by his sprout and waved. "Grow big, little sprout," said Milo.

Hunter loved his little blue truck. He took it to school for playground time. He pretended the truck could zoom down the slide. Zoom, zoom, it went.

Then it was time for snack. Hunter sat on the bench to eat. After snack, he looked in his pocket. The truck was not there. "Oh no," said Hunter. "Where did my truck go?"

The playground was big. There were kids running everywhere. Hunter wanted to run and look all by himself. But then he saw his teacher, Miss Ana. She was standing by the fence. Hunter walked to her first. "Miss Ana, I lost my blue truck," he said. "Will you help me look?"

Miss Ana smiled. "What a polite thing to do, asking me first. Let's look together." They walked past the slide. They looked under the swing. Then Hunter saw something by the sandbox. It was small and blue. "There it is!" he shouted. His heart felt warm and happy.

Hunter hugged his truck. "Thank you, Miss Ana," he said. She held out her hand. "Let's go line up together," she said. Hunter put the truck safely in his pocket and held her hand all the way.

Chloe stood in the kitchen by the back door. Snow was falling outside, all wild and white. Mom said, "Time for your coat." Chloe wanted to put it on all by herself.

She pushed her arms in. One arm hid inside the sleeve at first. She shook it and shook it. Out came her hand. Now for the zipper. She pulled it up, up, up. Then it stopped. It was stuck on her red sweater.

Chloe pulled hard. Still stuck. She took a breath. She pulled the zipper back down, just a little. Then she tugged her sweater free. The zipper slid up, up, up to the very top. Chloe smiled at Mom. "I did it," she said. Mom opened the door, and Chloe stepped out into the soft white snow.

Felix petted the big brown dog. The dog was soft and a little stinky. Then Felix smelled lunch. Soup! His tummy said yum.

Felix walked to the table. Mama said, "Not yet, Felix. Where are you going?" Felix looked at his hands. They had dog hair on them. He wondered what to do.

"Wash my hands!" said Felix. "Yes," said Mama. "Wash your hands." Felix went to the sink. Mama turned on the water. It was warm but not hot. Felix got the soap. He rubbed and rubbed.

"Sing the song," said Mama. Felix sang the ABC song. He sang it slow. Bubbles covered his hands. One bubble fell to the floor. Pop! Felix kept singing. When the song was done, he rinsed the soap off.

Mama gave him a towel. His hands were clean and warm. Then Mama put the soup on the table. Felix climbed into his chair. He picked up his spoon. "Clean hands, yummy soup," said Felix. "Clean hands, yummy soup," said Mama. Then Felix took a big slurp.

Daniel sat in his car seat. Today they were going to the library. Yesterday he had lost his doll there. Maybe it was still there now.

"Are we there yet?" asked Daniel.
"Not yet," said Mama. "Soon."
Daniel watched out the window. One red car. Two green trees. One big blue bus. "What does soon mean?" he asked.
"Soon means in a little while," said Mama.
So Daniel counted things to pass the time. One cow. Two fences. One yellow house. He pulled his hat down over his ears. The car went around one more corner. Then the library door came into view.

"Here now!" said Daniel. He ran to the desk. The librarian held up his doll. "Found it yesterday," she said. "Storytime starts soon," she added.
Daniel sat on the mat with his doll. He counted to ten. Then the story lady clapped her hands.
"Soon was not very long at all," whispered Daniel to his doll.

Abigail could not find her bunny. Bunny was her favorite toy. She looked under her bed. No bunny there. She looked in her toy box. No bunny there either.

"Where did you see bunny last?" asked Mom. Abigail thought hard. She remembered something. She had bunny at snack time. She ate crackers at the little table. Then she went to play on her slide outside.

Abigail ran to the snack table. She got down on her knees. She peeked under the table. There was bunny! Bunny had fallen down. Bunny was sitting by the chair leg. Abigail grabbed bunny and hugged him tight.

"I found him!" she said. Mom smiled big. "You remembered where you had him," said Mom. "That helped a lot." Abigail nodded. Then she put bunny on the table. She got one cracker for herself. She got one cracker for bunny too.

After snack, Abigail took bunny outside. She held bunny in her lap at the top of the slide. "Ready, bunny?" she said. Down they went, whee, all together.

Ellie went to the pet store with Dad. She saw a little gray kitten in a cage. "Can we take him home?" she asked. Dad smiled. "Yes, he can be your first pet." They bought a soft bed, a small bowl, and a bag of food.

At home, the kitten drank and drank. Then he went to sleep. Ellie played with her blocks near him. Later she looked at the bowl. It was empty! Not one drop was left.

"Kitty, are you thirsty?" she asked. "I will get you more." She carried the bowl to Dad. "Please fill it up." Dad turned on the tap and filled it with fresh, clean water. Ellie set the bowl down. The kitten ran over and drank it all. "We will fill it every day," Ellie said. "Then you will never be sorry and thirsty." Dad nodded. "Good helper," he said. The kitten licked Ellie's hand and purred like a tiny motor.

Grandpa lived in a house with a big kitchen. On a rainy day, Alexis put on one red sock and one blue sock. Then he ran to the kitchen.

"Can I have grapes?" he asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "You can have three grapes."

Alexis looked at the bowl. "The big ones?" he asked. "Or the little ones?"

"Three is three," said Grandma, smiling.

Alexis picked three big grapes. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." He put them on his plate. He ate them all up.

Then he picked three little grapes. He counted again. "One, two, three." Still three! Big or little, three was three.

"Grandpa wants grapes too," said Alexis.

He counted four grapes this time. "One, two, three, four. Grandpa gets one more than me!"

Grandpa clapped his hands. "Thank you, Alexis. Four grapes for me."

Grandma poured milk into a small cup. Alexis heard the milk go glug, glug. Outside, the rain went tap, tap, tap on the window.

"Let's sing the counting song," said Grandpa.

They sang together. "One, two, three, four, five." Alexis held up his fingers, one by one. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

"Now wash your hands," said Grandma, "and we will bake bread."

Alexis counted the soap bubbles. "One, two, three, four, five!"

Grandma laughed. "You count everything, Alexis."

"Ten kisses for Grandma!" said Alexis. He gave her one big kiss. "One," he said.

Leon had three little paint pots. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue. Red, yellow and blue, that was all.

Leon wanted to paint a rainbow. But a rainbow needs green. Leon looked and looked. No green pot. "Sorry, Leon," said Mama. "That is all the paint we have."

Leon dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He made a yellow sun. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue paint. He made blue water below the sun.

Then something happened. The blue water turned green where it touched the yellow sun. Leon leaned close. Green! Soft, leafy green, like the deep ocean waves in his book.

Leon clapped his hands. He painted a green tree. He painted green grass. "Green, green, green," he said, and laughed.

Mama hung the painting on the fence. Leon stepped back to look. The yellow sun sank down behind his green, green tree. "I made green," Leon said. "All by myself."

Hayden went to the pharmacy with his dad. His tummy felt funny, so they came for medicine. At the door there was a little sink. A sign said, "Wash your hands."

Hayden wanted to wash his hands all by himself. He turned the tap. Dad put his hand under the water first. "Not yet," said Dad. Hayden waited. Dad turned the tap a little more. "Now it is warm," said Dad. Hayden put his hands in. The water felt like a warm bath.

Then Dad poured soap into Hayden's hands. "Let's count to twenty," said Dad. They counted, "One, two, three, four, five." The soap made white bubbles. The bubbles looked like little clouds. "Ten, eleven, twelve." The water began to rain down on the bubbles. "Nineteen, twenty!" Hayden rinsed all the bubbles away.

A woman in a white coat gave Hayden a sticker. It had a bear on it. "Next time, I will wash my hands too," said Hayden. Dad smiled and held his hand as they walked out.

Connor opened his brown suitcase on the big hotel bed. "We go to the beach tomorrow!" he said. He pulled out his little swimsuit. It had fish on it.

Then he looked out the window. White snow was falling. Lots of snow. "Oh no," said Connor. "No beach?"

Dad came over and looked out too. "The beach is far away, kiddo. Here it snows. We need warm things." He dug in the suitcase. He found Connor's mittens and his puffy coat.

But the mittens were small. They were for the baby cousin. "Too little!" Connor yelled. He wiggled his fingers. They would not fit.

Mom knelt down beside him. "Let's check the other bag." Connor helped her look. He pulled out a sock. Then a truck. Then, at the bottom, he found his big blue mittens!

He put them on. They fit just right. The next morning, Connor wore his coat and mittens in the snow. He made a snowball and threw it at Dad. "Got you!" said Dad, laughing. "Again!" said Connor.

Eva sat on the red rug at school. Miss Tam put on a song. It had a steady beat, like this: clap, clap, clap.

Eva clapped her hands. First she clapped too fast. Then she clapped too slow. Miss Tam clapped the steady beat. Eva watched. She clapped, clap, clap. Her hands matched the song now.

Then Miss Tam sang a rhyme. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Eva knew that line. But the second line slipped away. "How does it go?" she asked.

"Sing it with me," said Miss Tam. So they sang. Then they sang it again. Then again. Eva sang the rhyme many, many times.

After lunch, Eva sat by the blocks. She sang the rhyme all alone. The second line popped out. "How I wonder what you are!" It came by itself, like a huge yawn.

The song played again. Eva clapped the steady beat and sang every word. Miss Tam gave her a thumbs up.

"Again?" said Eva. "Again," said Miss Tam.

Weston ran into Grandma's kitchen. He wanted to paint a pumpkin for the fall table. Grandma had red, blue, yellow and green paint. But there was no orange paint!

"How will I make my pumpkin?" Weston asked. Grandma smiled. "Try mixing two paints," she said. Weston stared at the little cups. It was a puzzle. He picked blue and yellow first. He stirred them with his brush. Green! "That is not orange," he said.

Then he tried red and yellow. He stirred and stirred. Orange! His brush made a big round pumpkin shape. "Grandma, look!" he shouted. Grandma held it up to the window. The painted pumpkin glowed like fire. Weston laughed and painted a green stem on top. "This is my favorite one," he said.

Aiden sat on Grandpa's big soft couch. The room smelled like warm popcorn. Everyone was shouting at the TV. "Go, go, go!" they yelled.

Aiden pointed at the screen. "Who has the ball?" he asked. The men all looked the same to him. He counted them. "One, two, three, four. Too many men!"

Grandpa laughed. "Look at the shirts," he said. He held up his mug. "Blue like this, that is one team. Yellow, that is the other team."

Aiden looked hard. The yellow shirt man ran. "Yellow man has the ball!" he said. Grandma clapped. "That's right, Aiden!"

The yellow man kicked the ball far. "Goal!" everyone yelled. Aiden jumped up and down. Uncle Sam gave him a high five. Aiden's finger tapped Uncle Sam's hand. Tap, tap, tap.

Later Aiden painted a picture at the little table. He drew one team in blue. He drew one team in yellow. "Blue team, yellow team," he said. He held the paper up to Grandpa.

"Look, Grandpa! I can tell them apart now."

Grandpa gave him a thumbs up. "Blue team scores!" said Grandpa, and he pointed at the paper with his sharp pencil.

Wren sat at the big table. She had a pencil and some paper. "I want to write my name," she said. "All by alone." Mama sat next to her. "You can try," said Mama. "I am right here."

Wren held the pencil in her fist. She pressed down hard. She made a big W. Then the pencil tip snapped off. The pencil would not write anymore. "Oh no," said Wren. "It broke!"

"Why did it break?" she asked. "Let's look," said Mama. She gave Wren a new pencil. This time Wren pressed soft and slow. The W came out wiggly but whole. The tip stayed on. Wren made a face of surprise. Then she laughed.

She wrote W, then R, then E, then N. "Wren!" she said. "That is me!" She held up the paper. Mama clapped. Wren wrote her name again, soft and slow, all by herself at the table.

Jasmine stood by the school kitchen door. It was her first day. She held her lunch box tight. The cafeteria was big. Very big. A lady in a yellow apron came out. She carried a tray of tasty apple slices. The lady smiled at Jasmine.

"Are you a teacher?" Jasmine asked in a tiny voice. "Yes, I am Teacher Meg," said the lady. "I look after the children in your class." Teacher Meg held out an apple slice. Jasmine took it. It was sweet and crunchy.

Jasmine felt bigger somehow. She skipped to a table. A boy sat there all alone. "Hello, I am Jasmine," she said, loud and clear. "Want some apple?" The boy grinned and took a bite.

Hazel went to the store with Dad. She held her bunny in the cart. But then the cart bumped over a bump. Bunny fell out! Hazel looked down. Bunny was not there.

Hazel looked by the apples. No bunny. She looked by the bread. No bunny. Dad walked slow so she could search. They passed the milk, so cold and white like a little lake in a jug. Still no bunny. Hazel wanted to cry.

Then Dad put a bag of carrots in the cart. The bag made a soft lump. Hazel peeked inside the bag. There was bunny! Bunny had fallen into the carrot bag. Hazel pulled bunny out and hugged her tight.

"Found you," Hazel said. Dad smiled. On the way home, Hazel put bunny inside her own coat pocket. She patted the pocket with her small hand. "Stay in there," she said. Bunny's ears poked out, soft and warm.

Maya turned four today. Her party was at the park. There was a big table with cake. Her friends came running up the grass.

Presents sat in a pile. Maya opened the first one. It was a little red truck from her friend Ben. She put it down fast. Then she grabbed the next box. Ben's face went sad and quiet.

Maya's mom knelt down beside her. "Do you like the truck?" she asked. Maya looked at Ben. "Should I say something to him?" she asked. Mom nodded. Maya ran back to Ben. "Thank you for the truck!" she said. Ben smiled big. "You can push it in the dirt," he said.

Then they sang the birthday song. Maya felt happy, not sick from worry anymore. Ben poured sand near the truck. Some sand did spill, but that was okay. Mom wiped it up. Maya pushed the red truck to Ben. "Your turn," she said. "Vroom!" said Ben.

Jackson wanted to play at the park. But the sky was not sunny today. Gray clouds sat over the swings. Big drops began to fall. Rain patted the slide. Rain patted Jackson's head too.

"Come here," said Grandma. She opened her umbrella. It went pop over their heads. Jackson looked up. The rain hit the umbrella. The rain did not hit him. "We share," said Grandma, and they walked under it together.

The wind blew a leaf past them. It spun like a small red top. Jackson picked it up. "This leaf stayed dry under here," he said. Grandma smiled. "You keep it," she said. The rain kept falling on the grass. But Jackson and Grandma stayed dry all the way home. Jackson held the leaf tight.

Muhammad sat at the dinner table. His plate was full of rice. He took a big bite. He drank his milk. Then he yawned a big yawn.

Muhammad wanted to wear his fire truck shirt to bed. It was his favorite shirt. He wore it at the park. He wore it at school. He asked Dad, "Can I sleep in my fire truck shirt?"

Dad said, "Sleep time comes after bath time. Let's get you clean and cozy."

After dinner, Dad filled the tub with warm water. Muhammad splashed and played with his yellow duck. Dad washed his hair. Then Dad helped him dry off with the big soft towel.

Muhammad pulled his fire truck shirt from the chair. It was stiff and a little scratchy. He held it against his cheek. Then he looked at his pajamas on his bed. They were soft like his teddy bear. He touched the pajamas. He touched the shirt again. He put the shirt back on the chair.

"I will wear pajamas," said Muhammad. He put them on all by himself. The pajamas had little stars on them. He climbed into bed and hugged his teddy bear.

"The stars are for sleeping," said Muhammad. Dad smiled and turned off the light.

Arthur ran up to Mia's door. He could not wait to play.

Mia had a big toy dragon on the floor. "Roar!" she said. "The dragon is scary."

Arthur stopped. He wanted the dragon to be nice. "Can the dragon be friendly?" he asked.

Mia thought. Then she smiled. "Yes! The dragon is friendly. He lives in a blue house."

Arthur clapped. Now they both liked the game!

Mia put a blanket on the floor. "This is the dragon's nest," she said. Arthur put the dragon inside. Then he tucked a teddy bear in next to it. "The bear is the dragon's baby," Arthur whispered. Mia giggled.

The baby bear got sleepy. "What will help him sleep?" Mia asked.

"I know!" said Arthur. He patted the bear's back, slow and soft. He hummed a little song. The bear closed his eyes. "Shh," said Mia. "The baby is sleeping."

Then the doorbell rang. Ding dong! It was the pretend mailman. That was Mia's big brother with a box. "Mail for the dragon's house!" he called.

Arthur ran to get it. Inside the box was a paper crown. "A party hat!" he said. "The dragon is having a birthday!"

Mia put the crown on the dragon's head. "Happy birthday, dragon!" they both shouted.

Then Arthur whispered, "Shh, not too loud. The baby is still sleeping."

Mia nodded. They sang the birthday song very, very quietly. The dragon blew out the pretend candles all by himself.

Athena went to the backyard with Dad. Dad was cooking at the grill. "Stay close to me," said Dad. Athena stayed close to Dad.

Then Athena saw a butterfly. It flew to the far fence. Athena ran after it. She ran and ran. She could not see Dad anymore. The tall grass was all around her.

Athena stood still. She could not see Dad. Dad could not see her either. She felt a little scared. So she turned around. She walked back the way she came. She counted her steps. "One, two, three." Soon she saw Dad again. Dad waved his big hand.

"There you are," said Dad. He gave her a hug. The grill made a hot sizzle sound. Athena did not go near it. Dad said the grill was hot, and he held the long spoon himself. Athena watched from her safe spot on the step.

Then they heard a train far away. Choo, choo! Athena loved that sound. She sat with Dad on the step. He put a warm bun on her plate. It was not hot like the grill. It was just warm and neat. Athena took a bite. "Good," she said. Dad smiled and hugged her again.

Ayla sat in Grandma's cozy reading nook. It was cloudy outside, so they would play inside. Grandma held up a card with a big S. "This letter says sss," said Grandma. "Can you find things that say sss?"

Ayla looked around the room. She saw her sock on the rug. "Sss-sock!" she said. Grandma smiled and clapped.

Next Ayla ran to the window. The clouds were thick, but a little sun peeked through. "Sss-sun!" said Ayla. Grandma clapped again. Two things!

What else? Ayla tipped over her small shoe. No, that was a shoe. Then she saw her toy bucket. It was full of soft sand from the garden. She poked it with her finger. It felt warm and bumpy. "Sss-sand!" said Ayla. Grandma laughed and hugged her.

"You found three," said Grandma. Ayla held up the S card. "Sss," she said, and gave the card a big kiss.

Lea stood by the slide. It was her first day of school. Her tummy made a little growl. "I am hungry," she said. She wanted to grab her snack right now.

Her teacher, Miss Ana, knelt down. "First we play," said Miss Ana. "Then we all eat together. School has a snack time." Lea held her teacher's hand.

Lea pushed a toy truck. The truck rolled fast. She patted a fluffy toy animal. She went down the slide, not too high, just her size. Her tummy growled again.

Then Miss Ana rang a little bell. "Snack time!" she said. Lea sat at the small table with the other kids. She opened her bag. She took a bite of banana. It tasted so good. "We played, and now we eat," said Lea. Miss Ana smiled and gave her a cup of water.

Jasmine stood far from the hoop. She threw the beanbag. It missed. She threw it again. It missed again.

"Big throw," said Dad. "Try again."

Jasmine took three little steps closer. One, two, three. She threw the beanbag. It went in! The hoop went swish.

Jasmine jumped up and down. Dad clapped his hands.

Then Dad held out a big red ball. "Catch it with both hands," he said. He rolled it slow. Jasmine held out her arms. One hand, two hands. The ball bumped her tummy and she grabbed it.

"Now throw it back," said Dad. Jasmine threw it high. Dad caught it and licked his ice cream. Their furry dog, Biscuit, barked at the ball.

"One more," said Jasmine. "One more hoop, one more catch, one more dog."

Biscuit wagged his tail.

Ellie sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap. "I don't want a pinchy arm," said Ellie. Mommy held her hand. "The nurse will be quick," said Mommy. The nurse came in with a small tray. "One, two, three, all done," said the nurse. One, two, three! Ellie felt one tiny poke, and then it was over. "You were so brave," said Mommy. "That was smart of you to hold still."

Then the nurse peeled open a little paper. It was a bandage with stars on it. She pressed it on Ellie's arm. "A star bandage," said the nurse. "Just for you." Ellie looked at it. The nurse had made the spot all better with one little sticker.

Afterward, Mommy took Ellie to the ice cream shop. Ellie got pink ice cream in a cup. It was cold and sweet. A fire truck went by outside, with a loud siren. Ellie held up her arm. "Look at my stars," she said to the lady at the counter. "One, two, three, four!" The lady clapped her hands. Ellie licked her ice cream and smiled.

Emile went to the vet with his mom. There was a small puppy in a cage. The puppy had soft brown ears. "We can take him home," Mom said. Emile gave the puppy a kiss on his head. The puppy wagged his tail.

The vet held up a little tag. It was shiny and round. Emile picked a blue one. The vet wrote their phone number on it. The tag went on the puppy's collar. It made a tiny tinkling sound.

At home, the puppy ran in the yard. Then he found a hole in the fence. Off he went. Emile felt scared. Soon a neighbor knocked on the door. She held the puppy. "I called the number on his tag," she said. Emile hugged the puppy tight. "I love you," he said. "And I love your tag." The puppy licked his cheek.

Nathan woke up early. Today was the big festival. He looked at his little pile of clothes.

"What should I wear?" he asked Mama.

Mama laid out two shirts. One was old and soft. One was red and gold, with a shiny dragon on it. Nathan touched the dragon. It felt bumpy under his fingers.

He put on the red shirt. Then he took it off. Then he put it on again. Mama waited. She did not hurry him.

At the festival, the street smelled like sweet buns and flowers. Nathan saw Grandma in her long silk dress. He saw Uncle in his white coat with gold buttons. He saw cousins in bright, twirly skirts.

"You look like us," Grandma said with a big smile. "We all wear special clothes today."

Nathan looked down at his dragon shirt. His cousin had a dragon too. They held hands and walked up the little hill together.

Then the drums began. Boom, boom, boom. The dragon danced down the street, and its tail was wet from the morning rain. Nathan clapped and clapped.

"I picked this shirt," he told his cousin. "I picked it all by myself."

Luna ran to the bookmobile. She picked a book about a red truck. The librarian gave her a little card. "Your first library card," she said. Luna smiled big.

"I want to keep the truck book forever," Luna said.

The librarian shook her head. "The book has to come back on its due day," she said. "Then another kid can read it too."

Luna held the book tight. "But I love it," she said.

"You can take it home now," the librarian said. "Bring it back, and then you can borrow a new one."

At home, Luna read the truck book three times. Mama helped her move it to a safe shelf. When the due day came, Luna put the book in her bag. "It is not mine," she said. "It goes back."

The bookmobile was not empty. A boy stood there, waiting. "I want the truck book," he said.

Luna gave it to the librarian. "Here," she said. "He can read it next."

"Thank you," said the boy. He sat down and opened the book.

Luna picked a new book about the moon. "This one is my gift for today," she said. The librarian laughed and stamped her card.

Clara sat at the big art table. She had a box of markers. She wanted to draw a butterfly. It would be pink and blue, with big wings.

Clara drew the wings. Then she drew more wings. The marker slipped. A blue line went right on her hand. Clara looked down. Was the blue line stuck on her skin forever?

"Look at my hand," Clara said. Her teacher, Mia, came over. Mia did not look worried at all. She smiled. "Let's go to the sink," said Mia. "What do you think will happen?"

Clara ran to the sink with Mia. Mia turned on the water. She helped Clara rub her hands with soap. Round and round went the bubbles. Clara watched the blue line. It began to fade. Then it was gone! Her hand was clean again.

"Where did the blue go?" Clara wondered. She looked at her hand. Then she looked at the markers. Maybe she should test it again. Clara drew one small dot on her finger. A cute little pink dot. She carried it back to show Mia. "This one can wash off too," Clara said. "I made it. And I can un-make it!" She wiggled her clean fingers at the butterfly on the table.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Maeva was so happy. She held his hand all the way to the park. The swings were far away, so they walked slowly.

"Want to swing?" asked Grandpa. "Yes!" said Maeva. Grandpa pushed her high. She could see the ducks on the pond. Then they went home for bread and milk. Grandpa had a bath. Maeva heard water splashing.

Then Grandpa yelled, "Oh dear! Where is a towel?" Maeva ran to the bathroom door. "I know!" she said. She opened the cupboard. It was low, just her size. She took out a soft blue towel and pushed it under the door. "Thank you, Maeva!" said Grandpa. "You are a good helper."

The next day Grandpa needed the soap. Maeva showed him the shelf. Then he needed a spoon, and she showed him the drawer. Grandpa laughed and laughed. At the park again, Maeva found a shiny red feather by the bench. She put it in Grandpa's pocket. "For you," she said. Grandpa grinned. "You show me everything, little host."

Jack walked home with Dad. He held the little dog's leash. The dog was small and brown. His name was Bingo.

Bingo wagged his tail on the sunny street. Jack had a chocolate coin in his pocket. He wanted to give it to Bingo. "Treat for you!" said Jack.

Dad shook his head. "Not that one," he said. "Chocolate can make dogs very sick. Dogs are never given chocolate." Dad held out a shiny bag. Inside was a bone-shaped dog treat. "Offer this instead," said Dad.

Jack held the treat on his flat hand, like a spoon full of cereal. Bingo took it gently. Then Bingo licked Jack's fingers. Jack laughed and began to sing a happy song. Birds sang too, from the big green tree.

At home, Dad poured water into a shiny bowl. Bingo drank it all up. Jack patted his soft head. "Good dog," said Jack. "I will keep you safe."

Julia held her teddy bear, Ben. Bedtime was here. But Ben looked sad. His mouth was turned down. Julia knew that face. Mama made that face when she lost her keys.

"Are you sad, Ben?" she asked.

She looked under the bed. She found one red sock. She stuck the sock on Ben's paw like a mitten. Ben still looked sad. Julia made a frown too. Then she made a big smile. Ben did not smile back. Teddies cannot move their mouths.

Then Julia saw it. Ben's other paw was empty. His little blue shirt was gone! It had fallen behind the pillow.

Julia pulled it out. She dressed Ben in his shirt. She hugged him close. He smelled sweet, like soap and sleep.

"Now you are happy," Julia said. She tucked him in. His soft head rested by her cheek.

"Night night, sweet Ben," said Mama from the door.

Julia closed her eyes and whispered, "Big smile in the morning."

Jacob ran into the backyard with his grandpa. The grass was green and soft. Jacob wanted to find a brown bug.

He looked under a big leaf. He looked by the old red pot. Then he saw something small on the ground. It was shiny and black. It was a little lighter.

Jacob wanted to pick it up. His hand went out. But then he stopped. He remembered something. Matches and lighters were only for grown-ups.

"Grandpa!" Jacob called. "Come and see!" Grandpa came right away. He looked at the little black lighter.

"Thank you, Jacob," said Grandpa. "You did not touch it. That was safe and smart." Grandpa picked up the lighter. He put it high in his pocket.

Grandpa sat down on the step. Jacob sat next to him, close and safe. Grandpa shared his big sun hat with Jacob. They sat and looked for bugs together.

A little brown bug crawled up the step. "There he is!" said Jacob. Grandpa smiled and held Jacob's hand.

Paisley stood at the toy shelf at daycare. She wanted all ten blocks for her tower. Ten blocks made a tall, tall tower.

She picked up one block. Then two blocks. Then she stopped. What came after two? She looked at her hands. She squeezed her eyes. The next number hid from her, like a cat under a bed.

Her friend Milo sat close by. "Sing it," said Milo. "Sing the shoe song." Paisley knew the shoe song. It went with a clap. She clapped and sang, "One, two, buckle my shoe." The words felt like a joke that tickled her ears. One rhymed with two in the song, and the song pulled the next number out.

"Three!" said Paisley. She put down block three. She sang the song again with Milo. "Three, four, shut the door." Four blocks sat in a line. The song kept giving her numbers, five and six, then seven and eight, then nine and ten.

The tower stood tall and wobbly. It smelled like soap and wood. Milo clapped a loud clap. The tower tipped over and fell with a big crash. Paisley laughed and rubbed her toes, because one block had landed on her shoe.

"Again," said Milo. Paisley picked up one block, then two, and sang the shoe song again, all the way to ten.

Brooks was on the swim team. He had a towel with sheep on it. He hid his goggles in the towel after every practice.

At the pool, the water was cool and blue. It smelled like chlorine. Brooks kicked his legs and splashed. His coach said, "Big arms, Brooks!"

One day Brooks asked his dad, "How long is the team?" Dad held up the schedule. It had lines and numbers. Dad pointed to the top. "This was our first practice." He pointed to the bottom. "This is our last game." Dad let Brooks count the games left. Brooks touched each line. "One, two, three games left!"

So the team was all of it. Every practice. Every game. From the first line to the last line.

Brooks swam at the last game. The water went swish, swish. He touched the wall and looked up. Dad waved the sheep towel high in the air. "Last one, Brooks!" Dad called. "Then we get ice cream."

Charles sat at the dinner table. He saw a big plate with blue flowers. Mom had painted the flowers long ago. The plate was Sam's special plate today.

Charles wanted it. He reached out fast. He took the plate right off Sam's mat. "Hey!" said Sam. His face went red. He put his head down on his arms.

Charles looked at Sam. Then he looked at the plate. He pushed it back across the table. "Sam, may I have the flower plate?" he asked. Sam sat up. He smiled a little. "You can have it after me," said Sam. "Then we can take turns." Dad gave Charles a plain white plate. It clinked when it touched the table. The warm bread smelled sweet.

Charles ate his bread. The plate went back and forth, back and forth, back and forth. Sam laughed. Charles laughed too. Baby Ivy fell asleep in her chair. "Can we use the flower plate tomorrow?" Charles asked. "Yes," said Sam. "You can ask me again then." Charles took one more bite and slid the plate over to Sam.

Aiden put on his boot. He pulled and pulled. Then Grandma laughed. "One boot is enough inside," she said. "We need to go to the big hall now."

At the hall there were tables and bowls of rice. Aiden wanted to eat fast. Grandma held his hands. "First we say itadakimasu," she said. "People in Japan say it before eating. It gives thanks for the food."

Aiden tried. "Ita... dakki... moose!" Everyone giggled. "Was that true? Did I say it?" he asked.

"Not quite," said Grandma. "Try again, slow."

"Ita-da-ki-ma-su," said Aiden.

"That's it!" Grandma clapped.

Then the bowls went click, click, click. Everyone picked up chopsticks together. Aiden ate his rice. "Grandma, do we say it again for more rice?"

"No, silly boy. Once is just right."

Aiden grinned and held out his bowl. "More, please!"

Kayden wants a story. He runs to Grandpa with his book. "Read to me, please!"

Grandpa pats the chair. Kayden sits close. He hears Grandpa's chair go squeak, squeak. His ears hear that. His nose smells warm soup in the pot. Mom made soup for the cold winter day.

But Grandpa does not open the book. Grandpa looks and looks. "Where are my glasses?" he says. Kayden touches the soft cushion with his hands. No glasses there. He looks under the blanket with his eyes. There they are! He gives them to Grandpa.

Grandpa puts them on. Now he opens the book. He reads the whole story, nice and clear. Kayden licks his lips. He tastes sweet apple after the story. "Grandpa, do the glasses help you?" asks Kayden. Grandpa smiles. "Yes, they help me see the words." Kayden hugs him and counts, "One story, one apple, one happy Grandpa!"

Blake was at daycare. She wanted to build a big tower. She put the blocks in a box one by one. Then baby Sam came over. Sam pulled the blocks out of the box. "Hey!" said Blake. "My blocks!" Sam laughed and clapped.

Miss Jo came to talk with them. "Sam is small," she said. "You are big. He wants to play too." Blake watched Sam drop a block out of the box. Then Blake put one in. Sam took it out. In went a block. Out it came. It was like a fast game, then a slow game.

Blake had an idea. She gave Sam one box alone. Sam put blocks in. He took them out. He was happy. Blake built her tower next to him. It grew tall. Sam patted the top block. "Yay!" said Blake. "We did it, Sam."

Theodore went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about a spider. "Find the picture," said the librarian, Miss Amy. Theodore looked and looked. He found a book with a spider on the front. He opened it in the middle. "That is not the start," said Miss Amy. "Turn back to the front." Theodore turned the pages, one, two, three. The first page said: The words go from front to back.

"Who made up this spider?" Theodore asked. Miss Amy pointed to the cover. "The author wrote the words," she said. "See the name? That is the author." Theodore read the name out loud. Then he turned page after page, one, two, three, all the way to the end.

The spider in the story fell asleep. Theodore leaned on his mom. "I like the author," he said. "Can we bake cookies at home?"

Sofia stood in the school hallway with her mama. It was her first day of school. The hallway smelled like new crayons. Sofia held a red backpack on her back.

A big yellow bus stopped outside the window. Sofia pressed her nose to the glass. Could she see the children? Yes! They sat in little seats, two by two. One boy stood up. He wanted to wave out the window. Then the driver spoke to him. What did she say? The boy sat back down in his seat. His hand came out the window and waved from where he sat.

"Look, Mama," said Sofia. "He waves and he sits." The bus door opened with a whoosh. The children came out one by one. The waving boy ran past Sofia in the hallway. He had a red jacket, red like her backpack.

"Were the seats comfy?" Sofia asked him. The boy nodded. "You get to sit the whole way," he said. Sofia smiled. Maybe she would ride the bus one day too. She gave her mama a hug and walked to her classroom door.

Clara ran to the music corner at school. A big purple drum sat there, just her size. She hit it once. Boom! Clara laughed. She hit it again and again. Boom, boom, boom!

Ben put his hands over his ears. He ran to the rug and sat far away. Clara stopped. She felt confused. She loved the drum, but Ben did not.

She walked over to Ben. "Too loud," he said. Clara looked at her drum. Then she looked at Ben. Maybe they could like different things.

"Come with me," she said. Ben followed her to the toy shelf. Clara found the magnet toys. Click! One magnet jumped onto another. Ben smiled a big smile. Clara was excited. "You try," she said.

Ben stuck two magnets together. Click! Now the quiet sounds filled the corner. Clara clapped. Ben filled a long chain, all purple and blue.

Then the chain stuck to the chair leg. Neither of them could pull it off. Ben laughed so hard he fell over. Clara laughed too.

The teacher came by. "You two look happy," she said. Clara nodded. "Ben likes quiet. I like loud," she said. She held up the magnet chain. "We both like this!"

"Want to drum soft?" asked Ben. Clara tapped the drum very slowly. Pum, pum. Ben tapped too. "I like that," he said.

Clara grinned. Two friends, one drum, both smiling.

Zayn put on his red shirt. It was team day at the community center. One, two, three, four, five kids ran onto the floor. The coach blew her whistle.

Zayn did not know where to stand. He stood by the door. The ball flew past him. "Zayn, come here," the coach called. She pointed to a spot on the floor. "Stand right here." Zayn stood on the spot. The ball came again. This time he caught it. He threw it to his friend Mia. She waved her arms high.

How did that happen? Zayn looked at the coach. She showed Ben where to stand too. Then she showed Sam. Then the whole team knew.

After the game, they drank cold water. One, two, three, four, five cups. Zayn fell down on the mat, laughing. "Same spot next week?" asked the coach. "Yes!" said Zayn.

Maya ran into the garage. She found a little flute in Daddy's old bag. It was white and had holes on top. "I will play a song!" she said.

Maya blew into it. Squeak! The sound was not a song. It was a squeak. Maya tried again. Squeak! "My flute is silly," she said. Then she looked at her fingers. One finger was not on a hole all the way. She put it down flat. She blew once more. Toot! A real note came out! Maya jumped up and down.

She lifted one finger. Toot, a new note! She put the finger back. The old note came back. She lifted a different finger. Another new note! "Listen, Daddy!" she called. Daddy ran in fast. Maya played toot, toot, toot. She said, "This one is my song. It goes toot and toot and toot!"

John sat in his big car seat. The car went fast, then slow. "Stop," said Mom. The car stopped at the snack shop.

John was hungry. Mom bought him a cold drink and a warm muffin. The sun was hot outside. The drink was cold in his hands.

Mom filled a little cup with water for John. She poured it slow. The cup got full, all the way to the top. Then Mom showed John the other cup. It had nothing in it. It was empty. John looked at the full cup. He looked at the empty cup. He took a little sip. Now the full cup was not so full.

Back in the car, John saw a big dog and a small dog outside the window. Mom had a bone in a bag for the big dog at home. "We will give him this," she said. John held his cup with two hands. He took small sips, one by one.

The cup was light now. Soon it was empty. Mom wiped his mouth with a clean, soft cloth. The car went fast again. John waved his empty cup at the small dog going by.

Ethan was a knight at school. His cape was a red towel. He had to save the teddy bear from the block tower. But the way was blocked. Maya and Sam stood in the door, building a long train.

Ethan tried to squeeze past. He bumped the train. A car fell off. "Oh no," said Ethan. "Sorry, Sam." Sam picked up the car. He put it back on the train. Ethan stepped back. Now what?

Then he remembered the magic words. "Excuse me," said Ethan, in his best gentle knight voice. Maya smiled. She moved her feet to the side. Sam moved too. The way was clear! Ethan walked past, slow and careful, like a cat.

"Thank you!" said Ethan. He ran to the tower. He lifted the teddy bear up high. "The bear is safe!" The class clapped. Ethan bowed in his red cape. "Excuse me," said a small voice behind him. It was Maya, holding two cookies. "Do you want one?" Ethan grinned. "Yes, please!"

Colton ran to the guessing table at daycare. Miss Ana had a big smile. "Close your eyes," she said. "Feel and guess!"

Colton shut his eyes tight. He could not see a thing. But his ears heard his friends giggling. His nose smelled the orange slices for snack time.

Miss Ana put something in his hands. Colton touched it with his fingertips. It felt bumpy all over. "A pinecone!" he shouted. He opened his eyes. Yes! It was a pinecone!

Next came something soft and light. His fingertips said soft like a baby chick. "A feather!" It was a feather. Last came something cool and smooth, like a stone from the creek. "A rock!" Colton laughed.

"You can feel with your fingers!" said his friend Mia. Colton nodded big. At snack time he licked his orange slice. Yummy and sour! Then he touched his messy, sticky hands and giggled all the way to the sink.

William put on his small swim vest. It was morning at the pool. His swim team was ready to play a ball game in the shallow water.

The coach blew her whistle. "Pass the ball to your friends!" she said. William kicked his legs and stayed close to his teammate Mia. The water was cool and splashed his chin.

Mia threw the ball to William. He reached out his hands. The ball hit his fingers and went plop into the water. It bobbed away. William's face went hot. He wanted to hide.

But then his team began to shout. "Try again, William!" said Mia. "You can do it!" said Ben. Even the coach clapped her hands. William grabbed the ball from the water. He took a big breath. He threw it back to Mia.

Mia caught it! Everyone cheered again. William laughed and splashed his feet. Now it was Ben's turn. Ben missed the ball too. The ball went over his head and splashed the coach.

"Try again, Ben!" William called out loud. He clapped his wet hands. Ben picked up the ball and smiled. The game went on until the morning sun was high. "One more throw," said Mia, holding up the ball.

Lily ran to the reading corner. A big red book sat on the shelf. The cover felt rough, like a cat's tongue. She opened it. A dragon filled the page. The dragon blew fire at a castle. "Wow," said Lily. "Big fire!"

Lily wanted this book. She hugged it to her chest. She walked to the desk. "I want to keep it," she said. The librarian smiled. "You can take it home," she said. "You just need a card." Lily patted her pockets. "I don't have a card," she said. Her tummy felt wobbly. The librarian laughed. "Today you get your very first one!"
