Lily said her name. The librarian typed it. Then she handed Lily a small blue card. Lily held it up high. "My card!" she said. "Look what it does!" The librarian put the book in a bag. "The card lets you take books home," she said. Lily clapped. "Then the dragon can come to my house!"

That night, Lily's coat hung on its hook. The rough red book sat on her bed. Daddy read one page. The dragon blew fire again. Lily giggled and pulled the blanket up to her chin. "He can't get me," she whispered. "He is just paper." Then she patted the dragon's nose and said, "Good night, dragon. Back to the library tomorrow."

Today was Ellie's birthday party in her classroom. Her mom helped her hang paper stars on the wall. Her dad brought a big cake. Friends came in with balloons. Even the class owl puppet sat on the shelf, watching.

A new boy named Sam ran up to Ellie. "How old are you?" he asked. Ellie held up her fingers. She looked at her hand. "One, two, three," she counted. Three fingers stood up. "No, wait," she said. She wiggled her little finger up too. "One, two, three, four!" Sam laughed and held up four fingers too. "We are the same!" he said.

Then all the friends held up four fingers. "Happy birthday, Ellie!" they shouted. Ellie blew out the candles with her dad's help. She was not three anymore, and her fingers showed it. "Four fingers for four years," she said, and she wiggled them at the owl puppet too.

Nathan sat at the big writing club table. He had a wide piece of paper and a pencil. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

He gripped the pencil in his fist. He made a line for the letter N. But the line was fat and fuzzy. "Why is my line so big?" he asked. Miss Amy leaned close. "Let's look at your pencil," she said. The tip was dull and flat.

Miss Amy took the pencil to the sharpener. She turned it around and around. Then she gave it back. The tip was small and pointy now. Nathan made his line again. This time it was thin and neat.

He wrote N, then A, then T. "I did it!" he said. Miss Amy put a little hat sticker on his paper. Nathan smiled so wide. "Can I write it again?" he asked. "Yes," said Miss Amy. "Write it one more time." And he did.

Jordan planted seeds in the school garden. He made a deep little hole for each one. Then he patted the soft dirt on top.

Every day Jordan ran to the garden. He looked for his seeds. Nothing came up. The dirt was dry and hard. Next to him, Mia had little green leaves. She held a watering can.

Jordan wanted green leaves too. He found his own small watering can. He gave his seeds a gentle drink of water. He sat in a circle with his friends to wait.

The next day, Jordan ran to the garden again. Something tiny and green was peeking out of the dirt. Jordan clapped his hands. "Hello, little plant," he said. He filled the watering can again. "Would you like to share my water?"

Lucy went to the park with her dad. Grandma was coming to meet them there. Lucy could not wait. She felt so excited. She jumped up and down. She bounced on her toes. She shouted, "Grandma! Grandma!" But Grandma was not there yet.

Lucy looked down the path. She looked with one eye, then two eyes. No Grandma. Lucy felt sad. Her jumps got smaller and smaller. Then a big dog ran near, and Lucy felt scared. Dad held her hand. The dog's owner called it back. Lucy felt angry at the dog for a minute. Then it licked her shoe, and she laughed.

"You are bouncing a lot," said Dad. "Let's wait in a calm way." They sat on the bench. Lucy colored with her chalk on the ground. She drew a big red heart for Grandma. She waited. She waited some more. Waiting felt long, but her chalk kept her hands busy.

Then a voice said, "Is that heart for me?" It was Grandma! Lucy jumped up one more time, because now jumping was just right. Grandma picked her up and hugged her tight. "I saw your red heart all the way down the path," said Grandma. Lucy smiled a big smile.

Margot sat on the big red cushion. The soccer game was on TV. Everyone was there. Dad was there. Grandma was there. Even her cousin Ben was there. Dad carried a plate of warm popcorn. He set it down on the low table. "Careful, it is warm," he said. Margot took one small piece and blew on it.

The players ran and ran. They kicked the ball. Then Margot heard a loud sound. Tweet, tweet! She covered her ears. "Why did everyone stop running?" she asked. "The man in the black shirt blew his whistle," said Grandma. "Watch." Margot watched. The whistle blew again. Tweet, tweet! The players stopped. They stood still like statues.

Margot wanted to try. She held her toy whistle. Tweet, tweet! she blew. Ben laughed. Nobody stood still. Dad kept munching popcorn. Grandma kept waving her sock in the air like a lazy flag. Margot laughed too. "My whistle does not stop Dad," she said. She blew it again. Tweet, tweet! Ben jumped up and hurried to the kitchen for juice. "Look!" said Margot. "It stopped Ben!"

Michael was at Grandma's house. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. Grandma put the pumpkin on the table. She gave him a brush.

Michael looked for orange paint. The orange jar was empty. "Oh no," said Michael. "No orange."

He found a jar of red paint. He found a jar of yellow paint. He put red on the pumpkin. Then he put yellow on top of the red. He moved his brush round and round.

The pumpkin turned orange! Michael opened his eyes wide. "Look, Grandma!" he said. Grandma smiled. "What a big orange pumpkin," she said.

Michael dipped his brush again. Red, then yellow, round and round. He painted a slimy green worm on his pumpkin too. Then he held it up to the window, so the sun could see.

Everly sat in a big red seat. Her mama sat next to her. On the stage, a woman began to play a quiet song on a violin. Everly liked it a lot. She wanted to clap right away. So she clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap.

A man in front turned around. He put one finger near his lips. Everly stopped clapping. She looked at mama. "Wait," mama whispered. "Watch the song. It is not over yet." So Everly waited. The music went up and down. It went soft and slow. Then it stopped. The stage got very still. Now the man in front began to clap. Then everyone clapped at once. Everly clapped too. It was like a game. The song ends, and then the hands go.

Next came a fast song. Everly wanted to play this game too. She listened hard. The song had a steady beat. She tried to clap along with it. She clapped too fast. She tried again. Too slow. She kept trying. Then her claps landed right on the beat. Clap, clap, clap, clap. She was with the song. Mama clapped along too.

At the end, the woman on stage sang a song Everly knew. It was about a star. Everly sang the words from memory. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Her voice was small but strong. The song ended. Everly held her hands up high. She waited and waited. Then the whole hall clapped, loud and long. Everly clapped the biggest clap of all. "Again," she said. "Sing it again."

Ethan wanted his bedtime story. He ran to get his book about a dog. Dad was still typing on his computer. So Ethan tried to read it himself. He opened the book. But he opened it from the back. The pages looked all mixed up. The dog was wet. Then the dog was in his bed. Then the dog began to bark at nothing. Ethan turned a page. The dog was lost. Ethan turned another page. The dog was home. "That is not right," said Ethan. Dad came over. He sat on the edge of the bed. Ethan held up the book. "It is all jumbled," he said. Dad tapped the front of the book. Ethan looked. The front had the dog's happy face on it. Ethan flipped the book over. He opened the front cover. There was page one. The dog woke up in the morning. Ethan turned the pages one by one. The story went along, calm and long, all the way to the back. The last page said good night to the dog. Ethan yawned. He handed the book to Dad. "Read it again," he said, "from the front."

William jumped into the car with a big bag. "Time for Grandma's house!" said Mom. The bag held gifts for Grandma's new puppy. William could not wait.

The bag tipped over on the seat. Everything fell out! William reached for the toys. A ball rolled under his feet. A squeaky duck sat on his lap. Then he found a bouncy sock. William laughed. "Socks don't go with toys!" He waved the sock in the air.

"Silly me," said Mom. "That sock fell in from the laundry. Socks go with clothes, like shirts and hats." William put the sock in a little pile with a hat and a shirt. Then he made a toy pile. Then a food pile, with crackers and a banana.

"Grandma will love her snacks," said Mom. "And the puppy will love that duck." William hugged the duck. It let out a big squeak. "Beep beep!" said William. "Almost there," said Mom, and pointed out the window at Grandma's red door.

Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds a heavy box under the toy shelf. He pulls it. He pulls again. The box does not move. "Too big for me," he says.

Miss Ana brings a small pillow. It has a soft feather inside. Carter lifts it up high. It is so light! He puts the pillow on top of the heavy box. Now the box is a big, round bottom. The pillow is a small, soft top.

The tower is dirty, so Miss Ana wipes it with a wet cloth. The cloth is cold on Carter's hand. He waits while it dries. He waits some more. Then he pushes his tower slowly across the rug. Slow, slow, slow. Ben runs fast past him. Carter laughs and keeps going slow. "My tower can ride on top," he says, and pats the soft pillow.

Hailey wanted to play blocks with Grandpa. She ran to the big room. "Grandpa!" she shouted. The baby was asleep in the little bed. The baby woke up and began to cry. Hailey felt sad. The baby was sad too.

Mommy picked the baby up. She rocked her soft and slow. Grandpa held up one finger by his mouth. Hailey looked at the sleeping baby. She took a big breath. Then she made her voice very small. "Grandpa," she whispered. "Play blocks now?" The room stayed quiet. The baby closed her eyes again.

Grandpa smiled and sat down on the floor. Hailey gave him the red blocks. He gave her the blue ones. They took turns putting one block on top. The tower grew tall. Outside, a truck went down the street. Inside, it was still nice and quiet. "More blocks," Hailey whispered.

Gabriel was at Grandma's house. Snow fell all morning. Gabriel wanted to draw the snow.

He took white paper and a red crayon. He drew his red sled. He drew his yellow hat. He drew green trees. But the snow would not show up. The white crayon looked like nothing on the white paper.

"Try blue paper," said Grandma. Gabriel found blue paper. He drew with the white crayon. The snow showed up! It looked soft and fresh, just like the snow outside. He added a red scarf and a yellow sun.

Grandma hung the picture by the window. Outside, a small bird landed on the snow. It left tiny marks, like little footprints. Gabriel laughed. "Now the snow has pictures too," he said.

Blake went to the garden center with Dad. She picked a young tomato plant. It had green leaves and a little stick.

Blake wanted to plant it in her pot. She filled the pot with soft brown soil. Then she saw a weed growing in the pot. "Go away, weed," she said.

Blake pulled the weed. Up it came. "Look!" she said. Long stringy roots hung down. "It has little feet!" Dad laughed. "Those are roots," he said. "A plant's roots grow down into the soil."

Blake tapped her tomato plant out of its cup. She saw roots there too. She made a deep hole. She set the roots down into the dark soil. She patted the soil with her hands.

The sun came out. Blake watered the pot. One drop, two drops, a big number of drops. "Grow, tomato," she said. "Grow your feet down low."

Soon a red tomato grew. Dad picked it. Blake took a taste. "Yum," she said. "My feet helped you stand up!"

Madelyn wanted to go to Lily's house. She wanted to go now. "Can we go now, Mama?" she asked. "Not now," said Mama. "We go tomorrow. First you sleep, then it is tomorrow." Madelyn frowned. Tomorrow felt far away.

Mama had an idea. She gave Madelyn a letter to draw on. "Draw a picture for Lily," she said. Madelyn drew a red cat and a big sun. She dropped her crayon under the table. She picked it up and kept drawing. The picture was very good.

Then Madelyn waited. She watched the sun go down out the window. She ate her dinner. She had a bath. She put on her soft pajamas. "Is it tomorrow now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "Sleep first, then tomorrow."

Madelyn got in bed. She put the letter by her shoes so she would not forget it. The letter was not stuck under anything. It sat right on top. Madelyn closed her eyes. She slept all night. In the morning the sun was up. "Is it tomorrow?" she asked. Mama smiled. "It is tomorrow now." Madelyn grabbed her letter. "Lily's house today!" she said. Mama took her hand. "Yes, today we go."

Harper went to the pharmacy with Dad. A sneaky germ had made her tummy sick. The pharmacist gave Dad some medicine. Then the pharmacist said, "Wash your hands, little one. Count to twenty with soap."

At home, Harper got the soap. She rubbed and rubbed. One, two, three, four. She counted all the way to twenty.

Then she looked at her hands. "Why are they still slippery?" she asked.

Dad smiled. "Try the water."

Harper held her hands under the water. The water washed the soap away. Her hands were not slippery anymore. They felt clean and smooth.

"Now can I eat my crackers?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Your hands are ready."

Harper pointed at the sink. "The soap went down the hole!"

A boy walked by with his mom. "Bye, slippery soap!" Harper called. Then she took a big, quick bite of her cracker.

Matteo did not want to sleep. He stood at his window. Snow was falling. Snow fell on the trees. Snow fell on the fence. Matteo pressed his face to the cold glass.

Today had been a good day. Today he made a snowman. Today he drank warm cocoa. Matteo had one more thing he wanted. He wanted to sled tomorrow. But first he had to sleep.

"Where does today go?" Matteo asked Dad. Dad tucked the blanket up to Matteo's chin. Dad kissed his warm cheek. "Sleep now," Dad said softly. "Sledding comes later." Matteo closed his eyes. He slept and slept.

When Matteo woke up, the sun was bright. He ran to the window. "Is it tomorrow?" he called. "It is tomorrow," said Dad. "And the snowman day? Now we call that yesterday." Matteo jumped up and down. Yesterday he made a snowman. Today he would sled. "Get your boots," said Dad, and held the door open wide.

Ethan stood at the snack table at school. He wanted to count the apples. His teacher put them in a line. Ethan pointed and counted, "One, two, three, four, five." But then his finger jumped back. "Six," he said, pointing at the same apple again. The girl next to him shook her head. "There are five apples," she said. Ethan frowned and looked at the line.

He tried again. This time he watched his finger. He touched each apple one time. "One, two, three, four, five." He did not touch any apple twice. Five! He counted them again just to be sure. One tap for each apple, and one number for each tap. He smiled big.

Then the teacher held up two bowls. One had crackers, one had grapes. "Which has more?" she asked. Ethan counted the crackers. He counted the grapes. "The grapes have more!" he said. He tapped his finger on the bowl and laughed.

Eleanor woke up excited. Today was Diwali! Grandma called her to the table. On it sat little clay lamps called diyas. There were so many! Eleanor touched one. It was cool and smooth.

"Can I help?" Eleanor asked. "Yes, you can help," said Grandma. Eleanor set out the diyas in a row. One, two, three, four, five. They all sat dark and empty.

"Who will make them glow?" Eleanor asked. Daddy struck the match. He tipped it into the first diya. A little flame popped up! Then he lit the next one, and the next. One flame made the whole row glow. The night outside was dark, but the room was bright. Eleanor clapped her messy, floury hands. "Happy Diwali!" she shouted. Grandma laughed and hugged her tight.

Eliana went to the art gallery with her mama. Big paintings hung on the walls. One painting was all red. One was all blue. One was all yellow. "Red, blue, yellow," Eliana said softly, like a song.

In the corner was a table with paint pots. Eliana dipped her brush in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow. She made a green line on her paper. Her eyes went wide. "Mama, look! Blue and yellow made green!" Then she made purple with red and blue.

Next to the table hung a little painting of a monkey. The monkey looked thirsty, holding a red cup. Eliana touched the monkey's cup. Her finger came back with red on it. A small fingerprint sat on the painting now. A gallery lady came over. "That paint is still wet," she said. "This one is dry. You can touch the frame."

Eliana sat down to paint a new monkey. This time she kept her fingers on her own paper. She waited while her green paint dried. Then she pointed at it. "Dry!" she said. "All done, green."

Sophie went to the garden with Grandma. She had little seeds in her hand. "Plant them here," said Grandma. Sophie pushed the seeds into the soft brown dirt. Then she patted the dirt down, pat, pat.

Sophie wanted her plants to grow. But day after day, nothing came up. "Where are my seeds?" she asked. "Wait," said Grandma. "Rain will help." The rain came down, drip, drip. The warm sun came out too. Soon little green leaves popped up. The plants grew tall. They curled up a stick like a pig's curly tail.

One day Sophie saw something green hanging on her plant. "What is that?" she asked. She picked it. It felt bumpy. Sophie turned it over in her hands. Then she popped it open. Inside was a row of little round peas! Sophie smiled big. "Look, Grandma!" she said. Grandma laughed and ate one. "Sweet peas from Sophie's garden."

Elias wants to make soup for his family. He and Dad go to the big community kitchen. There is a long table and many pots.

Elias picks a carrot and a potato. He puts them in the pot. Then he picks a big white onion. "This one," he whispers, like a little mouse.

Dad cuts the onion with his knife. Elias stands back, where it is safe. Then Dad rubs his eyes. Water runs down his face.

Elias feels worried. "Dad, are you sad?" he asks. "Did the soup make you cry?"

Dad laughs a soft laugh. "No, no," he says. "It is just the onion. Onions can make eyes water."

Elias looks at the onion. He looks at Dad's wet eyes. He blinks his own eyes. They feel fine. Dad did not cut an onion near him.

The soup bubbles. A grown-up stirs the hot pot. Soon the soup is ready. Mom and baby sister come to the table. They eat the warm soup. It is yummy.

Baby sister makes a funny face. Dad smiles at her. His eyes are all dry now.

Elias holds up the onion. "This made you cry," he says.

"I will cut it far away next time," says Dad.

Elias giggles and spoons more soup into his bowl.

Sara sat at the kitchen table. Grandma put a bowl of soup in front of her. The soup was too hot, so Grandma blew on it. Sara would wait.

While she waited, Sara played a game. "My eyes see," she said. She looked at the steam. It went up high. "My ears hear." She listened to the pot on the stove. Bub, bub, bub.

Then Grandma said, "Sniff, sniff." Sara sniffed with her nose. The soup smelled like carrots. "Mmm," said Sara. "I smell with my nose!" She touched the warm bowl with one finger. It was still hot, so she pulled her hand back.

At last the soup was ready. Sara took a small sip. It tasted yummy. "Grandma," she said, "my tongue tastes it!" Grandma laughed. Outside, a dog began to bark. Sara pointed at the window. "My ears hear that too!" she said.

Isla went to the playground with her towel. She wanted to play the opposite game with her friend Tom. Tom said a word. Then Isla had to shout the opposite. Tom said, "Big!" Isla looked at the big slide. She shouted, "Small!" and pointed at the small slide. "Yes!" said Tom. He laughed and clapped.

They ran to the swings. Tom said, "Fast!" Isla pumped her legs. Her swing went fast. Then she let it slow down. "Slow!" she shouted. Tom said, "You got it!" Next Tom said, "Hot!" He pointed at the sun on the bench. Isla touched the cold metal bar of the swing. "Cold!" she shouted. "Right again," said Tom.

Then Tom said, "Awake!" Isla stood very still. She thought hard. She closed one eye. Then she opened both eyes wide. "Asleep!" she shouted. Tom fell over laughing. "That was the best one," he said. Isla bowed on her swing. "Let's play more tomorrow," she said. Tom nodded and grinned.

Samuel's class went on a shape hunt. Miss Patel said, "Find me a circle!" Samuel found a round clock on the wall. "Find me a square!" He found a square block, red and smooth.

Then Miss Patel said, "Find a rectangle." Samuel frowned. What did a rectangle look like? He looked and looked. Then his friend Lily pointed at the door. "That's one!" Samuel ran to the door. He touched the top side. He touched the bottom side. He touched the two long sides. Four sides! Then he pressed his finger in each corner. One, two, three, four. Square corners, just like his block. The door was a rectangle!

Samuel was so quiet while he counted that Lily started to giggle. "You look like a sleepy cat by that door!" she said. Samuel heard a coat zip open behind him. Tom pulled off his coat and laid it flat on the rug. "Look, my coat is a rectangle too!" Everyone laughed and clapped. Then Miss Patel opened the door. "Snack time," she said, and twelve happy kids ran through the big rectangle at once.

Hannah sat on the big train with Mama and Dad. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap. Hannah liked to watch the rain slide down the glass.

Then her tummy made a squeeze. "I need to pee," she whispered. "Do we stop at a rest stop now?" In the car, they always did that. Daddy would park, and everyone would hop out and stretch.

Mama smiled a big smile. "Come with me," she said. She took Hannah's hand down the little aisle. Then she opened a small door. It was a tiny bathroom, right on the train!

"A bathroom on wheels!" said Hannah. She giggled so much she almost forgot to pee.

When she came out, Dad was holding something behind his back. "Look who came along," he said. It was Hannah's yellow sock monkey, waving from a seat by the window. "He watched the rain the whole time," said Dad.

Hannah gave the monkey a big squeeze and sat down to watch with him.

Olivia wanted to paint at the little table. Her brother Sam wanted to paint too. But there was only one big brush left.

"Who gets the brush?" Olivia asked herself. "We both get a go," she said. "One after another."

So Olivia went first. She painted a cloudy sky on her paper. Sam watched and waited. Then she put the brush down. "Your turn, Sam," she said.

Sam went next. He painted a red wall with a door in it. Olivia watched and waited. Then it was her turn again.

Outside, the rain stopped. Sam looked at the window. "Can we play now?" he asked.

"Yes," said Olivia. She helped Sam fix the paint lid. It was tight, so she pushed with two hands. Click!

They ran to the door. "You first," said Sam. "No, you first," said Olivia. They both laughed and went out together.

Ellie ran to the plate to bat. She was so excited to hit the ball. "Wait, Ellie!" said Coach Ben. "Come back here first."

Ellie ran back. Coach Ben held up a white helmet. "Put this on," he said. Ellie put the helmet on her head. It felt big and warm.

Then Ellie batted. The ball flew far! Everyone clapped. "We might win!" said her friend Sam. Ellie smiled under her helmet. She patted it with her little hand. "My helmet," she said. Coach Ben gave her a thumbs up. Ellie ran to first base, and the helmet stayed snug on her head the whole way.

Logan ran into the baby store. His shoes went tap, tap on the floor. "A new baby is coming!" he said. Mom held his hand. "We need tiny things," she said.

They found a cozy blanket. They found a little sock. Then Logan saw a big doll in a basket. The doll looked like a real baby. Mom said, "You can practice."

Logan patted the doll. Pat! Pat! The doll's head tipped over. Mom sat down next to him. "Watch me," she said. She touched the doll's hand with one finger. She moved it slow and soft.

Logan tried. He touched the doll's hand with one finger. Soft. Slower. The doll stayed still. "I did it!" said Logan. "Gentle hands!"

Then the doll made a sound. "Waa," it went. Logan jumped. "The doll talks!"

"The baby will talk too," said Mom. Logan touched the doll's cheek with his soft finger. "I will touch you like this," he whispered. "Nice and slow."

Mila sat at the big art table. She drew a big yellow apple. Ben sat next to her. He drew a big yellow apple too.

Miss Rosa said, "Time to put the paintings on the wall." Mila put her painting down. Ben put his down too. The two paintings touched on the table.

Then Mila looked. She saw two yellow apples. She could not tell which one was hers. "Which apple did I paint?" she asked.

Miss Rosa said, "Let's look very closely." Ben pointed at his paper. His paper had letters on it. The letters said BEN. "That one is mine," he said. "My mom helped me write my name."

Mila looked at her paper. It had no name on it. It was just a yellow apple. "Mine is this one," she said softly. "It has no name."

After that, Mila got a small pencil. She wrote M-I-L-A at the top. She sent her painting to the wall with the tape. Her name rode on top of the apple, all the way up.

Brooks ran to the playground. He wanted to play house. His friend Mia was there by the little play kitchen. "Let's play house," said Brooks. "I want to be the parent," said Mia. "I want to be the parent too," said Brooks. They both stood still. They both frowned.

Then Mia had an idea. "You be the parent first," she said. "Then we switch. I will be the baby now." Brooks liked that. He picked up the pot and stirred it. The pot went clink, clink, clink. Mia lay down near the little bed. "Time to sleep, baby," said Brooks. He patted her head. One pat, two pats, three pats.

"Now we switch," said Brooks. Mia jumped up. She was the parent now. Brooks was the baby. He crawled to the toy bear and hugged it tight. Mia covered the bear with a small blanket. "The baby bear is cold," she said. Brooks rocked the bear back and forth. The bear went rock, rock, rock.

They played until the sun went low. "Same time tomorrow?" asked Mia. "Yes," said Brooks. He thought about tomorrow all the way home. "I can be the baby again," he said to his mom. "Or the parent."

Lena sat in a big blue chair. The waiting room had a fish tank. A little orange fish swam past her nose. Lena was awake early today. Today she would see the dentist for the first time.

A nurse called her name. Lena held Mama's hand. The dentist showed Lena a small cup of water. Then Lena brushed her teeth with minty paste. Her mouth got full of white foam. It tasted like mint. Lena closed her mouth to swallow it.

Then she stopped. She leaned over the sink. She pushed the foam out with her tongue. "Good job," said the dentist. "You spit it out." Lena picked a green card with a star on it. The nurse gave her a sticker too. On the way home, Lena smiled at the orange fish in her mind.

Clara went to the community centre with her dad. There was a big table with crayons. Clara sat down on a small chair.

Her friend Mia sat down too. Miss Anne gave them each a tray. Clara counted her crayons. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. "I have five crayons." Mia counted hers. "One, two, three, four," said Mia. Clara had more. Clara smiled.

Clara drew a tall tree and a little car. Then the bell on the wall began to ring. Snack time! Miss Anne gave each girl one strawberry. Clara ate her strawberry. It was sweet and red.

Then Clara looked at her tray. One crayon was gone. It had rolled under the table. Clara picked it up and put it back. Then she counted again. "One, two, three, four," she said. "One crayon less, one number less." She took it away once more and counted. "One, two, three."

Mia slid her tray next to Clara's. "Now we both have four," said Clara. Mia laughed. The girls lined up all eight crayons in a tall, tall tower, and Clara counted every one.

Raphael stood by the lake pool. The water looked cool and shiny. His teacher, Mia, smiled at him.

"Put your face near the water," said Mia.

Raphael shook his head. "Will it tickle my nose?" he asked.

"Try it and see," said Mia.

Raphael leaned down. He took a big breath. Then he blew out through his mouth. Glub, glub, glub! Big bubbles popped up all around his chin.

Raphael lifted his head. "Bubbles!" he laughed. "My mouth made them!"

He blew again. More bubbles came. They grew big, then they went pop.

"Look, Mia! More bubbles!"

After the pool, Dad helped Raphael tie the strings on his shoes. Raphael looked at the lake. "Dad, can I blow bubbles in the lake too?"

"Not yet," said Dad. "First you blow them here, at the pool."

Raphael grinned and blew one more big bubble.

The lights went out. Matthew stood in the backyard with his dad. The house was dark. The TV would not turn on.

"How will we watch the bus show?" Matthew asked.

Dad clicked a flashlight on. A bright circle popped onto the grass. "No TV tonight," Dad said. "What else can we do?"

Matthew looked at the dark house. Could a puzzle work with no lights? Dad shined the flashlight on the porch table. Mom brought out a game with a big red box.

"Does a game need light from the wall?" Matthew asked.

"Let's find out," said Mom.

They opened the box. The flashlight lit up the board. Matthew picked a new card. He moved his little dog. It was his turn, then Dad's turn, then Mom's turn. The game worked and worked.

Mom clapped. "No plugs anywhere," she said.

Matthew laughed. He shined the flashlight on his dog piece himself. "You don't need the wall," he told it. The moon stayed up above them, big and white, watching the game.

Aubrey woke up hungry. She wanted toast with butter. She wanted to butter it all by herself.

Daddy made the toast. The toast was warm and golden. He gave Aubrey the butter and a dull knife. Aubrey pushed the butter on the toast. The butter was cold and hard. It tore a hole in the toast. "Oh no," said Aubrey. "My toast has a hole."

Then Aubrey saw the butter dish on the counter. That butter had sat out all night. It was soft. She tried again. The soft butter slid right across the toast. No holes! "Look, Daddy, it's smooth," she said.

Next came the milk. Aubrey held the cup with one foot planted steady on the floor. She poured slowly. Not one drop spilled. The dog barked, happy for breakfast too. "He wants some," said Aubrey. Daddy filled the dog's bowl.

Aubrey bit into her toast. It was yummy and not stinky at all, like her brother's socks. She laughed. "More toast, please," she said, holding up her cup.

It was story morning at daycare. Zoey wanted the cat book. The one with the sweet little cat on the cover.

She ran to the bookshelf. So many books! She pointed. "That one? That one? That one?" Her teacher shook her head.

Zoey patted the covers. She turned one book over. The pages flapped. Upside down!

Then she saw it. Big letters on the front. She knew those letters. "Z... O... E... Y?" she asked.

Her teacher laughed. "That says Little Cat." Zoey looked at the big words. "Little Cat," she said slowly. "Little Cat is the book's name!"

"Can I have Little Cat, please?" she asked. "Yes!" said her teacher.

Zoey sat down. She opened the front cover. Page one, page two, page three. The sweet little cat said, "Meow."

"Little Cat," said Zoey. "That is your name."

Eliana sat in her car seat. She held her small toy cat. "Today we see the dentist," said Mama. "Will he like my teeth?" Eliana asked. "I think so," said Mama. The car stopped. They went inside.

The dentist had a big chair. It went up and up. Eliana climbed in with help. Then a bright light came on over her head. Eliana squinted. "Too bright," she said. The light made her eyes feel funny.

The dentist smiled. He gave her tiny sunglasses. "Try these," he said. Eliana put them on. Now the light did not hurt her eyes. She opened her mouth wide. The dentist looked inside. "I can see all your teeth," he said. The bright light helped him see.

"Open big like a lion," said the dentist. Eliana opened very big. "I see clean teeth," he said. "You taste your food with those teeth, don't you?" Eliana giggled. After, Mama gave her a sticker. Eliana put it on her toy cat. "Now kitty has sunglasses too," she said.

Eliana stood at the gate of the school playground. It was her very first day. She wanted to play on the big red slide. But a long line of kids stood there first. Eliana's tummy felt jumpy like a stormy sky.

She looked around. Then she ran to the front of the line. "My turn!" she said. But a boy named Sam shook his head. "No cutting," he said. "We all follow the rules. Miss May told us." Miss May blew her whistle. "Sam is right," she said. "Line up, please."

So Eliana went to the back of the line. She waited. She counted one shoe, two shoes, three shoes. Soon it was her turn. The slide was fast and bumpy. "Whee!" she yelled. Sam slid down next to her. "Your turn again?" he asked. Eliana grinned and said, "Yes, after you!"

Brooks sat in his cozy car seat. A big blue plane flew over the car. "The dentist is far away," said Mama. Brooks was going to the dentist for the very first time.

At the dentist, a kind lady asked Brooks to open his mouth. Brooks opened it a little bit. Then he closed it to say, "Is this right?" The lady could not see his teeth. "Try again," she said with a smile.

Brooks took a big breath. He opened his mouth wide, like a lion's roar. Now the lady could see every tooth. She counted them one by one. Brooks jumped down from the big chair. "I did it!" he said. Mama gave him a soft hug. He got a little sticker shaped like a tooth.

Lillian wanted to find her happy face. Where could it be? She looked in the hall mirror. First she made a big smile. "There it is!" she said. The mirror girl smiled too.

Then Lillian made a sad face. Her mouth went down, down, down. The mirror girl looked sad too. Lillian made an angry face, all scrunchy. Then a scared face, with wide eyes. Then an excited face, jumping up and down. The mirror jumped with her.

Papa came to see. "Look, Papa!" said Lillian. She showed him every face. Papa tried one too. But his face looked funny, not sad and not mad. Lillian laughed. It was a surprise face! "What is that one?" she asked. Papa laughed too, and the mirror held two laughing faces.

Edouard stood in his bedroom. Today he would get his first library card. He put on his blue sweater. "I am ready," he told Mama.

At the library, a kind lady gave him a small card. It had his name on it. Edouard ran to the shelves. He found a big book about dinosaurs. "A DINOSAUR BOOK!" he shouted. Then he saw a girl reading at a table. He saw a man reading by the window. Edouard looked at their quiet faces. He made his voice very small. "A dinosaur book," he whispered. Mama smiled and nodded. The lady stamped his book. Edouard held it tight with both hands.

Back home, Edouard sat on his bed. He opened the dinosaur book. He picked up his crayons. He began to draw a big green dinosaur in his own garden picture. "This is the best day," he whispered.

Parker ran into the playroom. He had big news. "A dragon!" he shouted. "At the park!"

Mia was talking first. She was telling about her teddy bear. Parker talked over her. "Dragon, dragon!" he said. Then Mia stopped talking. She folded her arms. Parker had missed the end of the teddy story. Now Mia looked sad, and nobody was talking at all.

Parker sat on the rug. He put his hands in his lap. He watched Mia's mouth and waited. Mia told the end. The teddy hid in a dark cave and found a flashlight. "The end," said Mia. Then she smiled at Parker. "Your turn now," she said. Parker took a big breath. "A green dragon flew over the park!" he said. "It waved at me!" Mia clapped her hands. "Again, again!" she said.

Parker was at school. It was paint time. He wanted to paint green grass.

Mia wanted green grass too. They looked for the green paint. The green pot was empty. "Oh no," said Mia. "No more green."

Parker had a plan. He got the blue pot. He got the yellow pot. He put blue on his brush. He put yellow on top. He mixed them on the paper. "Look!" said Parker. The paint turned green. Green grass!

Mia smiled. "Let me try." She mixed blue and yellow too. Her grass was green. Parker kept painting. He painted green grass, and a yellow sun, and a blue slide.

At play time, Mia went down the big slide. Parker slid down too. Then he ran back up the old wooden steps. "Again!" he said.

Teacher Kim hung the paintings up to dry. "Beautiful grass," she said. Parker looked at his green grass. "I made green," he told Mia. Mia laughed. "Mix it again tomorrow!"

Hailey wanted to feed her pet rabbit, Clover. But first Mom called her for lunch. Mom cut the sandwich with a safe knife. The pieces were triangles.

"A triangle," Hailey said. She touched one corner. "One." She touched another. "Two." She touched the last one. "Three."

"Three corners," she said. "Three sides, too." She counted the sides. One, two, three. Then she took a big bite.

After lunch, Hailey made shapes for Clover. She folded a paper square. She cut out a circle. She pulled a napkin into a rectangle. "Which one is like my sandwich?" she asked. She held up the triangle. "This one! It has three corners."

Clover hopped over and sniffed the triangle. Hailey laughed. "You like triangles too," she said. "Here, Clover. One corner for you."

Sophia was three years old. Today she went to the bowling alley for her birthday. "Happy birthday, Sophia!" said Grandma. There were balloons and cake and a big shiny spoon for the ice cream.

Sophia pushed her ball down the lane. The ball rolled and rolled. It hit the pins. All the pins fell down! "Strike!" everyone cheered. The ball made the pins fall. Sophia jumped up and down. She rolled the ball again. The pins fell again.

Then Daddy brought out the cake. He lit the candles with a match, all by himself. Sophia counted the candles. "One, two, three, four," she said. "Four candles? I am three!"

"You had a birthday today," said Mommy. "Now you are one year older."

Sophia looked at the candles. Four candles for four years. She smiled a real big smile. "I am four!" she shouted.

"Make a wish," said Grandma. "But don't forget to blow." Sophia blew out the candles. Out they went, one by one.

"Happy birthday to me," sang Sophia. "I am four, I am four, I am four!" Then she picked up her spoon and took a big bite of cake.

Natalie put on her red team shirt. She ran into the backyard for soccer. Coach Maria was there. So was a man in a striped shirt. He held a little whistle.

Natalie kicked the ball. Then Ben kicked it. He used his hands to knock it into the net. The man blew his whistle. "No hands," he said.

Natalie frowned. She sat down on the crunchy grass. A soft feather floated by her shoe.

"Why did he stop the game?" Natalie asked.

"His job is to watch the rules," said Coach Maria. "He helps us play fair."

Natalie stood up. She kicked the ball again. This time she used only her foot. The whistle stayed quiet. The man gave her a big thumbs up.

Natalie laughed and kicked the ball to Ben.

Levi loved his blue socks. He wore them at school all day. He ran in them. He jumped in them. He painted in them. Now his socks had red and green paint spots. They felt sticky too.

At nap time, Levi pulled off his socks. He dropped them on the floor. Then he saw something. His friend Milo tossed his socks into a basket. Swish! They landed inside. "That looks fun," said Levi. He picked up his sticky socks. He lifted them high. He aimed at the basket. He threw. The socks hit the edge and fell out.

Levi laughed. He tried again. This time the socks went in. Swish! The basket held Milo's socks too. After school, Teacher Amy carried the basket to the washer. Levi gave the basket a gentle hug. "Bye bye, socks," he said. "Come back clean!" Teacher Amy smiled. "They will," she said.

Mila wanted to play with her big teddy bear. But she could not find him. She looked under the small chair. She looked in the slow toy train. No teddy.

Then Mila found a puddle on the floor. The water was cold on her toes. Her socks were wet. "Where did the water come from?" she asked. Mama came in. "The big dog splashed his water bowl," said Mama. "He wagged his tail and tipped it over."

Mila laughed. She took off her wet socks. She put on dry socks, fast. Then she found teddy behind the big basket. She hugged him. "Wet socks off, dry socks on," she said. She said it again, "Wet socks off, dry socks on." Then she rolled the slow train, early for teddy's tea party, all the way to the small chair.

Isla wanted to be the rocket ship today. But Tom said, "You have to count first." Isla did not know how.

At circle time, Miss Jo sang a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." Isla sang too. She counted the beads on the table. She counted six, seven, eight. She counted nine crayons, then one more. "Ten!" she said.

Outside, Tom made a rocket from a big box. "Pretend we are going far away," he said. "Past the cow in the field!" Isla climbed in. "Count down," said Tom. "From ten."

Isla took a big breath. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" She jumped up so high. "I did it!" said Isla. "Next time I count to the moon."

Beau sat on the small stage in the school auditorium. A big drum sat in front of him. His teacher, Miss Ada, gave him two soft drumsticks. "You can play," she said.

Beu hit the drum very hard. BOOM! The sound was huge. A baby in the back row woke up and began to cry. Beau looked at the baby. He felt his face get warm.

He tried again, this time with a little tap. Tap. The sound was small and soft. The baby blinked and stopped crying. Beau tapped again, soft as a whisper. Tap, tap. Miss Ada smiled. "That sound is just right," she said.

Beau played a slow song with his soft taps. The baby fell back to sleep. Beau looked at his drumsticks and whispered, "Soft taps make soft sounds. That's true." Then he tapped the drum one more time, very gently, and listened.

Jack ran to the sand pit at the park. He wanted to build a big castle. There was one box of round buckets and shovels.

Jack took all the buckets. He took all the shovels too. His friend Mia had nothing to hold. Mia sat down and put her hands in her lap. She watched the sand with sad eyes.

Jack looked at Mia. Then he looked at his tall pile. One friend had all the toys. One friend had none. That did not feel right.

Jack gave Mia a red bucket. He gave her a blue shovel too. Mia smiled and began to dig. Soon she had a tall tower. Jack had a tall tower too. Side by side, the towers stood like a gate.

Then Tom came to play. He had nothing at all. Jack thought fast. He held out a green shovel. "You can dig with me," Jack said. Tom dug a deep, cool hole. He made a round moat around both towers.

Three friends played in the sand. Everyone got a chance. The castle grew bigger and bigger. At the end, Jack clapped sand off his hands. "Best castle ever," said Mia.

"Same time tomorrow?" asked Tom. Jack nodded and grinned.

Arlo stood in the backyard with his big red ball. Today he had his first game. The ball had to go up and through the hoop. That was how his team got a point.

Arlo threw the ball. It hit the hoop and fell down. He threw it again. It hit the edge and bounced away. "Why won't it go in?" he asked. Maybe the ball was too low? He tried one more time. Too low again. The ball rolled to the grass.

Arlo picked up the ball and looked at the hoop. It was way up high. What if he threw it way up high too? He bent his knees. He pushed the ball up, up, up. The ball sailed through the hoop and dropped down. It went in! It went in! Arlo clapped his hands.

Dad came out with a juicy apple slice. "Big throw!" he said. "You got the ball through the hoop. That's a point for your team." Arlo took a bite and chewed. Then he lined up his ball again. "Watch me," he said. He bent his knees and pushed.

Declan sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. "I see the park!" he said. Mama parked the car. Declan's bike was in the back. His helmet was in the back too.

Declan jumped down. He ran to his bike. He held the handle bars. He wanted to ride right away. Then he saw his helmet sitting in the car. He went back and got it. Mama helped him clip it on. It sat snug on his head.

Declan pushed the pedal. The bike went fast. Then his foot did slip off the pedal. He wobbled and fell down. But the helmet was on his head. His knee got a little bump. It was okay. "Good try," said Mama. "You got your helmet first." Declan got up. The air felt fresh on his face. He pedaled again. This time he rode all the way to the big tree.

"Look at me, Mama!" he called. "I did it!"

Jack had big news. He had a new puppy! The puppy was small and white. Jack named him Socks.

The next morning, Socks did not eat. He just sat there. "Is Socks sick?" Jack asked. Mom felt his nose. "He feels warm," she said. "We need a doctor."

Jack was worried. Socks could not talk to a people doctor! They walked to a special building. Jack opened the door and his eyes got big. A cat sat in a box. A rabbit sat in a lap. A bird dropped one white feather on the floor. "Mom! This doctor has pets everywhere!"

A kind lady in a green coat came out. "I am the vet," she said. "I am a doctor for animals." She looked at Socks. She felt his tummy. She gave him a little drink. "He has a small cold," she said. "He will be fine."

At home, Jack fed Socks his food. Socks gobbled it all up. He wagged his tail and begged for more. Jack laughed and clapped his hands. "Good boy, Socks!" he said.

Levi found a big cardboard box in the living room. He climbed inside it. Then his friend Mia came over. She wanted the box too.

"I want it to be a boat," said Mia.

"But it is my car," said Levi.

They both held the box. It wobbled. Nobody could play.

Then Levi had an idea. He asked, "Can we take turns?"

"Yes!" said Mia. "First the car."

Levi sat in the box. "Beep beep!" he said. Mia pushed the box a little. The box slid on the floor. Zoom!

Then it was Mia's turn. "Row, row," she said. Levi made waves with his arms. The boat rocked side to side.

Next Levi remembered his teddy bear. Teddy needed a home. So the box became a house. Levi put teddy inside. Mia added a block for a table. She gave teddy a pretend crunchy cracker.

"Teddy is happy," said Levi.

Then Mama called, "Snack time!" Levi and Mia ran to the table. The box sat still, waiting. After snack, the box could be anything again.

"Next it will be a train," said Mia.

Levi smiled. "Choo choo!"

Isaac sat at the dinner table. He had two feet. But he had one sock on. The other sock was missing. "I want my sock," said Isaac.

Mama said, "Look under your chair." Isaac looked. There it was. One little sock. "A sock needs its partner," said Mama. Isaac held up both socks. "One sock and one sock," he said. "A pair!" Mama nodded. "A pair means two."

Isaac counted his toes as Mama put the socks in the wash. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. Then the other foot. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten toes, all warm.

The wash machine made a swishy noise. Isaac listened. Then it was time to eat. Papa set down the plates. "One for Mama, two for Papa, three for Isaac," said Papa. Isaac picked up his spoon. He tapped it once, then twice. "Early dinner tonight," said Mama. Isaac grinned and took a big bite of noodles. "Ten more bites," he said.

Elijah sat on the bench with Dad. The ice rink was cold and loud. His breath made little clouds. On the big TV screen, a soccer game was on. Mom gave him fresh popcorn from the machine. His friend Mia sat close by.

A player ran up to the net. "He has to kick it over!" Elijah said. He watched and waited. The ball went low. It rolled on the grass. Elijah held his popcorn tight.

The ball went right into the net. The net moved and swayed. The crowd on TV went wild. Mia clapped her mittens together. The horn at the rink beeped too, for the ice skaters.

"Again, again!" Elijah said. He wanted to see one more. They waited a long time. He ate popcorn, one piece at a time. Then another player ran fast. He kicked the ball low again. The net caught it, soft like a kiss on a blanket. Elijah jumped up so fast he almost dropped his popcorn. Dad caught the bag just in time.

"Right in the net," Elijah whispered. He kept his eye on the screen.

Margot wanted a story before bed. She picked her big cat book. She opened it. She opened it at the back. "That is the end," said Mama. "Books start at the front." Margot flipped to the front. The words sat in rows, like little ants.

At daycare, her friend Sam had a new book. It opened the other way. "It goes this way," said Sam. He slid his finger from right to left. "That is Hebrew," he said. Margot peeked. The words marched a different way. "Silly words," she said. "They walk the wrong way!" Sam laughed. "Not wrong. Just their way."

At home, Margot found her crayon. She drew one cat, two cats, three stinky cats. She made letters under them. "I will read it to you," she said. She opened her book from the right. She tapped each mark. The cat on the bed began to sink down, sleepy. "Once," read Margot, "there was one stinky cat."

Theodore went to the store with Mama. He saw a big red ball in the middle of the shelf. He wanted it so much. "Can we get the ball now?" he asked.

"Not now," said Mama. "We can get it later. First we need bread and milk."

Theodore held Mama's hand. They found the bread. They found the milk. "Is it later yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Mama. They walked past the dark coffee corner. Theodore did not kick his feet. He waited.

At last Mama said, "Now it is later. Let's go get your ball." She reached up and took the red ball down. Theodore hugged it tight.

"Today you got a ball," said Mama. "Yesterday we got apples. Tomorrow we can play with the ball at home."

"The ball is mine today!" said Theodore, and he smiled all the way to the car.

Noah had a red ball and a little toy horse on the grass. Today his team would come to practice in the backyard. Noah did not want to practice. "I want to play with my horse," he said. His dad smiled. "You can guess what we do at practice," Dad said. "I guess we throw the ball," said Noah.

The team came. They threw the ball to each other. Noah dropped it the first time. He dropped it the second time too. Then he threw it again and again. His hands learned to close at the right time. At last he caught the ball. "I got it!" he said.

On Saturday the team had a game. The sun was warm. A boy on the other team threw the ball far. Noah ran. He put out his hands. He caught it, just like at practice. Everyone clapped. "You were not late today," said Dad. Noah held the ball up high. "Practice made my hands ready," he said, and he ran to play again.

Daniel put his hands in the bowl. The dough was soft and very sticky. It stuck to his fingers like glue. "Oh no," said Daniel. "The bread is broken!"

His mom laughed a little. "Push it," she said. "Then fold it over." Daniel pushed the dough with his palm. He folded one side over the other. The dough felt smoother each time. He pushed and folded some more. Soon his fingers were clean. The dough was soft like a pillow.

Daniel made a round ball. "Look, Mom! I fixed it!" His mom put the ball on a safe tray. The teacher slid the tray into the big oven. Later the bread came out warm and puffy. Daniel held a piece for his dad. "I pushed it and folded it," he said. "Then it turned into bread!"

Leon sat on the big red couch at Mr. Kay's house. Everyone was watching the game on TV. The crowd on the screen was very loud.

"Who is winning?" Leon asked.

"The blue team," said Grandpa.

Ten minutes later, Leon asked again. "Who is winning now?"

Grandpa laughed. "My memory is like a frozen berry. It will not budge!"

Leon bit his snack and looked around the room. Then he saw it. A big sign on the TV, with numbers on it. The blue team had a big number. The red team had a small number.

Leon pointed at the sign. "Look! The blue team is winning!"

"That's the scoreboard," said Mr. Kay. "You found it all by yourself."

Now Leon did not need to ask. He just looked up at the numbers.

"Blue team is winning!" he shouted. "Blue team is winning again!"

Grandpa covered his ears and grinned. "Okay, okay. You are the score king now."

Leon took a string from his snack bag and held it up like a tiny flag. "Blue team! Blue team!"

Gabriel woke up excited. Today was park day. He put on his red shoes all by himself. "Park! Park!" he sang.

Then he heard rain. Tap, tap, tap on the window. Gabriel looked out. Big drops fell down. No park today. His face felt sad. His eyes got wet too. "The rain took my park," he said.

Mama gave him a hug. "We can still play," she said. "Let's build a fort." Gabriel was angry at the rain at first. He stomped his foot. Then Mama pulled the big blanket off the bed. Gabriel grabbed his soft chair. They made a fort together.

"Come in, come in!" said Gabriel. Inside, he had his teddy bear and a little flashlight. The flashlight was too bright and scared him for a second. He covered it with his hand. Then it was a soft glow. "Cozy," said Gabriel. Mama laughed, and he laughed too.

The rain still tapped outside. But now Gabriel was happy. His sad feeling had gone away. "Fort day is good too," he said. He hugged teddy tight and crawled in deeper.

Wesley ran into the band room. He was going to play a violin today. His mom gave him a wave from the door. Wesley picked up the violin. He held it upside down. He tapped the strings. Plink, plonk. The sound was very silly. Wesley laughed. He tried again. Plink, plonk. Still silly. He swung the bow in the air like a stick. Still no pretty music. Wesley frowned. "Violin, you are mixed up," he said. Then Miss Poppy came over. "Let me show you how to hold it," she said. She turned the violin the right way up. She helped Wesley put it under his chin. Wesley pulled the bow. The violin sang. A long, sweet note filled the room. Wesley played it again and again. "Mom, listen!" he called. His mom clapped loud. After the lesson, she gave him a crunchy apple for the walk home. Wesley hummed his note all the way.

Myles stood by the back door. He wanted to wear his sun hat and play outside. But the sky was full of clouds. "Where did the sun go?" he asked. "Maybe the clouds are hiding it," said Dad. Myles watched and waited. He saw a big gray cloud. It looked like a naughty turtle, slow and round.

Then the wind came. It was windy now! The leaves spun around. Myles felt the wind push his hair. "The wind is moving the clouds," he said. The big cloud slid away. The sun popped out! It was sunny again.

Myles put on his sun hat. He ran to the sandbox. The warm sun made the sand hot on top. "The sun makes things warm," said Myles. Then the sky turned dark again. Little drops fell. It was rainy now. Dad called, "Come get your rain boots!" Myles stomped in the puddles.

Sophie sat in the car. She sat in her deep car seat. Mom sat in front with a little bundle. The bundle was Sophie's new baby brother.

"I will hold him," said Mom. "He is so little." Mom looked at the baby all the way home. Sophie looked out the window.

At home, Dad said, "Cookie time." He gave Sophie a cookie. The baby slept. Mom fed the baby. Sophie ate her cookie alone.

"I miss you, Mom," said Sophie. "You held me before." Mom put the baby in his bed. Then Mom sat next to Sophie. "Come here," said Mom. Mom gave her a big hug.

Sophie hugged her back. Then the baby made a sound. Mom laughed. "He is calling you," she said. Sophie tiptoed to the bed. The baby grabbed her finger. "He likes me," said Sophie. Mom smiled and held them both.

Madison found a box of old balls in the shed. "I will make a rainbow," she said. She picked up a red ball. She set it on the grass. Red went with red.

Next she found a blue ball. Blue went with blue. Then a yellow ball. Yellow went with yellow. Soon she had three piles, neat as can be. A green ball went in its own spot. "You are the grass color," she told it.

A little green snake slid by her shoe. Madison held very still. The snake was green too. "You can sit with the green ball," she whispered. The snake slid away into the bushes. A red ball was hiding in the blue pile. Madison laughed. She moved it to the red pile. Then she shut the shed door tight. "Night night, rainbow," she said.

Luca ran into the backyard. He wanted his blue ball. He had a big game to play!

But the ball was gone. Then he saw it. It had rolled under the old tent. The tent was very dark inside. Luca reached in with one hand. He felt something round. He pulled it out fast.

The thing was not blue. It was not a ball at all. It was a red bucket! Luca laughed. He reached in again. He felt a shovel. He felt a soft rag. He pulled the rag out and used it to clean the bucket. Then he felt one more round thing. He pulled it out into the sun. It was blue! It was his ball!

Luca jumped up and down. "The tent played hide and seek," he said. "And I won!" He threw the red bucket over his arm and ran to show Dad before bed. Dad clapped his hands. "Big news," said Dad. Luca was happy all the way to the door.

John sat at the art table. He wanted to draw a sun. The sun needed a big circle in the middle. John drew and drew. But his circle came out wobbly and curly. It did not look like a sun. It looked like a wiggly worm.

John put down his crayon. Then he saw Maya next to him. Maya was tracing around her cup. She moved it slowly with one finger on top. When she lifted the cup, there was a perfect circle on her paper.

John picked up his own cup. He put it down on his paper. He traced all around the bottom. He lifted the cup away. There it was. A big round circle. John added curly rays and a happy face.

The teacher walked by with the hot glue gun. She held it up high. "This can burn," she said. "Only I touch it." John kept his fingers far away.

He held up his sun. "Look, Maya! A real circle!" Maya smiled and traced her cup again.

Benjamin was playing house at daycare. He made a big pile of soft blocks. The blocks were his pretend mountain. His teddy bear was going to climb the mountain. "Climb, teddy, climb!" said Benjamin.

Then teddy fell off. He dropped right onto the floor. Mia saw it. Her lip began to shake. "Teddy fell!" she said. "He is hurt. He is scared."

Benjamin picked up teddy. He squeezed teddy tight. He patted teddy's soft head. "There, there," said Benjamin. "A hug helps."

Mia stopped crying. She wanted a turn too. She held teddy and rocked him. "Teddy feels better now," she said.

The teacher smiled. "Teddy can have a pretend snack too," she said. She handed them a tiny pretend cake.

"Teddy is hungry," said Mia. "Teddy will eat the cake!" said Benjamin.

Then teddy climbed the mountain again. This time he got all the way to the top.

Camille wanted to see the bubbles. Mama was going to fill the pot with water. Camille stood by the door and watched.

"One step, two steps, three steps back," said Mama with a smile. Camille took three steps back. She was brave, but she stayed far away.

Mama put the pot on the stove. Soon the water went pop, pop, pop. Little clouds rose up from the pot. Camille saw the steam touch the window. The window got warm and foggy. Camille put her hand near her own cup of cold milk. Cold, not hot. Then she looked at the steam far away. Hot, hot, hot.

"Can I see the bubbles?" asked Camille.

"Come hold my hand," said Mama. Camille held Mama's hand. She peeked at the pot from far away. The bubbles went bloop, bloop, bloop.

"One cloud, two clouds, three clouds," said Camille, counting the steam. It floated up, up, up, like a dream.

"The steam is hot, so we stay back," said Camille.

Mama kissed her head. "Yes, my smart girl."

Camille watched the steam dance until it was time for warm oatmeal.

Aurora ran into Grandma's house. Everyone was there! Aunt Mia was stirring a big pot. Grandma was setting out plates. The whole table smelled like bread and soup.

"Today you can lead the blessing," said Grandma. Aurora clapped her hands. She was so lucky! She had waited all year for this. But then Grandma began to sing. The blessing was a song, not just words.

Aurora opened her mouth. She tried the tune. It came out wrong! The notes went up when they should go down. Uncle Ben smiled at her. "Take your time," he said. "We can wait."

Aurora took a big breath. She thought of the song in her head. Then she tried again. This time the tune came out right! The whole family sang with her. Their voices filled the room. Baby cousin Sam kicked his feet to the song.

When the song ended, everyone said, "Amen!" Grandma kissed Aurora's head. "Now we eat!" said Aunt Mia. She carried the pot to the table, and Aurora passed out the spoons.

Rehmat went to the bank with Mama. She wore her red coat. The wind blew at the big doors. The wind made her coat fly open, flappy flappy, like bird wings.

"My coat is being silly," said Rehmat. Mama laughed. "You can fix it," she said. Rehmat looked down. She saw the little zipper tab. She pulled it up, up, up. The two sides of her coat came together. Click, click, click. Now the coat was closed. No more flapping.

Inside the bank, it was warm. Rehmat felt proud. She unzipped her coat a little bit, then zipped it again, just for fun. Zzzzzip. A man at the desk smiled at her. "You are a fast zipper," he said. Rehmat giggled.

After the bank, Mama bought Rehmat a shiny red apple. Rehmat held it in her zipped-up coat. "Sorry, apple, no room in there," she teased. She carried the apple in her hand instead. She skipped all the way home.

William loved his little red truck. He brought it to summer camp in his backpack.

At camp, a boy named Sam saw the truck. Sam reached out and grabbed it. "My turn!" said Sam. William grabbed it back. "No, it's mine!" Then the truck fell on the grass. Both boys looked at it.

Their teacher, Miss Ada, came over. She knelt down. "Sam, you can ask first," she said. Sam took a big breath. "Can I have a turn, please?" William held the truck tight. He did not want to let go. But he counted to ten, slow and quiet. Then he put the truck in Sam's hands.

Sam rolled the truck through the cool, green grass. He made a loud brmmmm sound. Then he gave it back. "Your turn," said Sam. William smiled. Taking turns felt good.

The next day, William's friend Ben came to play at camp. William left his red truck at home, tucked safe on his shelf. He brought a friendly blue ball instead. "Let's roll it!" said William. Ben rolled it first. William waited. Then it was his turn.

Violet ran to school after breakfast. She was not late today. Outside, her friends were playing hide-and-seek.

"I will count," said Violet. "You go hide." She closed her eyes. "One, two, three!" Her friends ran. "Four, five, six!" They were still running. "Seven, eight, nine, ten!" Violet opened her eyes. Little Ben stood in the open. He had not found a spot.

"You counted too fast," Ben said. "We need time to hide."

"Okay," said Violet. "I will count slowly." She closed her eyes again. "One... two... three..." Her friends tiptoed away. "Four... five... six..." She heard soft steps behind the big tree. "Seven... eight... nine... ten!" Ready or not, here she came.

Ben was gone now. He was under the slide. Sam was behind the tree. Mia was by the wall. Violet found them all, one by one.

Then it was Ben's turn to count. Violet ran fast to hide. She heard him counting slowly, so she had time. She squeezed behind the bush just as he said, "Ten!"

"I found you, Violet!" Ben called. Violet laughed and popped out. "Count slowly again," she said. "That is the best way to play."

Violet held Mama's hand at the door of the big house. Inside, people were singing. Little lamps sat in rows along the front. Their small flames flickered like tiny stars.

"Can I light one?" Violet asked.

"Flames are for grown-ups," said Grandma. "But you can pick one for me to light."

Violet looked at all the lamps. Some were tall. Some were small. One had a red flower painted on the side. "That one," she said, pointing. "The flower one."

Grandma took a long match. She struck it carefully. A little flame jumped up on the match. Then Grandma touched it to the wick. The lamp with the flower lit up bright.

Violet watched with wide eyes. The match made the lamp glow. "It worked!" she said.

"You picked it, and I lit it," said Grandma. "We did it together."

Grandma blew out the match. The lamp kept shining. Its warm light made a soft circle on the wall. The flames were not scary at all. They were calm and small, and Grandma's hands held them safely.

Violet stood by her lamp while the people sang. She watched her flower flame dance. "Good night, little light," she whispered. "Stay warm until we come back."

Luka was at summer camp. He sat at a big paint table. He had a pot of yellow. He had a pot of blue. He wanted to paint his mother a picture. He dipped his brush in the yellow. He made a big yellow sun. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue. He wanted a blue sky. But the sky came out green. Luka blinked at it. "Green?" he said. His friend Mia was shy. She peeked at his paper and smiled. Luka looked at his pots. The yellow pot was all green now. He tried to pull the green apart with his brush. He stirred and stirred. The green stayed green. "It will not come back," he said softly. The teacher gave him new pots. Luka was careful this time. He kept a little yellow in a cup. He kept a little blue in another cup. Then he mixed the rest. Green again! Luka laughed. He painted his mother a sun, a sky, and a green grass snake. "Look, Mom," he said. "I made a new color!"

Joshua ran into the cooking classroom. Today he would make bread for his family. "One, two, three, four cups of flour," he counted.

First came the stirring. Joshua loved to stir. Round and round went the spoon. The batter looked like soft mud. It smelled sweet like cake.

Now he needed butter. Joshua got some from the fridge. He tried to spread it on his bread. The butter was hard. It tore a big hole. "Naughty butter!" said Joshua.

Miss Amy put the butter on the counter. "We will wait," she said. Joshua waited. He counted to ten. Then he touched the butter. It was soft now. It spread like a dream.

Joshua carried the warm bread home. "I made this!" he said.

Clara loved her classroom. It had one big window and two small windows. At nap time, Miss Paz pulled the curtains shut. The room went dark. "Night, night," she said, and everyone slept.

Clara woke up. The room was dark. She thought it was night. "Night means home," she said. She looked for her coat. She walked slow, slow, slow, past the sleeping mats. A moth with one dusty wing sat on the wall. It looked just as mixed up as she felt.

Clara tugged Miss Paz's sleeve. "It is night," she said. "I want to go home." Miss Paz smiled. "Come and see," she said. She opened the curtains, one, two, three. The sun came in. The room turned bright and warm. The moth flew fast out the door. Outside, the day was wide and wild with light.

"Day," said Clara. "Not night. Day and night are not the same." She put her coat back. She lay down on her mat. She closed her eyes and waited, nice and slow, for snack time.

Parker made a painting at school. He wanted to give it to his mom as a gift. But the paint was wet. "The paint is not dry yet," said Miss Ana. "You can take it home later." Parker put it on the shelf to wait.

After lunch, Parker had nap time. He slept a long time. When he woke up, he said, "Is it morning now?" Miss Ana smiled. "No, Parker. It is afternoon now. A day goes from morning, to afternoon, to evening, to night." Parker looked out the window. The sun was lower in the sky.

"Where is my painting?" he asked. "It is right here," said Miss Ana. It was not missing after all. The paint was dry now. Parker carried his gift to his cubby. "I will give it to Mom today," he said.

Miles sat in the family car. He held his blanket tight. “First haircut today,” said Mom. The car stopped at the salon.

Inside, a chair went up and down. Miles climbed in. The hairdresser sprayed his hair. It felt wet and cool. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little curls dropped onto the cape. One curl landed on Miles’s hand. He picked it up. Mom held out a small envelope. She tucked the curl inside. “A little hair from your first haircut,” she said. “To keep.”

Miles watched the envelope close. “That curl is mine?” he asked. “Yes,” said Mom. “Now we can look at it any time.” Miles put the envelope in his pocket. He marched back to the car with his blanket. In his pocket, the little curl rode home.

Anna looked in the sandbox. No bunny. She looked behind the slide. No bunny. Her soft bunny was lost on the school playground.

Anna looked by the swings. No bunny. She sat down on the short wall. "Bunny is lost," she said. Her big sister Lily came over. "I will help you look," said Lily.

Anna and Lily looked by the park gate. No bunny. Then Dad came to pick Anna up. "I will help too," said Dad. Now three people were looking. Anna looked under the bench. Lily looked by the big tree. Dad looked in the little playhouse. Then Anna heard Dad call, "Come here!" There was bunny, sitting on the shelf. Anna hugged her bunny tight. "More looking eyes found you," said Anna. Lily smiled and helped Anna fold bunny's ears down soft.

Charlie was at Sam's birthday party. There was a big red truck on the rug. Charlie wanted the truck. But Ben had the truck first.

Charlie reached out fast. Her hand almost grabbed it. Her teacher, Miss Ana, sat down next to her. "You can have a turn next," Miss Ana said. She set a little timer on the table. Charlie watched the timer. Tick, tick, tick.

Then the timer rang. Ben held the truck up high. He looked like he might toss it. Charlie held her hands out, soft and open. Ben put the truck in her hands, gently, one wheel at a time. Charlie smiled. The truck had a scratch on its side. She turned it over. The wheels felt bumpy. She rolled it across the rug. It bumped over her leg and kept going.

Soon the timer rang again. Charlie stood up. She walked to a girl named Mia. "Here," Charlie said. She handed the truck over, gently, just like Ben had done. Mia hugged the truck. Then something surprising happened. Mia rolled it back to Charlie, so they could both play.

Miss Ana clapped her hands. Charlie sat close to Mia. They rolled the truck back and forth. Then they all had cake.

Milo went to the park with his dad. There was a big hoop on the grass. There were beanbags in a basket. Milo wanted to throw one in.

He threw the beanbag up high. He thought it would bounce. He thought it would bounce right into the hoop. But it did not bounce. It went flop, down on the grass.

Milo picked it up. He threw it again. Flop. Then he stood close to the hoop. He threw it soft and straight. The beanbag went in. It landed with a little flop right inside.

Then Dad brought a big ball. "Catch with both hands," said Dad. Milo held out both hands. The ball was too fast. It bumped his tummy. He sat down and felt dizzy for a second. Dad sat down too. "Try again," said Dad.

Milo stood up. He held out both arms. Dad rolled the ball slow. Milo caught it with both hands. He hugged the ball tight.

"You did it," said Dad. Milo laughed and threw the ball back.

Lillian went to the cultural center with Mama and Baba. It was Lunar New Year. There were red lanterns everywhere. Lillian held Mama's hand.

Then the drums began. Boom, boom, boom! They were so noisy. Lillian jumped and covered her ears. "Too loud," she said. Mama held her hand tight. Baba pointed at the door.

A big lion came in! It was red and gold. Its big mouth opened and closed. The lion moved to the drum beat. Lillian peeked at the lion. Boom, boom! The lion stomped. Boom, boom! The lion jumped high.

Lillian let go of her ears. She looked at the lion. She clapped one time. Then she clapped again. The lion shook its head at her. Lillian laughed. Baba clapped too. Mama clapped too. Lillian clapped with the noisy drums, boom, boom, boom.

The lion came close. It blinked its big eyes at Lillian. Lillian patted its soft nose. "More drums," she said. The drums went boom, boom, boom.

Eli sits at the little table at daycare. He wants to write a note for Grandpa. Grandpa picks him up after snack. Eli holds his crayon. He writes letters all across the top of the paper. The letters run on and on, like one long worm.

Miss Amy sits next to him. "Can you read it to me?" she asks. Eli looks at his paper. He tries to read it. "Ilovyougranpa," he says fast, all in one breath. He frowns. "Grandpa can't find the words," Eli says.

"Where does one word stop?" Miss Amy asks. Eli points. "I. Love. You." He makes a space with his finger after each word. He writes the note again. This time he leaves a space between the words.

At pickup, Grandpa reads the note out loud. "I love you, Grandpa." He gives Eli a big hug. "You wrote this all by yourself." Eli smiles and holds the paper up high.

Lena stood on her stool in the kitchen. Today was Dad's birthday. Lena was going to make the cake!

She cracked the eggs. She poured the flour. She stirred and stirred. The batter was runny and wet.

"Yuck!" said Lena. "This is not a cake. It is soup!"

She thought about Dad's fox cup. It had a fox on it. Dad would want a real cake, not soup.

"Will it ever be a cake?" Lena asked Mom.

"Watch and see," said Mom.

Mom slid the pan into the oven. Lena sat on the floor and watched. She could not see inside.

Then the kitchen began to smell warm and sweet. Lena sniffed and sniffed.

The timer rang. Mom put on her big mitts. She pulled out the pan.

It was a cake! A real cake! Lena could poke it. It was soft, not runny.

"It worked!" Lena yelled. "The soup turned into cake!"

That night, Dad cut a slice. Lena took a big bite.

"Best cake ever," said Dad. "Happy birthday to me!"

Henry put on his red shoe. Then he put on the other one. "Are we going on the big trip now?" he asked. "Yes!" said Dad. "We are going to the airport!"

Henry sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. The sky looked dark and stormy. "Will the rain stop us?" he asked. "No," said Mom. "Planes can fly after rain."

Soon they got to the airport. Henry saw the big planes. They were huge! He wanted to run to them. He took one step. Then he saw all the people. So many legs, so many bags!

Henry stopped. He ran back and grabbed Dad's hand. "Hold hands," he said. Dad smiled and held on tight. They walked close together, all the way.

At the window, Henry saw a plane go up into the sky. "Look, Dad! It's flying!" said Henry. Dad lifted him up high. "Our plane is next," said Dad. Henry squeezed his hand even tighter.

Ibrahim looked out the big window. He saw white snow falling down. "Snowy day!" he said. He put on his boots and his coat. He ran outside with Dad.

Ibrahim made a snowball with his bare hands. Brrr! His hands felt cold. They were very, very cold. He ran back to Dad. Dad helped him put on his red mittens. Then his hands felt warm again. "Good mittens," said Ibrahim. He made a new snowball. This one was big and round.

Then Ibrahim heard a funny beep, beep, beep. It came from the porch. It was his toy robot! Mom had set it outside in the snow. The robot beeped and its lights blinked. "My robot sees the snow," said Ibrahim. He remembered to bring it inside. He held it in his warm, mitten hands all the way to the door.

Kinsley went to the park with her dad. She wanted to play with the red ball. But the red ball rolled away from her. It rolled under the slide. The slide was wet and slippery. Kinsley could not reach the ball.

"Please help me, Dad," she said. Dad reached under the slide. He got the red ball out. He gave it to Kinsley. "Thank you," said Kinsley. Dad smiled.

Then a boy named Ben came over. Kinsley passed the ball to him. Ben ran off with the ball. He ran all the way to the sandbox. Then Ben stopped. He turned around. He came back and said, "Thank you!" Kinsley laughed. She passed the ball again. Now they took turns. Dad sat on the square bench and watched. The sun came out. The slide was dry. "My turn," said Kinsley, and up she went.

Evelyn sat on the red rug. Mama put on a song. The song went clippety, clippety, clippety.

Evelyn wanted to clap along. She clapped fast. Then the song got mixed up. Mama smiled. "Try clapping when I clap," she said.

Mama clapped one, two, one, two. Evelyn watched her hands. Evelyn clapped one, two, one, two. The claps fit the song. Evelyn laughed and clapped some more.

Then Mama sang a rhyme. "The cat sat on the mat. The cat put on a..." Mama stopped. "What comes next?"

Evelyn thought hard. She looked at her toy box. A hat sat on top of the blocks. "Hat!" said Evelyn. "The cat put on the hat!"

"Hat sounds like mat," said Mama. "You found it." Evelyn put the hat on her own head. Then she sang the whole rhyme, all by herself.

"Again!" said Evelyn, and she clapped one, two, one, two.

Paisley held Mama's hand at the shelter. Cats and dogs sat in little rooms. They were all waiting for a family. Paisley walked past a big dog. She walked past a fluffy cat. Then she saw a small gray kitten. The kitten put one paw out. "Hello," said Paisley.

The kitten came home with them. Paisley wanted to feed her right away. But the kitten hid under the sofa. "She is scared," said Mama. "Let's make her a soft spot." Paisley put a little blanket by the sofa. Then she put down a small bowl of food. Paisley waited very still.

The moon came up in the window. The kitten peeked out. She sniffed the blanket. She sniffed the bowl. Then she climbed onto the blanket and ate. Paisley saw it all. Her soft spot made the kitten come out.

Paisley sat by the blanket with her own yummy snack. The kitten finished eating. She walked to Paisley and rubbed her small head on Paisley's knee. "Good night, kitten," Paisley whispered. The kitten curled up on the blanket and closed her eyes.

Olivia got to school with her coat on. Teacher Sam pointed at the big clock. "Time to play inside!" Inside, Olivia ran and jumped. She got warm.

Olivia wanted her coat off. She pulled the little zipper tab. She pulled it down, down, down. The coat opened all by itself! Olivia slid her arms out. Then she was not too warm anymore.

Later it was time to go outside. Olivia put her arms back in the sleeves. She pulled the tab up, up, up. The coat closed. She did it all by herself.

Teacher Sam smiled. "Nice work, Olivia. You did that all alone."

Olivia looked at her friend Ben. His coat had a different zipper. His was red. Hers was blue.

"My turn again tomorrow," said Olivia. She zipped it up one more time.

Georgia put on her big farm hat. The hat was loose and wobbled on her head. "I want to help today," she said.

Farmer Ada smiled. "Can you sort these for me?" She put a feather, a pinecone and a small blanket on the grass. "Put the soft ones here. Put the rough ones there."

Georgia picked up the pinecone. It poked her fingers. She set it down fast. Then she touched the feather. It was light and soft like a kiss. "Soft!" she said. She put it in the soft pile. She touched the blanket. It was warm and soft too. "Soft," she said again.

The pinecone waited in the grass. Georgia touched it one more time. Her fingers said poke, poke. "Rough," she said. She put it in the rough pile all by herself.
