Farmer Ada clapped. "Your hands can tell you that," she said. Georgia patted her own fingers. Then she sniffed the feather. She smelled hay and sunshine. "My nose knows things too," she said. She hugged the soft blanket tight.

Axel sat at the dinner table. He wiggled a tooth. It felt loose. "It is almost missing!" he said. Mom smiled. Dad put carrots on Axel's plate.

"How many days until Saturday?" Axel asked. Saturday was pancake day. He could not wait. "Count with me," said Dad. Axel held up his hands. He touched each finger, one by one. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven fingers stood up tall.

"Seven days make a week," said Dad. Axel frowned. He counted again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Still seven. He touched his thumb last. The loose tooth wiggled again. "So Saturday comes after all seven days?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. Axel jumped in his seat.

Then Axel began to sing. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" He sang it twice. He ate his carrots fast. "I will not forget," he said. "Seven days. Then pancakes." He touched his thumb one more time and grinned. The tooth wobbled like a tiny door.

Milan ran to school with a big question. "Is today the library day?" he asked his teacher. She smiled and said, "Yes, today is the day. Today is happening right now." Milan jumped up and down. Yesterday he had waited and waited. Tomorrow would be too late. Today was here.

The class walked to the library. Milan held his coin tight in his pocket. He wanted to cook up a plan for story time later. First, the teacher read a bright book about trains. Then the librarian said, "Now you may pick your own book." Milan looked and looked. The shelves were tall. He pulled one book out. Too big. He tried again and again. His friend waited with him, patient and quiet.

At last Milan found a small red book. He gave his coin to the librarian for the late fee, just like Mom had shown him. "Now we read," said the teacher. Milan sat down on the soft rug. He opened his book, and the first page showed a bright yellow truck. "Later I will read it to my mom," Milan said. "But now I read it here."

Jaxson ran to the table. Lunch was there. He could smell the warm noodles. But his hands were muddy from the yard. He touched the table, and one brown mark showed up. His mama saw the mark. "Hands first," she said. She pointed to the sink.

Jaxson went to the sink. Mama turned on the water. It felt cool and soft. He rubbed his hands. One, two, three rubs. The mud went down, down, down. Now his hands were clean and pink. He dried them on the small towel. It was soft like a cloud.

Jaxson came back to the table. He held up his hands. No mud now. He ate his noodles. They were warm and yummy. Then he saw something. His fork had a noodle hanging off it. It swung like a little rope. Jaxson laughed.

After lunch, Jaxson helped pick up his plate. The water in his cup made a tiny wave. His baby sister, a little girl with one tooth, clapped her hands. "Ba!" she said. Jaxson clapped too. Then he asked for more noodles. "More, please," he said. Mama smiled and filled his bowl again.

Zoe packed her little red bag. "We go to the big park today!" she said. Daddy opened the car door for her. Zoe climbed into her seat. Mama buckled her in. The wheels went round and round on the road.

At the park, Zoe saw tall trees. She saw a big lake. A deer walked near the water. Zoe waved at the deer. It looked at her and walked away. "Bye bye, deer," said Zoe.

Mama held up her phone. "Smile, Zoe," said Mama. Click! The phone took a photo. Zoe saw her own face on the little screen. "That is me!" she said. Zoe pointed at a big rock. "Photo the rock too, Mama!" Click!

The sun went down. Zoe was very tired. Daddy carried her to the car. "I miss the deer," said Zoe. Mama opened the photos. "Look, here is the deer," she said. Zoe touched the screen. "Deer!" she said, and smiled. In the morning, Zoe looked at the photos again. "More park photos, Mama," she said. "Yes," said Mama. "All day long."

Hayden wants to brush his teeth like a big lion. He holds his little toothbrush with both hands. The sink is cold when he touches it. Brrr! Then Mama turns the tap for him. She puts her hand under first. "Too hot," she says. She waits. She turns the tap a little. The water gets warm.

Hayden brushes his teeth. He roars like a lion at the mirror. Then he sees something on the shelf. Small red dots in a bottle. They look like candy. Hayden reaches up. "Wait," says Mama. She takes the bottle down. "These are not candy. They are special medicine. Only a grown-up gives it to you." Hayden puts his hands behind his back. He looks and looks at the red dots. He does not touch them.

Mama puts the bottle high up on a shelf. Hayden points at it. "Medicine," he says. "Only a big person." Mama smiles. She hands him his special lion cup. Hayden drinks his cool water. "Roar," he says.

Aaron brought his red car to school. At play time, he rode the big tricycle around the playground. Then he played in the sandbox. Then he went on the slide. "Where is my car?" Aaron said. His pockets were empty.

His teacher, Miss Kim, came over. "Where did you go first?" she asked. "The tricycle," said Aaron. He walked back to the tricycles. He looked under the wheels. No car. Next he had played in the sand. He walked to the sandbox. He dug gently with his hands. Still no car.

The sky was cloudy, but the sand was dry. "One more place," said Aaron. He walked to the slide. He looked at the bottom. There, in the grass, sat his red car! "I went back to every place, in the same order," Aaron said. Miss Kim clapped. "You found it, Aaron!" Aaron held his car up high and ran to show his friend Ben.

Asher skipped to the sink at summer camp. His team was about to eat watermelon. The teacher, Mia, said, "Wash your hands first, Asher."

Asher turned on the water. He rubbed his hands fast. Then he looked. There were no bubbles. He looked again. No bubbles at all.

"Where are my bubbles?" he asked.

Mia smiled. "Try the soap, little one."

Asher picked up the soap. He rubbed it on his hands. He rubbed and rubbed. Bubbles popped up, small and white. More bubbles. More and more.

"Bubbles!" said Asher. "Look, look!"

He counted with Mia. One, two, three. They counted all the way to twenty. The bubbles sat on his hands like a cozy little cloud.

Then Mia helped him rinse. The bubbles went down, down, down. His hands were clean and shiny.

At the table, Asher ate his watermelon. It was sweet. After eating, he ran back to the sink.

"My turn for bubbles!" he said. And he rubbed the soap and water, and the bubbles came again.

Billie helped Mom in the kitchen. Mom turned on the stove. "Is it hot?" Billie asked. "Yes, very hot," said Mom. Billie stood back and watched. Mom cracked eggs into a bright yellow bowl. "We need more eggs," said Mom. "Let's go to the store."

At the store, Billie's arms wanted to swing. She swung them as she walked. Then she looked up. Mom was not there. Billie did not see her coat. She did not see her shoes.

Billie saw a lady at the checkout. The lady had a bright vest on. Billie walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," she said. The lady smiled and picked up her phone. Soon Mom came around the corner. "Billie! There you are," said Mom. She gave Billie a big hug. "Can I help with the eggs now?" Billie asked. "You can hold the carton," said Mom. Billie held it all the way to the car.

Mya went to the storytime room. It was her first day to get a library card. She wanted a book about trucks. She looked on the low shelf. One book, two books, three books. No trucks. She looked on the round table. No trucks there either.

A man in a striped shirt waved at her. "I am the librarian," he said. "I work here. I help people find books." Mya said, "I want trucks." The librarian walked with her to a big shelf. He pulled out a red book. Trucks! Then he pulled out a blue one. More trucks!

"Now let's make your card," he said. Mya stood very still. He typed her name. The card came out of the machine. It had a little paint spot on it, orange and shiny. Mya clapped her hands.

The librarian stamped her book. "Bring it back soon," he said. Mya hugged the book to her chest. On the way out, she saw a small striped cat sitting by the door. The cat blinked at her book. Mya whispered, "One truck book, one library card, one cat. Best day."

Luka sat in the small room at the doctor's office. He wanted to show the doctor he was a big boy. So he counted what his body could do.

"My eyes see the chart. My ears hear the beep. My nose smells the soap." The doctor smiled. Then she held up a lemon slice. "Taste this," she said.

Luka thought of orange juice. Orange juice was sweet. So the lemon would be sweet too! He put it on his tongue. His whole face scrunched up. Sour! He drank some water fast.

"Was it sweet?" asked the doctor.

"No! It was sour!" said Luka.

"Then what did your tongue do?" she asked.

"My tongue tasted the sour lemon!" He touched the lemon too. It felt bumpy and cold.

The doctor gave him a sticker. It showed a fish. "That fish can swim," said Luka. He pressed the sticker on his hand. His fingers felt it stick. At home, he would tell Mama all about his day. First eyes, then ears, then nose, then tongue. "And my hand too!" said Luka.

Jordan put on his red boot, then his other boot. "Hurry!" said Dad. "The big game is on!"

At the restaurant, a giant screen glowed. Everyone sat at one long table. The screen showed men running with a ball. Jordan looked around. The fans in blue stood up. They clapped and cheered loud.

The blue team scored. Jordan jumped up too. He clapped and yelled, "Yay, blue!"

The whole table went quiet. Then Grandpa laughed. "We like the red team, buddy!"

Jordan giggled. He had clapped for the wrong team!

The red team got the ball. They ran fast. They scored! Jordan clapped hard. Everyone at the table clapped too. The waiter brought a frozen ice pop for Jordan. It was red all the way through. Jordan held it up. "This one is mine!"

Madison stood at the running track. She had a red beanbag and a hoop on the grass. A little pig was printed on her shirt. Her friend Theo waved from far away.

"Watch me, Theo!" said Madison. She looked at Theo and threw. The beanbag went sideways. It missed the hoop.

"Where did it go?" Theo asked.

"It went that way," said Madison. "Next time I will look at the hoop." She held the beanbag straight in her hand. She looked at the hoop. She threw. The beanbag went in.

Theo clapped. Then he tossed her the big ball. Madison used both hands. She caught it.

"Again!" she said. Theo threw it high. She caught it again.

"Now we can go swim in the pool," said Theo. They ran off together, hand in hand.

Leon went to the hair salon with his dad. It was his very first haircut. Leon sat in a big chair. The chair went up, up, up. Then Leon saw a fish tank. It had blue fish and yellow fish. Leon turned to look at the fish. Snip, snip, went the scissors. But Leon's head turned too, and the hair came out all crooked on one side.

The hairdresser said, "Oops, little fish watcher." Leon felt worried. His dad held his hand. "The fish will wait for you," Dad said. Leon counted the fish. One, two, three fish. Then he sat very still, like a statue. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell down like soft little raindrops. This time it came out neat and even all around.

The hairdresser sprayed water. It made a mist. In the mist, Leon saw a tiny rainbow. "Look, Dad, a rainbow!" he said. Dad smiled and clapped. When the haircut was done, Leon got a sticker. He walked to the fish tank. He counted again. One, two, three fish, still swimming. Leon waved goodbye. "Bye-bye, fish," he said. "Bye-bye, rainbow." Then he and Dad went home.

Iris wanted to go to the park. It was right across the road. She could see the swings from the window.

First she had to take a bath. Dad ran the water. He put his hand under the tap. "Hot," said Dad. "We wait for it to get warm." Iris touched the cold towel. It felt cool on her toes. Dad poured the water. He checked it again. Then Iris got in. The water was warm and nice.

Iris saw a shiny cup on the side of the tub. She reached for it. "Not that one," said Dad. "It has soap and sharp bits inside." Dad put it up high. Iris splashed instead.

After the bath, Iris put on her socks. Then they went out to walk to the park. The road was busy. Cars went by fast. Iris saw the swings. She wanted to run. But she stopped at the curb. She looked up at Dad. She held out her hand.

Dad smiled. He took her hand. They crossed the road together. Iris held on tight the whole way.

At the park, Iris ran to the swings. "You did it!" called Dad. He pushed her high. Iris laughed and kicked her feet.

Arlo woke up and looked out the window. The backyard was white. The swing was white. The grass was white too. "Where did my yard go?" he asked. "It is under the snow," said Mom. Arlo got his boots. Mom helped him tie the laces. She made each knot tight.

"Time for school!" said Arlo. He got his backpack. Mom shook her head. "No school today," she said. "It is a snow day. A snow day means school is closed because of snow." Arlo put down his backpack. "A snow day," he said. "Can we play in it?" "Yes," said Mom.

Arlo stomped in the snow. His boots went crunch, crunch. He picked up a handful. It was cold and soft. He dropped some on the ground. It fell in a little white pile. He picked up more and dropped it again. The pile grew bigger. "Look, Mom! More snow makes a bigger pile!" Then he pushed it and patted it. It became a round ball. "Can we make it huge?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Let's roll it."

They rolled the ball across the yard. It grew and grew. The cat, their pet, watched from the fence. The snowball was as big as Arlo now. Mom found two sticks and a carrot. Arlo pushed them in. "A snowman!" he said. He patted its round tummy. The snowman smiled with his stick arms waving in the wind.

Liam wants to draw a cat today. He walks to the tablet shelf in the computer lab. He picks up a tablet with one hand. The tablet tips and slides. It almost falls. Liam grabs it fast with his other hand. Now he holds it with two hands. It feels tight and steady in his arms. It does not slip at all.

Liam carries the tablet to the little table. He sits down slowly. He holds the tablet flat on the table. Then he presses the round button on the bottom. The screen lights up. Liam smiles. His teacher, Miss Ana, nods from her desk.

Now Liam needs the drawing app. He taps the green square. It opens. Colors fill the screen. Liam picks the purple crayon on the screen. He draws one ear. He draws the other ear. He draws whiskers, long and wiggly. The purple cat looks sleepy.

Liam draws three more cats. The room is quiet. His friend Sofia taps her screen too. Her tablet makes a soft bird song when she picks yellow.

Then the timer on the wall beeps. Time to clean up. Liam taps the big red X. The app closes. He presses the button on the bottom. The screen goes dark. He stands up and holds the tablet with two hands, one on each side. He walks slowly to the shelf.

Liam sets the tablet down soft as a kitten. He pats it once. "Night night, cat," he says.

Edouard brought his book to school. He held it tight under his arm. "Can you read my book?" he asked Miss Lila. "Yes," she said. "Let us open it at the front."

Miss Lila turned page one. Then page two. Then page three. "Look," said Edouard. "A dog! Is it a pet?" "Yes," said Miss Lila. "The words say it is a pet."

Then they came to a page with only a big picture. "Read this one!" said Edouard. Miss Lila looked and looked. "I cannot read this page," she said. "There are no words on it."

Edouard leaned close. He saw the picture. He saw no little black marks. "Where are the words?" he asked. "On the next page," said Miss Lila. She turned it. There were the words. She read them all out loud. "Again!" said Edouard. He hugged his book tight.

Owen did not want to be at the doctor. He sat on the big bed and made a grumpy face.

"Let's play a game," said Dr. Kim. "Show me your eyes." Owen blinked his eyes. He saw a red bird outside the window. "Good looking!" said Dr. Kim.

"Now your ears." Owen heard a beep from the hall. Then he heard his tummy rumble. That made him laugh.

"Smell this," said Dr. Kim. Owen sniffed with his nose. It smelled like bread. "That is my lunch," she said, and she laughed too.

She gave Owen a little cup. He stuck out his tongue. He tasted sweet juice. "Yum," said Owen.

Then Dr. Kim touched his arm with a soft brush. Owen felt it with his skin. "You are good at this game," she said.

"But I have one more," said Dr. Kim. "Take off your shoes and socks." Owen took them off. She pointed at the floor. There was a green mat with soft bumps.

Owen stepped on it with his bare toes. The mat tickled his feet. He giggled and jumped up and down. "It is like soft grass!" said Owen. "My feet can feel too!"

"That is the best answer of the day," said Dr. Kim. She gave him two stickers. Owen put one on his toes.

Claire wanted to paint a dog at daycare. But the paint cups were empty. "We will fill them later," said Miss Jo. "Painting is now," said Claire. "Now we play blocks," said Miss Jo.

Claire played the block game. She stacked them tall. Then Max came over. "I went to the park tomorrow," said Max. He stopped. He thought. "No. Yesterday. I went yesterday." "Yesterday is done," said Claire. "It is behind us." She pointed at the wall. The sun picture for yesterday was cloudy and gray. Today's sun picture was up high.

"Now it is later," said Miss Jo. She set out red paint and yellow paint. Claire sat down. She painted a big dog. It had red ears. "Today I paint," said Claire. "Tomorrow I can paint a cat." She held up her paper. "Look at my dog!"

Zoey wanted to build a toy car at daycare. She found a small box and some cardboard. She cut four square wheels all by herself. She taped them on tight.

Zoey pushed the car on the rug. It would not go. She pulled it back and pushed again. The square wheels just slid. Why would the car not roll?

Then Zoey looked across the room. Ben had a toy truck. Its wheels were round like circles. Round wheels go round and round, she thought. She looked at her square wheels. Squares had pointy corners. Would pointy corners stop the rolling?

Zoey asked her teacher for help. The teacher was brave with the big scissors and cut four round circles. Zoey taped them on. She gave the car a push. It rolled across the rug, all the way to the fish tank. The fish wiggled at the wall. Zoey laughed and chased her car. "Go, go, go!" she said.

Anna sat at Grandma's big table. There was warm bread in a basket. Anna took a piece and put it in her mouth.

Then Anna looked up. Grandma was quiet. Papa was quiet. Aunt May was quiet. Everyone's hands were folded. Everyone was waiting. Anna's cheeks went hot. She put her bread down on her plate.

Anna pointed at the bread. "Why is everyone waiting?" she asked.

"We say thank-you first," said Grandma. "Then we eat."

Grandma held Anna's hand. Aunt May held Anna's other hand. Papa bowed his head. "Thank you for this bread," Grandma said. "Thank you for the wheat. Thank you for the sun. Thank you for the farmer and the cow who gave us milk to drink."

"A cow helped?" whispered Anna.

"A young cow," said Grandma with a smile. "She is learning too."

Then Grandma squeezed Anna's hand. "Now we eat."

Anna picked up her bread again. It was still warm. She took a big bite.

"Next time," said Anna, "can I say the thank-you?"

Grandma nodded. "Next time it is yours."

Anna looked at the bread basket. It was empty now. But then Aunt May opened the oven door with her big mitts. Out came a whole pie.

Anna clapped her hands. "Thank you, pie!" she said.

Alexander stood by the bus stop with Grandma. He held his blue coat in his hands. "Can I put it on all by myself?" he asked.

"Yes, you can try," said Grandma. Alexander pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. He pulled the coat close. The zipper was tricky. He tried once. He tried twice. Then the zipper went up, up, up. "I did it!" said Alexander. He felt like he could win a big race.

Little drops of rain began to fall. Tap, tap, tap. Alexander wondered, where could his head go? Then he saw the soft part on the back of his coat. He grabbed it and pulled it up over his head. The rain tapped on top, but his hair stayed dry. "Look, Grandma! My head is hiding!" he said. A tired little turtle walked by with a boy. The turtle had a shell over its back. "The turtle has a coat too," said Alexander. The bus came, and they climbed on together.

Elizabeth loved snack time at daycare. Today Miss Ana put green peas on every tray. One, two, three trays. Four trays with peas.

Elizabeth saw Mia look at her peas. "Yuck!" Mia shouted. Miss Ana's face went sad. Mia tried again. "No, thank you," she said, quiet and small. Miss Ana smiled. She took the peas away and gave Mia a banana instead.

Elizabeth blinked. A big shout made a sad face. A small "no, thank you" made a happy face.

Then Miss Ana held out peas to Elizabeth. Elizabeth sat up straight like a butterfly sitting on a flower. "No, thank you," she said. Miss Ana smiled big. "Would you like apple slices?" "Yes, please!" said Elizabeth.

She munched her apples. One, two, three, four slices gone. "Thank you!" she said. Miss Ana laughed. "You are welcome."

At play time, Elizabeth pretended to be a butterfly. She flapped her wings over to Mia. "Would you like a pretend flower?" she asked. "No, thank you," said Mia. "Would you like a pretend apple?" Elizabeth gasped. "Yes, please!"

Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. First, Olivier went to the airport with Mama. They stood in the arrivals area. That is where families wait for people coming off a plane.

Olivier watched the big doors. The doors opened. A man in a red hat came out. "Grandpa!" said Olivier. But it was not Grandpa. The doors opened again. A lady with a big bag came out. "Grandpa?" said Olivier. It was not Grandpa either. Then the doors opened one more time. It was Grandpa! Grandpa picked Olivier up and hugged him tight.

The next day, they went to the park. Grandpa brought bread crumbs. Olivier dropped a crumb on the ground. A little pigeon ran over and pecked it up. Olivier dropped another crumb. Another pigeon came running. "I drop it, and the pigeon eats it!" said Olivier. He dropped crumbs one by one. More and more pigeons came. Soon there were pigeons all around his feet.

Grandpa laughed and laughed. "You make the pigeons come," he said. Olivier dropped one last crumb. A little brown bird flew down too. Then Olivier took Grandpa's hand and said, "Pigeons first. Swing next!"

Henri sat at the long table in the big hall. The table sat on a hill, and from the window Henri could see the thick green grass outside. Everyone was waiting for the potluck lunch to start.

Grandma stood next to Henri. "We hold hands now," she said. "Then we say our blessing together." Henri had a spoon in his hand. He wanted to hold Grandma's hand. But his hands were full.

Henri looked at the spoon. He looked at Grandma's open hand. He put the spoon down on the table. Now his hand was free. He reached out and took Grandma's hand. She smiled at him.

Dad held Henri's other hand. Everyone at the table held hands. They closed their eyes. They said the blessing together. Henri said the words he knew. His voice was small but clear.

Then everyone said, "Amen," and picked up their spoons. Henri picked up his spoon too. "I did it," he said. Grandma gave him a warm hug.

Bennett stood in the pool changing room. He pulled his small blue bag. He wanted to get to the water fast. "Swim time!" he said. He started to run.

"Walk, please," said Dad. Bennett stopped. Why walk? The pool was right there! Bennett looked down. The floor was wet. It was shiny and slick.

Bennett took one big step. His foot slid a little. Whoa! The wet floor was slippery. Walking kept him steady. Step, step, step. His feet stayed right under him.

Bennett kept walking all the way to the pool. He held Dad's hand. Would the pool floor be slippery too? Bennett put one toe in the water. Then he splashed his whole foot. "The water is warm!" he said.

Dad laughed. Bennett laughed too. He would walk on wet floors. And he would swim and swim.

Sofia carried her little blue bag to the pool. The pool was right by the beach. The sand was warm. The water looked so big and shiny. "Today I will learn to swim!" said Sofia.

She ran to the pool. A boy was standing by the door. "Stop!" said the lifeguard. "Shower first!" Sofia looked at the shower. "Why do I need a shower?" she asked. "I am going to get wet anyway!" The lifeguard smiled. "Pools ask swimmers to shower first. Go on, try it."

Sofia stood under the shower. Water ran down her arms. It was warm and tickly. Then she stepped into the pool. The water felt just right. Her teacher held her hands. Sofia kicked her legs. Splash, splash, splash! "I am swimming!" she shouted. A furry dog watched from the beach. It wagged its tail.

"Did you see me?" Sofia called to her mom. "I showered, and then I swam!" Her mom clapped and waved.

Eleanor ran to the park with her dad. Her shoes went hop, hop, hop on the path. She used her eyes to look around. She saw a red ball by the slide.

Then her ears heard something. Sizzle, sizzle! "What is that?" she said. Her dad pointed at a grill. A mom was cooking there. The mom was a grown-up, so she was the one by the hot grill. Eleanor stayed back with her dad.

A new smell came to her nose. Eleanor sniffed and sniffed. "I smell corn!" she said. The mom laughed. "Yes! Corn!" Eleanor was happy. Her nose knew first. Then her eyes saw the yellow corn on the plate.

The mom gave Eleanor one piece to touch. It felt bumpy and warm. Her dad blew on it to cool it. Then Eleanor took a little bite. Yum! Her tongue tasted the sweet corn.

"Thank you," said Eleanor. The mom smiled at the small child with curly hair. Eleanor waved her hand and said, "Bye, corn!"

Grandma came to stay for a whole week! Anna jumped up and down. "Grandma, what will we do?"

"We will make my special bread," said Grandma. "My mama made it too."

Anna clapped her hands. "I want to help!"

Grandma put flour in a big cup. Anna poured it in the bowl. Plop! Flour dust went everywhere. "How messy!" said Anna. She laughed and laughed.

"Now we mix," said Grandma. Anna stirred the sticky dough. Round and round she went.

"Can I touch it?" asked Anna.

"Yes, squish it," said Grandma. Anna squeezed the dough. It was soft like a pillow.

Grandma put the pan in the hot oven. "You stay back here," she said. Anna watched from her stool.

The kitchen began to smell warm and sweet. Anna sniffed and sniffed. "Grandma, it smells so good!"

Ding! The bread was done. Grandma set it on the counter. Anna waited until it cooled.

Then Grandma tore a piece and handed it over. Anna took a big bite. "Mmm!" she said. "Grandma's bread!"

"Now you know my way," said Grandma. "One day you will make it too."

Anna hugged the warm loaf. "Tomorrow can we make it again?"

Grandma smiled. "Yes, my little baker."

Brielle woke up and looked out the window. The sun was shining bright. "It is sunny today," she said. She put on her sun hat. The hat had a big brim and a red bow.

Brielle and Mama went outside to play. The wind began to blow. It blew her hair. It blew the leaves. Then it blew her hat right off her head!

"My hat!" said Brielle. The hat went fast across the grass. It rolled and tumbled. Brielle ran after it. The wind pushed it more. Brielle ran faster. At last the hat stopped by a bush. Brielle picked it up and held it tight.

Then the sky got dark. Little drops began to fall. "It is rainy now," said Mama. They ran inside fast. Brielle watched the rain from the window. Her hat sat on the table, all safe and dry.

Rain pitter-pattered on the glass. Brielle put her nose close to the window. A drop ran down the other side. "Hello, rain," said Brielle. She waved at the drop. It slid past her finger like it wanted to play.

Riley went to the park with her dad. The wind blew hard. Her hair went up, up, up. Dust flew around in the air.

"I want to sit on the swing," said Riley. She sat down. The wind puffed dirt into her face. Riley closed her eyes fast. She blinked and blinked. When she opened her eyes, she looked in the little mirror in dad's bag. Tiny bits of dust sat on her eyelashes. "Look, Dad! My eyelashes caught the dirt!" she said.

The wind pushed the swing. The swing went back. The swing went forward. Riley heard it squeak, squeak, squeak. She touched the cool metal chain. She smelled popcorn from the snack cart. "Can we get some?" she asked. Dad said yes. The popcorn was warm and salty on her tongue.

A little ladybug landed on her hand. Its feet tickled her skin. Riley held very still. Then it opened its wings and flew away. "Bye, little bug!" she called, waving her hand.

Eliana ran into the big hall. Balloons hung from the roof. Thick paper chains went all around the room. Grandma was setting out cups.

"Why is everyone here?" Eliana asked. "Is it a party for the balloons?"

Grandma laughed softly. She took a photo from her bag. "Look at this little baby," she said.

Eliana looked. The baby had tiny hands. "Who is that?"

"Guess," said Grandma.

Eliana held the photo up. She looked at her own hand. It was the same hand, only bigger now. "It's me!" she said. "That was the day I was born."

"So today we sing for that day," said Grandma.

Outside, snow began to fall past the window. Dad carried in the cake. He lit three little candles. Everyone sang.

Eliana blew them out. Then she took Grandma's hand and they slid across the smooth floor, all the way to the cake table.

"I want to see the baby photo again," she said.

Isaiah went to the store with Mama. He saw a big basket full of apples. He wanted one apple very much. He reached out and grabbed at the bin. An apple rolled onto the floor.

A boy named Sam picked it up. Sam held the apple out to Isaiah. Isaiah took it fast, without a word. Sam's face went sad. Isaiah looked at Sam's hands. They were empty now.

Isaiah remembered something. "Please," he said, "would you like a turn to pick one too?" Sam smiled big. They took turns picking apples, one by one. Isaiah put two apples in the basket. "We can share these," he said. Mama said, "I will keep one for later."

At the street window, Isaiah saw the bread man. "Bread, please," said Isaiah. The bread man laughed and gave him a small warm roll. What a surprise! Isaiah broke it in half and gave some to Sam.

Elliot wanted a tea party. He wanted a big one, with all his toys. He looked in the toy box. Out came Bear. Out came Duck. Out came Bunny too. He set them in a circle on the rug.

Then came the problem. Where was the tea? Elliot ran to the kitchen. He asked Daddy for tea. Daddy said the kettle was too hot for little hands. Elliot felt sad. A tea party needs tea. Or does it?

Elliot looked at his tea set. The little cups were empty. He picked up the teapot anyway. He tipped it over Duck's cup. He made a pouring sound. "Glug, glug, glug." Nothing came out. But Elliot said, "Tea for you, Duck!" He tipped it again over Bear's cup. "Glug, glug, glug." "Tea for you, Bear!"

Duck got her cup first. Elliot held it up to her beak. "Sip, sip," he said. Then he said, "Careful, it's pretend hot!" He blew on the empty cup. He blew on Bear's cup too.

Then Daddy brought a plate. On it was a juicy orange, all cut up. "Real snacks for the tea party," said Daddy. Elliot clapped. Bear got a pretend cake. Duck got a pretend cake. Elliot got real orange. It was the best tea party ever. "More tea, anyone?" said Elliot. "Glug, glug, glug."

Grayson was going on a big trip. The car was packed. Dad put in the tent. Mom put in the snacks. Grayson put in his spotted toy dog.

The car went zoom, zoom, zoom. Then it stopped. "Oh no," said Dad. "This is not our road." Mom looked worried. Grayson looked out the window. Trees. More trees. No campsite.

Dad took out a big paper map. He spread it open. Grayson peeked at it too. The map had roads. The map had places. Grayson pointed his little finger. "There is a lake," he said. Dad looked where Grayson pointed. "Yes! The lake is by the campsite!" said Dad. He found the road to the lake. The car turned. The road went the right way.

They counted as they drove. One lake. Two tents. Three happy people. "We are here!" Grayson yelled. He hugged his spotted dog. Mom set up the tent. Grayson handed her the pegs, one by one. Dad pointed at the map on his knee. "You found our way, Grayson," he said. Grayson grinned and patted the paper.

Grandma was making mooncakes for the festival. Luke stood on his little stool. He watched her fold the dough over the sweet filling. "Can I taste one now?" he asked. "Not yet," said Grandma. "These are for tonight."

Luke saw a mooncake on the counter. It was still warm. He reached out his hand. Grandma caught him gently. "We wait," she said. "We eat them together under the moon."

Luke wanted to wait, but it was hard. He helped instead. He pressed the dough flat. He made a small nest for the filling. Grandma put the cakes in the oven. The kitchen smelled sweet.

At last it was night. The moon was big and round. The family sat outside. The plate was full of mooncakes. Luke took one big bite. It was even better because everyone was there. "More moon!" he said. Grandma laughed and gave him another piece.

Charlotte was getting her very first haircut. She sat on a big chair at the barbershop. The chair could roll across the floor. Charlotte liked that.

Then she saw the scissors. They were shiny and sharp. "Will it hurt?" she asked.

"Let's see," said the barber. He snipped a tiny bit of hair. Snip. Charlotte waited. Then she waited some more. "I don't feel anything," she said. "Nothing at all?"

"Nothing at all," said Mommy.

Charlotte sat up tall. "Do it again," she said. Snip, snip. She did not feel a thing. The scissors cut the hair, and the hair just fell down. It landed on her cape like soft little pieces of string.

"My bike has a weak bell," said Charlotte. "It goes ding very softly. But your scissors go snip very loud!"

The barber laughed. "You are a brave one," he said. He cut and cut. Soon Charlotte had short curls all around her face.

She looked in the mirror. "New hair!" she said. She patted her curls with both hands.

"Can we come back next time?" she asked Mommy.

Mommy smiled. "Yes," she said. "We can come back."

Charlotte rolled the big chair one little roll, then hopped down.

Jayden sat at the paint table at summer camp. He wanted to make a picture of a big green hill. But he had no green paint. He only had red, yellow, and blue. "One, two, three," he said, tapping each cup.

He painted blue on his paper. Then he painted yellow on top. It turned green! He was so happy. But his paper got soggy and started to break. "Oh no," he said. His hand felt sticky and stuck to the page.

Miss Amy came over. "Try this tray," she said. "It is a palette. It holds your paint. You can mix colours on it first." Jayden put yellow on the palette. He put blue next to it. He stirred them with his brush. Green!

He painted a big green hill on fresh paper. "Green!" he said. "My hill is green!"

Hailey was at the grocery store with Dad. It was cold outside. Very cold.

"I want to wear my coat," said Hailey. "I will do it myself."

Dad smiled. "Okay. You try."

Hailey grabbed her red coat. She pushed her arm in. Then she pushed her other arm in too. It went into the same sleeve!

"Look, Dad! I am a one-arm girl!" She laughed and wobbled around. Her coat hung funny, like a flap.

"That is a silly coat," said Dad, laughing too.

Hailey pulled her arm out. She looked at the coat. It had two sleeves. Two!

"Where does this arm go?" she asked.

"Try the other hole," said Dad.

Hailey slid one arm in one sleeve. She slid her other arm in the other sleeve. It was true! The coat felt right now.

She pulled the zipper up. Up, up, up. It clicked at the top.

"I did it!" she said.

Then Dad held up a small juice box. "A drink for the car?"

"Yes! Can I drink it in the garden at home?"

"Sure," said Dad. Hailey zipped her coat again, just to hear the little click.

Hudson sat at the little table in the art room. He wanted to paint grass for his sheep. But he had no green paint. He looked in the cup. Red. Yellow. Blue. No green.

Hudson scratched his head. He looked at the yellow cup. He looked at the blue cup. He dipped his brush in the yellow. He painted a big yellow blob. Then he dipped his brush in the blue. He painted right on top of the yellow blob.

He waited. He watched the paint. Slow, slow, the blob turned green. Green like the grass outside. Hudson tapped his brush on the cup. "Green!" he said. He painted long green grass for his sheep.

Then he tried again. Red and yellow made a big orange blob. He tapped his foot like a little song. Blue and red made purple. Hudson painted purple grapes next to the green grass. He held up his paper. "Look at all my colours," he said.

Henri sat on the train with Mama. The train went clack, clack, clack. Henri held his cup of milk. He drank a little sip. Outside, a sheep stood in a green field. "Where are we going?" Henri asked. "To the beach," said Mama. "We will see the big water."

The train stopped. Papa carried the bag. Henri held Mama's hand. They walked on warm sand. It went squish, squish under his feet. Far away, the water moved up and down. A big wave rolled in. Then it rolled back out. Henri saw the water go in and out, in and out.

"I want to splash now," Henri said. He let go of Mama's hand. He started to run to the water. Papa caught his hand. "Wait," said Papa. "I come to the water with you." So Henri waited. He watched the waves. His legs felt weak from waiting so long. Then Papa took off his shoes. Papa held Henri's hand tight.

They walked to the water together. A wave came up to Henri's toes. It was cold and tickly. Henri laughed and jumped. Splash, splash! Mama sat on the sand and waved. Henri waved back. "I am splashing!" he called. Papa held his hand, and the water went in and out around their feet.

Dylan ran to the park. The sun was warm on his face. The grass smelled fresh and green. He pushed his feet through the soft sand. He felt excited.

He saw his friend Mia by the swing. Mia wanted to go high. She kicked her legs hard. Then she jumped off too fast. She tripped and fell in the sand. Mia began to cry big tears. She looked sad.

Dylan felt scared for her. But he walked over. He sat down next to her in the warm sand. "Are you okay?" he asked. Mia stopped crying. She rubbed her knee. "It hurts a little," she said. Dylan patted her back softly. Mia gave a small smile.

Then they got up together. They walked to the sandbox. It was full of smooth sand. "Let's build a big hill," said Mia. The weather was warm and the sky was blue. They dug with their hands. Mia laughed out loud. "You are my good friend," she said.

Alice sat in her car seat. Today they were going to the farm shop. The bags in the back were heavy with apples. Alice looked out of the window. A cow stood by the fence. "We came here yesterday," said Mom. Alice remembered yesterday. Yesterday she had petted a soft sheep.

"When do we see Grandma?" asked Alice. "Tomorrow," said Mom. Alice held up one hand. She counted on her fingers. "Today, tomorrow," she said. "One, two." Then she kept going. "And five more days after that." She counted and counted. Her fingers ran out at five. She still needed more days. She held up her other hand too. "Six, seven," she said.

"Seven days," said Alice. "That is a whole week." She said it again to hear the sound in her mouth. "A week has seven days." The car went bump over a little hill. Alice's fingers went up and down.

"Now we are almost at the shop," said Mom. "Later we will buy apple juice." Alice watched the gate come closer. The cow moved its tail. "Hello, cow," said Alice. "We came yesterday, and we are here today."

Everly did not want to sleep yet. "Is it tomorrow now?" she asked.

Mom shook her head. "No, it is today. Today you played in the water. Today you tasted the lemon and made a sour face."

Everly giggled. She remembered the sour lemon. "When does tomorrow come?"

"After you sleep," said Mom.

Everly frowned. "How will I know when?"

Mom pointed at the clock on the wall. "The clock shows what time it is."

Everly looked at the clock. The short hand was at eight. "Now it is eight," she said.

"Yes. Later the hand will move. Sleep comes first."

Everly got into bed. She watched the clock. The hand did not move. She closed her eyes a little. Then she peeked again.

The hand moved a tiny bit. Everly smiled.

"Mom! It moved!"

"Shh, it is sleepy time," Mom whispered.

Everly hugged her bear. The clock ticked softly. Tick, tock, tick.

"One more peek," said Everly. The hand moved again. Her eyes closed all the way.

"Goodnight, clock," she said.

Anthony went to the library with Grandma. Yesterday he got a book about trucks. Today he wanted a book about dogs. "We can find one now," said Grandma.

Anthony saw a big rug. He saw a little chair. He saw a sign with a dog on it. One dog, two dogs, three dogs on the sign.

"Storytime starts soon," said a lady with a basket of books.

"What is soon?" Anthony asked Grandma.

"Soon means we wait a little bit," said Grandma. "We can look at trucks first."

Anthony turned one page. He turned two pages. He turned three pages. Then he heard clapping. Storytime was starting now!

Anthony sat on the rug. The lady read about a hungry dog who found a cake. "Yum, yum," said the dog in the story. Anthony laughed.

After storytime, Grandma said, "Storytime again tomorrow." Anthony smiled. "Tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow too?" he asked. Grandma held his hand. "Yes. Now let's pick your dog book."

Ellie sat at the dinner table. The table was warm from the pot. Dad set down her plate. The peas rolled round and round.

"Can I have a cookie now?" asked Ellie. "Not now," said Dad. "The cookie is later. Now is for dinner." Ellie put her hand on the table. The plate was hot from the pot, so she pulled her hand back fast. Dad touched the plate too. "I will wait," he said. "The plate is hot now, but it cools."

Ellie ate one pea. Then she ate three more. "Yesterday I had peas too," she said. "Yes," said Dad. "Yesterday is all done. Today is now." Ellie tapped her spoon. Tap, tap, tap. "Is tomorrow now?" she asked. "No," said Dad. "Tomorrow is after you sleep."

Ellie drew a boat on her placemat with her finger. A little boat on invisible water. "The boat sails now," she said. Dad smiled. "That is a fine boat." Ellie did not want to get upset, but she wanted the cookie very much. She ate her carrots. She ate her rice, one bite at a time.

Then her plate was empty. Dad put a cookie on her plate. "Now it is cookie time," he said. Ellie held the cookie in both hands. She took a big bite. "Now the cookie is in my tummy," she said. Dad laughed and turned off the big light. "And later," he said, "we will read your boat book."

Lincoln stood alone in the nursery. His new baby sister was in the crib. She was very small. She made a little crying sound.

Lincoln wanted to help. Babies like crackers, he thought. So he went to fetch his cracker from the table. He held it out to her. "Cracker?" he asked. The baby kept crying. She turned her small face away.

Mom came in. "She is hungry," Mom said. Mom picked up a bottle. It was warm from the warm water. Mom held the bottle for the baby. The baby drank the milk. Her crying stopped. Her eyes went soft and sleepy.

Lincoln watched. Then he knew. His sister did not eat crackers yet. She drank milk. So Lincoln went to get his toy bunny. He set it by the crib, close to her. "For when you are big," he said. The baby made a small happy sound.

Michael got to school with his red bag. He was a little shy at the door. His teacher smiled and said good morning.

It was dress-up time. Michael wanted to be a fireman. He found a big black coat. He found shiny red boots. He pushed his feet into the boots first. Then he tried to push socks on top. The socks slid off. He fell over on the rug and laughed. He pulled the boots off. He put the socks on first. Then the boots went on. They stayed on. He stood up tall.

At lunch, Michael ate his apple and bread. He could smell the soup in his cup. After lunch, the class lay on mats for a rest. Michael did not sleep. He watched his friend Lily draw a cat on the computer with the teacher.

At home time, Michael put on his coat. He pointed at his socks. "Socks first," he said to his mom. "Then boots." His mom laughed. Michael marched out the door like a fireman. "Nee naw," he called. "Nee naw."

Sofia sat in the car seat. She held her toy rabbit by one soft ear. "Rabbit has to see the dentist too," she said. Mama smiled. "First you, then rabbit watches."

"I have a loose tooth story," said Mama. "One tooth, two teeth, twenty little teeth." Sofia counted along softly. One, two, three. The car smelled like orange peels from breakfast. Outside, a big truck went by. Vroom.

At the dentist, Sofia lay back in the chair. It went up. It went down. "Open wide," said the dentist. Sofia opened her mouth. The dentist held up a tiny mirror on a handle. It was small and shiny. He put it in Sofia's mouth. He turned it this way and that way.

"Your teeth look good," he said. "The backs too?" asked Sofia. "Yes. The mirror shows me the backs of your teeth." Sofia reached out one hand. "Can I see?" The dentist put the little mirror in her palm. Sofia looked into it. She saw her own eye, big and round. She saw rabbit's fuzzy face too.

In the car, Sofia held the mirror up to rabbit's mouth. "Open wide," she said. "One tooth, two teeth, all clean." Mama buckled the seat belt and started the car.

Charlie stood at the basketball court with a big bag of beanbags. She wanted to throw them all by herself. She threw one, two, three into the hoop. A boy named Sam waited and waited.

"More beanbags," said Charlie. She held the bag tight like a magnet on the fridge. Sam's face went sad. His shoulders drooped low.

Then Charlie looked at Sam. She looked at the long line of beanbags. She handed one to Sam. "Your turn," she said. Sam threw it and the beanbag went in. He jumped up and down. "Your turn now," said Sam.

So they took turns. One person throws. Then the next person throws. Charlie threw a beanbag, and then Sam threw a beanbag. They counted together. One, two, three, four, five.

Then Daddy rolled a big ball to Charlie. She patted the ball with both hands and caught it. She laughed. She rolled it back to Sam so he could try.

Sam caught the ball too. He gave Charlie a pat on the back. "Good catching," he said. "Again tomorrow?" asked Charlie. Sam smiled and picked up the last beanbag.

Lincoln ran to the school garden. Today he would plant carrot seeds. His teacher, Ms. Rosa, gave him a small shovel. Lincoln dug little holes in the dirt. He dropped the seeds in, one by one. "Grow, grow, grow!" he said.

Every day Lincoln watered the dirt. Then one morning, green leaves popped up. Lincoln clapped his hands. But wait. Little green leaves grew everywhere, even between his carrots. What a puzzle! "Those must be weeds," said Lincoln. "Weeds grow where I don't want them." He pulled some out. Then he saw a tiny leaf right where a carrot should be. Was it a weed too? He did not want to hurt his carrot.

"Ms. Rosa, is this a weed?" Lincoln asked. Ms. Rosa knelt down. "Look at the rows," she said. "Your carrots grow in a line. That leaf is in your line." Lincoln smiled big. It was a baby carrot! He patted the dirt around it. "You get to stay," Lincoln told the leaf. Behind him, a line of little green tops waved in the wind.

Nora was at Grandma's house. Lunch was ready. Grandma had made crunchy toast with jam. Nora ran to the table.

"Wash hands first," said Grandma. "We count to twenty." Nora held her hands under the water. She wanted toast now, not later. She started to march back to the table.

"Nora, we scrub with soap for twenty seconds," said Grandma. "Let's count together." They put soap on their hands. "One, two, three." They rubbed and rubbed. The bubbles grew big and white. Nora watched the bubbles cover her fingers. "Ten, eleven, twelve." The clock's little hand moved a tiny bit. "Nineteen, twenty!"

"Done!" said Nora. Grandma gave her the answer to her tummy's growl. Warm toast, sweet jam. Nora took a big bite.

"After lunch, we wash again," said Grandma. Nora nodded. She held up her soapy hands and said, "One, two, three!"

Riley was at Grandma's house. She wanted to find the room with the big toy box. Grandma had five rooms upstairs, but which one?

Grandma said, "The toy box hides behind door five. You will know it when you see it!"

Riley looked at the first door. It had a big 1 on it. She looked at the next one. It had a big 2. Then a 3. Then a 4.

At the last door, Riley stopped. It had a big 5. She held up her hand. "One, two, three, four, five," she counted, wiggling her fingers. Five fingers. And a 5 on the door!

She pushed the door open. Inside was the toy box, and a soft blanket on top. Grandma had made the blanket quiet and cozy. "You found it!" Grandma laughed from the hall.

Riley hugged the blanket. "Five fingers, five door," she said. Then she counted ten toys, one by one, all the way to ten, and lined them up on the bed.

Emmett was in the kitchen with Grandma. Grandma wanted to make a berry smoothie. Emmett wanted to help.

"First, wash the berries," said Grandma. Emmett touched the berries. They were cold and bumpy. He smelled them. "They smell sweet!" he said. He tasted one little berry. "Yum. Sweet and sour."

Then Grandma plugged in the blender. Mom always plugged it in, not Emmett. Grandma said, "Ready? Here we go."

The blender made a big, loud noise. Brrrrr! It was very loud. "Too loud!" shouted Emmett. He put his hands over his ears. Press, press.

The loud sound got smaller. It was quiet now. Emmett peeked at the blender. Then he took one hand off his ear. The noise got big again. He put his hand back. Small again. One hand off, one hand on. "Grandma, my hands make it quiet!" he said.

"Yes, ears under hands, quiet ears," laughed Grandma. She stopped the blender. "One, two, three scoops of smoothie," she said. Emmett counted too. "One, two, three!"

Emmett looked at the pink cup. He heard the last little buzz die away. He smelled the berries again. He touched the cold cup. He tasted the smoothie. "Best loud machine ever," he said.

Grandma laughed. "After our snack, we can sweep the floor. The berries made a wild mess." Emmett looked down. Berries everywhere. He got the little broom.

Hazel wanted her animal book. She could not find it anywhere. She looked in the toy box. She found a ball. She found a red truck. No book.

Then Hazel had a big idea. "I will make a library," she said. She set her toys in a straight line on the bench. Trucks went with trucks. Animals went with animals. She put her stuffed bear with the lion. The bear made a soft sound when she squeezed him.

Next she sorted her play food. Apples went with bananas. The pretend peas went with the pretend corn. "These are for eating," she said. "But not really eating."

At last she found the book shelf box. The animal books were all together in one spot. There was her book, with a tiger on the cover. Hazel sat down by the bear and the lion. She read them the tiger page, twice.

Leah loved the beach. She played in the sand all morning. She made a crunchy sand cake with shells on top. The sea was big and splashy. Leah could not swim yet, and she wished she could.

That afternoon, Mom took her to the local pool. A kind teacher named Rosa waited in the water. "Today we will float on our backs," Rosa said. Leah looked at the water. It was deep. She held the pool wall tight.

"What if I sink?" Leah asked. Rosa smiled and held out her arms. "I will hold you while you float," she said. Leah lay back into the water. Rosa's hands held her back, warm and steady. Leah did not sink. She floated, looking up at the big blue sky. "I'm floating!" she called. Rosa laughed softly. "Yes, you are." Then Leah kicked her feet, and they moved together across the pool, all the way to the steps. "Again," said Leah, holding out her arms.

Victor wanted to build a house for his toy bird. He picked a square block. He put it on the floor for the wall. Then he found a triangle for the roof. "The roof can fly up high," said Victor, and he placed it on top.

His friend Mia came in. She pointed at a block on the rug. "That is a new shape," she said. The square was turned. One corner pointed up. Victor looked at it. He turned it back down. "Look," he said. "It is the same square." Mia clapped. "A square is a square!"

They made the house together. Victor put a rectangle at the door. Mia set a circle by the window. The bird sat on top. Victor gave the bird a kiss on its head. "Next we need a bed," said Mia. She handed him one more little square.

The lights went out. The whole house turned dark. Jules stood still in the hall. He could not see his own feet.

"Mom, the lamps stopped!" he called. Mom came with slow, careful steps. She held baby Anna on her hip. "The power is out," Mom said. "We need our flashlight." Dad patted the shelf by the door. He patted the table, too. No flashlight there.

Jules thought hard. He asked, "Where is it hiding?" Then he knew the answer. "The kitchen drawer!" he said. He took Mom's hand. They went together, step by step. The drawer slid open with a soft sound. Inside was a long, hard shape. It was cold and smooth. "I found it!" said Jules.

Mom clicked the button. The flashlight lit up. A round spot of light planted itself on the wall. Jules gasped. The lamps were still dark. The house was still dark. But the flashlight shone anyway! "It works with no power," Jules said. Mom smiled. "That is true."

The light made a circle on the floor. Jules moved his hand in front of it. His hand made a bunny shape with long ears. Anna laughed and kicked her feet. Mom made a dog shape next. Jules laughed too.

They sat on the rug together. The flashlight glowed warm and steady. Dad found some bread and apple slices. They had a picnic right there in the dark. The lights stayed off all night. That was fine. The little light was enough. "Bunny is sleepy," Jules whispered. He made the bunny lie down on the rug.

Natalie ran into the nursery. A new baby was here! He was her baby brother, Sam.

Sam lay in his flat little bed. Natalie wanted him to smile. She made a funny face. Sam did not smile. Then Sam began to cry. Loud cries! Big tears!

"He is not talking," Natalie said. Then she had an idea. Babies cannot talk yet. Maybe the cry was his way of asking! "Does he need milk?" she asked. Mommy said, "Let's try." Mommy gave Sam a bottle. Sam drank and drank. The crying stopped. Sam made a small, soft sound. Then he closed his eyes and went to sleep.

Natalie tiptoed out. She got her paper and glue. She made a card. She drew a road on it, so Sam could follow it home to her. Mommy taped the card on the wall by the flat little bed. "For Sam," said Natalie. "When he wakes up."

Aiden found a book at school. It had a dog on the front. He wanted to read it to his friend Mia. Aiden sat down and opened the book. He put his finger at the right side of the page. He tried to say the words. They came out all mixed up. Mia looked upset. "That is not the story," she said. Miss Polly came over. She did not say much. She took Aiden's hand and put his finger at the left side of the page. Aiden slid his finger across, left to right. This time the words came out smooth. "See the dog run," he read. Mia smiled and clapped. Aiden lifted the page and turned it. "Next page," he said. "I have an idea. We read all the way to the back." They read together, page by page, until the dog found his bone.

Hunter had a big red drum. He wanted to bang it loud. He lifted the sticks up high. BANG! BANG! BANG!

Dad came running. "The baby is sleeping," Dad whispered. "She needs quiet now."

Hunter looked down the hall. The baby was small in her crib. She rubbed her eyes. A bird outside the window flew away fast.

Hunter wanted to play slow and soft. He tapped the drum. Tap. Tap. Tap. That was quiet. The baby stayed asleep.

"Can I do one loud bang?" Hunter asked.

"One," said Dad.

Hunter raised the sticks. He made his loudest BANG. The baby woke up and cried loud too.

"Oops," said Hunter. He tapped quiet again. Tap. Tap.

The baby blinked. Then she yawned. Then she went back to sleep.

Dad patted Hunter's head. "My quiet drum man," he said.

Hunter grinned and tapped his toes instead.

Madelyn wanted to build a house for her toy sheep. She found a block with three sides. "That is a triangle," she said. She found a block like a door. "That is a rectangle." She found a round ball. "That is a circle." Then she found a flat cracker-shaped block. Was it a square? She was not sure.

She cut a piece of string. She laid it along one side. Then she laid it along the next side. The string fit just the same. She laid it on the third side, and then the fourth. The string still fit just the same. All four sides matched.

"A square!" said Madelyn. She set it on top for a roof. But the roof looked weak and wobbled. She turned the square block so it sat flat. Now it did not wobble at all. The sheep went inside. "Good night, sheep," said Madelyn.

Everett sat at the dinner table. The soup was hot. Mama said, "Blow on it." Everett blew with his mouth. Then he touched the bowl with one finger. "Warm now," he said. His fingers felt the smooth bowl.

He heard a slurp. Papa was slurping his soup. Everett laughed. His ears liked that sound. Then he smelled something sweet. His nose went up, up, up. "Cookies!" he said. His eyes looked for them. But the kitchen was dark. It was hard to see. "Where are the cookies?" he asked.

"I will turn on the light," said Papa. Click. The light went on. Now Everett could see. There they were, on a rough wooden plate. Everett took a small bite. "Yum," he said. His tongue tasted cinnamon. It tasted like summer. Mama tapped her spoon. Ding! Everett tapped back. Ding, ding!

Austin sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He saw a poster of an ear. He heard a baby cry in the next room. He touched the squishy seat with his hand.

The nurse gave Austin a sticker and a strawberry. Austin sniffed it with his nose. It smelled so sweet. He took a bite. Yum! It tasted sweet too.

Then his mother held his nose for a silly game. "Hold still," she said. Austin bit the strawberry again. It tasted plain, like nothing much. He made a funny face.

The nurse laughed. Austin let go of his nose. He took another bite. Sweet again! He saw that his nose made the taste strong.

Austin got down from the chair. He put the sticker on his shirt. "More strawberry," he said.

The nurse opened a little fridge. Inside was one more strawberry, big and red. What a surprise!

At home, Austin yawned. His mother said, "Time to sleep soon." Austin held his strawberry in his hand. He sniffed it one more time with his nose. Sweet dreams smelled like strawberries.

Raphael was at school. He was painting a big star. It was yellow. Then his friend Ben grabbed the brush. Ben painted right over the star. Raphael felt angry. His face got hot. He pushed the paint cup away and sat in the corner. He did not say anything. His teacher, Miss Ana, came over. She sat down next to him. "Raphael, can you tell me what is wrong?" she asked. Raphael looked at his shoes. "Why should I tell her?" he thought. Then he said, "I feel sad. My star is all gone." Miss Ana nodded. "Let's look," she said. The yellow star was still there. It was hiding under the blue paint. Miss Ana got a clean brush. Raphael painted the star again, even brighter. It looked real. He felt happy now. "My star is back!" he said. Ben said, "I like it." Raphael smiled. "Want to paint with me?" he asked. Ben said, "Yes!" So they painted side by side.

Lennon sat at the snack table. Her jar of applesauce had a tight lid. She pulled and pulled. The lid did not move.

"Try asking for help," said her friend Milo.

How could words open a jar? Lennon wondered. She decided to try.

"Can you help me, please?" she asked Miss Rosa.

Miss Rosa smiled. "Of course." She turned the lid. Pop! It came off.

"Thank you," said Lennon.

Miss Rosa said, "You said the magic words. Those words help big people know you need them."

Later, Milo spilled his cup. Milk ran across the table. He looked at his shoes.

"Sorry," said Milo.

"It's okay," said Miss Rosa. She wiped the table with a cloth.

At play time, Lennon saw her spotted phone toy under the shelf. It was too far for her hand. Could words work again?

"Can you help me, please?" she asked.

Miss Rosa reached down. She got the phone out.

Lennon held the phone up high. "It worked again!"

Cooper sat in the middle of the back seat. Mommy drove the car. Cooper wanted his water cup. It was on the floor. "Help, please, Mommy," he said. Mommy reached back at the red light. She gave him the cup. "Thank you," said Cooper. Mommy said, "You're welcome." Cooper blinked. That was a new thing to say!

He drank some water. Then the car went bump. Water splashed on his shirt. "Sorry," said Cooper. "That is okay," said Mommy. The car was quiet. Cooper counted cars out loud. "One car. Two cars. Three cars."

Then Cooper laughed. He had an idea. "Mommy, what do I say after thank you?" he asked. Mommy smiled. "You say you're welcome," she said. Cooper practiced. "Thank you, cup. You're welcome, Cooper." Mommy laughed too. The car drove on, nice and warm.

Gabriella put on her little apron. Today she would bake muffins for her family. The community kitchen smelled like warm bread and old apples. Her grandma helped her mix the batter. Gabriella stirred slowly. She watched the flour hide inside the wet mix.

"Who will tell us when the muffins are done?" Gabriella asked. Grandma pointed to a round timer. "We can ask that little friend," she said. Grandma turned the dial, and it made a tick, tick, tick sound. Then the muffins went into the big oven. Grandma slid the tray in herself, because ovens are very hot.

While they waited, the family played a game at the long table. Gabriella matched red cards and blue cards. She laughed when Papa made a silly face. Soon the game got very busy. Everyone forgot to watch the clock.

Then the timer rang out loud. Beep, beep, beep! "The muffins!" said Gabriella. She clapped her hands. Grandma put on her big mitts and took out the tray. The muffins were golden and warm. Gabriella gave one to Mama, one to Papa, and one to Grandma. She bit into her own muffin. "The little friend told us," she said, "and we did not burn them."

Rowan wanted to help make sandwiches. Mama gave him bread, cheese, and a spoon. "Can I cut the bread?" he asked. "I will use the knife with you," said Mama. Her hand held his hand.

First Rowan looked for a corner to start cutting. The bread was a square. It had four corners. He put the knife on one corner. Then Mama gave him a round cracker. "Cut this one," she said. Rowan looked for a corner. He looked and looked. There was no corner anywhere. A circle is round and has no corners. "No corner!" said Rowan. "No corner," said Mama. She smiled.

Rowan cut the square bread into two triangles. He cut the cheese into a long rectangle. Then he made a face on his plate. The crackers were circles for eyes. The water cup tipped and the water did not spill, because the cup was round and it rolled back. Rowan sang a little song. Mama closed the bread bag. Then Rowan took a big bite of his sandwich face. "Yum!" he said. "Yum!" said Mama.

Isla stood in the bathroom with Mama. It was time to wash her face. But Isla did not want water in her eyes. "I will close my eyes," she said. "Then the water can't get me." She covered her eyes with her hands.

Splash! Mama washed her face with warm water. Isla could not see the towel. She could not see Mama. She could hear the water drip, drip, drip. She could smell the soap. Her tummy felt a little funny. "Mama?" she called.

"I am here," said Mama. Isla opened her eyes. She saw Mama smiling. She saw the soft blue towel. She touched the towel. It was warm and fluffy. "Water went splash," said Isla. "My eyes were closed. I could not see!" She giggled. Mama dried her hands and made the sink all tidy. "Now we can buy a little towel just for you," said Mama. Isla hugged the blue towel tight.

Colton stood in the big restaurant kitchen. The cook, Rosa, had made warm toast. She put a small knife with butter in front of him. "Can I try?" Colton asked. "Yes, you can," said Rosa. Colton held the knife. He spread the butter. The butter made the toast shiny.

Next came the milk. Colton lifted the little jug. He poured slowly. Too fast! Milk splashed onto the table. A small puddle sat there, white and shiny like snow. Colton frowned. "What now?" he asked. Rosa pointed to a blue cloth with a turtle on it. Colton took the cloth. He wiped the puddle. The table was dry again.

Colton picked up the jug once more. This time he tipped it just a little. The milk went into the cup. Not one drop fell. Colton smiled and took a big drink of milk.

The lights went out at the farmhouse. Everything went dark. "Wow!" said Kai. He wanted his teddy bear.

Kai ran to the kitchen. Bump! He hit a chair. "Ouch," said Kai. Dad came fast. "In the dark, we walk slowly," said Dad. "Hold my hand."

Kai held Dad's big hand. They took one slow step. Then another step. No bumps! They found the flashlight. Dad clicked it on. "A light!" said Kai. "So pretty!"

Mom lit the fireplace. The room turned warm and orange. "Let's have a dark party," said Mom. They sat on the rug. They ate crackers. Kai hugged his teddy bear.

Then the lights came back on. The whole house glowed. "Yay!" said Kai. He clapped his hands. "More dark party tomorrow?"

Cooper ran fast into the playroom. His big red ball was gone! He looked under the small chair. He looked in the toy box. No ball. Then he heard a funny sound. Flap, flap. It came from the closet. The closet door was open. Cooper peeked in. The cold air tickled his bare toe. "Ball!" he said. The big red ball sat inside, next to Daddy's shoe. Cooper pulled the door wider and grabbed it. The door swung shut with a soft click. Now it was closed. Cooper pushed it. Open. He pulled it. Closed. Open, closed, open, closed. He laughed. It was like a game. Then he pushed it shut and held it there. He sniffed the air. He could smell soup. Daddy was cooking in the kitchen. Cooper ran to see, slow at the door, then fast across the floor. "Daddy, my ball was hiding," he said. Daddy stirred the pot and smiled. Cooper stood back, far from the sharp edge of the counter, and watched the steam rise.

Jasmine sat at the big table. She had paper and crayons. She wanted to draw a picture for a party. Mom was making a cake for the party, and Jasmine was hungry for cake.

First she drew the sun. She picked the yellow crayon. Round and round went the sun. Yellow sun on white paper.

Next she drew the grass. She picked the green crayon. Green grass, soft and long. She patted the paper with her hand, soft like grass.

Now she wanted the sky. She picked the gray crayon. She held it up. Then she looked out the window. The sun was shining. The sky was not gray at all. The sky was blue. Jasmine put the gray crayon down.

She picked the blue crayon. Slowly, slowly, she made the sky. Blue sky over the green grass. Blue sky by the yellow sun.

Mom came over. "What a pretty day," said Mom.

Jasmine held up her paper. "Look, Mom! Blue sky!" She marched around the table, holding her picture high.

"Let's hang it up for the party," said Mom.

Jasmine smiled at her picture. Yellow sun, green grass, blue sky. She clapped her hands. "Party day!"

Julia looked out the window. The sky was gray. Then rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. Julia saw big puddles on the path. She wanted to jump in them. "I will wear my boots," she said.

Julia pulled on her red rain boots. One boot, two boots. She put on her yellow rain coat. It had a triangle pocket. Julia held Mama's hand. They went outside.

The rain went pitter patter. Julia found a puddle. She stepped in it. The water went splash. Julia looked at her socks through the boot tops. They were dry! Her feet were warm and dry. "Dry feet, dry feet," she sang.

Then the wind blew. It blew Julia's hat right off. The hat flew down the path. Julia waited. She watched it land in the grass. Then she walked over slowly and picked it up. She put it back on her head.

The rain stopped. The sun came out. It was sunny now. Mama said, "Look up." Julia saw a rainbow in the sky. It had red, and yellow, and blue. Julia held her hat on her head and smiled. "Hello, rainbow!" she said.

Felix wanted the dog book. He loved the big brown dog on the cover. But today Sam had it first.

Felix waited on the rug. He watched Sam turn the pages. Sam turned one page at a time. He started at the front. He went to the back.

At last Sam held the book out. "Your turn," Sam said.

Felix took the book. Miss Jo sat down next to him. "Read it to me," said Felix. Miss Jo read the words on the page. The dog ran to the salty sea. The dog got wet. Felix laughed.

Then Daddy came to pick Felix up. Felix held up the book. "Read it again," he said.

Daddy read the same page. The dog ran to the salty sea again. The dog got wet again. Felix clapped his hands.

"Same words!" said Felix. "Miss Jo said the sea. You said the sea too."

Daddy turned the page, and there was the dog, shaking water everywhere. Felix laughed so hard he fell over on the rug.

Connor sat at the dinner table. He had chicken on his plate. He also had peas and milk. Then he saw something stuck to his sleeve.

It was a little feather. Soft and white. "Look, Mom!" said Connor. "A feather!"

"Where did that come from?" Mom asked.

Connor thought hard. He thought about his toy box. His monkey had soft fur, but no feathers. His ball had no feathers. His teddy had no feathers either. Then he thought about the backyard. A bird had been there this morning. The bird was pecking near the fence.

"The bird!" said Connor. "The bird has feathers. One fell on me!"

Mom laughed. "A bird feather on a chicken night," she said. "That is a funny dinner surprise."

Connor put the feather in his pocket. "Maybe the bird wants it back," he said. "Can we leave it on the fence after dinner?"

Mom smiled. "Yes," she said. "But first, eat your peas."

Connor ate one pea. Then two. Then all of them. The feather waited in his pocket, ready for the fence.

Jordan stacked the soft blocks at daycare. He made a tall tower. It was a good tower.

His friend Mia ran over. "Come to my house!" she said. "We can play in my snow fort."

Jordan wanted to go now. He ran to Teacher Ana. "I go to Mia's house now!" he said.

Teacher Ana shook her head. "Not today, Jordan. It is sleepy time first. Tomorrow is the day after today. You sleep tonight, and then it is tomorrow."

Jordan looked out the window. The winter sun was bright. But sleep came after the sun went away. He would have to wait.

Jordan ate his snack. He played with trucks. He wondered, "Is it tomorrow yet?" Teacher Ana laughed. "Not yet. Now is still today."

After nap, Jordan's daddy came. "Can it be tomorrow now?" Jordan asked. "Not yet," said Daddy. "First we eat dinner. Then you sleep. When you wake up, it is tomorrow."

Jordan ate his dinner. He put on his soft pajamas. He closed his eyes.

Then he opened them again. The sun was up! "Is it tomorrow?" he asked. Daddy smiled and nodded. Jordan ran to find his shoes. "Mia's house!" he shouted. "Today is the day!"

Evelyn sat at the big art table. She was painting a lion. The lion was round and yellow. It had a soft mane and a happy face.

Now Evelyn wanted grass under the lion. She looked for green paint. She looked in the red cup. No green. She looked in the blue cup. No green there either. Evelyn had blue paint and yellow paint, but no green.

Her friend Milo saw her sad face. "Try mixing," he said. "Stir them together." Evelyn put blue paint on her brush. Then she put yellow paint on it too. She stirred and stirred in the tray. The paint turned bubbly. Then it turned green!

Evelyn dipped her brush in the green. She painted tall grass under the lion. Milo clapped his hands. Evelyn painted more grass, and more, and more. "It works!" she said. The lion sat in a big green field.

Zoey sat at the dinner table with her father. The peas rolled on her plate. They were bumpy and fun to touch.

Then Zoey saw something. A tear ran down her father's cheek. Another tear came after it. His face looked sad.

Zoey felt scared. Why was her father crying? She put down her spoon.

Then she had an idea. She picked up her soft toy dog from her chair. She held it out to him. "You can hold Barky," she said.

Her father wiped his eyes. He took the toy. He hugged it close. Then he smiled a big smile.

"You made me feel better," he said.

Zoey felt excited. She clapped her hands. After dinner, she chased Barky around the rug, and her father laughed and laughed.

Henry went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so the sandbox was wet. Now the sun was out, and the sand was just right for digging. Henry wanted to dig a big, big hole. He started to dig. He dug and dug. "Look, Dad! My hole is getting deep!" Dad smiled and sat on the bench. "I will wait here," said Dad. Henry found a smooth white stone in the sand. It was his treasure. He put it in his sweater pocket. He wondered where his hole would go when he went home. Would it still be there later? Would it be there tomorrow?

At bedtime, Henry asked Dad, "Where did today go?" Dad said, "After you sleep tonight, today will be called yesterday." Henry thought about that. His hole was at the park right now. But tomorrow, his digging day would be yesterday. He hugged his stone and closed his eyes.

In the morning, Henry ran to the window. The sun was up. "It is today now!" he said. "And my digging is yesterday!" At the park, his hole was still there. But the rain had filled it with water. Two ducks were swimming in it. Henry laughed. "My hole is a pond now!"

Stella found a big red book at daycare. It had a bear on the front. The bear held a blue umbrella.

"I want to know who drew the bear," Stella said.

She opened the book. First she looked at the very front. There were little marks there. "Those marks are words," said her friend Tom. "Words tell us things."

Miss Ana came over. "Do you see the names?" she asked. "One name is for the person who wrote the words. One name is for the person who drew the pictures."

"Who draws the pictures?" asked Stella.

"That person is called the illustrator," said Miss Ana. She pointed. "Here is the illustrator's name. Liz Park drew this bear."

Stella smiled. She put her finger on the name. Then she turned the first page. Then the next page. The pages went front to back. The bear found his umbrella at the end!

"I can draw a bear too," said Stella. She marched to the art table. It was a noisy room, full of kids. She picked up a pencil.

She drew a bear with a red hat.

"Look, Tom!" she said. "I am the illustrator."

Layla was building a tower of soft blocks. Her cat, Milo, sat near her. "Tall, tall," said Layla. She was happy.

Then the lamp went click. The room got dark. Layla could not see her blocks. She felt scared. Her tummy felt tight. She heard a new sound too. Tap, tap, tap. It came from the window. Layla held her teddy tight.

"Mama," she called. "I am scared." Mama came fast. She took Layla's soft hand. They stood by the window together. Tap, tap. It was just a branch in the wind. "It is a tree," said Layla. She felt excited. Mama fixed the lamp so the room was light again. The tower was still standing! Layla gave it one more block. "A different color," she said. Milo purred, and Layla clapped her hands.

Felix went to the band room with his dad. A big drum sat by the wall. Felix wanted to play it.

On the stand was a paper full of dots. Little dots, up and down, on lines. "What are those?" Felix asked. His dad said, "Those are notes. Let's find out what they do."

Felix hit the drum. Boom! He looked at the paper. He hit it again. Boom, boom! His dad pointed to a dot. "Play here," he said. Felix played. Then Dad pointed to another dot. Felix played again, slower.

The dots went up. Felix played louder. The dots went down. Felix played soft, like a bird landing. A bird sat at the window. It tilted its head.

Felix felt upset when he missed a dot. He waited. He tried again. Boom. That one was right.

The bird sang one little note. Felix laughed and played it back.

Aubrey woke up early at Grandma's house. She reached for her bunny. Bunny was not there. "Oh no," said Aubrey. "Bunny is lost."

Aubrey looked under the blanket. She looked in her cup drawer. Grandma said, "Grandpa found a basket of things. The things go in a box. People can come get their things back." Aubrey said, "Bunny could be there!"

Aubrey held Grandma's hand. They walked to the big box by the door. Aubrey peeked in. There was a hat. There was a mitten. There was a shoe. And way at the bottom, there were two soft ears. "Bunny!" cried Aubrey. She pulled him out and gave him a big hug.

Grandpa came in with two cups of milk. He sat down to share the milk with Aubrey. Bunny sat on her lap. Aubrey gave Bunny a little sip, pretend sip. "Bunny was in the box," said Aubrey. Grandma smiled and clapped her hands. "Bunny is home now," Aubrey whispered to him.

Mohamed sat at the kitchen table. He had big paper and red paint. He wanted to paint a flower for his mom.

Mom put out the brushes. "Put on your old shirt," she said. Mohamed shook his head. He sat down fast. He dipped his brush in the red paint.

He painted one petal. Then another petal. A big drop fell. It fell right on his shirt. His clean white shirt now had a red spot. "Oh no," said Mohamed.

Mom brought him an old blue shirt. Mohamed pulled it on over his own shirt. He painted more petals. Drips fell on the blue shirt. His own shirt stayed clean. No more red spots.

He painted the flower all red. Then he made a stem. Mom helped him sort the brushes in a cup. Mohamed held up his paper. The flower was big and bright.

Mom smiled. "Now let's wash that little red spot," she said. Mohamed looked at his blue shirt. It had ten spots. He laughed. "The old shirt caught them all," he said.

Ruby went to the garden center with Dad. It was a noisy place, full of trucks and water hoses. Ruby picked tiny plants for her garden. She got tomatoes, carrots, and peas.

Ruby and Dad planted them in the dirt at home. Ruby put the tomato plants in one row. Then she watered every leaf. The next morning, Ruby ran outside. Little green sprouts were everywhere. But now every row looked the same. "Dad, where did the tomatoes go?" she asked. Ruby could not tell them apart. She sat down in the grass and frowned.

Then Dad handed her some sticks and paper. Ruby drew a red tomato on one paper. She drew a long orange carrot on another. She drew green peas on the last one. Dad taped each paper to a stick. Ruby pushed a stick into the dirt by each row. Now each spot had a picture above it.
