Every day Ruby checked her labels. She poured water on the tomato row. She poured water on the carrot row. The plants grew tall. Ruby held up a ripe red tomato. "This one grew right here," she said, pointing at her picture stick.

The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jules stood on the grass in the backyard. "I can't see anything!" he said. "How will I find my ball?"

Dad came out with a big blanket. "We can wait out here," said Dad. "One, two, three, we count the dark away."

Jules squinted. "Is that a bush? No, that's the swing." He blinked. Then he blinked again. The swing came out of the dark, slow and soft. He could see it now.

"One, two, three," he counted. "I see the swing! I see the sandbox! I see my toy fish in the sand!"

"That fish is not real," laughed Dad. "Real fish swim. That fish naps in dirt."

Jules tiptoed over. He picked up the fish. His eyes could see the door now too. "Dad, look! The dark got softer!"

Just then the porch light blinked back on. The whole backyard lit up like morning. Jules held up his fish. "Hello again, house," he said. "Hello again, grass."

Carter sat on the kitchen floor. He had a little toy pig and a tiny toy slide. He wanted the pig to go down the slide. "Whee!" said Carter.

The pot on the stove was hot. Mama's hand moved the pot. Carter stayed far away. The stove was hot, but the floor was cold. Two different things.

Now the pig could slide. Carter put the pig at the top. The pig's head was pointing down. He let go. The pig bumped his nose. "Oh no," said Carter.

Carter picked up the pig. He turned the pig around. Now the pig's feet went first. He let go. The pig slid down. "Whee!" The pig landed soft on his feet.

"Again!" said Carter. He moved the pig back up to the top. "Feet first, pig."

Milo went to the library with his mom. He wanted a book about a big red fire truck. But he could not read yet. All the books had marks on the front.

Milo picked a book. He opened it at the back. The pages felt strange. The words ran the wrong way. His mom turned the book around. She flipped the pages from the front. "We start here," she said. Milo watched. First page, then next page, then next.

Then Milo saw a card on the wall. It said "Milo." He touched the letters. M, i, l, o. Later he found a paper on a busy desk. It said "Milo" too. He looked and looked. The letters were the same. Same M. Same i, l, o. Same order both times.

Milo ran back to his mom. "That is my name," he said, pointing. "It says Milo." His mom smiled. They sat under a tall tree picture by the window. She opened the book at the front. Milo turned page after page. At the end, a dog chased a red fire truck down the street. Milo clapped. "Read it again," he said.

Victoria was at the beach with her family. The wind blew her hat right off. Daddy caught it and laughed.

Next to the beach was a little pool. Victoria's big sister Maya swam in the deep end. Maya went under the water and came up smiling. Victoria wanted to go there too.

"Wait, wait, wait," said the swim teacher, Miss Jo. "You start here." Miss Jo pointed to the shallow end. Victoria stood there. The water came up to her tummy only. She blew bubbles. She kicked her legs. She tried again. Then she tried again.

Victoria looked at the deep end. Maya stood there, and the water went up to Maya's shoulders. Victoria looked at her own water, up to her tummy. The pool was small at one end and big at the other.

Victoria picked up a wet leaf from the pool edge. It felt slimy. She gave it to Daddy, and he did not let it break.

"Watch me!" Maya called from the deep end. Victoria watched. Then she practiced her kicks some more. Kick, kick, kick. Miss Jo held her hand.

"Tomorrow we try more," said Miss Jo. Victoria nodded. The wind blew softly on the water. "See you tomorrow, deep end," Victoria said.

Grandpa was coming to stay for a week. Jaxon waited by the back gate. He held his toy snake in his hand.

The car pulled up. Grandpa got out and opened his arms. Jaxon hid behind the big tree. He was afraid to hug. What could he do instead?

He looked at his snake. The snake could not hug. But the snake could wave! Jaxon lifted the snake's tail and waved it in the air. "Hello, Grandpa!" he said.

Grandpa waved back. "Hello, Jaxon!" he said. Then they ran to the sandbox to play. Grandpa dug a big hole. Jaxon filled it with sand. When Mom called them in for lunch, Grandpa held out his arms. This time Jaxon ran right into the hug.

Logan stood by the big hotel pool. The water was blue and sparkly. Logan wanted to swim, but his tummy felt funny. "The water is deep," he said.

Dad held out his hand. "Hold the edge with me," said Dad. Logan held the cool, wet wall. "Now kick your legs," said Dad. Logan kicked. Kick, kick, kick! Big splashes flew up. Water drops landed on Dad's shirt. Dad laughed. "You splashed me!" he said. Logan kicked faster. More splashes! One splash was so big it went over Dad's hat.

"I did that!" said Logan. "Yes, you did," said Dad. Logan felt proud. He held the edge and kicked and kicked. Then Dad lifted him up in a hug. Logan was warm and cozy in his towel, which had a cute fish on it, every color of the rainbow. "More kicking tomorrow," said Logan. Dad smiled and kissed his wet hair.

Sienna went to Grandma's hair place with Grandma. "My turn today," said Sienna. She wanted short hair like Grandma's.

The big chair was too tall. Sienna climbed nothing at all. She stood on her toes. The hairdresser, Miss Jo, could not reach her hair. "Hmm," said Miss Jo. "You are too short for the big chair."

Miss Jo brought a booster seat. It was red and small, like a little mountain for sitting. Sienna sat on it. Now she was tall. Now Miss Jo could reach her hair.

Snip, snip, snip. The scissors went snip. The cape was tight around Sienna's neck. "I think I look like Grandma," said Sienna. Grandma laughed. "Almost," said Grandma. "Almost like me."

Sienna looked in the mirror. "Short hair," she said. "Just like Grandma." Miss Jo put the booster seat away. "Same seat next time," said Miss Jo. "Yes," said Sienna. "My red mountain seat."

Cooper went to the big game with Dad and Grandma. The ice was so shiny. The players zoomed fast on their skates. Cooper clapped and clapped.

Then Cooper saw a man in a striped shirt. "Who is that?" he asked. The striped man did not have a puck. He just skated around and watched. He watched and watched. Cooper pointed. "Look, Grandma! He watches everything!"

One player pushed another player. The man in the striped shirt blew his whistle. Toot! The game stopped. The pusher had to sit down. Cooper jumped up. "Dad! His whistle made them stop!"

Later, a player fell. The striped man did not blow the whistle. That fall was okay. The game went on. Cooper colored a picture of the striped man at home. He drew a black and white shirt, like a smelly old zebra, Dad said, laughing. Cooper held up his picture. "He is the watching man," said Cooper. "Toot, toot!"

Grayson ran to the playground with Mama. He wanted to go down the big slide first. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Grayson held her hand. He could hear the swings squeak, squeak, squeak.

Then Grayson saw the water fountain. The sun made the metal hot. He put his hand near it. "Ouch," said Mama softly. "That is hot. Let me feel it first." Mama touched the metal. "Too hot for you," she said. Grayson nodded and kept his hands to himself.

At home, it was bath time. Grayson wanted to jump right in. But he remembered the hot fountain. He stopped at the edge. "Wait," said Grayson. "You check it, Mama." Mama put her hand in the water. "It is warm, not hot," she said. Grayson touched it too. It felt warm like a soft blanket.

Grayson got in the bath. His rubber duck floated by. "This is a real bath," said Grayson. After the bath, they had warm pizza together. "I waited," said Grayson. "You did," said Mama, and she kissed his wet hair.

Jacob ran into the kitchen. The table smelled like warm bread. Grandma set the big bowl down.

"Time for the blessing," said Grandpa. "Fold your hands, Jacob."

Jacob folded his hands. He wanted to peek. He peeked! Grandpa's eyes were closed. Grandpa's head was bent down low. Grandma's eyes were closed too. Jacob opened his eyes very wide.

Then Grandpa said, "Amen." Everyone looked up. Grandpa smiled at Jacob.

"You peeked!" said Grandpa. "I saw you, silly boy."

Jacob giggled. "Your eyes were shut, Grandpa!"

"So they were," said Grandpa. "Try it again. This time, you close your eyes too."

Jacob squeezed his eyes tight. Everything went dark. He heard Grandpa's voice. He heard the snow tick against the window. He heard his tummy rumble.

"Amen," said Grandpa.

"Amen!" said Jacob.

Then Grandma said, "Bread for Jacob! One piece, two pieces."

Jacob did not skip the blessing next time. He closed his eyes first. He said "Amen" loud like a big drum. Grandma clapped, and the bread was warm and soft in his hands.

Oliver walked home with a small cage. Inside was his new bunny, Fluffy. Fluffy had soft white fur and a tiny pink nose. Oliver held the cage with both hands.

At home, Oliver gave Fluffy a carrot. Fluffy nibbled it fast. "You like carrots," Oliver said. Then Oliver wanted a snack too. He ran to the cookie plate. He reached out his hand.

Then Oliver looked at his fingers. They had bunny fur on them. He turned around and walked to the sink. He washed his hands with soap and water. The water ran, and his hands got clean. Then he picked up a cookie. It tasted nice.

Mom said, "Fluffy needs clean straw now." Oliver helped put the straw in the cage. It did not hurt his hands at all. After that, he washed his hands again. Fluffy watched him from the corner of the cage. "Good night, Fluffy," Oliver said. Fluffy twitched her little nose.

Lillian could not find her bunny. Bunny was her best toy. She wanted to sleep with bunny at nap time. "I will look," said Lillian.

First she looked under her shirt pile. No bunny there. Then she looked in her little bed. No bunny there. Then she looked by the cold window. No bunny there. She looked in three places, and her tummy felt sad.

Then Lillian saw something gray. It was not bunny. It was her daddy's warm sock. "That is Daddy's sock," said Lillian. Daddy was looking for it. So Lillian picked up the sock. She carried it to Daddy. Daddy smiled big. "Thank you, Lillian," he said.

Daddy bent down low. He looked under the big soft chair. "Come here," he said. Lillian peeked too. Bunny was there, sleeping with the sock's twin sock. Lillian hugged bunny tight. She hugged Daddy too. "Two socks, one bunny," said Lillian. "All found."

Carter sat on the big soft couch. Grandma was next to him. Uncle Ben was on the floor. On the TV, a big game was on. The players slid on bright ice.

Carter looked hard at the screen. "Where is the ball?" he asked. He watched and watched. He saw the players carry long sticks. Then he saw it. The sticks hit a small flat black disc. It slid fast across the ice. It was not a ball at all. It was a different shape, flat like a little pancake. "I see it!" said Carter. He pointed at the screen.

The puck slid into the net. Everyone jumped up. "Good goal!" they cheered. Grandma gave Carter a high five. The clock on the wall said it was bedtime soon. Carter waved at the TV. "Thank you, puck," he whispered. "That was fun."

Jasper sat very still on the swing. He wanted to win the listening game. Mama said, "Tell me what your ears can do."

Jasper cupped his hands over his ears. "Ears!" he said. Then he heard something. Tweet, tweet. "A bird!" he said. "My ears heard it!"

Mama smiled. "What else can your ears do?" Jasper listened hard. The wind went whoosh. The leaves went rustle, rustle. "I hear the wind!" said Jasper. Then he heard a bark. "Molly!" he yelled. The dog ran around the corner.

"Now try your other senses," said Mama. Jasper touched the warm swing rope. "My hands feel it," he said. He sniffed the air. "I smell flowers with my nose." He looked up. "My eyes see a bright yellow butterfly!"

The butterfly landed on Jasper's shoe. It sat very still. Jasper looked at it. Then it flew up and touched his nose. Jasper laughed. "That tickled," he said. "My nose knows butterflies!"

Florence ran to the shape table at school. Miss Patel had put out a big hunt. "Find a circle, a square, a triangle and a rectangle!" she said. Florence clapped her hands. She loved hunts.

She found a square block first. Then a triangle roof from the toy house. Then a rectangle door. But where was a circle? Sam held up a tiny button. "This can't be a circle," he said. "The clock on the wall is a big circle. This is too small."

Florence looked at the clock. She looked at the button. She put the button on her shirt. She walked far away from the clock. The clock looked small now, small like the button! "It is a circle," she said. "Big circle, tiny circle. Both circles!" Sam laughed and paid her one red crayon to use the button for his hunt.

Then Florence found a circle that was alive. A bird had made a nest up in the tree by the window. The nest was round too. "A circle nest!" she shouted. Miss Patel said the nest was safe and warm, high up in the tree. Florence drew a square, a triangle, a rectangle, and two circles. One was big. One was tiny. She held her paper up high. "All shapes found!"

Charlie woke up and looked out the window. The street was white. Snow was on the trees. Snow was on the cars. It was a snow day!

Charlie put on his boots. He put on his big red coat. Mom put on her mittens too. They went out to the snowy street.

"I will make a snowman," said Charlie. He patted the snow. He patted and patted. But the ball fell apart. The snow was dry and soft. It would not stick. Charlie tried again. The ball fell apart again. "Try again later," said Mom. So they made snow angels. They waited. They watched the sun shine on the snow.

Later, Charlie picked up a handful of snow. This snow felt a little wet. He squeezed it in his mittens. It stuck! He patted a big ball. It stayed in a round shape. He patted another ball on top. Mom put a hat on the snowman. Charlie found two small stones for eyes. The snowman stood tall.

"Hello, snowman," said Charlie. One of his ear muffs slipped off as he waved. "Peek at me!" Charlie said, and he hid behind the snowman. Then he popped out. "Boo!" The snowman stood still and quiet, all afternoon long.

Ruby had a cough. Today she would see Doctor Lin.

In the waiting room, Ruby looked with her eyes. She saw a big fish tank. She heard a quiet hum with her ears. She sniffed with her nose. "I smell soap!" she said.

A nurse gave Ruby a small paper cup. Inside was one little ice cube. Ruby touched it with her fingers. It felt so cold! She dropped it fast into her water cup. Plop!

"That was cold!" said Ruby.

"Now open wide," said Doctor Lin. Ruby stuck out her tongue. "Say ahh," said the doctor. Ruby did it. Her tongue was for tasting, and it tasted cold water after the ice.

Doctor Lin touched Ruby's neck with warm hands. Then Ruby got a cool bandage on her arm. She touched the soft sticker. "I did it!" said Ruby. She waved bye-bye to the fish.

Joseph was wide awake at school. He looked out the window. "Sunny today," said Miss Kim.

The class went outside to play. The sun was very bright. Joseph made a little frown. His eyes went squint, squint. He could not see the ball.

"I don't like the bright sun," he said.

Miss Kim reached into the play box. She pulled out a yellow sun hat. "Try this," she said.

Joseph put the sun hat on his head. The hat made shade over his face. His eyes opened wide. "I can see now!" he said.

He ran to the ball and kicked it far. His friend Ben clapped. "Good kick!" Ben said.

Then the wind blew. Leaves flew around. Joseph held his hat with one hand. The sun stayed bright, but his face stayed shady.

Later, clouds came. Rain began to fall. "Rainy now," said Joseph. Everyone ran inside fast.

At the window, Joseph watched the rain. He still wore his hat. "Sunny hat, rainy day," he said with a giggle. Miss Kim laughed too. "Let's find the rain boots next," she said.

Livia sits in the big waiting room. Mama sits next to her. "Is it our turn yet?" Livia asks. "Not yet," says Mama. "We wait here until they call your name."

Livia waits. She waits some more. The fish tank goes bubbling, bubbling, bubbling. A nurse taps on a computer. Then the nurse opens the door. "Livia!" she calls.

Livia runs to the door. "That's me!" she says. In the small room, the nurse says, "Time for your shot. It will be quick." Livia squeezes her bear. The nurse counts, "One, two, three." Pop! It is done. "All finished!" says the nurse. Then she opens a drawer and hands Livia a sparkly sticker. "A unicorn!" Livia shouts. "Now we go home and show Papa!"

Penelope was in the backyard. She had a big red apple for a snack. She took small bites. Then a green apple fell from the tree. Plip! It rolled on the grass.

Penelope wanted to make a street for her toy cars. She got her broom. She began to sweep the patio. Sweep, sweep, sweep. Now the patio was clean. She lined up her blue car and her yellow car.

Dad came out to help. He held up a red cup. "Red means stop," said Penelope. Both cars stopped. Dad held up a green leaf. "Green means go!" Both cars zoomed across the clean patio. The blue car went fast. The yellow car went slow around the red apple.

Then Dad picked up the green apple. "Green means go," said Penelope. Dad rolled it gently on the ground. The green apple rolled and rolled, right past the blue car. "The apple wins!" said Penelope. She waved the green leaf high in the air.

Cooper ran onto the soccer field. His team wore blue shirts. The other team wore red shirts. Cooper wanted to score a goal. He looked for the ball.

The ball rolled to his feet. Cooper looked up fast. He saw a red shirt. He kicked the ball to the red shirt. "Oh no," said Cooper. The red player took the ball away. The coach blew the whistle. Cooper got a drink of water. The sky was pretty and blue, like his shirt.

The ball came back to Cooper. This time he looked for blue shirts. He saw a blue shirt near the goal. He kicked the ball to the blue shirt. The blue shirt was his friend Sam! Sam kicked the ball into the net. "Blue shirts," Cooper said. "Blue shirts," Sam said. They jumped up and down.

Hudson was three today. His party was at the bowling alley. Mom held his hand at the big door.

Then his friend Ben cried. "I was scared we were lost," Ben said. Hudson had an idea. He showed Ben the card in his hand. Hudson had drawn a bowling pin on it. The card said the party was at the bowling alley. "See? We are in the right place," Hudson said. Ben wiped his eyes. He pointed at the card. "It says bowling alley. This is the bowling alley!" Ben smiled big.

Dad picked out a small blue ball for each boy. It was safe and light. Hudson pushed his ball. It rolled and rolled. Down went the pins. Boom! Everyone clapped. Ben clapped loudest of all. Then Mom brought out a big cake. Hudson blew out his candles with Dad right beside him. "Happy birthday, Hudson!" everyone said.

Florence stood in the backyard. Dad put a red hoop on the grass. He gave her a small beanbag. Florence threw the beanbag. It fell next to the hoop. She got it and tried again. This time it went in! Florence jumped up and down.

Then Dad rolled her a big blue ball. Florence held out one hand, like the big kids do. The ball bounced off her hand. It rolled away past the flowers. "My turn again," said Florence. She ran after the ball.

Dad rolled the big ball again. This time Florence held out both hands. The ball landed right in them. She held it tight. "I caught it!" she said. Dad clapped his hands.

Florence threw the beanbag in the hoop two more times. The wind began to blow the leaves around. Dad said it was time for soup inside. Florence hugged the big ball. The cat sat by the hoop, asleep in the sun. "Wake up, cat," said Florence. "Come and watch me."

Lena wants the crackers at snack time. She sees two boxes on the shelf. Both boxes look the same. She cannot tell which one has crackers.

Teacher Mia holds her hand. "Let me show you something," she says. She points at the front of a box. "These words say crackers." Lena looks at the letters. She points at the other box. "What do those words say?" she asks. "Those words say oats," says Teacher Mia. So Lena takes the cracker box. She was right. Crackers inside!

At story time, Lena picks a book. She opens it from the back. The pages seem mixed up. Teacher Mia turns the book around. "We start at the front," she says. Lena opens the front cover. There is the bear! "Read it," says Lena. She taps the words with one finger, like Teacher Mia does.

After story time, Lena kicks a soft red ball in the yard. Then it is lunch. Lena holds her spoon. She uses it to eat her noodles. On her lunch box there are words too. "Those words say Lena," she says. Teacher Mia smiles. "Yes, they do." Lena traces the letters with her spoon handle, very slowly, one at a time. Then she takes a big bite of her noodles.

Jaxon sat in the family car. Mom buckled him in. "First haircut today," she said. The sun did shine on the road. "Snip, snip, snip," said Jaxon. "That is the sound of a haircut."

At the salon, a lady named Roz put a cape on Jaxon. He sat up tall. Roz picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. One bit of hair fell. Two bits fell. Three bits fell. Then Jaxon began to squirm. He wiggled his shoulders. He scratched at his neck. "Hold still, little one," said Roz. But Jaxon could not hold still.

Roz stopped and looked. Tiny bits of cut hair sat on his neck. She took her soft brush. Brush, brush, brush. She swept the bits away. Jaxon stopped wiggling. His neck felt fine now. He sat up tall again. Snip, snip, snip. One bit, two bits, three bits. When they fell on the floor, he did not itch at all.

Jaxon looked in the mirror. His hair was short and neat. "I look like a big boy," he said. Roz smiled. Mom gave him a sticker shaped like an egg. He held it all the way to the car. "Snip, snip, snip," he said, and Mom laughed. Jaxon was happy.

Rosalie ran to the art room. Today was paint day! She wanted to make something new.

"Red, yellow, blue," said Teacher Mia. Rosalie pointed to each cup. She knew all three names now. She wanted a green tree, but there was no green paint.

First she made a card for her father. She wrote a big R on it in red. Then she dipped her brush in yellow. She painted a yellow leaf. Then she dipped the same brush in blue. She swirled it on the paper. The paint turned green! "Look!" said Rosalie. "Yellow and blue made green!" It was true. Her tree was green.

At home time, Rosalie left her brush in the red cup. The next day she picked it up. The brush was stiff. It was hard like a stick. It would not bend. "Oh no," said Rosalie. She could not paint with it.

Teacher Mia brought water. Together they washed the brush. The red paint came out. The brush was soft again. Rosalie laid it on the rack to dry. Then she ran to her seat. "Green tree today!" she said. She held up her clean brush, ready to paint.

Naomi wanted to read a story to her bear. She picked a beautiful book from the shelf. She held it up for Bear to see.

"One, two, three, here we go!" she said. But the pictures looked funny. The moon hung at the bottom. The cat stood on its ears. Naomi laughed and laughed. "Silly cat, upside-down cat!"

She turned the book around. Now the moon was at the top. The cat sat on its paws. The little black marks sat in neat rows on each page. Naomi pointed at them. "This says moon," she told Bear. "This says cat."

She turned one page, then another, then another. Front to back, all the way to the end.

"Now you, Bear," she said. She propped the book on his lap. Bear stared at the pages. His head tipped to one side.

"Oh no, Bear!" Naomi giggled. "You forget which way is up!"

She kissed his fuzzy head and turned off the light. "Goodnight, moon," she whispered. "Goodnight, upside-down cat."

Jules was hungry for warm bread. Mama said, "The bread is baking. It is almost late for snack time." Jules waited by the oven door. He did not touch it. It was hot, and Mama was the one to open it.

Something smelled so good. Jules sniffed with his nose. Then he wanted to see his sniffing place. He climbed no. He stood on his step stool instead. He looked in the little mirror by the sink. He looked and looked. His nose had two little holes. Two! He peeked again. Yes, two holes, one on each side. "Do I have two?" he asked himself. He counted them in the mirror. One, two. Yes!

The oven timer went ding. Jules covered his ears with his hands. What a loud sound! Mama knocked on the oven top. "All cool," she said. She cut a slice of bread for Jules.

Jules touched the bread. It was soft and warm. He took a bite. Yum! His tongue tasted the warm bread. "Mama, did you hear that ding?" he asked. "I did," said Mama. Jules took another big bite.

Evan was at the school playground. It was his very first day. His teacher, Miss Kim, blew a whistle. "Time to go inside," she said. The children ran to the door. Evan ran too. He ran fast, way out ahead.

At the door, Evan got stuck. So many feet! So many kids! He could not find a space. Miss Kim held up her hand. The line stopped for a break. She smiled at Evan. "Find your spot," she said. Evan looked. There was a gap, right behind a girl with a red backpack. He stepped in. His feet fit just right.

The line walked and walked, down the hall. Light came in the big windows. The red backpack bounced in front of Evan. The girl looked back. "Hold my hand at the door?" she asked. Evan took her hand, and they walked in together.

Leo has a little garden on the balcony. He has a pot of lettuce and a pot of carrots. His watering can is orange, just like a pumpkin. Every morning, Leo gives the plants a drink.

One hot day, Leo runs outside to play. He forgets to water his garden. He plays trucks with his friend Sam instead. Then Leo looks at his pot. "Oh no," says Leo. The lettuce is drooping. It hangs down like a sleepy cat.

Leo runs to the sink. He fills his orange can. He pours water on the lettuce, slow and careful. The sun goes down. The next morning, Leo peeks at the pot. The lettuce stands up tall and waves. "Good morning, lettuce," says Leo. He fills the can again, just in case.

Elizabeth did not want to sleep. She wanted to play with her blocks all night. "One more tower," she said. "Two more towers."

Mom said, "Bedtime now, sweet girl." Elizabeth had a bath first. The water was warm. Mom washed her hair. Then Elizabeth put on her soft pajamas. She zipped the zipper all by herself. Zip, zip, zip. Mom read one book, then two books. Elizabeth closed each eye, one at a time. Then she fell fast asleep.

The next morning, Elizabeth woke up happy. She ran to her blocks. She built one tall tower, then two, then three. Her arms felt strong. "Where did my big energy come from?" she wondered. She ate her breakfast. She drank her milk. Then she built the tallest tower ever. "Mom, look!" she called. "My tower goes up, up, up!"

Milo hurried up the steps to Grandma's house. Grandma had a big surprise for him. She held a soft cloth bag. "Put your hand in," said Grandma. "Tell me what you find."

Milo put his hand in the bag. He felt something round and smooth. "A ball!" he said. He pulled it out. He looked at it. The ball was blue. "I thought it was red," said Milo. Grandma laughed a kind laugh. "Try another one," she said.

Milo put his hand in again. He felt something small and round. "A marble!" he said. He took it out and looked. The marble was green. His fingers could feel the shape. But his fingers could not tell him the color. Only his eyes could do that.

Milo played the game again and again. He found a yellow car. He found a red block. Each time, he had to look. He and Grandma took turns. Grandma felt a smooth stone. "What color is it?" she asked. Milo peeked. "It is yellow!" he said. Grandma smiled.

Soon it was time for Milo's nap. Grandma tucked him in with the blue ball beside his pillow. "Close your eyes," she said softly. Milo closed his eyes. The whole world went dark. "Grandma," he whispered, "I can't see the colors now." Grandma kissed his head. "Sleep well, little one," she said.

Iris is at school. It is time for a snack. She eats a red apple. Crunch, crunch. "The apple is crunchy," says Iris.

Then Iris needs the toilet. She goes through the little door. She uses the toilet. She runs out fast to play with blocks.

Her teacher smiles. "Iris, did you flush?" Iris stops. She forgot! She goes back. She pushes the handle. Whoosh, the water swirls down. "And now?" asks her teacher. Iris looks at her hands. "Now I wash my hands!" She washes with soap. Bubbles, bubbles.

At nap time, Iris lies on her little mat. She thinks about the whoosh. After the toilet, we flush and then wash. She did both steps today.

Iris wakes up and puts on her shoes. "I can do it," she says. Then she asks, "Can I have more crunchy apple?" Her teacher laughs and says yes.

Jasper's class had ten toy cars. Jasper wanted to count them all. He lined them up on the rug. He touched each car. "One, two, three, four," he said. Then he stopped. He forgot what came next.

His friend Mia came over. Mia is in the big class. She has a big sister at home. Mia knelt down by the cars. She patted the fifth car. "Try again," she said. "One, two, three, four..."

Jasper looked at the cars. He touched them one by one. "One, two, three, four, five!" he said. His face felt warm and happy. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" All ten cars were counted. Miss Ella clapped from her chair. Jasper stood up and hugged the cars. "Ten cars," he said. Mia smiled. "You did it," she said.

Aaron was at Grandma's house. He was playing with his blocks. Then he sniffed the air. Something smelled sweet.

"Grandma, I smell cookies!" he said.

Grandma smiled. "Your nose knows first," she said. "Follow the smell to the kitchen."

Aaron could not see the cookies yet. But his nose knew. He walked down the hall. The smell got bigger and bigger. He pushed the kitchen door open. There was Grandma, taking warm cookies from the oven with her big mitts.

"You found them," said Grandma. "Your nose found them before your eyes."

Aaron laughed. "Nose for smelling! Eyes for seeing!" Then he held up his hands. "Hands for touching." He touched a cool plate. He pointed to his ears. "Ears for hearing." Just then the phone did ring, and Grandma had to get it. Aaron waited for her answer, then clapped.

"Ears heard the phone!" he said.

"Right, not wrong," said Grandma. "And what is your mouth for?"

Aaron took a small bite of a cooled cookie. "Tasting!" he said. "Mmm. My nose found them. My mouth says thank you."

Alexis ran into Grandma's house. He had been digging in the yard. His hands were brown with dirt. He wanted to hold the new baby. The baby was asleep in Grandpa's arms.

"Hold her! Hold her!" said Alexis.

"Wait," said Grandpa. He did not move.

Alexis looked at his hands. Dirt was under his nails. Dirt was on his knees too. He held his hands up to show Grandpa.

Grandma took Alexis to the sink. She turned on the water. Alexis made soap bubbles. He scrubbed and scrubbed. A bubble flew up and landed on his nose. "You look like a frog," said Grandma. Alexis laughed. The bubble popped.

Then Grandpa sat down on the big chair. He put a pillow on Alexis's lap. Then he set the baby down, very slow and soft. The baby opened her eyes. She made a tiny sound, like a mouse.

"Hello, sister," said Alexis.

The baby grabbed his shirt. She held on tight. She would not let go.

"That is not a toy," Alexis told her. "That is my shirt."

Grandma smiled. "She thinks you are her teacher," she said. "You will have to work hard."

Alexis patted the baby's back, soft like a feather. The baby closed her eyes and went to sleep, still holding his shirt.

Zoe went to the health clinic with her mom. The nurse had a friendly smile. "First we weigh you," she said.

Zoe stepped on the scale. She wiggled her toes. She bounced her knees. The numbers jumped up and down. "Why does it move?" Zoe asked. The nurse said, "Let's find out."

"Stand very still," Mom said. Zoe took a big breath. She stood still like a tree in the garden. The numbers stopped jumping. One number stayed. "That is how much you weigh," said the nurse.

"I did it!" said Zoe. Mom clapped.

Then it was time for Zoe's shot. Zoe squeezed her mom's hand. The nurse said, "Be still, just like on the scale." Zoe stood still. The shot was quick. It was done!

The nurse opened a drawer. She gave Zoe a shiny star sticker. Zoe stuck it on her shirt. "Can we come back?" Zoe asked. "Next year," said Mom, laughing.

Jaxson ran into the kitchen in his pajamas. He opened the tall cupboard. He saw the cookie jar. "Cookies! Cookies for breakfast!" he called.

Mom shook her head. "Breakfast comes first," she said. "It is the very first meal of the day. Cookies are not breakfast."

Jaxson pouted. He wanted cookies. Mom held up two boxes. "You can pick," she said. "Eggs or oatmeal?"

Jaxson pointed at the eggs. Mom cracked them near the stove. Jaxson stood back and watched from his chair. The eggs sizzled and jumped. "The eggs are dancing!" he laughed.

Soon the plate was on the table. Jaxson took a big bite. "Yum," he said. "Eggs are my breakfast."

After breakfast, Jaxson had a bath. He got dressed in a tidy shirt. Then he asked, "Cookie now?"

Mom smiled. "Maybe after lunch, silly goose."

Jaxson whispered to the cookie jar, "Wait for me."

Olivier was at Grandma's house. His little blue bunny was gone. "Where did bunny go?" he said.

He looked under the table. No bunny. He looked in the big chair. No bunny. "Bunny, where are you?" he did call. Grandma said, "Maybe bunny is naughty and hiding." Olivier laughed. He looked and looked.

Then he saw a basket by his little bed. He peeked inside. There was bunny! "Found you!" said Olivier. Grandma smiled. "Let's put bunny in this basket every day," she said. "Then you will know just where he is."

The next morning, Olivier woke up. He peeked in the basket. Bunny was right there, waiting. Every day after that, bunny slept in the basket. And every day, Olivier knew just where to look. "Good morning, bunny," he said, with a big hug.

Xavier sat at the little red table. Miss Ada put the tablet in front of him. "Can you turn it on?" she asked. Xavier pressed the big button. The screen lit up. He clapped his hands. He had made that happen!

Xavier wanted to draw. Miss Ada showed him the drawing app. He tapped it with one finger. A white page opened. Now he wanted a red sun. He looked at the colours at the top. He tapped blue. His finger made a blue line. "Not blue," said Xavier. "Sun is red."

His friend Mia leaned over. "Try the red one," she said. Xavier tapped the red circle. He drew a big round sun. It was red! He laughed and drew red rays all around it.

Then the teacher rang the bell. Time to clean up. Xavier pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He carried the tablet to the shelf, holding it with both hands like a bowl of soup. "Bye bye, sun," he said.

Zoe sat in the waiting room. She was not sick at all. Her nose was fine. Her tummy was fine. But the nurse said Zoe needed a shot today. Zoe hugged her teddy bear tight.

"Why do I need a shot?" Zoe asked. "I am not sick."

The nurse smiled a soft smile. "It helps protect your body," she said. "It keeps you from getting some sicknesses."

Zoe thought and thought. Then the nurse gave the shot in Zoe's arm. It felt like one tiny pinch. Zoe squeezed her teddy and it was done. The nurse put on a special blue bandage with stars.

After that, Zoe skipped down the hall with Mama. "Teddy needs a shot too," she said. She tapped his fuzzy arm. "There. Now he will stay well, just like me. We can go back to my class."

Zoe waved her star bandage at the door.

Joshua went to the park with his red ball. He also brought Bunny, his soft toy. Joshua put Bunny on the bench. Then he ran to play.

He kicked the ball. It was hard to kick far. A big kid helped him. They took turns and did not share well at first. Then they made a game of it. Soon Joshua was tired. He went back to the bench.

Bunny was not there! Joshua looked under the bench. He looked by the tree. A kind man held up Bunny. "Is this yours?" he asked. He pointed at the tag. Mommy had written Joshua on it. "It says Joshua," the man said. Joshua hugged Bunny tight. "Thank you," he said. He held Bunny with one hand and the ball with the other, all the way home.

Max put on his little blue apron. Today he would make pancakes for his family. His tummy made a happy grumble.

The teacher held up a card. "This is the recipe," she said. "It tells us what to do." Max looked at the steps. Flour, milk, egg, stir, stir, stir. One step, then the next step.

But Max was in a hurry. He poured the flour. He poured the milk. He skipped a step and did not put in the egg. The teacher cooked the pancakes on the hot pan. Max watched from his safe spot.

Flip! The pancake came out flat. Flat as a rain puddle on the floor. "Oh no," said Max. "Flat pancake!"

They read the recipe again. Step one, step two, step three. This time Max put in the egg. Stir, stir, stir.

The new pancake puffed up big and round. Mama took a bite. Papa took a bite. Max clapped his hands. "The recipe helped!" he said. "More please!"

Arya went to the library with Dad. Story time was today. Miss Lena put paper on the big table. "We will make a little house," she said.

Arya picked a red paper. It was a square. It had four sides, all the same. She held it up. "Look, Dad. A square!" Dad smiled and nodded.

Miss Lena showed how to fold. Arya folded her square paper in half. She pressed the fold with her fingers. Then she opened it a tiny bit so it would stand up. "Oh!" said Arya. Now it was not a square. It was a rectangle. The paper looked like a little roof. Arya put it on the table. It stood all by itself.

Next to her, a boy named Sam frowned. His paper would not stand up. Arya watched him. He had not folded it yet. "Fold it in half," she said. "Like this." Sam folded his square edge to edge. He pressed it down. His paper stood up too. "It's tall now!" said Sam.

Miss Lena gave them triangle stickers for windows and a circle sticker for the sun. Arya put the circle sun on top. Then she gave Sam one more triangle, because he had none. Arya spun her little house around on the table. "My house can spin!" she said. Dad laughed and clapped his hands.

Arthur rode the city bus with his mama. He held his toy bunny on his lap. Then the bus went bump, bump, bump. Arthur looked down. The bunny was gone!

Arthur ran up the aisle. He ran back down. He looked fast, fast, fast. Where could the bunny be? He peeked under one seat. Then another. But he ran so fast, his eyes missed things.

Arthur stopped. He took a big breath. "I will look one seat at a time," he said. He looked under seat one. Snow was melting off someone's boots there. He looked under seat two. Only a bit of dirt. He looked under seat three. There was his bunny, lying neat and still!

Arthur picked up the bunny and hugged it tight. "I found you," he whispered. The bus doors opened with a whoosh.

Alexander wanted Grandpa to read the owl book. Grandpa picked it up. He squinted at the page. "Wait," he said. He went to the table.

Grandpa put on his glasses. Then he read the first page. His voice was big and warm. Alexander heard every word. The owl went "hoo, hoo" in the story.

Alexander wondered about the glasses. Did they help Grandpa? He wanted to find out. Grandpa put the glasses down on the couch. Alexander picked them up very carefully. He put them on his own nose.

The room looked funny. Everything looked big and blurry. Alexander laughed. "The glasses are for Grandpa," he said. He gave them back. Grandpa put them on and read the rest of the story. Alexander touched the soft book page. He smelled popcorn from the kitchen, where Mom made a snack. He tasted a warm bite. Then he pointed at the owl. "Read that part again," he said.

Ibrahim woke up in the morning. He ate his bread and egg. Then Mama said, "Teeth time, one, two, three!" Ibrahim brushed his teeth up and down. "Good teeth," said Mama, and she smiled.

At night, Ibrahim had his bath. The water was warm. Mama helped him wash his hair. Then he put on his soft pajamas. He did not rip them. He was careful. Papa lit a small fire in the big lamp. No, wait, Papa turned on the lamp. The room felt warm and cozy. Ibrahim got into bed. Mama pulled the blanket up. "One, two, three, sleep," she said.

Then Ibrahim sat up. "Wait," he said. "My teeth!" He hopped out of bed. He ran to the bathroom. He brushed his teeth, up and down. "Good boy," said Papa. Ibrahim got back into bed. He closed his eyes. "Teeth in the morning," he said. "Teeth at night." Then he went to sleep.

Edouard wanted to count all his blocks. He sat on the playroom floor. "One, two, three," he said. He stacked the blocks up high. "Four, five, six." The tower was getting tall!

He found more blocks under the chair. Dirt was on one block. He wiped the dirt off with his sleeve. "Seven, eight, nine." Only one more block to find! He looked in the toy box. He looked behind the bear. There it was, sitting all alone in the corner.

"Ten!" Edouard shouted. He had ten blocks! He wanted to write the number ten on his paper. He drew a nine first. Then he rubbed it out. Ten did not look like that. He tried again, slow and careful. He wrote a one, and then a zero. "One, zero," he read out loud. Ten needed two numbers! He held up his paper and jumped. "Mama, look! Ten!"

Eliana wished for one more turn with the blue truck. Her brother Milo had it now. "My turn," said Milo. Eliana waited. She tapped her toes while she waited.

Then Milo rolled the truck to her. "Your turn," he said. The truck felt bumpy under her hand. It smelled like crayons. Eliana pushed it fast, and it hit the block tower with a crash. Both of them laughed.

A bell rang. Time to clean up. Eliana ran to the door. Then she stopped. The blocks were still on the floor. She had played with them. So she went back. She put the blocks in the red bin, one by one. Milo put the truck away too. Then Milo found something under the rug. It was Eliana's lost yellow pencil. "For you," he said. Eliana hugged it tight and smiled.

Nathan stood at the little pool by the lake. The water was blue and warm. He wanted to jump in right away.

"Not yet," said his friend Daisy. "Look. There is no teacher here."

Nathan looked around. He saw the empty pool. He saw the big lake. He saw cows in the green field. The cows did not swim. They just stood in the shade.

Then Nathan saw a duck. The duck sat in the shallow water. It flapped its wings. It liked to bathe there in the sun.

"My turn soon," Nathan whispered to the duck.

At last Miss Lily came. She carried a big red float. She sat down by the pool. "Now I am watching you," she said. "You can get in."

Nathan held the red float. He kicked his legs. The water went splash, splash. His feet came up. He was floating!

"I did it!" he said. Miss Lily clapped. Nathan felt happy and warm. The duck splashed its wings too, and Nathan laughed and laughed.

Emmett sat at the kitchen table. Mama set down a big pot of soup. Papa put out four orange bowls. Baby sister Ada banged her spoon.

"Can I do the special words?" Emmett asked. "Like Coco does?"

Papa smiled. "You mean bon appétit? In France, people say it before a meal. It means have a good meal."

Emmett wanted to say it too. He tried. "Bon... bon apple tea?"

Ada laughed and clapped. Mama laughed too, softly.

"Try again," said Papa. "Bon. Ap. Pé. Tit."

Emmett counted on his fingers. One, two, three, four sounds. "Bon. Ap. Pé. Tit."

"Bon appétit!" said Papa.

"Bon appétit!" said Mama.

"Ba!" said Ada, waving her spoon.

Emmett said it one more time, all by himself. Then Mama ladled soup into his orange bowl. Papa gave Ada a soft piece of bread. Emmett picked up his spoon like a big boy.

"Bon appétit, Ada," he said.

Ada blew him a kiss through the steam.

Joshua sat in the music classroom. He wanted to play a big growly bear. His teacher, Miss Amy, stood near him. "Try the piano," she said.

Joshua pressed a key on the right. It made a high sound. That was not a bear. That was more like a little bird. He pressed a key on the far right. Another high sound. Still not a bear.

Joshua scooted down the bench. He pressed a key on the left. It made a low sound. He pressed the far left key. It made a very low sound. "Growl," said Joshua. Miss Amy laughed. "That is a big bear," she said.

Then Joshua played the high keys again. "Tweet, tweet," he sang. Miss Amy clapped. A car honked outside. Joshua stopped and smiled. He played one low key, soft and slow. "Good night, bear," he said.

Mila was going on a trip with Mama and Papa. Her teddy bear, Boo, rode in her backpack. They were off to a campsite with trees and a little tent.

First they had to fly on a big plane. At the airport, Mama put the bags on a moving belt. The belt carried Mila's backpack into a machine. The backpack went in, but it did not come out. "Boo!" said Mila. "Where is Boo?" Her tummy felt tight.

Mila stood on her toes and watched the machine. The belt moved and moved. Then, out came her backpack, on the other end. Mila opened the zipper. Boo was still there, soft and warm. "Boo came out!" said Mila. She hugged him tight. The man at the desk smiled at her. Mila felt proud. She put Boo back in the backpack and held it close.

At the campsite, the tent went up under the stars. Mila put Boo inside, safe and snug. "Night night, Boo," she said. "You rode the machine. You came back to me."

Zachary wanted to draw a big red truck. The tablet sat on the shelf, all dark and quiet. He pressed the round button at the bottom. The screen lit up, bright as morning. His mom had shown him how once, and now he could do it himself.

He tapped the little paint pot. The drawing app opened. He picked red and drew two round wheels. He drew a long truck body. He drew a driver with a funny hat.

Then the screen went black. All his truck was gone. "Where did my truck go?" he asked. Mom came over and looked. "It got tired," she said. "It needs charging." She took the charger and plugged it in for him. A small green light came on. Zachary watched from the couch and drank his juice slowly. He did not forget his truck. He waited.

After snack, the screen woke up. There was his truck, just as red as before. Zachary laughed out loud. He drew a fast dog running next to the truck. Then he was done. He pressed the button again, and the screen went dark and quiet. He carried the tablet back to the shelf with both hands.

"That was fast," said Mom. "You put it away all by yourself." Zachary patted the shelf. "Night night, tablet," he said.

Oliver sat at the kitchen table. Grandma put down two rows of buttons. One row was long and spread out. One row was bunched up close.

"That long row has more!" Oliver said. "It goes all the way to the honey pot!"

"Let's count," said Grandma.

Oliver touched each button. "One, two, three, four, five." The long row had five.

Then he pushed the close row together. He counted again. "One, two, three, four, five." That row had five too.

"Same!" Oliver said. He laughed out loud.

He spread the bunched row apart. It looked big now. He pushed it back. It looked small. He counted again. Five. Five. Five.

Then Grandma slid a soft toy bee across the table. "Count these," she said.

Oliver counted fast. "Six bees, four buttons. Bees have more!"

He clapped his hands and counted them all again, just to hear the numbers go.

Charles was sleepy. He rode the bus with Grandma. He hugged his blue string. His toy bunny was gone.

"Where is Bunny?" Charles asked. He looked down. The bus seat was dark under there. He could not see anything at all.

The bus driver stopped the bus. She had a little flashlight. "Try this," she said. Grandma helped Charles hold it. The light made a bright circle. Now Charles could see under the seat! There was Bunny, hiding in the dark.

"My Bunny!" said Charles. He did not throw his string. He put it in his pocket, safe. He hugged Bunny tight.

The driver smiled at him. "Good thing the light found him," she said. Charles gave Bunny a kiss on his soft ear. The bus went bump, bump, down the road. Bunny's ears went up and down. Charles laughed. He waved his string at Bunny. Bunny rode home all the way in Charles's warm arms.

Nova sat at the craft table at summer camp. She was drawing a picture of a snowman. She drew one ball, two balls, three balls. "Snow!" she said. "Snow in my picture."

Then Nova drew the snow. She pressed her pencil down very hard. She wanted the snow to look very white and very full. SNAP! The pencil point broke off. It rolled under the table.

"My pencil!" said Nova. "Oh no."

Her friend Ben laughed, kind and soft. "Your pencil got tired," he said. "It went to sleep."

Nova got a new pencil from the teacher. This time she pressed gently. The pencil did not snap. The snow came out soft and gray and pretty.

"One ball, two balls, three balls," said Ben.

"And one snowman," said Nova. She held up her old toy bunny. "He is in the snow too."

Ben drew a tiny carrot for the snowman's nose.

Sofia and Mama went to the bank. It was cold outside. "Time for your coat," said Mama. Sofia held her coat up high. She put one arm in. She put the other arm in. Now came the hard part. The zipper.

Sofia pulled the zipper tab up. It did not move. She pulled again. Still nothing. Why would it not go? She looked down at the coat. The two sides were apart at the bottom. Little bits of paper seemed to float in the air near the big machine. That was funny. But her zipper was not funny.

She looked very closely. One side of the zipper had a tiny box at the bottom. The other side had a little end. What if the end went into the box? She slid the end in. Click. It fit! Then she pulled the tab. Up it went, all the way!

"My zipper is not weak anymore," Sofia said. "It is strong!" Mama smiled. They walked out into the cold. Snow began to fall. Sofia patted her coat. "I did it all by myself," she said.

Rowan ran to the playground in his blue shirt. The sun was warm. The slide was shiny. He counted the swings. One, two, three. Then he saw a big red kite in the sky. It danced and pulled. A girl named Mia held the string. Rowan wanted to hold it so much.

He ran fast and grabbed at the string. Mia pulled it back. "No," she said. Rowan felt scared and hot in his face. His friend Sam came over. Sam said, "You say may I first." Rowan looked at the kite. He took a breath. "May I have a turn, please?" he asked.

Mia smiled. "Yes, you may," she said. She put the string in his hand. The kite pulled like a big dog. Rowan laughed. "Thank you, Mia," he said. Then he tripped on the grass and tumbled down. "Sorry, kite," he said, and Sam helped him up. "Thank you," Rowan said again.

They took turns, one, two, three, four. The wind went whoosh. The kite went up and up. "May I fly it now?" asked Sam. "Yes, you may," said Rowan. He held the string tight and watched the red tail wave.

Amira sat at the big table at math club. In front of her was a red bucket full of buttons. Her friend Leo had a blue bucket.

"Want to see who has more?" asked Leo.

"Yes!" said Amira.

She grabbed some buttons from her bucket. She put them in a row. "One, two, three, four," she counted. Leo lined his up too. "One, two, three," he counted.

Amira looked at both rows. Her row was longer. "I have more!" she said. Then she wondered, what if Leo had one more?

Miss Dana came by with a little cup of buttons. Leo picked one button and put it at the end of his row.

"Count again," said Miss Dana.

"One, two, three, four," said Leo.

Now the rows were the same size. Amira tapped her chin. Hmm. Leo got one more, and now they had the same.

Miss Dana held out one button to Amira. "Here, Amira. One more for you."

Amira put it at the end of her row. She counted slowly, touching each one. "One, two, three, four, five." She jumped up. "Now I have more again!"

Leo laughed. "I want one more too!"

"Okay," said Amira. "I hope there are enough buttons."

Iris went to Mama's office. On the desk was a big tablet. Iris wanted to draw a monkey on it. She did not know how to begin.

Mama turned the tablet on for her. The screen lit up with small pictures. Iris looked for the drawing app. One small picture had a paintbrush on it. She tapped it with her finger. The drawing page opened. Iris tapped the green color. A green line followed her finger. She drew a monkey with a long tail. She gave it a sharp yellow banana.

Then it was time for lunch. Iris tapped the top of the screen and the app closed. She put the tablet on the soft mat, face up, just like Mama showed her. Then she ran to the lunch table. "My monkey has a big smile," she said.

Isabelle went to the big hall with Mama. There were lanterns on the walls. There were people everywhere. Isabelle saw a table with sweet cakes. She let go of Mama's hand. She began to walk to the cakes.

The hall was full of legs and coats. Isabelle could not see Mama. She stopped. Her tummy felt funny. She stood very still by a chair.

Then Isabelle saw Mama's red scarf. Mama turned around. She came back fast. "Isabelle, hold my hand," said Mama. Isabelle reached up and held on tight.

They walked to the cake table together. Mama picked a little cake. Isabelle sat on the chair to eat it. The cake was sweet. Isabelle held Mama's hand all the way home.

Weston sat at the dinner table. His tummy made a little growl. "More rice, please," he said. Mama smiled and put rice on his plate. "Thank you," said Weston.

Then Weston reached for the big spoon. The spoon slipped. Bloop! Rice fell on the floor. "Sorry," said Weston. Papa said, "That is okay. Let us clean it up." Weston helped wipe the floor with a cloth. The cloth tickled his fingers like a soft feather.

Next, Weston wanted the red cup. It was too far away. He stretched and stretched. His chair wobbled like a little storm at sea. "Help, please," said Weston. Papa reached over and gave him the red cup. Weston took a big drink. "Ahh," he said. "Yummy water."

Then Grandma came in the door. Weston hid behind his hands. Grandma waved at him. Weston peeked out. "Hello," he said. Grandma clapped her hands. She gave him a tiny orange from her pocket, like a little sun. Weston held it up to the light. "Hello, orange," he whispered, and he took a great big bite of his rice.

Mohamed sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. "Where are we going?" he asked. "To Grandma's house," said Mama. "She is making soup." Mohamed watched the trees go by. The sun made his seat warm. "Hot," he said, and pulled his hand away. The window was cool when Mama opened it a little. Warm seat, cool wind. The same car had two different feelings.

At Grandma's house, the big pot sat on the stove. Grandma stirred it with a long spoon. Mohamed looked at the stove. It did not look like anything at all. Was it hot? Was it cold? He could not tell. He put his hands behind his back. "Grandma, is the stove hot?" he asked. Grandma held her hand up high, far from the pot. "Yes, it is still hot," she said. "Only I touch the stove. You can watch from here." Mohamed stood by the door, close to Mama. The soup went bubble, bubble.

Later the pot was empty. Everyone ate the soup. It was warm and good. In the car going home, Mohamed felt sleepy. "Talk about it tomorrow," said Mama softly. Mohamed had a dream about bubbles, big and round, going up, up, up.

Luca lived on a farm with his grandma. One sunny morning, grandma gave him three little seeds. "Plant them here," she said. Luca dug a small hole. He put in one seed, two seeds, three seeds. Then he patted the soil down, pat, pat, pat.

Every day Luca went to look. "Where are my seeds?" he asked. Grandma said, "Wait, little one. They need rain and sun." So Luca waited. The rain came. The sun came. A naughty goat came too, but grandma shooed him away before he could nibble anything.

On the sixth day, Luca ran to the garden spot. Something green was poking up out of the soil. It was very small and very new. "Grandma, come quick!" Luca called. He ran across the yard. "A little green thing came up!"

Grandma knelt down beside him. "That is a sprout," she said. Luca looked at it. "A sprout," he said. "One sprout, two sprouts, three sprouts!" He counted them with his finger, one, two, three.

Luca made a picture of his sprouts. He drew the brown soil and the green tops. Then he showed it to the ducks by the pond. The ducks were busy watching grandpa fish in the water. Luca held up his picture anyway. "Look," he said. "My sprouts are growing."

Snow fell outside the window. Kinsley wanted to watch it fall. She pushed the couch to see better. Behind the couch, she saw a small hole in the wall. It had two little slots. It looked like a tiny face.

Kinsley wanted to touch it. She lifted her finger. Then she remembered. Fingers never go in there. She put her hand behind her back. She ran to find Grandma.

"Grandma, come see," said Kinsley. "There is a hole behind the couch." Grandma came right away. She looked at the wall. "That is an outlet," said Grandma. "Thank you for telling me, not touching it." Grandma put a safe cover on it. It clicked into place.

"Now it is closed," said Grandma. Kinsley touched the cover. It felt smooth and cool. The cover did not open for her finger. It stayed shut.

Grandma gave her paper and paint. Kinsley painted white snow. She painted the couch. She painted the outlet with its new cover, and it looked just like the true thing. Then she held Grandma's hand, and together they watched the snow.

Miles stood in the pool changing room. He put on his little blue swimsuit. "Time for swim class," said Dad. Miles held his yellow owl towel. "Can the owl swim too?" asked Miles. "No, but he can watch," said Dad.

At the pool, Miles wanted to get out. He pulled on the wet edge. His arms slipped. His feet splashed. He could not get out. "This is hard," said Miles. His teacher pointed to the metal ladder. Miles put his feet on the ladder steps. Up, up, up he went. "I did it!" said Miles.

He slid back into the water. Then he climbed the ladder again. "Is the ladder easy?" asked Dad. "Yes!" said Miles. "The ladder helps me!" He hugged his owl towel. "Good tries, Miles," said Dad. Miles smiled big.

Paisley wanted a story at bedtime. She ran to her shelf. But the book felt wrong. It was not her book.

Dad came in. "Where did my book go?" Paisley asked. "The one with the funny dog."

"Maybe you left it at school," said Dad. "But here is a library book. We can read this one."

Paisley looked at the cover. There were little marks on it. "What are these?" she asked. Dad pointed. "Those are words. That name says Eric. He made up the story."

Paisley touched the name with her finger. "Eric made the dog?" she asked.

"This Eric made this book," said Dad. "Your book has a name too."

Dad opened the book at the back. Paisley shook her head. She turned the pages herself. She turned them until she got to the front. The first page had a picture.

"Start here," she said.

So Dad read, and Paisley listened, and the pages turned one by one to the end.

Zayn put on his red shoe. "I need the other one," he said. Mom laughed and found it under the couch.

At the library, a lady gave Zayn a little card. It had his name on it. "My own card!" said Zayn. He picked a book about a big, juicy strawberry. The lady scanned the card. Zayn hugged the book all the way home.

Daddy read the book three times. Then Zayn took it back to the library. He slid it into the return slot. The book went down, down, gone. "Bye, book," said Zayn. Then he looked for his shelf. He wanted a new book about trucks. He held it up. The lady smiled. "Your card again?" she asked. Zayn gave her the same little card. It worked! Zayn jumped. "It's a magic card," he said. "Not magic," said Mom, "but pretty great." Zayn hugged the truck book tight.

Wesley wanted to play a game. Daddy put three things on the bath mat. "Close your eyes," said Daddy. Wesley shut his eyes tight.

First he touched a stone. His fingertips slid round and round. It felt smooth. "A stone!" said Wesley. He opened his eyes. Yes, it was a stone.

Next his fingertips found bumps. Bumpy all over. "The pinecone!" He was right again.

Then something soft tickled his fingers. It felt like a little feather. Wesley laughed. "The feather!" Daddy clapped.

Daddy held up a toothbrush. Wesley saw its straight handle. He heard the tap run. The toothpaste smelled like mint. He put a little on his tongue. It tasted cool. Then he chewed his breakfast dream away and brushed every tooth. Daddy said, "All clean, big boy." Wesley smiled at himself in the mirror.

Emmett went to the grocery store with Dad. They pushed a big cart. Emmett picked a carton of eggs. He held it with two hands, so soft, so slow. At home, Emmett wanted to make pancakes for the family. "I can help," he said. Dad said, "Let's build the batter together." Emmett poured the flour. It made a white puddle in the bowl. Then Dad said, "Now we need an egg." Emmett took one egg. He tapped it on the bowl. Tap, tap. The shell cracked open. The egg slid out into the bowl. But a little piece of shell fell in too. Emmett saw it sitting there. He got a spoon. He scooped the shell bit out. He tried once. He tried again. He got it! Dad stirred the batter. Dad poured it on the hot pan, because pans are for grown-ups. Emmett watched from his stool. The pancakes bubbled and flipped. Soon there was a tall stack. "Tasty," said Mom, taking a big bite. Emmett smiled and put one more egg on the table. "We can crack another," he said.

Everett sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted a sticker, but first he had to wait. The wait felt long. He looked around with his eyes. He saw a man with a bandage on his arm. He heard a phone ring with his ears. He smelled something like soap with his nose.

Then the nurse came in. "Time to check you," she said. She let Everett touch the paper on the bed. The paper was smooth and it made a crinkly sound. Everett touched it with his fingers. The nurse smiled. "Good looking, good listening," she said.

Next she held up a little cup. "This is lemon juice," she said. "You can try a tiny taste with your tongue." Everett thought of orange juice. Orange juice was sweet. So lemon juice must be sweet too. He stuck out his tongue and tasted it. He scrunched up his whole face. "Sour!" he said. "Sour, sour!" The nurse laughed, and the man in the hall laughed too.

Everett got his sticker at last. It was a shiny star. He stuck it on his hand and looked at it with his eyes. "Sour lemon," he told his mom. "Sour lemon, sweet sticker."

David climbed the tall steps of the school bus. He found a seat by the window. His backpack sat on his lap. Today was his first day of school!

The bus went bump, bump, bump. David saw a dog out the window. He saw a red truck. Soon the bus stopped at school. A big door waited at the top of the steps.

Inside, David saw blocks and paint and a tiny play kitchen. His teacher smiled and said, "Good morning, David!" Then David needed to go to the bathroom. He looked around. He could not find it. Where was it? He asked himself, "Who can help me?"

He walked to his teacher. "I need to find the bathroom," he said. "I will show you," she said. She took his hand. They walked down the hall. The bathroom was right there! David washed his hands all by himself.

At play time, David built a tall tower of blocks. A girl named Mia knocked it over by accident. "It's okay," said David. "I can ask the teacher if I need help." After snack, David drew a picture of the school bus. He could not reach the red crayon. Mia got it for him. Then the teacher rang a bell. "Time for the bus!" she said.

David ran to the bus with his class. He waved at his teacher. "See you tomorrow!" he called. The bus went bump, bump, bump all the way home.

Victoria sat at the table. She had oatmeal and a banana. The sky outside was cloudy. Victoria sniffed. She sniffed again. Then she sniffed a third time.

"My nose is drippy," said Victoria. She wiped it on her sleeve. Mom brought a box of tissues. Mom pulled one tissue out. "Try this," said Mom. Victoria held the soft tissue. She blew her nose. One big sniff, and the tissue did the work. "My nose feels better now," said Victoria. She hoped the drips were all gone. She looked out at the big tree.

"I need a tissue," said Victoria next time. She took one, then two, then three tissues. She made a little pile. "One for me. One for Bear. One for Bunny," she said. Mom smiled and gave Bear a pat.

Madelyn wanted apple juice. She sat at the table. Her cup was empty.

"Give me juice!" said Madelyn.

Daddy kept cutting the apple. He did not bring the juice. Madelyn tried again.

"Juice, please," said Madelyn.

Daddy smiled. "Juice coming up!" He poured the juice into her cup. Madelyn took a big drink. "Thank you," she said. "You are welcome," said Daddy.

Then Madelyn tipped her cup. The juice spilled on the floor. "Oh no," said Madelyn. "Sorry, Daddy."

"That is okay," said Daddy. "Please get the towel." Madelyn ran to the drawer. She got the small towel. She wiped the floor all by herself.

Then Madelyn wanted to feed the dog. "Please come here," she called. The dog ran over. It began to bark. "Thank you," said Madelyn, and she put food in the bowl.

After lunch, Madelyn felt sleepy. The dog was already asleep by the door. Daddy carried Madelyn to her bed. "Can you read to me, please?" she asked.

"Yes," said Daddy. He opened the book. Outside, a butterfly flew past the window. Madelyn watched it until her eyes closed.

Mia ran into the baby store. "The baby is coming soon!" she said. Mom smiled. "We need a little bed," she said. Outside it was windy, but inside the store was warm. Mia liked the tiny socks. She held one up. It was smaller than her thumb.

Then Mia saw a doll. It had a soft head. She picked it up. The doll's head flopped down. It flopped to the side. Mia gasped. "Oh no!" she said. She held the doll again. This time she put her hand under its head. The head stayed still. "I have an idea," said Mia. "I will hold the baby like this."

A lady walked by with a real baby. She had her hand under the baby's head. Mia watched. The baby's head did not flop. "Just like my doll!" said Mia. Mom picked out a little blanket. It had white snow dots all over it. Mia carried the blanket to the car, and the doll rode home with her hand under its head.

Edouard stood in the music room. A drum sat in front of Miss Pia. "Today we clap," she said. She tapped the drum. Boom, boom, boom.

Edouard clapped too fast. His claps ran ahead of the drum. "Too quick, Edouard!" said his friend Tom. Tom laughed, but not in a mean way. Edouard clapped too slow. His claps fell behind. He frowned.

Then Miss Pia sang a little song. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." The words were short. The ends of the lines matched. Star, star, are, high. Edouard clapped with the song. Boom went his hands. One clap for each beat. His claps fit!

"Can I sing it by myself?" he asked Tom. "Try it," said Tom. Edouard sang the whole song. He did not forget one word. He clapped all the way too. Miss Pia played a long drum roll. "Our star!" she said. Edouard took a bow, just like a big singer, and Tom clapped for him this time.

Alexander went to the baby store with Mama. "The new baby needs things," said Mama. Alexander wanted to pick a toy. He found a red cup with a duck on it. "The baby can drink from this!" he said. He also found a shiny pinwheel. "The baby can watch it spin!" Mama smiled. "Babies sleep a lot," she said. "Maybe the baby will sleep now."

At home, the baby came. Alexander held the pinwheel up. "Look! Spin!" he said. But the baby was sleeping again. Alexander waited. He blew the pinwheel softly. Still the baby slept. "Does the baby sleep all day?" he whispered. He spun the cup round and round on the table. It made a little sound. The baby opened one eye.

Then the baby made a small noise. "He is awake!" said Alexander. Mama put the baby in her arms. Alexander touched the baby's tiny hand. The baby held on. Alexander laughed. "Now we can play," he said. "But just a little bit." The pinwheel sat on the shelf, waiting for tomorrow.

Madison put on her red team shirt. The sun was warm on the court. Her shoes went squeak, squeak on the dry ground. "I think it will be a good day," she said.

The game started. Madison ran and bounced the ball. She threw it up. It did not go in. The other team got more baskets. The coach blew the whistle. The game was over.

The other team jumped and smiled. Madison felt mad. She wanted to stomp her foot. "Do we have to keep playing?" she asked. "No," said Coach Amy. "Now we line up."

Madison stood in the line. Each player on her team gave a high five. Each player on the other team said, "Good game." Then it was Madison's turn. She heard herself say it too. "Good game."

The girl in the blue shirt smiled at her. "Your bounce pass was nice," the girl said. Madison stood taller. She looked up at the sky. The weather was still warm. She waved to the blue team as they walked away.

Ava sat at the art table. She had a small pile of stickers. She wanted to put a sticker on her toy block.

The block had lost its color in one spot. Ava wanted to fix it.

She put one sticker on the top. It was a square sticker on a square face. Then she put one on the bottom. She turned the block over and over.

"Look, Ava," said Teacher Mia. She held the block up. She did not say more.

Ava counted the stickers. "One, two, three, four, five, six." The block had six faces. Each face was a square. Six square faces, six square stickers!

Then Ava saw something else. Her friend Sam had a round ball. Ava pressed a sticker on it. The sticker peeled off. It would not stay on the curved skin of the ball. A square sticker likes a flat face.

Ava laughed. "The ball will not take my sticker," she said.

Teacher Mia smiled. "You can give the ball round stickers instead."

Ava took out a circle sticker, a triangle sticker, and a rectangle sticker too. She put the circle on a round lid. She put the triangle on a paper hat. She put the rectangle on a little door.

Then she set the block on the table. "Six stickers, six squares," said Ava.

Sam clapped his hands.

Milan went to the store with his dad. He wanted a book about trucks. He saw a bin of little books by the door. A blue book had a big truck on the front. Milan picked it up.

He sat down on the floor to look. He opened the book from the wrong side. The pages felt odd. The truck picture came at the end, not at the start. The story seemed all mixed up. Milan turned the book over. Now the truck was on the front cover. He opened it from the front. The first page showed a little red truck. Page by page, the truck drove to a big hill.

"Can we get this one?" Milan asked. Dad said, "Yes. Let's go fetch a basket." Milan held the blue book tight. It did not fall, not even once.

Josephine loved the monkey song. But today the monkey toys were up high on the shelf. She could not reach them. "Can you help me?" she asked Miss Ana. "Yes, I can," said Miss Ana. She took down the five little monkeys and poured them into Josephine's lap. They tickled her hands.

Josephine lined them up on the rug. Five monkeys, side by side. She sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!" She made one monkey fall off. Bump. Now she saw four monkeys on the rug. She sang again, "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed!" Another monkey fell. Bump. Now there were three. Then two. Then one. Then none.

A boy named Sam watched. His face looked grumpy. "Where did the monkeys go?" he asked. "They fell off the bed," said Josephine. "Each one went bump." Sam sat down next to her. Together they counted one, two, three, four, five. All the monkeys came back to the rug.

Miss Ana clapped her hands. "Sing it one more time," she said. Josephine held the monkeys like a warm little nest in her hands. She counted them softly. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she lifted the first monkey high and began, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed..."

Adam was at the playground. He saw a big red truck. A boy named Sam was pushing it. Adam wanted the truck very much.

Adam grabbed the truck out of Sam's hands. Sam's face got red. Sam started to cry. Big tears ran down his cheeks. Adam looked at Sam. Sam did not push the truck anymore. He just cried and cried.

Adam gave the truck back. "Truck?" he asked. "My turn, please?" Sam wiped his tears. He nodded his head. "Okay. Wait for your turn," said Sam. Adam sat on the bench. He watched Sam push the truck down the slide ramp. It was noisy and fun to hear.

Then Sam ran back. "Your turn now," said Sam. Adam pushed the truck fast, fast, fast. "Thank you, Sam!" said Adam. Sam smiled. Then Sam asked, "My turn, please?" Adam gave the truck back. Now they took turns, over and over, until the sun went down.

Beatrice sat on Grandma's big soft chair. Grandma's tablet lay on the table. It was dark and still.

Beatrice wanted to draw a ball on it. She pushed the screen with her whole hand. Nothing happened. The screen stayed dark. She pushed again, hard. Still nothing. "Hmm," said Beatrice. "How does it wake up?"

Grandma tapped the little button once. The screen lit up. "Now you try," said Grandma. Beatrice tapped the button with one finger. Click! The screen woke up. "It likes my finger," said Beatrice.

She saw the little paint pot picture. She tapped it once with one finger. The drawing app opened. Beatrice drew a big red ball. She drew a soft gray cat too.

Then she was done. She swept her finger over the screen and made a curvy sun. "All finished," she said. She gave the tablet to Grandma. Grandma put it away in the drawer, safe and snug.

"More drawing tomorrow?" asked Grandma. Beatrice nodded. "Yes! With my one finger," she said, and held it up high.

Lucy ran into the playroom. Her big teddy sat on the small chair. "Today we slide!" said Lucy. She had a little slide right there, next to the doll bed.

Lucy climbed up, up, up the ladder. Then she zoomed down, fast. "Again!" she shouted. Her friend Ben came in. He held a warm cup of cocoa. "Mama made it," he said. "It was too hot, so we waited."

"Watch me!" said Lucy. She went up slow. Then she went down fast. Her arms opened wide. "Look, Ben!" Ben laughed and clapped. He put his cup on the shelf, far from the slide.

Lucy went up again. But her foot hit the cup handle. Oh no! The cocoa began to spill. Mama ran in fast. She grabbed the cup. "All safe," said Mama. Lucy climbed up the ladder one more time. Down, down, down she went. "Up and down!" she sang.

Ava held her teacher's hand. It was her first day of school. Her shoes were pink. Her bag had bread inside for snack time. "Will you stay with me?" Ava asked. "I will stay close by," said Miss Kim.

Outside, Ava saw the big slide. She ran to it fast. A boy named Sam was at the front. He went down. Then he ran back to go again. But Miss Kim showed him the back of the line. Ava got in line behind two friends. She waited. She watched. Each friend went down, one at a time. Then it was her turn. Whee! Down she went, fast as a bird.

Ava ran to the back of the line again. Soon it was her turn one more time. "The line works," said Ava. Sam smiled and stood behind her. "My turn next," he said.

Norah wants to make pancakes. She stands on her stool at the big counter. Dad holds the bowl.

"Can I pour the flour?" asks Norah.

"Yes," says Dad. "Pour it in."

Norah tips the cup fast. Whoosh! A big white cloud puffs up. The cloud lands on her nose. It lands on Dad's nose too. Norah looks at Dad. Dad looks like a snowman.

"You have a dusty nose," says Norah. She giggles.

"You have one too," says Dad. They laugh and laugh.

"Now I will pour slow," says Norah. She tips the cup little by little. No cloud. No dusty nose. The flour goes softly into the shiny bowl. Norah stirs the batter round and round.

Dad cooks the pancakes on the hot stove. Norah waits in her safe spot. Soon the pancakes come to the table.

Mama takes a bite. "Mmm," says Mama. "What is the name of the cook?"

"Norah!" says Norah. "The girl with the floury nose."

Gabriel wanted to build a big tower. His friend Mia came over to play. Mia was building a tower too.

Gabriel ran to get more blocks. Oh no! His foot bumped Mia's tower. The blocks fell down. Crash!

Mia sat very still. Her lip went tight and small.

Gabriel looked at the blocks. He looked at Mia. What could he do?

"Sorry, Mia," Gabriel said.

Mia looked up. "Okay," she said. "Sorry is good."

Then Gabriel picked up a block. He put it at the bottom. "You build," he said. "Then me."

Mia stacked one block. Gabriel stacked one block. Then Mia. Then Gabriel.

"What color next?" asked Gabriel.

"Red," said Mia.

Gabriel found the red block. He gave it to her. She laughed. The tower grew so tall. It was taller than their teddy bear!

Then Daddy came in. He wiggled his fingers near Mia's toes. "Tickle, tickle!" he said.

Mia giggled. Gabriel giggled. The tower wobbled and fell down again.

"Uh oh!" said Gabriel. "Blocks again?"

"Yes, blocks again," said Mia.

They both picked up blocks together. This time the tower had two builders. It stood up straight and tall.

Iris sat at the dinner table. She wanted the big bowl of carrots. It was near Daddy.

Daddy held up one carrot. "One," said Iris. Daddy held up two carrots. "Two," said Iris.

Soon Iris had carrots on her plate. She counted them. "One, two, three, four." Then she ate one. "Now one, two, three," she said. Daddy smiled.

Mama set down the peas. "How many peas, Iris?" she asked.

Iris pointed at each pea. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." Eight peas!

Then Grandma asked, "How old are you, Iris?"

Iris held up three little fingers. Then she said the number word out loud. "I am three!"

"Three!" said Grandma. "And next year you will be four."

The clock on the wall gave a little ring. Dinner time was over.

Iris put her three fingers near Grandma's plate. "One, two, three peas for you," she said, and pushed the bowl close.

Penelope went to the store with Mama. She held the shopping list. "I can help," she said. "Yes, you can," said Mama.

Penelope dropped the picture basket by accident. It was on a low shelf. All the pictures fell out. Oh no! Apples, balls, cows, bread, ducks, teddy bears. What a mess!

"I will fix it," said Penelope. She made a pile of animals. Cow, duck, sheep. She made a pile of toys. Ball, teddy bear, drum. She made a pile of foods. Apple, bread, milk. Each pile had its own friends.

Mama came back. "Where did the mess go?" she asked. Penelope laughed. "It is not a mess now! Look, look, look!" She pointed at her three piles.

"You sorted them," said Mama. "Now help me shop. Find the foods we need." Penelope found the bread. She found the milk. She put them in the cart, one by one.

At home, Penelope made piles of her own toys. "Animals go here," she said. "Toys go there." Then she took her crayon. She drew a cow on the list. Mama laughed. "Is a cow a food?" she asked.

"No, Mama! A cow is an animal!" said Penelope. "Silly Mama." She kissed the cow picture good night.

Elias sat in a big chair at the mall. His hair was long and it went in his eyes. "I want to see," said Elias. "A haircut will help," said Mom. A hairdresser named Joy came over.
