Joy held up a soft cape. She put the cape around his shoulders. "Look, a superhero cape!" said Elias. He giggled and patted it. Joy began to snip. Little hairs fell down. They landed on the cape. They slid off his shirt and onto the floor.

Elias looked down. "The hairs did not get on me," he said. "No, the cape kept them off," said Joy. She brushed the hairs away. Then she turned the chair to the mirror. Elias saw his face. He could see! He smiled big. Mom took a photo. "New hair, happy boy," she said.

Charles wanted to draw a big sun. He went to get his crayons. But the crayon box was empty. Where did they go?

"Did you leave them somewhere?" Mom asked. Charles thought hard. Then he remembered. The crayons were in the car! He had taken them on the trip to Grandma's house. Charles and Mom went out to the car. The sun was bright and hot. The car felt hot too. Mom opened the door. Charles peeked inside. There was the box on the seat. He picked up a crayon. It felt soft. It bent like a worm! The orange one had gone flat and squishy.

"My crayons are bendy!" Charles said. Mom laughed. "Let's make something new," she said. She carried the box inside. Charles drew his sun with the bendy crayons. The soft tips made fat, smooth lines. It looked like the sun was glowing. "I like my sunny-day crayons," Charles said. He held one up to the window. It bent back and forth, back and forth.

Mohamed's teddy, Bruno, fell on the floor. "Are you sick, Bruno?" Mohamed asked. "Yes, I think you are."

Mohamed got his toy cup. He held it to Bruno's mouth. "Drink your medicine," he said. "Drink it all up." Bruno did not drink, but Mohamed pretended he did. "Good job, Bruno!"

Then Mohamed got a small blanket. He tucked Bruno into bed. "Sleep now," he said. "Sleep, sleep, sleep." He patted Bruno's soft head.

At lunch, Daddy made soup. It was hot, so Daddy blew on it. Mohamed watched. Then he blew on his toy cup too. "My soup is hot, Bruno," he said. "Wait for it."

After lunch, Mohamed looked at Bruno under the blanket. "Do you feel better?" he asked. He made a small voice. "I feel better."

Mohamed smiled. "Time for one more nap." He lay down next to Bruno. "Sleep, sleep, sleep," he whispered. And the room got very quiet.

Evan sat in the backyard with his paint pots. His friend Mia came over with her crayons. Mia held up a dark blue crayon. "This is not blue," she said. "Blue is like the sky."

Evan looked up. The morning sky was light blue. He looked at his paint pot. That blue was dark. He dipped his brush and painted a big wet stripe on the paper. "Look," he said. "Dark blue." Mia dipped her crayon next to it. "Light blue," she said.

They lined up all the blues on the grass. Light blue, blue, dark blue. "They are all blue!" said Mia. Evan painted one more stripe. It was a polite little stripe, small and neat, just for Mia. The paint smelled like rain. A bee buzzed by the yellow flowers, and Mia laughed.

"Red next?" asked Evan. He held up the red pot.

Sarah went to the big hall with her family. The hall had a Christmas tree. It was tall and green. Sarah wanted to hang the ornaments all by herself.

She put a red ball on one branch. Then she put a star there too. Then a little wooden boat. Soon one branch was full. The branch bent down low. "Oh no," said Sarah. "The branch is too heavy."

Grandma came to help. "Try another branch," said Grandma. Sarah hung the red ball up high. She hung the star on the other side. The soft little boat went on a low branch. She counted them: one, two, three. Now the ornaments were all around the tree. The branches stood up tall again.

The tree looked pretty from every side. Sarah smiled and hung one more star, way up high, where everyone could see it.

Colton wanted his favorite book at bedtime. It was the book about the duck. But the shelf was full of books, and he could not find it.

Colton pulled out a book. He opened the front cover. He looked at the first page. This book had a bear in it. Not the duck book. He put it back. He took out another one. He opened it slowly, front cover first. That one had a truck. Not the duck book either.

"Colton, it is bedtime soon," said Dad from the hallway. Colton kept looking. His tummy felt a little jumpy. He wanted the duck book so much.

Then he saw the big words on the front of a book. The words said "Little Duck." Dad had pointed to them one night. Colton ran his smooth finger under the letters. He opened the front cover. Page by page, the duck swam. The duck made its boat float on the pond.

Colton climbed into bed with the book. He turned each page, one at a time. Dad sat down beside him. "Read it," said Colton. Dad started at the front. "Little Duck," he read, "went out one morning."

Arnaud ran to the block corner at school. Tom was already there. Tom had all the blocks.

"Can I play too?" asked Arnaud.

"You can play later," said Tom. "Now I am making a robot."

Arnaud sat down on the small red chair. He looked at the clock. The big hand moved a tiny bit. Was it later now? He went back to Tom. "Is it later yet?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Tom. "My robot is not done."

Arnaud sat down again. He watched Tom stack the blocks. The robot got taller and taller. Where would its arms go? Then Tom picked up the loud drum from the toy shelf. He banged it twice. Boom, boom.

"That is my robot voice," said Tom.

Arnaud laughed. He found a box and began to fill it with crayons. He drew a robot with big square feet. He gave it red eyes and four wheels. The drawing took a long time. He colored the wheels and then the sky.

He looked up. Tom's tower was done. "Is it later now?" Arnaud asked.

Tom looked at the blocks. He looked at Arnaud's drawing. "Yes," said Tom. "It is later now."

They sat down together. Arnaud filled the robot's tummy with blocks. Tom made the loud drum go boom, boom, boom.

"Tomorrow," said Tom, "we can make a spaceship."

"Today is robots," said Arnaud. "Tomorrow is spaceships. And yesterday we made nothing at all."

Tom hit the drum one more time. "Boom," he said. "Robot says yes."

Norah came home with a small cat. The cat was gray and soft. Norah hugged her teddy bear tight. "Where will the cat sleep?" she asked. "In this soft bed," said Dad.

Then Norah had a worry. "Where does the cat go potty?" Dad set a box on the floor. It was full of sand. Norah poured a little more sand in. The cat sniffed the box. The cat stepped in. The cat dug a small hole.

Norah waited. The cat used the box! Then the cat covered the hole with sand. "Wow," said Norah. "That is so smart." Dad smiled. "You are smart too," he said. "You helped make the cat's potty." Norah patted the cat's head. The cat purred like a tiny motor.

Kinsley sat on the playroom floor. She wanted to make a card for Grandma. The card needed a pink flower on it. She looked in her paint box. She found red paint. She found blue paint. She found yellow paint. She found green paint. But there was no pink paint.

Kinsley made the grass first. She painted green grass at the bottom. She painted a yellow sun up high. Then she tried to paint the flower. She dipped her brush in the red paint. She made a red flower. She shook her head. "Grandma wants pink," she said.

Then she saw the white paint jar. She put red paint in a cup. She added a little white paint. She stirred it round and round. She heard a swishy sound. The paint turned pink! Kinsley clapped her hands. She painted a big pink flower.

Then Kinsley washed her brush in the water. The water turned pink too. She laughed. She painted three small pink flowers next to the big one. Mom came in to look. "A pink flower for me?" said Grandma's voice from the door. Kinsley held up the card and ran to her.

Weston ran to the playground with Dad. He saw the tall slide. His tummy felt funny. "I am scared," he said. The slide looked so big.

Dad sat on the bench. "I was scared of slides too," said Dad. Weston stopped. He looked at Dad. Dad was big. Dad was tall. Dad had been scared? Weston thought about that. Grown-ups had feelings too!

Weston held Dad's hand. He walked to the slide. He touched it with one finger. It was cool and smooth. Dad stood close by. Weston climbed one step. Then two steps. His heart went fast, but it felt like happy-fast now.

Down he went! Whee! He laughed and laughed. "I did it!" he said. He was so excited. Then he saw a little girl crying by the swing. Her ice cream had fallen. Weston felt sad for her. Dad had a napkin. He wiped her hands. She smiled.

Then a small dog ran by with a red hat in its mouth. The dog dropped the hat right on Weston's head. Weston laughed again. Dad laughed too. "Home time," said Dad, and Weston held his hand all the way.

Zoey sat in the big salon chair. Her feet did not touch the floor. Today she would get her first haircut.

The hairdresser was named Mia. Mia had a silver comb and small scissors. Zoey was scared of the scissors. "They look pointy," she said.

Mia smiled. "Just watch what I do first," she said. She combed a piece of Zoey's hair. Comb, comb, comb. Then one little snip. Zoey counted on her fingers. "Three combs, then a snip!" she said.

Mia did it again. Comb, comb, comb. Snip. Zoey counted every time. The counting made her forget to be scared.

Then Zoey saw something. The comb made her hair flat and tidy before each snip. The snipped hair fell in neat little pieces, not big messy ones. They slid down like soft rain.

"Your hair is very neat," Zoey said.

"You helped," said Mia. "You kept counting for me."

At dinner that night, Zoey ate a lemon and made a sour face. Then she smiled. "Three combs, then a snip," she said, and she combed her doll's hair with her fingers.

Aubrey wanted to do it all by herself. Daddy had made the toast, and now it sat on her plate. "Can I put on the butter?" she asked. "Yes, you may," said Daddy. Aubrey picked up the little knife. Daddy held it with her, and they spread the soft butter together. The toast turned shiny and gold.

Next came the milk. Aubrey held her cup in one hand. She tried to pour with the other hand. The cup wiggled. The milk made a puddle on the table. "Oops," said Aubrey. She set the cup down on the table first. Then she poured. The cup sat still. The milk went right in, all the way to the top. Not one drop spilled.

"Look what I can do!" said Aubrey. Daddy clapped. Aubrey took a big bite of her buttery toast. Then she drank her milk, sip by sip.

Juliette sat at the art table. She wanted to make a paper sailboat. She had a brown square of paper. She also had a long rectangle for the boat.

But a sailboat needs a sail. Juliette looked and looked. She needed two triangles. She had no triangles at all.

Miss Amy came over. "Hold your square still," she said. She took the scissors. "Scissors are for grown-ups." She cut from one corner to the opposite corner. Then Juliette saw them. Two triangles! The square had made two triangles.

Juliette tapped the triangles on the table. Tap, tap. She glued one triangle on top of the rectangle. The sail stood up tall.

Then she drew a tree on green paper. She added a brown root going down into the dirt. "Don't taste the glue," said Miss Amy. "I won't," said Juliette.

She put her sailboat in her cubby. She could not wait to show Mama. "Look at my sail," she whispered to the boat.

Oliver went to the big cultural center with his mom and his grandma. Today was Hanukkah. The room smelled like pancakes and apples. There were pretty blue and gold flags on the walls.

A tall man stood by a menorah. It had holders for eight candles, plus one more candle in the middle. Oliver wanted to help. "Can I light one?" he asked.

"Grown-ups light the candles," said the man kindly. "But you can count with me." The man used the middle candle to light two little candles. They popped and glowed. Oliver counted out loud. "One, two!" The flames made warm light on his face.

"You know what my secret job is?" said the man. "I come back every night. And each night, we light one more candle." Oliver's eyes got big. "So tomorrow there will be three?" he asked. "And then four?"

"Yes," said the man. "All the way to eight." Oliver held his grandma's hand tight. "Can we come back tomorrow?" he asked. "I want to count again." His grandma smiled. "We will come back," she said. Oliver waved to the little flames. "See you tomorrow, candles."

Evan sat at the paint table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. But there was no orange paint.

Evan looked at the cups. Red paint. Blue paint. Yellow paint. Green paint. No orange at all. He frowned at his paper.

His friend Mia came over. "I know a trick," she said. She put red paint on the brush. Then she added yellow paint. "Now stir it," she said.

Evan stirred slow, then fast. The paint turned orange! "It looks neat!" said Evan. He hurried to paint his pumpkin.

Mia made a green leaf for the top. Then she looked at her paper. "I want purple," she said.

Evan smiled. "Try the trick," he said. Mia stirred blue and red. It turned purple! "Whoa," said Mia.

Their teacher hung both pictures on the wall. Evan pointed at his pumpkin. "Orange is red and yellow," he told her. "I made it myself."

Violet got to daycare in the morning. The sun was low and small. She hung her coat on her little hook. Her friend Ben was already there. They built a tall tower in the block corner.

After lunch, the class lay down for a nap. Violet slept for a long time. When she woke up, she rubbed her eyes. The light in the room was big and gold. "It is morning," said Violet. "Time for breakfast."

Miss Ana smiled. "Look out the window," she said. The sun was high and bright. "It is not morning now. It is afternoon."

Violet looked out. The sun had moved. It was not where it was before. The day had gone on and on, past morning, all the way to afternoon.

"Now we have a cold snack," said Miss Ana. She poured milk into little cups. Violet drank hers slowly. The milk was cold and good.

"After snack we play outside," said Miss Ana. "Later, your mommy comes."

Violet played in the sand. Then the door opened. Mommy stood there with her big bag.

"Mommy! It is afternoon now," said Violet. "And now it is going home time."

Felix put his itchy sweater sleeve up high, out of the way. Mom put two soft white slices into the toaster. Felix waited and counted. "One, two, three," he said. Pop! The slices jumped up. Felix looked and looked. The bread was not white now. It was brown. It crunched when Mom tapped it. "The toaster made it brown and crunchy," he whispered. Mom set the toast on his plate. Felix took the butter knife. He spread, spread, spread, slow and smooth. The butter went soft and melty. Then he held the milk jug with two hands. He poured, a little, a little more. Not one drop spilled. He drank it all and smiled. "Again tomorrow," said Felix. Mom laughed. "We can buy more bread, and you can spread again."

Ruby was at Nana's house. Her tummy was rumbling like a tiny drum. Nana put rice and peas on the table. "Yum!" said Ruby. She picked up her spoon, fast.

Nana held up her hand. "Wait, little one," she said. "We say Bismillah first." Ruby put her spoon down. It went clink on the plate. "Bismillah," Ruby tried. It felt fuzzy in her mouth, like a new sock on the wrong foot. Nana laughed a kind laugh. "Almost! Say it with me."

"Bismillah," they said together. Then Ruby took a big bite. The peas were sweet. Later, after her nap, they would drive to the park. But first, one more bite. "Bismillah," said Ruby, all by herself. Nana clapped her hands.

Amelia ran to the art room. She wore her new blue shirt today. She wanted to paint a big cat.

Teacher Sam held up a red paint pot. "This is red," said Amelia. Then she pointed to the yellow pot. "And that is yellow!" Teacher Sam smiled.

Amelia reached for a brush. Then she stopped. Paint could drip. Paint could splash. Her new shirt was her favorite shirt. She grabbed the big apron from the hook. She put it on all by herself. "Now my shirt is safe," she said.

She scooped red paint. She scooped yellow paint. She mixed them in her tray. The paint turned orange! Amelia clapped. Orange like a pumpkin. Orange like a fox.

She painted a big orange cat. One little drop fell on her apron. Amelia looked down at her shirt. Still clean and blue!

"Look, Teacher Sam!" she called, holding up her work. "My cat is orange and my shirt is still blue!"

Felix stood at the gate of the school playground. His new backpack sat on his back. It was very heavy. He could not walk fast. He wanted to run to the slide, but his feet went slow, slow, slow.

A girl named Mia ran past him. She looked at his big backpack. "Why is it so big?" she asked. Felix sat down on the wooden bench. He opened his backpack. Out came a toy bear. Out came a toy truck. Out came three picture books. The backpack got lighter. Felix put his toys in a safe pile.

Now his backpack was small and light on his back. Felix stood up. He ran to the slide with Mia. His feet went fast, fast, fast. He went down the slide and laughed. "I will remember," said Felix. "A backpack is for carrying, not for toys." Mia held his toy bear, and they went to play again.

Mason stepped onto the big school bus. He held his dad's hand tight. The doors closed with a soft whoosh. Mason sat by the tall glass window.

His tummy felt funny. It felt like little butterflies were in there. Mason looked down at his shoes. He did not say a word.

A boy sat down next to him. The boy had a blue backpack. The boy looked down at his shoes too. Mason tapped the glass with one finger. Tap, tap. The boy looked up. Mason smiled at him. Then the boy smiled back. Mason's tummy felt a little better.

Dad sat across the aisle. He leaned over softly. "My tummy felt funny on my first day too," Dad said. "I was nervous then. It was okay." Mason nodded. He looked out the window again.

The bus stopped by the school. Mason picked up his small backpack. He waved to the boy with the blue backpack. The boy waved back. They walked to the classroom door together. Mason put his hand on the door. He took one big breath. The butterflies flew away, little by little. He pushed the door open, and the room was full of toys.

"Look," said the boy. "Blocks!" Mason ran to see.

Grandma came to sleep in the guest bedroom. Elizabeth helped make the bed. She tucked the blanket in tight. "One pillow for you," she said. "One pillow for Ted the bear." Grandma laughed and put Ted by the window, where a bird was building a nest.

Each day they did things together. One, they baked bread. Two, they picked peas. Three, they read books in the guest room. Elizabeth loved having Grandma there.

Then the week was over. Grandma put her bag by the door. Elizabeth felt wobbly and sad. "Draw me a picture," said Grandma. "Put it in a letter. I will write back." So Elizabeth drew the bird's nest and the blue eggs. Mom helped her mail it. On Friday the phone rang. Grandma's voice said, "Your picture is on my wall!" Elizabeth ran to get her crayons.

Grayson looked out the window. Snow was falling on the grass. "No school today!" said Mom. Grayson clapped his hands. He wanted to find his toy plane. It was lost somewhere outside. He had left it after playing yesterday. Grayson put on his boots. Mom came outside with him. The snow was fresh and bumpy. Then Grayson saw marks on the ground. They looked like little holes in a row. "Look, Mom! What is that?" he asked. "Follow them and see," said Mom. Grayson stepped in the snow. His boots made marks too. His marks looked just like the other marks. He followed them step by step. The marks went past the big tree. They went up to the neighbor's door. There sat his red plane, safe on the step. Grayson laughed. "My feet made marks too, Mom!" They walked home side by side, two trails of footprints behind them, and the plane tucked under his arm.

Ryan sat at the little desk in the library. He had a red pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

He gripped the pencil in his fist. The letters came out wobbly. He tried again with two fingers, like the librarian showed him. That felt better.

Ryan started his R at the right side of the paper. He wrote A, then Y. Uh oh. There was no room left. The N fell off the edge of the page. Ryan made a sour face. "My name does not fit," he said.

He thought for a minute. He looked at the book next to him. The words started at the left side of the page.

Ryan got a new sheet. He started the R on the left this time. A, then Y, then A, then N. They all fit.

The librarian leaned over the desk. "Ryan," she read out loud. She drew a little star next to it. Ryan smiled and traced the letters one more time.

Zachary sat in the school computer lab. His teacher, Miss Ana, put a tablet on the table. "I want to draw," Zachary said. "But I don't know how."

"Press the round button," said Miss Ana. Zachary pressed it. The screen lit up. His eyes went wide. He tapped a green icon. The drawing app opened. "I did it!" he said.

Miss Ana gave him a cup of juice. He set it down next to the tablet. Miss Ana shook her head. She moved the cup to the far table. Zachary watched her. Then he nodded and kept drawing.

He drew a blue pond. He drew a yellow duck on the pond. "That's for you," he told Miss Ana. "I like it," she said.

At last it was time to go. Zachary pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He carried the tablet with two careful hands. He put it back on the shelf, all by himself.

"Can we sell my duck picture at the school fair?" he asked. Miss Ana laughed. "Let's print it first," she said. She held his hand and they walked out together.

Isabella wanted to sing the whole rhyme by herself. Miss Rosa had a shiny drum and a big smile. "Sing with me," said Miss Rosa. "One, two, three, clap!"

They sang very fast. "Hickory dickory dock, the mouse ran up the clock!" Isabella's words got all tangled. She said "hickory hickory dockery" and laughed. The words fell over like blocks.

Miss Rosa tapped the drum slowly. Booom. Booom. "Let's try it slow," she said. Isabella clapped with each slow tap. Her hands went clap, clap, clap. She sang, "Hickory... dickory... dock." The words came out just right. The mouse ran up the clock. The clock struck one. The mouse ran down. Then Isabella sang about a cat with a long tail. "Pussy cat, pussy cat, where have you been?"

Then Miss Rosa tapped the drum fast. Isabella sang the fast song too. Her feet jumped. Her pigtails flew up.

"I did it!" said Isabella. "Fast mouse. Slow mouse. I can do both!"

Miss Rosa tapped the drum one more time. Booom. Booom.

Jasmine ran to the door with her shiny red boots. "Can we go to the park?" she asked. "It is sunny today!"

"First we stop for sunscreen," said Mom. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn."

Jasmine stood still. Mom put white cream on her face, her arms, and her neck. Then they took the long walk to the park.

At the park, the wind blew. The wind made the leaves dance. "Why do the leaves move?" Jasmine asked. "The windy day pushes them," said Mom.

Jasmine looked up at the big sky. No clouds came. The sun stayed out all day. Her friend Ben came with a rain hat, but it was not rainy. "Take it off," Jasmine said, and Ben laughed.

When they got home, Jasmine looked in the mirror. Her skin was not red at all. She clapped her hands and said, "Sunscreen, sunny day, we can go again tomorrow!"

Samuel wanted to build a sand castle in the backyard. It was a sunny morning. He wore his sun hat. Then the sky turned gray. Big clouds came. The wind blew. Samuel's hat flew off. He ran to catch it.

"Rain is coming," said Mama. Samuel ran outside without his coat. The rain came down. His hair got wet. His shirt got wet too. He ran back inside.

Samuel put on his red raincoat. He put on his rain boots. Then he went back out. The rain fell on the raincoat. It ran down the sleeves. His body stayed dry. He looked under the coat. "Dry!" said Samuel. He stomped in a quiet little puddle. The rain went drip, drip, drip. Samuel built his castle in the wet sand.

Wyatt waited at the bus stop with Grandpa. The sun was bright and warm. Wyatt wore his sunny hat. Then the wind blew. It blew the hat right off! Wyatt laughed. "Come back, hat!" The wind pushed a leaf, too. Wind pushed the hat, and the hat pushed the leaf. What a silly wind!

Then dark clouds came. Rain began to fall. Grandpa opened the umbrella. Plip, plip, plop. Then Wyatt heard something. Rumble! It was thunder, loud and sharp. Wyatt wanted to stay and splash in the rainy puddles. But Grandpa took his hand. "Thunder says go indoors," said Grandpa. So they hurried home, fast, fast, fast.

Inside, they looked out the window. The rain fell and fell. Wyatt zipped up his cozy jacket. "Thunder told us to come in," said Wyatt. Grandpa smiled. "Yes it did."

Naomi wanted to win the shape game. "Find a rectangle," said Mom. Naomi looked around the playroom. Her round ball was not it. Her square block had four sides, all the same. That was not it either. Her triangle flag had pointy corners. Not it.

"I am thirsty," said Naomi. She walked to the door to get her cup. She stopped. She looked at the door. It was tall and flat. She put one finger on a corner. "One, two, three, four," she counted. Four corners. She ran her finger down each side. Four sides.

"Mom! The door is a rectangle!"

"You win the game," said Mom.

At snack time, Naomi pointed her fork at her toast. "That is a rectangle too," she said. She took a big bite.

Mohamed wanted his bedtime story. But where was his book?

"Here it is," said Papa. "Yossi gave you this one at daycare."

The book looked funny. It opened from the other side. Mohamed turned it over and over. Which way did it go?

He opened the front cover. The words were all at the wrong end! He flipped the book. Now the words sat at the start. "It goes this way," he said.

The story was about a little turtle. The turtle ate leaves. Then the turtle began to grow. It grew and grew.

Mohamed pointed at the marks on the page. "What are these?" he asked.

"Those are the words," said Papa. "They tell the story."

Mohamed traced the letters with his finger. The letters made words. The words made the turtle! He turned one page, then another. Each page had more story.

The turtle spun in a circle and felt dizzy. Mohamed laughed.

"One more page?" he asked.

Papa turned the page.

Sarah was at Grandma's house. Grandma poured milk into ten little cups on the table. "How many cups, Grandma?" asked Sarah. "Let's count them," said Grandma.

Sarah started at the red cup. "One, two, three, four, five." Grandma started at the blue cup at the other end. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six." They both pointed at cups, one by one, slowly.

"You got ten too?" said Sarah. "I got ten from my side!" She counted again from the middle cup. Ten cups again. She counted from the cat's side. Ten cups again. The gray cat sat under the table and washed his dirty paw.

"Now for the cookies," said Grandma. She put three cookies on one plate and six on another plate. "Which plate has more?" Sarah pointed at each cookie. "This one! This one has more." Grandma smiled and gave her the big plate. "One, two, three, four, five, six," said Sarah.

Brielle got to school early. Her teacher put a pencil on her table.

"Today we write your name," said Miss Kim. Brielle was so happy. She wanted to write her name all by herself.

Brielle picked up the pencil. She jumped up to show her friend Leo. The pencil point waved up in the air. Leo leaned in close to look. The point came near his eye. Miss Kim rushed over fast.

Brielle stopped. She looked at her pencil. She turned it around. Now the point faced down. She walked to Leo slowly, holding it that way. The point stayed far from his face.

"See my pencil?" said Brielle. "Point down."

"Nice holding," said Leo.

Brielle sat back down. She gripped the pencil near the tip. She made a big round B. Then two little r's. She wrote her whole name, one letter at a time.

"I did it!" she said.

Miss Kim smiled. "You counted seven letters," she said.

"Is that a joke?" asked Brielle. "My name is not that long!"

Brielle wrote her name again. It looked even better the second time.

Charlotte went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about dogs. Dogs had four legs and floppy ears.

She found a big picture book. On one page she saw a cow. On the next page she saw a fish. The fish had no legs at all.

"That fish is silly," said Charlotte. "It is not an animal. Animals have legs." She looked at the dog page. She looked at the cow page. Then she looked at the fish again.

Charlotte turned the wheel on the book rack. Round and round it went. All the animal books spun by. Dogs, cows, birds, and fish too.

"Fish live in the water," said Charlotte softly. "But they are still animals." She wanted to yell the good news. Instead she ran to her dad.

"Dad! Fish are animals!" she said.

"That's right," said Dad. "Want to check out that book?"

"Yes, please," said Charlotte. She hugged the big book. Then she picked one more, all about toy trucks and apples and bread.

At home she read the fish page twice.

Lennon held Mom's hand at the store. Yesterday they had no bread. Today the bread shelf was full.

"Is today the library day?" Lennon asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Today is the day. It is happening right now."

Lennon picked a small bread loaf. It felt soft, like a little mouse. She put it in the cart. She wanted to read her library book now.

"We go to the library later," Mom said. "First we pay now."

A man next to them had weak hands. His apples fell and rolled. Lennon picked up one apple. She held it out to him.

"Here," she whispered.

"Thank you, little one," he said.

They paid for the bread. Then Mom smiled.

"Now we go to the library. Today is the day."

Lennon skipped all the way to the car.

Ayla waited in a little room at the doctor's office. She wanted her sticker, but first the doctor had to check her. "Can you see my light?" the doctor asked. Ayla looked with her eyes. She saw the small light blink on and off.

Then the doctor held up a bell. Ding, ding! Ayla heard it with her ears. She sniffed with her nose when the doctor opened a mint tin. It smelled cool and sweet. The doctor gave her a tiny taste on a stick. It tasted like orange.

"Now one more check," the doctor said. She took off Ayla's shoes and socks. She set Ayla's bare feet on a soft green mat. "It feels like grass," the doctor said. Ayla wiggled her toes. The soft grass tickled her feet. She laughed out loud. "Grass feet!" said Ayla. The doctor laughed too, and gave her the sticker.

Mila sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her curly hair bounced as she looked around. On the wall there was a picture of a dog with a bandage on its arm.

"Today you get a shot," said Mom.

Mila frowned. She thought a shot would be very big. She imagined a needle as tall as the door. She imagined it would hurt for a long, long time. She held her bear tight.

"I don't want a big poke," said Mila.

The doctor came in. She held up a small needle. It was thin, like a little stick. It was not tall like the door at all.

"You can hug your bear," said the doctor. "Just look at him."

Mila hugged her bear. She looked at his soft ear. The doctor touched Mila's arm.

"One quick poke," said the doctor.

Mila felt a tiny pinch in her arm. Then it was done. The doctor put on a round bandage. It had yellow stars on it.

"That's it?" asked Mila.

"That's it," said the doctor. "All done."

Mila looked at her arm. The poke was already over. She had waited for something big. But it was just quick and small.

Mila showed Mom her star bandage. "It was fast," she said. "My bear got one too."

The doctor put a small bandage on the bear's arm. Mila smiled and walked out slowly, holding her bear up high.

Mateo ran into Grandma's house. He wanted to hold the new baby. Baby Rosa was sleeping in a little basket.

"I want to hold her now," said Mateo.

"Not standing up," said Grandma. "Come sit with me."

Mateo sat down on the soft couch. Grandma sat right beside him. Then she put Rosa in his arms. "See? You can hold her while you sit," she said.

Rosa was small and warm. She made a tiny sound. Her hand opened and closed. Mateo laughed. "She is trying to tickle me!"

Then Rosa spit up a little. It was slimy on Mateo's shirt. "Yuck!" he said. Grandma wiped it with a cloth. "Babies do that," she said, and she smiled.

Grandpa brought Mateo a glass of milk. Mateo drank it all up. He could not move with the baby, so Grandpa held it for him.

Rosa blinked her eyes. Then she fell asleep in Mateo's arms. He sat very, very still.

"Shh," said Mateo. "My baby is sleeping."

Leah stood in the pool changing room. She pulled on her swim suit all by herself. "Today I will swim," she said.

The pool was big and blue. A lifeguard sat in a tall chair. "Why does she sit up so high?" Leah asked her mom. "I want to see." Leah walked to the side of the pool. From the floor, she could see her mom's knees. Then she sat on the wide step. Now she could see more. Then she stood on the step and looked. From up high, she could see every swimmer in the pool. "I see the whole pool!" she said. The lifeguard was looking at everyone too.

Leah saw a small boy splashing near the rope. The lifeguard blew her whistle. She pointed to him. A grown-up swam over and helped him. "She saw him from up high," said Leah. The pool was quiet again. Leah jumped a little jump into the water. The lifeguard smiled down at her from the tall chair. "I can see you!" Leah called up.

Hudson stood in the big school gym. A red hoop lay on the floor. He wanted the beanbag to land inside it.

Hudson threw the beanbag high over his shoulder. It flew past the hoop. It landed far away with a thumping sound. Miss Kim picked it up. She smiled. "Watch me," she said. She held the beanbag down low. Her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped right into the hoop.

"Can I try that?" Hudson asked. "Yes," said Miss Kim. Hudson held the beanbag low. He swung his arm forward and up. The beanbag rose in the air. It landed on the edge of the hoop. "So close!" said his friend Milo.

Hudson tried again. His arm swung from low down, forward and up. The beanbag went up and fell into the hoop. "I did it!" Hudson said. Milo clapped his hands.

Next Miss Kim rolled a big blue ball to Hudson. He caught it with both hands. He laughed. "That throw was a little messy," Milo said, pointing at his own shoes. Hudson had stepped in a puddle from the rain. "That's okay," Hudson said. He threw the beanbag again. It landed in the hoop one more time.

Asher ran to the playground. He wanted the red swing. But a big girl was on it. Asher's face got hot. He stomped his foot. "I want a turn!" he shouted.

His dad knelt down next to him. "Let's try something," Dad said. "Breathe in slow. Now breathe out slow." Asher made a big breath in. He let it out like a sleepy dragon. Again, in and out. His hot feeling got smaller. His feet stopped wanting to stomp.

"Red swing is free!" the girl called. Asher felt excited. He ran fast. Dad pushed him high. "I see the whole park!" Asher said. He looked up at the sky. The clouds made a big white circle. He pumped his legs harder.

Then the swing went too high. Asher felt scared. "Stop, Daddy!" he yelled. Dad caught the swing. Asher climbed down slow. He sat in the sand and took one slow breath. Then he smiled. "Can we build a castle?" he asked. Dad sat down too. "Yes, let's build it big," he said.

Adam wanted to write a note for Grandpa before bed. He got his crayons and some paper. He wrote all his letters in one long line. "ILOVEYOUGRANDPA," the paper said.

Grandpa came to say goodnight. He held the paper close. He turned it upside down. Then he turned it back. "Hmm," said Grandpa. "The letters are all squished together like a big storm of letters."

Adam looked at his paper. "Can you read my note?" he asked. Grandpa shook his head slowly. "Not yet, little one."

Then Adam saw his bedtime book on the pillow. He opened the front cover. The words had little gaps in them. One word, then a small space, then another word. Adam put his finger on the gap. "There is a space here," he said.

Adam took his crayon again. He drew small spaces in his note. Now it said, "I LOVE YOU GRANDPA." Grandpa read it out loud in a big, warm voice. He gave Adam a hug.

"Stinky feet need washing too," said Grandpa, and he laughed. Adam laughed too. Grandpa tucked him in and read the book from the front to the back. Adam's eyes got sleepy. "Don't forget my note," Adam whispered. Grandpa put it right by the lamp, where he could see it.

Isiah sat at the little table in the school library. Miss Rosa put down a card with a big black B on it. "What sound does this make?" she asked.

"B," said Isaiah. Then he frowned. He wanted to write his own name, but he did not know how to start it.

Miss Rosa gave him a red crayon. Isaiah wrote i-s-a-i-a-h with a small i first. It looked wrong. His name did not look like his name.

Then Miss Rosa held up his name card. The first letter was a big I. It was tall and it seemed to shine on the paper.

Isiah rubbed out his small i. He drew a big I instead. "Isaiah!" he read out loud.

Miss Rosa clapped. Isaiah smiled and drew a ball next to his name, just for fun.

The bookmobile came to Ethan's street. It was a big blue bus full of books. Ethan held his mama's hand. He wanted a library card of his very own.

Inside, the shelves were tall. The books were way up high. Ethan could not see the covers. "Too high," he said. He stretched his toes. Still too high.

Then he saw something in the back. A little corner with tiny shelves. The books there had big, bright covers. One was about a squishy frog. Ethan could reach it all by himself. "Mama, small books! For me!"

The library lady smiled. "That is the children's area," she said. "Books just for young kids like you." She helped Ethan write his name. His new card was blue, just like the bus.

Ethan picked the frog book. "Can I take him home for lunch?" he asked. The lady laughed. "He can sit next to your sandwich." Ethan carried the book to the desk. The lady beeped it with her scanner. Beep!

Ethan waved to the bookmobile as it drove away. He hugged the frog book tight. "See you, froggy," he whispered.

James wanted to build a tower of ten blocks. He patted the carpet flat first. He put down one block, then two blocks. Then he stopped. "What comes after two?" he asked himself. He could not think of it. His big sister was singing on the rug. She sang, "One, two, buckle my shoe." James listened. Three! He clapped his hands. The song gave him the word. He stacked three, then four, then five. The tower wobbled. It fell down with a big crash. James giggled and started again. His sister sat close and sang with him. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" James put on the last block, quick, before it could tip. The tower stood tall. "Ten blocks!" said James. His sister patted his head. Then James counted them all again, touching each one. "One, two, three," he sang, all the way up to ten.

Bennett was at Grandma's house. Grandma was knitting a small blue blanket. "The baby is coming soon," she said. Bennett patted the tiny blanket. "Babies are so small," he said.

The next day, Dad took Bennett to the baby store. They pushed a big cart. Dad put in diapers. Then more diapers. Then even more diapers. Bennett counted them. "One, two, three, four, five, six!" A girl next to them stared. "Why so many diapers?" she asked her mom. Bennett listened hard.

At home, the baby came. Her name was Rosie. Rosie drank milk. Then Rosie made a wet diaper. Grandma changed it. Then Rosie drank more milk. Then another wet diaper. Grandma changed that one too. "Six diapers, then more," said Bennett. He put the diapers, one by one, into the basket.

Bennett picked up his pencil. He made a card for Rosie. Grandma helped him cut around the edges. One snip, then another snip. Rosie began to cry. She sounded sad. Bennett waited by her basket. Dad picked her up and rocked her. Soon Rosie went to sleep. Bennett laid the card beside her. "One baby, one card," he whispered. "Night night, Rosie."

Maya ran to the park with her bear, Bobo. She wanted to play house, but she had no house here. She looked around fast. She saw a big flat rock. She put Bobo on the rock. "This is your bed," she said.

Then she found a stick. She tapped the stick on the rock. "Time to eat, Bobo!" There was no food, really. But Maya made a face like she was stirring a pot. She held out her hand. "Here is your soup." Bobo said nothing. Maya pretended he ate it all up. She clapped. "You love soup!"

A boy named Sam ran over. He was holding his toy plane. "I am a pilot!" he said. He made a big zoom sound. Maya wanted to be on the plane too. But where could she sit? She looked at the ground.

She pointed at the wood chips. "This is the plane!" she said. She sat down and buckled an invisible belt. Sam sat next to her. He held his plane up high. "We fly to the beach!" Zoom, zoom! Maya heard the wind in the trees. It sounded just like a plane.

Then a dog ran by and grabbed Bobo! Maya jumped up. "My baby!" she cried. The dog dropped Bobo in the soft grass. Maya ran and picked him up. She hugged him tight. "We are home now, Bobo," she said. Sam zoomed his plane one more time over her head. "Good night, plane!" Maya called.

Emmett sat at the dinner table. He wanted grapes. "Can I have three grapes?" he asked. Mom said, "Yes, three grapes for you."

Mom put grapes on his plate. One, two, three. But these grapes were big, big, big. Emmett looked at them. Were big grapes still three? Maybe big grapes counted as more?

He counted them with his finger. "One, two, three," he said. He pushed them apart. Still three. He pushed them together. Still three! He giggled. Big or small, three was three.

Then Dad slid over a bowl. "Look what I have." Dad counted his grapes. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten little grapes!

Emmett leaned close. "Dad, do ten little grapes equal three big ones?" Dad laughed. "Count and see." Emmett pointed at his plate. "One, two, three." He pointed at the bowl. "Ten is more. Ten wins!"

Then Mom held up a rainbow cup. "Want three milk pours in here?" Emmett nodded. He watched the milk pour. "One, two, three," he said. He picked up a big grape and plopped it in. "Now it's a grape bath!"

Dad said, "You teach me something new every day." Emmett took a bite. "Three bites!" he said. "One, two, three."

Carter went to the store with Mom. He wanted to find the squishy red ball. "Stay with me," said Mom. Carter held her hand.

Then he saw the balls far away. He let go of Mom's hand. He skipped down the big aisle. He turned around. He could not see Mom. The aisle was too long. Carter looked and looked. He walked back the way he came. Then he saw Mom's blue coat. He ran to her fast.

"There you are," said Mom. "I like to see you." Carter held her hand again. They found the red ball together. It was soft and squishy in his hands. At the checkout, a man pushed a cart of hot soup. "Step back," said Mom. Carter stepped back and waited. He squeezed his new ball and smiled. "Home now," he said. Mom squeezed his hand. They walked out the door together.

Josephine sat at the art table. She picked up a red crayon. She drew a big red apple. Next to her, Ben drew a yellow sun. It looked warm and bright.

Josephine wanted to draw snow. She took white paper. She drew and drew. But her snow did not show up. The paper was white too. Her snow was hiding! She frowned. "I can't see my snow," she said.

Then she saw green paper in the bin. No, wait. She found blue paper. She drew soft white snow on it. Now the snow showed up! It was white on the blue. "Look, Ben!" she said. Ben smiled back. She drew a green tree under the snow. "I can share my blue paper," Josephine said. Ben gave her a hug. "That is not mean at all," he said. "That is nice." Josephine hung her picture up to dry.

Nova put on her clean dress. It was Eid morning. The street outside had flags and balloons. Music played, and it smelled like sweet bread.

Mama knelt down by the door. "When people come, you can say Eid Mubarak," she said. Nova practiced in a small voice. "Eid Mubarak." She tried again, a bit louder. Then the bell rang.

Nova opened the door. Auntie Ruby stood there with a sparkly bag. Nova took a big breath. "Eid Mubarak!" she said. Auntie Ruby smiled wide and hugged her. "Eid Mubarak to you too!" Then Uncle Ben came, and Nova said it again. Then Grandma came, and Nova said it once more.

Every time she said it, someone smiled at her. Then came a small surprise. A tiny cousin said it back to Nova, all by himself. Nova gave him a high five. "Eid Mubarak," she said, one more time.

Hayden sat at the paint table at daycare. He wanted to paint green grass. But the green paint pot was empty. "Oh no," said Mia. She was painting grass too. Mia looked grumpy.

Then Mia dipped her brush in blue paint. She dipped it in yellow paint too. She stirred them together on her paper. The paint turned green! Hayden leaned close. He saw the blue and yellow make green.

"One dip blue, one dip yellow," Hayden said. He stirred his own brush round and round. Green! He painted tall grass. Mia painted a bunny in the grass. The sun did shine in the window. Their teacher smiled at the wet green paintings. "Bunny!" said Mia. "Grass!" said Hayden. They hung the pictures on the wall to dry.

Aurora waited at the gate for her daddy. The sun was warm on her nose. Her tummy rumbled. She wanted her snack right now. But first, her teacher said, everyone must wash hands. Aurora felt worried. "I am too hungry to wait," she said. Her teacher smiled. "Washing is quick," she said. "Then we eat."

Aurora stood at the little sink. She pumped one drop of soap onto her palm. She rubbed her hands under the water. Bubbles grew! She rubbed more, and the bubbles got thick and white. She spread them on her chin. Now she had a fluffy soap beard! Milo stood next to her, looking sad. He had dropped his cracker at snack time. Then he saw Aurora's white beard. He giggled and giggled.

Milo pumped soap too. He rubbed his hands with water. Bubbles grew on his hands too. He made soap whiskers. "We are bubble bears!" he said. The teacher laughed. Then they rinsed all the bubbles off. The teacher helped them dry their hands on the soft towel.

Daddy was at the gate now. He lifted Aurora up for a hug. "Tonight we will have your bath after dinner," he said. "Can I bring my rubber duck?" Aurora asked. Daddy kissed her soapy-smelling hair. "The duck, the boat, and both of us," he said.

Clara ran to school. Today was scarf day! She could not wait.

"Look at my scarf," said Ben. His scarf was long. It went down to his shoes. Clara held up her scarf. It was short. It stopped at her tummy.

"I want a long scarf," said Clara. "Mine is too short for the cold wind." She tried to stretch it. It would not grow. She frowned.

Then Clara had a big idea. "Let's share!" She put her short scarf on her neck. Ben wrapped his long scarf around her too. Now Clara was warm from top to toes.

At art time, Clara wanted to draw an ocean. The ocean was so big! Her paper was so small. "I will draw a short wave," she said. She drew a little wave and a big wave. It looked like the sea!

At nap time, Clara was sleepy. She snuggled into Ben's long scarf like a blanket. "Warm," she whispered. "Nice and warm."

Violet put on her new swim suit. Mom drove her to the pool by the lake. The water looked big and shiny in the light.

Violet stood at the edge. She wanted to swim. But she did not want to put her face in the water. "What if the water bites my nose?" she asked. Her teacher, Miss Kim, smiled. "Watch me," said Miss Kim. She leaned down. She put her mouth near the water. Then she blew. Bloop, bloop, bloop! Big bubbles popped up.

Violet laughed at the bubbles. She leaned down too. She put her mouth close to the water. She blew. Bloop, bloop! The water did not bite at all. It made bubbles. Violet blew again, bigger this time. Mom clapped from her chair. Miss Kim held Violet's hand. "Again," said Violet, and she leaned down for more.

Paisley stood in the restaurant kitchen with her grandma. Grandma had warm toast on a big plate. "You can help," said Grandma. "Let's put butter on the toast."

Paisley picked up a little knife. Grandma held the knife too, so it stayed safe. Together they spread the butter. The butter went on soft and smooth. "Now watch," said Grandma.

Paisley looked at the toast. The butter was hard and yellow. Then it began to shine. Then it turned into a little wet puddle. Paisley touched the plate near the edge. "It's gone!" she said. "The butter ran away!"

Grandma smiled. "It melts on the warm toast," she said. "Look, it is still there. It is just soft now." Paisley leaned close. The butter had made the toast shiny all over. She took a small bite. The toast tasted good.

Next, Grandma gave Paisley a small cup. "Now we pour milk," she said. Paisley held the cup with both hands. Grandma held the little jug. They poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. "I did it!" said Paisley. Grandma clapped. Outside the window, a bird sat in a tree. Paisley waved at it with her milky cup.

Weston was hungry. The festival smelled like warm bread. His tummy made a big growl. "Was that a cloud rumbling?" asked Auntie May. Weston laughed. "That was me!"

They sat down at a long table. Many families sat there too. Weston saw big plates of rice and beans. He saw salty crackers in a bowl. He grabbed one cracker right away.

Then he saw that no one else was eating. Grandpa stood up. Grandpa said the family blessing. His voice was low and kind. Weston looked at his hand. He put the cracker down on his plate. He folded his hands and waited.

Grandpa said the last word. Then everyone picked up food at once. Weston munched his cracker. "It tastes better when we wait together," said Auntie May. Weston's tummy growled again. "There goes your thunder cloud," said Grandpa. Weston giggled so hard that a bean rolled off his plate.

The wind blew hard outside. Sienna stood by the window with Mama. The big tree bent and swayed. Then all the lights went out. The room went dark.

Sienna grabbed Mama's hand. "The dark came," she said. "The wind did it," said Mama. "It knocked out the power." They heard the wind howl again. Sienna listened hard. Papa came with a flashlight. He clicked it on. The light came back, small and bright.

They sat on the couch together. Sienna held her plastic bunny. She looked out at the wind, then at the dark lamp. "Wind blows, lights sleep," she said. Mama smiled and wrapped her in a soft blanket. The rain tapped on the glass. The flashlight glowed warm. Soon the wind grew quiet. All the lights popped back on. Sienna waved at her bright lamp. "Hello, light," she said.

Lincoln was at Grandma's house. His new baby sister was coming. Lincoln wanted to hold her, but he had to wait.

Grandma baked bread. Lincoln could smell it. The bread was warm and squishy. "Can baby sister eat bread?" he asked. "No," said Grandma. "Babies drink milk. Grown-ups feed her many times, day and night."

At night, Lincoln heard a small cry. Baby sister was awake. Mama fed her milk. In the morning, she cried again. Mama fed her again. "Baby eats one, two, three times, and more," said Lincoln. "Just like Grandma said."

Then Mama sat on the big soft couch. She put baby sister in Lincoln's arms. He held her very still. The baby made a tiny sound. Lincoln smiled and counted her little fingers, one, two, three, four, five.

Nicholas sat on his bed with his big bear book. He wanted Dad to read it. "Dad! Come read to me!" Dad came in and sat down.

Dad opened the book. He looked at the front page. Then he turned the pages one by one. He read from the front to the back. Nicholas watched Dad's eyes. They went along the little black marks. "Dad, what are those marks?" he asked. "Those are words," said Dad. "They tell me what to say."

Nicholas turned a page. This page had no marks on it. Only a big picture of a bear. "Read this one!" he said. Dad looked at the page. "There are no words here," he said. "Nothing is written on this page." Nicholas tapped the picture. "So the bear says nothing?" he asked. "The bear just looks," said Dad.

Nicholas turned to the next page. Little marks were there again. Dad read them out loud. The bear found honey! Nicholas clapped his hands. Then he turned back to the picture page. He made up his own words. "The bear is quiet," said Nicholas. Dad laughed. "That page is wrong," said Nicholas. "It has no words to read!" He turned the page and pointed. "Read this one, Dad. This one has words."

Amelia wanted the little toy mouse. It lived in the big red box. The box sat on the small rug.

Tom put blocks in the box. Plunk, plunk. Then Sam took blocks out. Plunk, plunk. The mouse hid under the blocks each time.

"How will I find my mouse?" Amelia asked.

"Look in the box," said Miss Kim.

Amelia looked in. She saw blue blocks. She did not see the mouse. "Was that fast or slow?" Tom asked, dropping one block.

"Fast!" said Amelia. She laughed. Then Sam pulled blocks out, slow, one by one.

Miss Kim brought warm soup for snack. "Careful, it is hot," she said. She blew on Amelia's bowl. Amelia touched her cold cup of milk. Hot soup, cold milk.

The box got empty. All the blocks were out. Amelia peeked in again. There was the mouse! Its gray ears poked up.

"Hello, mouse," she said. "Do you want to grow bigger?" The mouse stayed small, of course.

Amelia put the mouse in her pocket. Then she put all the blocks back in the box. In, in, in. The rug looked tidy at last.

Sam held up one red block and smiled. "Out again?" he asked.

"No, Sam," said Amelia. "In!"

Harrison went to the library with his mom. There was a big rug with pictures on it. Some pictures were animals. Some pictures were toys. Some pictures were foods.

A librarian gave Harrison a carrot, a plastic apple, and a plastic slice of bread. "Where do they go?" she asked. Harrison put the carrot with the toys. He put it next to the teddy bear. The librarian smiled and waited. Harrison looked and looked. Then he moved the carrot. He put it with the apple. He put it with the bread. "Apple, bread, carrot," he said. "Foods!" The librarian clapped.

Harrison picked up a black toy car. "Is this a food?" he asked. He answered himself. "No. It is a toy." He put the car with the toys. Then he sat down and made a vroom sound. His mom sat beside him and read him a book.

Anna climbed the big school bus. She held her lunchbox tight. It was red with a plane on it.

A boy sat down next to her. He had a red lunchbox too. It had a plane on it too!

"Oh no," said Anna. "Same lunchbox!"

The bus went bump, bump, bump. The two lunchboxes slid under the seat. Anna reached down. She picked one up. But which one was hers?

Then Anna looked at the lid. She saw letters there. "A-N-N-A," she read. "That is me! This one is mine!"

The boy looked at his lid too. "Tom," he said. "This one says Tom. That is me!"

Anna laughed. "Your name found your lunchbox," she said.

"My name is smart," said Tom. He grinned.

At school, the teacher helped them paint. Anna painted a big red plane. Under it, she painted her name.

"That is a smart picture," said Tom.

Anna held it up high. "Now everyone knows it is mine!"

Eloise sat on her bedroom floor. Her teddy bear, Blue, sat on the table. Eloise wanted to hug him. But Blue was too far away.

Then Eloise saw her big brother Tom in the doorway. Tom had a big frown. His mouth turned down at the corners. His eyebrows made little hills.

"Tom looks sad," Eloise said. She felt sad too. She did not want Tom to be sad.

Eloise pointed to Tom's face. "You look sad," she said.

Tom nodded. "I lost my toy truck," he said.

Eloise looked under the table. She looked by the bed. Then she saw something red under the blanket. "Look!" she said.

Tom's frown went away. Now his mouth curved up. He was happy! He hugged the red truck. Then he hugged Eloise too.

Eloise smiled big. She felt excited and warm inside. Tom put Blue in her lap.

Eloise hugged her bear tight. "Happy faces," she said. Tom laughed and clapped.

Sofia was going camping with her family. She packed her little bear in a bag. "Time to get in the car," said Mama. Sofia climbed into her car seat. She was so excited. She hugged her bear tight. But the straps hung loose. Nobody clicked the buckle.

Daddy sat in the front. He looked back. "Hmm," he said. "The car will not go yet." Sofia waited. The car was still. "Why is the car waiting?" she asked. She looked down at her seat. Then she heard it. Click! Daddy had buckled her straps snug and safe.

The car started to roll. "The car heard the click!" said Sofia. Outside, the trees went by. Sofia felt the soft strap on her chest. She held her bear on her lap. "Now we can pretend to drive far away," she said. "Beep beep," said Daddy, and they drove on.

Myles wanted the puppy book. It was up on his bed. He climbed up next to it, not on the shelf, and held the book in his lap.

The book was upside down. The dog in the picture looked funny. Myles turned the book over. Now the dog sat right side up. "Good dog," said Myles.

He put his finger on the words. He started at the right side of the page. He slid his finger along. The words went the wrong way. Dad sat down next to him. Dad took Myles's hand. He set the finger down at the left side of the page. "Try here," said Dad.

Myles slid his finger from left to right. The words marched along in a line, one after another. Dad read them out loud. "The puppy chewed his fresh bone all day." Myles laughed. The puppy had chewed a big hole!

Myles turned to the front page. He turned pages one by one, front to back. Each page had more words. Each page had more puppy. He slid his finger from left to right again and again.

At the last page, the puppy was asleep. "The end," said Dad. Myles hugged the book. "Read it again!" said Myles. Dad smiled and turned back to the front.

Luca stood at the bus stop with Mama. The sun came out. "Sunny now," said Luca. But the wind blew hard. His hat flew off. "Wind," said Luca. Mama picked up his hat. She put it back on his head.

Yesterday it had rained. Luca saw water on the ground. A big puddle sat by the bench. "Look, Mama! Water!"

"Rain made that puddle," said Mama. Luca stepped in the puddle. Splash! His shoe got wet. He stepped again. Splash, splash!

"My boot is wet," said Luca. He frowned. "Cold foot."

"We can fix that," said Mama. She opened her big bag. She pulled out dry socks. "I was ready for puddles." Luca sat on the bench. He chewed his cracker while Mama put the dry socks on his feet. Warm again!

Then Luca looked up. Little white flakes fell down. "Snow!" said Luca. Mama zipped his coat up high. She put his mittens on his hands.

"Snow makes the ground white," said Luca. He pointed at the bench. The snow sat on top, soft and thin.

The bus came around the corner. Luca jumped up like a spring. He held Mama's hand tight. They climbed the big steps together.

"Bye, puddle!" Luca called out the window.

Iris went to the pharmacy with Grandpa. The pharmacy sold soap, and Iris wanted the pink soap. "We need soap for hand washing," said Grandpa. Iris picked a pink bottle. "Good pick," said Grandpa. "You are so smart."

At home, Iris had to use the toilet. Then she ran to the sink. But the sink was too high. Her hands could not reach the water. "I can't wash!" she cried.

Grandpa brought a step stool. He set it by the sink. He stood right next to her. Iris climbed up. Now her hands reached the water! She pumped the pink soap. Grandpa said, "Wash while we count to twenty." They counted together. One, two, three, all the way to twenty.

The bubbles went down the drain. Iris held her hands up to the sun by the window. They were shiny and clean. "Now I can eat my sandwich," she said.

Daniel went to the park with Grandma. The sun was warm. The water in the little creek was cold. Daniel put one toe in. "Brrr," he said. He pulled his toe out fast. Cold water made him shiver.

Daniel saw something red by the bench. It was a little lighter. Grandma had one like it at home. Grandma used it for the big candle. Daniel did not touch it. He kept his hands in his pockets. He ran to Grandma. "I see something," he said. He pointed with one finger.

Grandma walked over slow. She looked down. She picked up the lighter. "Good boy," she said. "That is for grown-ups." She put it in her bag. Then they fed the ducks together. The ducks splashed in the water. Daniel laughed and clapped. Soon the sky turned orange. It was getting late. "Time to go," said Grandma. Daniel held her hand all the way home.

Jake had a cold. He had to blow his nose a lot. His tissues piled up on his bed.

Mom brought a small bin. She put it by his shoe on the floor. "Look," she said. She dropped one tissue in. Plunk!

Jake sat up. Could he do that too? He picked up a tissue. He held it up high. He let it go. It fell into the bin. Plunk!

Jake giggled. He found another tissue. This one was a little shy of the bin. It missed and landed on his shoe. Jake picked it up. He moved closer to the bin. He dropped it in. Plunk!

One tissue was stuck to his blanket. He pulled it off. He dropped it in. Plunk! Now the bed was all clean. The bin was full of tissues.

Jake clapped. "Look, Mom! All fixed!"

Mom smiled. "Nice work," she said. Then she held up one more tissue. "Can you do it again?"

Jake reached out his hand. "Drop it!" he said.

Henry sat in his car seat. The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow up a hill. The wind outside made a windy sound. Henry rolled down his window a little bit.

"My cup is empty," said Henry. He tipped it upside down. Not one drop came out. "I want it full," he said.

Dad stopped the car at a little shop. He bought cold water from the big fridge. Dad poured the water into Henry's cup. Henry watched. He poured too fast at first, and water splashed over the top. "Whoa," said Henry. Dad poured slow instead. The water went up and up. It stopped right at the top. The cup was full now, not empty.

Henry drank a little. The water was cold on a hot day. "We pay for the water here," said Dad, and Henry helped put the coins on the counter.

Back in the car, Henry held his full cup with two hands. He took one small sip. "Slow," said Henry. Dad smiled and drove slowly down the hill.

Bennett sat on the yellow rug in the music room. Miss Rosa played a song on her drum. "Clap along," she said.

Bennett clapped fast, fast, fast. His hands went everywhere. The claps did not match the drum at all. His friend Milo put his hands in his lap. "Too tricky," said Milo.

Miss Rosa played the drum again. Boom. Boom. Boom. Bennett closed his eyes and listened. He waited. Then he clapped one time with each boom. Boom, clap. Boom, clap. His claps landed right on the beat. "I did it!" he said. He took Milo's hands. "Listen first," said Bennett. "Then clap." They clapped together, boom by boom.

Then they sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" from memory. Miss Rosa hid her paper with the words, just to see. The boys sang every word. She gave them each a cup of milk. Bennett took a big drink and clapped one more time, boom.

Gabriel sat at the kitchen table. Mom gave him a big pencil and pink paper.

"I will write my name!" said Gabriel.

He held the pencil in his fist. He made a G. It came out wobbly. He made an A. It fell over like a sleepy cat. Gabriel frowned. His name looked wrong.

Mom put a pink eraser on the table. "Try this," she said.

Gabriel rubbed the eraser on the wobbly G. He looked close. The mark was gone! The paper was clean again.

"Again!" said Gabriel.

He rubbed out the sleepy A too. Then he held the pencil with his fingers, the way Mom showed him. He wrote G. It stood up tall. He wrote A. It sat up straight.

Gabriel jumped from his chair. He ran to the woman washing dishes at the sink.

"Look, Grandma! I wrote Gabriel!"

Grandma held the paper up high. "My clever boy!" she said.

Gabriel looked at his name on the pink paper. He smiled big. "I want to write it ten more times!"

Oliver sat at the dinner table. He wanted his peas to be a rocket ship. "Can peas fly?" he asked. "Let's try," said Dad.

Dad put ten peas on Oliver's plate. Brown bread sat beside them. Oliver pointed at each pea. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Dad said that was good counting.

"Now we go down," said Dad. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six." Oliver ate one pea each time. "Five, four, three, two, one." One pea was left. "Blast off!" said Oliver. He popped it in his mouth and jumped up from his chair.

"What was that?" Oliver asked. "A countdown," said Dad. "Again!" said Oliver. Dad fetched more peas, one by one, until the bowl was empty.

"Ten, nine, eight," said Oliver slowly. He waited between each pea. "Seven, six, five." Mom clapped her hands. "Four, three, two, one. Blast off!" The last pea went up, up, into Oliver's mouth.

Dad laughed. "My rocket boy," he said. "Bedtime countdown next. Ten, nine, eight..." Oliver giggled all the way down to one.

Evan wanted to sort his things in the backyard. He made three piles. One pile for animals. One pile for toys. One pile for foods.

First he put the apples in the food pile. "One apple, two apples," he said. Then he put the banana there too. The food pile was growing.

Next came the animals. A ladybug landed on a leaf. "Animal," said Evan. He heard a bird sing. "Animal," he said again. He watched a squirrel run up the tree. "Animal," he said, and laughed.

Then he held his favorite stuffed dog. It was brown and soft. He set it in the animal pile. He looked at the squirrel. It ran and jumped. He looked at his stuffed dog. It just sat there. It did not eat. It did not bark. It was not alive. Evan picked it up and put it in the toy pile, next to his red ball. "One toy, two toys," he said.

His dad came out with a snack. "Nice sorting," Dad said. "Can I ride my toy truck too?" Evan asked. Dad smiled. "After your snack," he said. Evan bit the apple and waved it at the toy pile.

Isabelle went to the farm with Grandpa. She wanted to find a gift for Mama. "Let us look," said Grandpa. They walked past the cows. Isabelle saw a shiny red apple in the basket. She picked it up.

"Now close your eyes," said Grandpa. Isabelle closed her eyes. "What do you hear?" "A duck," she said. She heard the duck quack. "Good. Ears hear," said Grandpa.

Then Grandpa held up a lemon. "Taste this," he said. Isabelle licked it. Her mouth went tight. "Sour!" she said. Then she licked a strawberry. "Sweet!" she said. "My tongue knows." Grandpa laughed.

Isabelle sniffed the hay. "Nose smells," she said. She touched the soft lamb. "Hands feel." She looked at the shiny apple. "Eyes see." She put the apple in her bag. At home, Mama bit the apple. "Sweet," said Mama. Isabelle clapped her hands. "My tongue said so first," she said. Mama gave her a strawberry from the bowl.

Ivy went to the library on a hot summer day. She wanted to draw on the big tablet there. But the screen was dark. She poked it. Nothing happened. She tapped it with two fingers. Still nothing.

A librarian named Sam walked by. "Try the little round button," Sam said, "on the side." Ivy found it. She pressed the button. The screen woke up. Ivy pressed it again, and the screen went dark. She pressed it one more time. The screen woke up again. "On and off, like a light," said Sam, laughing.

Ivy opened the drawing app. She drew a cat with a purple hat. Then she drew a dog with a pancake. When she was done, she remembered the little button. She pressed it, and the screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf.

"Bye, dark screen," said Ivy.

Josephine wanted the big red fire truck. It sat inside a big box on the shelf. The box looked fun. Maybe more trucks were hiding in there.

Josephine pulled the box. It did not move. She pulled again. Still no. The box was heavy. "Oof," she said. She sat down on the rug to wait and think. Her teacher came over. "Want some help?" she asked. "Yes please," said Josephine. Together they pulled one more time. Slowly, the box slid down. It made a big bump on the rug.

Inside was a soft yellow pillow. Josephine picked it up. Up it came, so easy! The pillow was light. She hugged it and carried it fast across the room. Then she walked back slow, so the pillow would not fall. Her friend Ben patted the pillow. "Soft," he said. Josephine kissed the pillow, right on the corner. "My light pillow," she said. "My big truck can ride on top." She set the red fire truck on the pillow and marched around the rug, holding it high.

Alexis sat at the big table. His friend Sam from school came for dinner. Alexis had his red car in his pocket.

After the food, Alexis put the car on the table. He pushed it fast. Vroom, vroom. Sam watched. Sam reached out his hand.

Alexis held the car tight. His tummy felt tight too. He wanted to grab it away. But then he sat still. He took one slow breath. Then two. Then three. His tummy felt soft again.

"You can have a turn," Alexis said. He gave Sam the car. Sam pushed it across the table. The wheels made a little sound. Sam laughed. Alexis laughed too.

"Watch this," said Sam. He rolled the car to Alexis. It bumped his cup. Alexis picked it up. It was his turn again. He washed his hands first, because they were sticky, and then he rolled the car back to Sam.

Daddy set down a plate of warm bread. It smelled good. Mom touched Alexis's ear gently and smiled at him.

"My turn, your turn," said Alexis. He rolled the car one more time, all the way across the tablecloth.

Jacob stood in the bathroom. Mom ran the bath water. Jacob put his hand near the faucet. "Hot water is for me to turn," said Mom. Jacob watched her feel the water. "Just right now," she said.

Jacob took off his socks. His toes touched the warm floor. He heard the water splash. He heard the tub fill up. Then he sniffed. He sniffed again. "Mom! I smell spaghetti!" "Yes," said Mom. "Dad is cooking it now." Jacob had not seen the spaghetti. But his nose knew first. He liked that.

Jacob got in the tub. The warm water touched his legs. He splashed with his hands. "Don't miss your ears," said Mom. She washed behind them. Then she dried him with his big furry towel. It was soft on his cheeks. Dad called from the kitchen, "Dinner, little man!" Jacob sniffed the air one more time and grinned. "Spaghetti time!"

Jaxon marched into the living room. The big game was on TV. Dad was there. Grandma was there. Uncle Ben was there too. Jaxon climbed onto the soft couch and clapped his hands.

"Go, go, go!" Jaxon shouted. One team wore red shirts. One team wore blue shirts. The red team ran and ran. They ran so fast! The blue team ran slowly, like a turtle. Then the blue team kicked the ball. It went into the net! The blue team got a point. Later, the blue team kicked it in again. Two points for blue!

The game ended. The whistle blew. "Red ran more," said Jaxon. "Red wins!" Uncle Ben laughed. "Look at the numbers," he said. He pointed to the big screen. The score said blue had two. Red had one. Blue had more points. Blue won the game. Blue got the shiny gold cup.

Jaxon clapped and jumped up and down. "Blue has more points! Blue wins!" Grandma gave him a hug. Dad put a red hat on Jaxon's head. "Maybe next time," said Dad. Jaxon grinned and shouted, "Let's watch one more game!"

Leah went to the library with her mom. She wanted a book about dogs. Where would a dog book hide?

Leah saw a shelf with a sign. The sign said "Animals." She found books with cats, elephants, and dogs. She patted the dog on the cover. "Hello, dog," she said.

Next to her, a boy named Sam was playing with blocks. He put all the red blocks in one pile. "Red here," he said. Then Sam laughed. He mixed them up. He put all the big blocks in one pile instead. The same blocks, but in a new way!

Leah looked at the shelves again. The animal books were all together. But she saw something new. On another shelf, books stood in a rainbow. Red books, then yellow books, then green books. Same books, different shelves!

"Mom, look," said Leah. "The books moved!" Mom smiled. "Someone sorted them by color today."

Leah picked her dog book. It was blue. She held it up to the blue shelf. "You belong here," she said, "but you come home with me."

At the desk, the librarian let Leah stamp the book. Thump went the stamp, right on the page. Leah touched her nose to the dog's nose on the cover. "Good dog," she whispered.

Ezra went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought warm bread, fresh butter, and a big carton of milk. "Can I have toast here?" Ezra asked. "Yes," said Dad. "I will teach you to make it."

Dad got bread and butter from the bread stand. He held the hot toast himself. Then he gave Ezra a small knife. Ezra spread the butter. He made it flat and smooth. "I did it!" said Ezra. "Now milk," said Ezra.

Ezra tried the big milk carton. It was too heavy. Milk nearly spilled. Dad saw Ezra's face. He poured some milk into a little jug. Ezra picked up the little jug. It was light in his hands. He tipped it slowly. Milk went into the cup. Not one drop spilled. Ezra took a sip. "Dad, was the big carton too big for me?" "Yes, little jug, little hands," said Dad. Ezra grinned and poured himself some more.

Jasper wanted to find his red ball. It was not on the shelf. It was not under the rug. That was a problem.

Jasper looked at the toy box. It was full of blocks. It was full of dolls too. He could not fit one more thing. "I guess I will make room," he said.

Jasper picked up a block. "You are a toy," he said. He set it on the shelf. He picked up a doll. "You are a toy too." He set it by the block. Soon the box had room. He peeked inside. There was the red ball, hiding at the bottom!

Jasper gave the ball a gentle pat. His little sister came in. She could not reach her doll. Jasper picked up the doll and handed it to her. She smiled big.

"Ball?" she said, pointing.

"Yes," said Jasper. "Let's roll it together."

Sienna sat at the craft table at summer camp. She wanted to make a paper sun. The sun needed lots of yellow strips.

"Can I use the big scissors?" Sienna asked. Ms. Rosa held up a small pair instead. "These are your safety scissors," she said. "They have rounded tips. I will watch you cut."

Sienna held the little scissors. Snip, snip, snip. A yellow strip fell down. Then another one. "Look, my sun is getting rays!" she said.

Then she saw something funny. Each snip made a strip fall. Snip, strip. Snip, strip. "It's raining paper!" said her friend Tom. He put out his bag to catch them.

One strip landed on Tom's head. "Now you have a yellow hat!" said Sienna. Tom laughed and shook it off. It fell into the bag.

"My hands are all dirty with glue," said Sienna. She wiped them on a wet cloth. Then she glued the strips around a yellow circle. Her paper sun was done.

Ms. Rosa hung it in the window. The real sun shone right through it. "Two suns!" said Tom. Sienna giggled and pointed. "Mine has better rays. Snip, snip!"

Sofia sat in the family car with her toy bunny. "Are we going to the doctor?" she asked. "The doctor checks my whole body!"

Mama smiled and drove fast. "We will hurry," said Mama. "We have a special visit today."

The car stopped at a new place. Sofia saw a big tooth on the door. A big tooth! She held her bunny tight.

Inside, a friendly woman said, "Hello! I am the dentist."

"A dentist?" said Sofia.

"The dentist is a doctor for teeth," the woman said with a smile.

Sofia opened her mouth wide, wide, wide. The dentist looked and looked. She counted Sofia's teeth. Then she gave Sofia a shiny sticker.

"A tooth sticker!" said Sofia. It was her favorite kind of surprise.

Bunny got a check too. "Open up, bunny," said Sofia. The dentist clapped. "Perfect teeth," she said.

Ellie sat at the big table. Grandma put warm bread in a basket. Grandpa held up his hands. Everyone got quiet.

"Who will say the bread words?" Grandma asked.

Ellie wanted to say them. She had practiced at home. She had practiced in the bath. "Me! Me!" said Ellie. Grandpa smiled. "Let's hear it, Ellie."

Ellie stood on her chair. "Sit down, sweet pea," said Grandma. "Feet on the floor." Ellie sat down. Then she said the words. "Hamotzi." Everyone said "Amen" together. Grandpa clapped. The bread basket went around and around.

After dinner, Uncle Ben showed Ellie his plate. It was empty. Hers was different. She still had bread on it. "Look," said Uncle Ben. "Your words started the meal. Then we ate it all up." Ellie looked at her bread. She took a big bite. Then everyone laughed. Ellie laughed too. "Again tomorrow?" she asked. "Again tomorrow," said Grandpa.

Lea sat at the big art table. She was making a paper crown. It had red stars and yellow dots.

"I will wear it home," said Lea.

First, one star. Second, one dot. Third, another star. She spread the wet glue. It felt cold and sticky on her fingers. It smelled like flour and water.

Teacher Mia sat close by. "Take your time," she said.

Lea wanted to try the crown on. She picked it up too soon. The stars slid. The dots slid too. The pieces came apart in her hands. Lea's lip wobbled. "My crown is broken," she said.

Teacher Mia knelt down. "It is not broken. Wet glue needs to dry," she said. "Let's set it flat and wait."

They laid the crown on the table. Lea counted the pieces. One, two, three, four. Then they watched the glue. It went from shiny to dull. Lea touched one star. It held!

Lea pressed the crown on her head. It stayed. It felt like a real queen's crown.

"My crown is full of stars," said Lea. "And it will not slide off!"

Teacher Mia smiled. "You made it all by yourself," she said.

Lea walked to the cubbies, crown shining, and held Teacher Mia's hand.

Nova sat at the long wooden table. Big bowls of soup sat in the middle. Everyone held hands. Nova did not know what came next.

Grandma squeezed Nova's hand. Grandma began to speak. She thanked the sun and the farmers and the soup. Nova waited. She wanted to eat, but she kept holding hands. When would the talking end?

Then Grandma said one word. "Amen." Everyone let go of hands. Everyone picked up spoons. Nova blinked. The waiting word meant the food could start.

The next week, Nova came back to the hall. She brought a small present for Grandma. It was a drawing of soup. Everyone held hands again. Nova listened hard. Grandma thanked the sun and the farmers. Nova waited and waited.

"Amen," said Grandma.

Nova laughed and grabbed her spoon.

Parker was at Grandma's house. He wanted to bake cookies for his family. Grandma said, "Let's make them together."

Parker helped mix the dough. He poured the sugar. He dropped in the blue bowl of chocolate chips. Some chips fell on the floor, and Grandma smiled and helped him pick them up.

The dough was ready. Grandma put the pan in the hot oven. Parker wanted to look inside. He reached for the oven door. Grandma said, "Stop. That is hot. A grown-up opens the oven." Parker stepped back and waited.

While they waited, Parker watched a bird fly past the window. The bird landed in its nest in the big tree. Parker sat very still so he would not scare it.

Then Grandma said, "The cookies are done." She put on her big mitts. She opened the oven door. The cookies looked golden and warm. Parker saw that Grandma always touched the hot oven, and he never did. He got to carry the plate to the table instead.

The family ate the cookies. Dad said, "These are the best cookies ever." Parker grinned and said, "Can we ride home with some for tomorrow?"
