Weston was in the backyard. He had a big pot and a wooden spoon. He wanted to make soup for his bear, Ted.

He found three pinecones. He put them in the pot. He poured in some water from the hose. Then he began to stir. "Soup is ready!" he said.

Weston lifted the spoon to his mouth. He wanted a big slurp. Just then Mom came out. "Stop, Weston," she said. "Pretend soup is for pretending." Weston looked at his spoon. The water was cold and muddy. He put the spoon down.

He sat on the square patio stone. He was sorry he almost ate it. "Let's pretend to slurp instead," said Mom. She sat down too. They slurped and slurped with empty spoons. Ted got a pretend drink too. Weston smiled. "More soup, please!" he said.

Rehmat wanted to play the shouting game with her big brother. He said one word. She had to shout the opposite word back.

"Ice cream is cold," said her brother. Rehmat thought and thought. "Then soup is hot!" she shouted. Her brother laughed and clapped.

Next he ran around the playroom, fast as a rabbit. Rehmat crawled like a sleepy turtle. "Slow," she said. Her brother nodded. "Fast and slow are opposites too."

Then Rehmat got it wrong. He said "big," and she said "big" back. Her brother shook his head. Rehmat felt grumpy. Her mouth turned down. She hugged her teddy.

Mama came in and sat on the floor. "Try again," said Mama softly. Rehmat looked at the teddy. Then she looked at her brother. He was big. The teddy was small.

"Small!" Rehmat shouted. Her brother pointed at her and cheered. "You got it!"

Rehmat giggled. She held up the teddy. "Big bear," she said. Then she squished it tiny. "Small bear!" Her brother laughed. Mama clapped her hands.

Rehmat snuggled between Mama and her brother. She whispered one more word to the teddy. "Soft," she said. Then she poked her brother's elbow. "Hard!"

Everett was four today. The whole family drove to Grandma's house. Grandpa blew up red balloons. One balloon popped and Everett jumped. Then he laughed.

"Time for cake," said Grandma. She lit the candles with a match. Everett watched from far away. The candles glowed. "Make a wish," said Grandma. Everett closed his eyes. He wished hard. Then he blew and blew. The little flames went out. Everyone clapped.

Then the singing began. "Happy birthday to you. Happy birthday dear..." Everett waited. Would they say his name? "Everett!" they sang. His very own name, right in the song. He hid his face in his hands. He was not mad. He was smiling a big smile. His cheeks felt warm. "Sing it again," he said. So they did. "Happy birthday dear Everett!" And he smiled behind his hands one more time.

Bennett ran in from Grandma's backyard. He had been spinning in circles under the big tree. His head felt dizzy and his shoes were full of grass.

"Grandma, I want to cook!" he said. Grandma was mixing pancake batter in a blue bowl. The batter smelled like vanilla and warm mornings.

"First, the sink," said Grandma. She pointed with her wooden spoon. Bennett looked at his hands. They had dirt on them. He turned the faucet. The water ran cool over his fingers. He rubbed the soap until white bubbles grew. He rinsed the bubbles away. Now his hands were clean.

Then Grandma let him stir. Round and round went the spoon. The flour and milk turned into smooth batter. "Look," said Bennett. "I made it change!"

Grandma cooked the pancakes on the hot stove. Bennett stood far back and watched. Soon the pancakes came to the table. They were golden and soft.

Bennett took a big bite. Then he felt something small in his pocket. He pulled out a tiny pinecone from the backyard. Grandma laughed. "That one is not for eating," she said. Bennett giggled and put it in the middle of the table, next to the syrup.

It was a big day for Audrey. Mom said, "Today we get your shot!" Audrey held Mom's hand. They walked into the pharmacy together.

A nurse smiled. "Hello, Audrey! Sit up here on the big table." Audrey climbed up. The table was tall and cold. She felt her tummy go tight. She wanted to hop right down.

Then Mom sat on a chair. Mom opened her arms wide. "Come sit on my lap," said Mom. Audrey slid down and snuggled in. Mom held her close, like a deep, warm hug. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." Quick! The shot was done!

"Was that it?" asked Audrey. She looked at her arm. There was a tiny pink bandage. The nurse poured a spoon of sweet syrup as a treat. Audrey drank it all up. "That was easy!" she said. Mom laughed and swung her high. On the way out, Audrey waved to the nurse. "See you next time!" she called.

Elijah stood by the cubbies at school. He pulled off his shoes. Then he pulled off his socks. He put them in his cubby. After snack time, he came back. He looked inside. He saw one tiny sock. Just one.

"Where is the other one?" said Elijah. MissAna knelt down beside him. "A sock needs its partner," she said. "Two socks make a pair." Elijah looked under the bench. He saw a red horse toy. He saw a crayon. No sock.

Elijah began to sing the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." He walked slowly along the wall. "Six, seven, eight." He looked at the little toy shelf. "Nine, ten." He froze. There, behind a tiny chair, was his sock!

Elijah picked it up. He held the two socks together. One sock, then the other sock. A pair! He put them on his feet. They were warm and soft. Then he ran to the rug. "Look, Miss Ana!" he said. "One for this foot. One for that foot!"

Peyton was at Grandma's house. She sat at the big table in the sunny room. Grandma put out red paint and a fat brush.

"I will paint a fish," said Peyton. She dipped the brush in the red paint. She painted a wiggly fish on the paper. Then she ran outside to see the dog.

The brush stayed in the paint cup all night. In the morning, Peyton picked it up. The brush was stiff. The bristles were hard and stuck together. "Oh no," said Peyton. She touched the brush. It would not bend.

Grandma brought a cup of water. Peyton dipped the stiff brush in. She swished it round and round. The water turned pink. The brush got soft again. The bristles were clean and fresh.

Peyton painted a new fish. This time she rinsed the brush right away. She put it on a towel to dry. "Good helper," said Grandma. Peyton smiled and painted one more fish, a big red one.

Rowan went to the big cultural center with Mom. The room was full of red and gold. Lanterns hung from the ceiling. They gave off a warm light.

Rowan saw his cousin Mei. Mei held a small red envelope. It was shiny and flat. Rowan wanted one too. He looked and looked. "Where is mine?" he asked.

Grandpa came over with a smile. He put a red envelope in Rowan's hand. Rowan wanted to open it fast. He pulled at the corner. Then he saw Mei. Mei bowed to her grandma first. She said, "Thank you." Only then did she open her envelope.

Rowan stopped pulling. He looked up at Grandpa. "Thank you," he said. Grandpa laughed and patted his head. Rowan opened his envelope. There was money inside! A shiny coin slid out into his palm. Rowan held it up to the lantern light. "Mei, look!" he said. Mei clapped her hands.

Audrey sat on a small red chair. She had a pencil and some paper. She wanted to write the letter K. Her name had a K in it, but she could not write it yet.

She tried once. The lines went the wrong way. She tried again. It still looked funny. Her pencil got stuck on the paper. Audrey felt sad. Then she saw a box of bumpy letter cards. She picked out the K card. The letter was big and rough. She put her finger on the card. She traced the top line down. She traced the little lines out. Her arm moved slowly, again and again.

Then Audrey picked up her pencil. She drew the lines on her paper. It was a K! Audrey smiled. "I can write my name," she said. She wrote the K one more time, very big, right in the middle of the page.

Jaxson sat at the dinner table. He had a big idea. He would bang his drum after eating!

"Can I play my drum?" he asked.

"Yes, after dinner," said Mom.

Jaxson was so excited. He ate fast. Then he got his drum. BOOM! BOOM! He danced in his chair. What a happy boy!

Then he heard a sound. It was a little cry. His baby sister was covering her ears. Her doll fell on the floor. Her face looked sad, then scared.

"Hmm," said Jaxson. "I love the drum. But she does not."

Dad picked up the baby. "She likes quiet sounds," he said.

Jaxson put the drum down. He picked up her doll. He made the doll dance, slow and soft. The baby stopped crying. She smiled. She clapped her hands.

Jaxson smiled too. Loud for him. Quiet for her. Two people, one table, two different feelings.

"More doll dance!" said Jaxson. The doll spun around and around.

Sadie ran to the bike at the playground. She wanted to ride it right away. She put her foot on the pedal.

Her grandma held up a helmet. "Sadie, come here first," she said. Sadie ran back. Grandma put the helmet on her head. It felt hard and smooth. The strap clicked under her chin.

Then Sadie rode the bike. She pedaled past the swings. Her nose picked up the smell of popcorn. A man was making popcorn in a hot pot. Grandma stood by him, but Sadie stayed back. The pot was far too hot to touch. Grandma carried the popcorn over in a paper bag. It was warm and good.

Sadie rode one more time around the path. Then her front wheel hit a small rock. The bike tipped. Sadie fell onto the soft ground. Bonk went her helmet on the path. Sadie sat still for a short minute. Then she stood up.

She touched her helmet with one hand. It had a little mark on it. "My head is okay," she said. She turned the bike upright. "One more ride," said Sadie. Grandma smiled and clapped.

Alexander stood in the sunny kitchen. He wanted to see the bubbles in the pot. Mom said the water was getting hot.

Alexander stepped close to the stove. The pot made a cloud of steam. The steam felt hot on his face. He jumped back fast.

"Ouch," he said. "That is very hot."

Mom picked him up. "Watch from here," she said. She set him on a chair far from the stove. Alexander held his pencil. He drew the pot and the bubbles on his paper.

The steam went up and up. The water went bump, bump, bump. Alexander saw that the steam came from the hot pot. When the pot got hot, the steam came out.

Mom made the noodles. She gave Alexander a bowl. He clapped his hands. Then he took a big bite.

"Hot pot, good noodles," he said. Mom laughed and gave him more.

Josephine ran straight to the library story room. Her friends Ben and Mia were there. "Let's play hide-and-seek!" said Ben.

"I will count," said Josephine. "You hide!" Ben and Mia ran to hide behind the big book shelf. Josephine counted, "One, two, three!" She counted very fast. Then she turned around. Ben and Mia were still standing in the open!

"You counted too fast!" said Mia. "We need time to hide."

"Okay," said Josephine. "I will count slow." Ben and Mia ran off again. Josephine counted, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." She counted slowly, like a song.

Now Ben and Mia were gone. Josephine looked behind the shelf. Not there. She looked under the table. Not there. Then she heard a giggle by the coat rack. "I see you, Mia!" said Josephine. "Look at you, hiding behind the coats!"

Mia laughed and laughed. "You counted slow," she said. "So we got to hide!"

"Who wants to count next?" asked Josephine.

Aubrey went to the computer lab with her class. The teacher said, "Today we learn tablets." Aubrey wanted to draw a cat on the screen. She had never done it before.

First she pressed the round button. The screen lit up. She pressed it again and the screen went dark. "Oops," said Aubrey. She pressed it one more time. Light again! Then the teacher helped her find the drawing app. Aubrey tapped it open. She mixed blue and yellow on the screen. Green! She drew one cat, two cats, three cats. "Meow," she said to each one.

Then it was time to go. Aubrey ran to the little couch and set the tablet down on the soft cushion. Ben came running to sit. "Wait!" said the teacher. She picked up the tablet just in time. "When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place," she said. Aubrey looked at the shelf. It had a green tag with her name.

Aubrey carried the tablet back. One, two, three, she counted the steps to the shelf. She set it on the green tag. It fit just right. "Good night, tablet," said Aubrey. The teacher smiled. "Happy tablet, happy shelf," she said. Aubrey waved at her three cats through the dark screen.

Julia stood by the big piano in the band room. She wanted to make a song. Her teacher, Mr. Bell, smiled at her. "Try the keys," he said.

Julia looked at the keys. Some were black. Some were white. She tapped a white key. It made a low sound. She tapped another white key. It made a new sound. Then she tapped a black key. That one made a sound too. She thought only white keys could play. But the black keys played!

Julia pressed only the black keys. One, then two, then three. The sounds went up and down. "It sounds like raindrops!" she said. A boy named Sam was upset because his drum was too big for him. Julia said, "Listen to my rain song." Sam stopped frowning. He tapped his drum very softly along with her.

Mr. Bell gave them both a thumbs up. Julia played her black keys again. Sam tapped his drum again. "Let's give our song a name," said Julia. Sam said, "Rain and Drum!"

Henry walked into his classroom. He held his dad's hand. His backpack felt heavy on his back. There were new toys on every table.

A boy stood by the blocks all alone. Henry wanted a friend to play with. But he did not know the boy's name.

Henry asked his dad, "What do I do?"

His dad said, "Go find out his name."

Henry took a big breath. He walked over to the blocks. "My name is Henry," he said. "What is your name?"

The boy smiled big. "I am Sam!" said Sam. "I like blocks. Do you?"

"Yes!" said Henry. They stacked the blocks up high. Then the tower fell down. Crash! Both boys laughed.

"Let's build a house," said Sam. "It can be a doctor's house. My mom is a doctor."

"Can I touch the doctor's door?" asked Henry.

"Only if you knock first," said Sam.

Henry knocked on the block door. Knock, knock. Sam opened it. "Hello, friend," said Sam.

"Hello," said Henry. He handed Sam one more block.

Grandpa had a big red dog named Bess. "B is for Bess!" said Grandpa. Evan wanted to read her name all by himself.

Grandpa wrote DOG on paper. Evan looked hard. "Bog!" he said. Then he laughed and laughed. "Bess is a bog!"

"No, no," said Evan again. He looked closer. The first letter had a round part. Which way did it face? He made his own fist. He turned it left. He turned it right. The round part of the b faced the same way as his right hand. The d faced the other way! "D, d, dog!" Evan shouted. "It says dog!"

Grandpa clapped. A shy gray cat ran under the chair. A feather floated down from Bess's tail. Evan picked it up. He held it like a pen.

"Now I can write too," said Evan. He climbed onto the tall stool. He drew a big D. Then a little d. Then the round part faced the wrong way, so he fixed it. "D is for dog," he said. "D is for door. D is for Grandpa's donuts!"

Bess barked one big bark. Evan laughed. "B is for Bess. B, b, bark!"

Matthew saw a big blue bus. It was full of books. "This is the bookmobile," said Mommy. "You can get your own library card today."

Matthew got a little white card. It had his name on it. He smiled and smiled. He picked a book about a red fire truck. "I want this one," he said.

The librarian put the book in a bag. Then Matthew saw a small slot in the side of the bus. A girl was standing by it. She held her book tight. "I don't want to let it go," she said. Her daddy held her hand. "Wave it goodbye," he said. The girl waved the book. Then she dropped it into the slot. It went in and made a soft sound. "Bye, book," she said. "See you soon."

At home, Matthew read the fire truck book three times. Mommy sang a little song about it. His tooth felt loose when he smiled big.

One week later, the bookmobile came back. Matthew ran to the bus. He held his fire truck book tight too. Then he remembered the girl. He waved his book. "Bye, book," he said. He dropped it into the slot. The librarian smiled. "Here is a new card for you," she said. It was a sticker of a fire truck.

"I did it all by myself," said Matthew.

Myles sat at the little table in art class. The sun was sunny outside the window. His teacher put out paper and paints.

"I want to paint a boat," said Myles. "But I can't make the sail." He looked at the circle stamp. He looked at the square sponge. Neither one looked like a sail.

His friend Nia was eating her lunch. Her sandwich was cut into triangles. "Look," she said. She pointed at one piece. Myles counted the corners with his finger. One, two, three. Then he counted the sides. One, two, three. A triangle had three sides and three corners, just like a sail.

Myles found the scissors-safe sponge with three sides in the tray. He dipped it in white paint. He pressed it on his paper. There was a triangle sail. He pressed it again for the other sail.

He painted a square boat under the sails. He painted a rectangle flag on top. Then he hopped up to show his teacher.

"The sail has three corners," said Myles. He pointed at each one. His teacher smiled and hung the boat on the sunny wall.

Ibrahim went to Adam's house. Adam's grandpa had a tablet on the table. It was big and shiny. Ibrahim wanted to draw on it.

He reached out his hand. Then he stopped. He turned to Grandpa. "Can I please use the tablet?" he asked.

Grandpa smiled. "Yes, you may. Good asking, Ibrahim."

Grandpa showed him the little round button. Ibrahim pressed it. The screen lit up like magic. "Ooh!" said Ibrahim. He touched the green shape that looked like a crayon. A big white page opened. Adam laughed. "Now you can draw!"

Ibrahim drew a fat blue cat. Then he drew a yellow sun with a funny face. The sun had squiggly legs. "Silly sun," said Ibrahim. He touched the screen again, and the page turned clean. "It went away!" he clapped.

"Time for a snack," said Grandpa. Ibrahim pressed the round button. The screen went dark and soft, like sleep. He put the tablet on the table, flat and safe.

Grandpa patted his head. "You learn fast," he said.

"Can we draw a dog next time?" asked Adam.

"A dog with a hat," said Ibrahim. Grandpa laughed all the way to the kitchen.

Charlotte wanted to draw a big hill. She was at her friend Milo's house. Milo had a tablet on the table. "Can I draw?" Charlotte asked. "Yes," said Milo. "Press the round button."

Charlotte pressed the button. The screen lit up. She heard a soft sound. "I did it!" she said. Milo's mom showed her the little drawing app. Charlotte tapped it. A white page opened. She drew a green hill with her finger. Then she drew a yellow sun over the hill.

The tablet blinked. The screen went dark. "It's tired," said Milo. "It needs the charger." Charlotte found the charger cord on the shelf. She carried it to Milo's mom. The mom plugged the charger into the wall. Charlotte put the tablet down on the table. "All done," she said. "I can draw the last cloud tomorrow."

Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. The chair leaned back like a rocket ship. The dentist had shiny tools and a little cup of water with ice in it. "First we wash our hands," said the dentist, Miss Kim. Grace wanted to be a helper. But when she got to the sink, she scrubbed for two seconds and turned off the water. "That was fast," said Miss Kim. Grace looked at her hands. The germs could still hide in her soapy fingers, and germs made teeth and tummies sick.

At camp, Grace had learned a song for the sink. She began to sing it, soft and low. "Happy hands, scrub and rub, soap and bubbles, scrub and rub." She kept scrubbing while she sang. The bubbles turned white and fuzzy on her hands. The song was long. The scrubbing was long too. At last she rinsed, and the water carried the bubbles away. Her hands felt smooth and clean.

"Now I can be a helper," said Grace. Miss Kim gave her a fuzzy sticker shaped like a tooth. Grace stuck it on her shirt. She sang the song again on the way out, just because she liked it.

Jayden was at home with Mommy. Mommy made hot cocoa. Steam rose from the cup. "Too hot," said Mommy. She put it far away. Jayden touched his milk cup instead. That one was cold. He liked cold.

"Today we buy a present for Grandma," said Mommy. Jayden held Mommy's hand. He stayed close all the way to the store.

The store was big. Jayden saw a toy train. He looked at the train. He looked up. Mommy was gone! Jayden stood very still. Then he saw the checkout worker. She had a blue vest and a kind face. Jayden walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," he said. The worker smiled. She spoke into her phone. Soon Mommy came around the corner. "Jayden!" She hugged him tight. "Stay close now," she said.

At home, Grandma opened her present. It was a thin, soft scarf. Grandma wore it right away. Outside, the snow began to melt on the sunny roof. Jayden waved at Grandma through the window. She waved back.

Sarah ran into the library. She wanted a book about dogs. Dogs were her favorite animals.

At the picture table, two kids were arguing. A boy held a card with an apple on it. "It goes with the fruits," he said. "No, it goes with the foods," said a girl. They each pulled a little. The card began to bend.

Sarah looked at the table. There was a picture of bread by the foods. There was a picture of grapes by the fruits. Then she saw something. There was a rough basket with two labels on it. One label said foods. The other said fruits.

"Put it here," Sarah said. She pointed at the basket. The boy set the apple inside. The apple sat in both groups at once.

"It fits," said the girl. "It fits two ways," said the boy. They clapped. Sarah clapped too.

Then Sarah found her dog book. She hugged it tight. "Home time," she said.

Joshua knocked on his friend Mia's door. Mia opened it wide. "Come see my shop!" she said.

Mia put toy food on a little table. "I am the shopkeeper," she said. She stood behind the table. "You be the shopper."

Joshua picked up a tiny pot. He stirred it with a big spoon. "I am making soup," he said.

Then Joshua wanted to be the shopkeeper. He stood behind the table. Mia said, "Now I am the shopper!" She held a little basket. She took a long time. She looked at the apples. She looked at the bread. Joshua had to wait and wait.

"I want to pick," said Mia. So Joshua waited some more. His feet felt tired. He sat down on a small stool behind the table.

At last Mia held up a toy banana. "This one, please!" Joshua put it in her basket. "Thank you for waiting at my shop," he said.

Then Mia gave him the banana back. "Now you are the shopper," she said.

Joshua laughed. Two people, two jobs, and they could swap! Joshua put the banana in his basket and walked to the play kitchen. "One soup, please," he said, and knocked on the little toy door.

Nicholas was at Grandpa's house. He found a big cardboard box. He wanted to play, but he did not know how to start. His cousin Mia was there. She sat on the rug and looked grumpy.

Nicholas asked, "How do we play?"

Grandpa said, "Try telling Mia what to play."

Nicholas stood by the box. He said, "Let's pretend we are bears!"

Mia jumped up. "Yes! I am a baby bear!" she said. Nicholas counted three toy cups for their pretend tea. Mia hugged a teddy and fed it.

"Let's pretend the teddy is sleepy," said Mia. They tucked him in the box.

Then Nicholas roared like a big bear. Mia laughed and roared too. Grandpa peeked in and said, "Two bears in my house! I will bring honey."

Max sat at Grandma's kitchen table. He had a big yellow pencil. He wanted to write his name, just like his big brother could.

"Can I write M?" he asked.

Grandma drew a big M. But it had small dots inside it. "Try this," she said.

Max held the pencil. Grandma moved his fingers. "Thumb here," she said. "Now go over the dots."

Max drew his pencil on the dots. The dots turned into a line. The line turned into an M! Max looked at it. Did his hand do that?

"Again," said Max.

He traced the dotted A. It worked too. He traced the X. Now his whole name sat on the paper.

"My name!" said Max. He held it up. "Dry it?" he asked.

"It will dry fast," said Grandma.

Max waved the paper in the air. His brother came in and looked.

"Did you make that?" his brother asked.

Max grinned and pointed at the M. "Me," he said. "All by me."

Willow ran to the dress-up corner at school. She wanted to play house. But Ben had the big apron, and Mia had the baby doll. Willow had nothing at all.

Then she saw a tall white hat on the shelf. She put it on her head. "I am the cook!" she said. Ben gave her a wooden spoon. Mia gave her the doll. "The baby is hungry," said Mia. Willow stirred a pretend pot. "Soup is ready!" she said. The doll got a bottle and went to sleep.

After rest time, Willow stayed awake. She wanted more pretend fun. She found a shiny red coat. She put it on and zipped it up. "Now I am a firefighter!" she shouted. Ben grabbed a toy hose. "We can rescue the kitty!" he said. Willow crawled on one knee behind the couch. "Come out, little kitty," she called. Mia held out her arms. "Meow!" she said. The kitty was safe, and everyone cheered.

Gianna was at Mia's birthday party. On the rug sat a big box of blocks. A boy named Leo grabbed the box first. Gianna wanted the blocks too. She reached out her hand to grab them.

Then she stopped. She thought hard. "Can we both play?" she asked. Leo looked at the box. "But there is only one box," he said. "Can one box be for two kids?" Gianna asked herself. She looked at the rug. It looked big and empty. "Let's make one big tower," she said. "Together?"

Leo nodded. "Together," he said. They sat side by side. Gianna put one block down. Leo put the next block on top. "One for you, one for me," said Gianna. "One for you, one for me," said Leo.

The tower grew tall. It got so tall it looked thin at the top. Then it wobbled. "Oops," said Leo. The blocks fell down with a clatter. The two friends laughed. "Let's dig in the box and start again," said Gianna. They built the tower up, up, up. Then they clapped. "We made it together," said Leo. "Best tower ever," said Gianna.

Emma stood by the camp table. She wanted to make pancakes for her family. Daddy was there to help. Daddy lit the little camp stove. Emma stayed back from the hot pan.

First came the flour. Emma tipped the bag. Too much flour puffed out. The bowl looked like a snow cloud. "Oh no," said Emma. "It went too fast."

Daddy handed her a big cup. "Fill this," he said. Emma scooped flour into the cup. She made it level with her finger. The cup held just the right amount. Then she used a little spoon for the sugar. One spoon, not a river of sugar. Daddy cracked the eggs. Emma poured the milk from her cup, slow and steady.

The batter went drip, drip into the pan. Daddy flipped each pancake. A green frog hopped by and watched too. Soon the pancakes were warm and golden. Emma took a taste. "Yum!" she said. "The cup helped me make them just right." Daddy gave her a big hug.

Olivia went to the garden center with her dad. The sun felt warm on her face. There were pots and seeds and little plants everywhere. Olivia picked a packet of carrot seeds. "I want a carrot garden," she said. Dad smiled and got a big bag of soft brown soil.

At home, they filled a long box with soil. Olivia poked little holes with her finger. She dropped one seed in each hole. Then she covered them up, pat, pat, pat. The soil smelled like rain. Dad said, "All done!" But Olivia forgot one thing.

Every morning Olivia ran to the box. She looked and looked. Nothing grew. The soil was dry and crumbly. "Where are my carrots?" she asked. Her tummy felt worried. Then she saw the sky. The weather was hot. The sun could burn her shoulders, dad said, so he put a hat on her head.

Dad handed her a small green watering can. It went "swish, swish," a soft, loud splash on the soil. Olivia watered the seeds every day. The soil turned dark and damp.

One morning, tiny green leaves popped up. Two leaves, then five, then ten! Olivia jumped up and down. "They grew!" she called. Dad gave her a thumbs up. Olivia patted the soil gently. "More water tomorrow," she said, and carried her little can inside.

Ivy sat on the grass by Grandpa Joe's stone. The stone was warm and dry in the sun. Mom set out bread, apples, and cheese.

"Now we hold hands," said Mom. "We say the blessing, like Grandpa Joe did."

Ivy held Mom's hand. She held Dad's hand. But her mouth stayed shut. The blessing felt too big for her. Dad said the words. Mom said the words. Ivy only listened.

She looked at the bread. She thought and thought. Who made this bread? A baker made it. Who grew the apples? A farmer grew them. The sun helped too.

Dad handed her the bread. "Your turn, Ivy. You can choose your own words."

Ivy took a big breath. "Thank you for the bread," she said. "One, thank you for the apples. Two, thank you for the cheese. Three, thank you for the sun."

Mom squeezed her hand. Dad smiled a big smile. Then Mom said, "One, thank you for Grandpa Joe." Dad said, "Two, thank you for Ivy's words."

Ivy felt the squeeze go around. Mom squeezed her hand. She squeezed Dad's hand. Dad squeezed back. The thank-you went around and around, like a circle.

Ivy bit her apple. It was sweet and cold. The wind moved the grass by the stone.

"Again tomorrow?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Every day."

Ivy waved at the stone. "Bye, Grandpa Joe. Thank you for the blessing."

Anna was playing outside on a windy day. Dust blew all around. Anna rubbed her face with her hands. Something small got in her eye. "Ouch," said Anna. It felt scratchy and sad.

Mama helped Anna blink and blink. Then the dust was gone. Anna looked in the little mirror. She saw tiny hairs on her eyelids. "What are these?" she asked. "They are my eyelashes," she said.

Anna blinked again. Her eyelashes went down, then up. They touched her cheek, soft as a feather. Did they stop the dust? Anna ran her fingers over them. She could feel them tickle.

Inside, Anna smelled warm cookies. She heard the timer ring. Mama gave her one cookie. Anna took a little bite. It tasted sweet. Anna smiled. She did not want to lose her cookie, so she ate it all up, blinking her happy lashes.

"Hello, little lashes," said Anna.

Jake was in the playroom with his friend Mia. They wanted to play house. Jake got the small blue pot. Mia got the gray blanket for the bed.

"I want to be the parent," said Jake. "I want to be the parent too," said Mia. They both held the pot. Neither one would let go. The pot went clunk on the floor.

Then Jake had an idea. "You can be the parent first," he said. "I will be the baby. Then we can switch." Mia smiled. She wrapped Jake in the gray blanket. He pretended to sleep. Then she fed him pretend soup from a little cup.

Next it was Jake's turn to be the parent. Mia curled up with her robot toy. She made the robot cry like a baby. Jake patted the robot softly. "There, there," he said. "Time for a nap." He covered them both with the blanket. Mia closed her eyes and snored a big pretend snore. Jake giggled and turned off the pretend light with a click.

Maverick ran to Grandma's toy box. He found a soft gray pig with a floppy ear. "Mine!" said his cousin Nia. "No, mine!" said Maverick. Grandma sat down between them. "Play pretend with it," she said. Nia held the pig first. She wrapped it in a small blanket. "The pig is sick," Nia said. Maverick felt the pig's ear. It was warm and fuzzy. He patted it softly. "The pig is sleeping," he said. "No, the pig is hungry," said Nia. Maverick made a sad face. Then he had an idea. "The pig is hungry, then sleepy," he said. Nia smiled and clapped her hands. "Yes! Then it swings on the swing!"

Nia found a tiny cup. Maverick fed the pig pretend oats. He made a little yum yum sound. Then the pig got very sleepy. Nia rocked it in her arms. "Shh," she whispered. Grandma hummed a quiet song. Maverick covered the pig with his own jacket. The pig's ear felt soft against his hand. "Goodnight, pig," said Maverick. "Goodnight," said Nia, in her most polite voice. Grandma gave them both warm hugs. "You two agreed on the game," she said. "That was kind sharing." Maverick snuggled close to Grandma. Outside, a bird sang at the window. The pig slept and slept. "Nice pig," whispered Maverick.

Austin ran to the playground. It was a big playground. Austin was small, but he could run fast. "Look at me go!" he said.

Dad sat on the bench with a big water bottle. "The sun is hot today," said Dad. Austin touched the slide. The slide was hot too. So he went to the little slide in the shade. That slide was cool. Down he went, slow and easy.

Then Austin saw a puddle. He jumped in it. Splash! His shoes were wet. His socks were wet. "My socks are all wet," said Austin. Dad opened his bag. "Here are dry socks," said Dad. Austin sat on the bench. Off came the wet socks. On went the dry socks. Dry socks felt warm and cozy. "Dry socks are better," said Austin. Dad laughed. "Let's go find the horsey," he said. Austin rode the bouncy horse up and down. He did not want to ride alone, so Dad held his hand. Then they walked home, slow and happy, all dry.

Emile sat at the big art table. He wanted to draw a sun. A sun needs a big round circle.

Emile picked up his crayon. He drew a circle. It came out wobbly. It looked like a squished egg. He tried again. Wobbly again. Emile frowned at his paper.

Then he saw Mia's cup on the table. It was a round cup. Emile held his paper next to it. He put his crayon at the bottom of the cup. He traced all the way around the bottom of the cup. He lifted the cup up. There it was. A big round circle! A real one!

Emile drew triangle rays around his circle. Yellow triangle rays, just like the sun. Mia drew a square window beside his sun. Tom drew a rectangle door. The teacher tapped the picture with her phone to show Emile's mom later. "Look at my sun!" Emile said. He held the cup up high.

Nova went to her friend Mia's house. Mia had a big cardboard box. "It's a car!" said Mia. She turned a paper plate. Vroom, vroom!

Nova shook her head. "It's a house," she said. She put her teddy bear inside. "Teddy lives here now."

"But I want a car," said Mia. "But I want a house," said Nova. They both frowned. The box just sat there.

Then Mia had an idea. "You go first," she said. "Then me." Nova smiled. She patted teddy and gave him a bottle. She crawled in and rocked him to sleep.

Then Nova climbed out. "Now it's your turn," she said. Mia jumped in. "Beep, beep! The bus is here!" said Mia. Nova ran around and waved. "Stop the bus! I want to ride!"

The box stopped. Nova climbed in too. Now the bus had two riders. They drove all the way to the kitchen for a snack.

Later, Mia's mom came in early to check on them. "Where did you two go?" she asked. Mia pointed at the box. "To the moon," said Nova. "And back," said Mia. "Room for one more," said Nova, and she held up teddy.

Sebastian stood in the backyard with a red beanbag. He wanted to toss it into the hoop on the grass. He threw it. The beanbag fell outside the circle. "Oh no," said Sebastian. He sat down on the step.

Then he got up. He picked up the beanbag. He threw it again. It missed again. He threw it one more time. It missed one more time. But his throw went closer to the hoop.

Sebastian was busy trying. Throw, pick up, throw again. Each time, the beanbag went a little closer. Then one throw went up and dropped right into the hoop. "I did it!" said Sebastian. He jumped with both feet.

Next Dad rolled him a big blue ball. Sebastian tried to catch it with both hands. It bumped his arms and fell. He tried again. It fell again. Then he held his hands out wide. The ball came right into them. Sebastian hugged the ball tight. "Again, Dad!" he said.

Eva ran to the swings with Grandma. The swings were near a tall forest of trees. One, two, three, she pumped her legs. The swing went high. "Look at me!" she said.

Next Eva wanted the slide. The sun sat on the slide. Grandma put her hand on it. "Too hot," said Grandma. They waited in the shade. They waited and waited. Eva counted clouds. One, two, three. At last the slide felt cool. Down Eva went. Fast!

Then Eva saw something on the picnic table. Little red dots, like candy. "Grandma, come look," she said. She did not touch them. Grandma looked. She put them in her pocket. "Good girl. Only a grown-up gives you medicine."

The gate stood open. Eva held Grandma's hand all the way home.

Liam ran into daycare. Today a firefighter was coming to visit! He felt so excited. He jumped up and down. He bounced on his toes. He shouted, "The firefighter is coming!"

Teacher Mia said, "Liam, you are so excited. But bouncing makes you extra noisy. Let's find a calm way to wait."

She put a big box of blocks on the table. "You can pat the table softly while we wait," she said.

Liam patted the table. Pat, pat, pat. It felt smooth and cool. He took a big breath. Then he patted again.

"The firefighter is coming," he said, nice and quiet this time.

Then the door opened. A firefighter in a big shiny hat walked in. Liam felt excited again. His feet wanted to jump! But he patted his knees instead. Pat, pat, pat.

"Hello, friends," said the firefighter.

Liam waved. "I waited so good," he whispered to Teacher Mia.

She smiled and gave him a hug. "You did, Liam."

The firefighter showed everyone her red truck through the window. It was big and loud and bright.

"Truck!" said Liam. He clapped his hands.

"Would you like to try on my hat?" the firefighter asked.

She set the big hat on Liam's head. It was heavy and warm. Liam grinned a big grin.

"I'm a firefighter!" he said.

At nap time, Liam curled up on his mat. He patted his teddy bear softly. Pat, pat, pat.

"The truck goes beep, beep," he said. His eyes closed.

Teacher Mia tucked his blanket in. "Sleep tight, big helper," she said.

Olivier dug a little hole. He dropped a seed in. Then he patted the soil on top. "Grow, little seed," he said.

Olivier came back the next day. Nothing was there. He came back after many days. A tiny green leaf peeked out! "Mama, look!" he said. He watered it with his small can.

A weed grew next to his plant. It had a pink flower on top. "I will pull you out," said Olivier. He pulled it, gently. Up it came. Long stringy roots hung from the bottom! "Wow," said Olivier. "What are these?" He touched them. They were soft and wet. His plant had roots down in the soil too, he thought. So that is how it held on.

Olivier patted the soil again. He ate a cookie by his little green leaf. "Stay in the ground, roots," he said. "Grow down deep."

Zoe sat at the paint table. She wanted to paint a magic sun. She had red, yellow, and blue paint.

"Red, yellow, blue," she said softly, like a song. She touched each cup as she named it. Then she dipped her brush in the yellow.

Zoe put a big yellow circle on her paper. It looked like the sun. Now she wanted orange. She had heard that red and yellow could make orange, like magic.

She dipped her brush in the red. She painted beside the yellow. But the red came out brown and muddy. Her sun looked dirty. Zoe frowned at it.

She looked at her brush. It was still yellow at the tip. She rinsed it in the water cup. The water turned cloudy yellow. The brush came out clean.

She dipped the clean brush in red. She painted a red stripe on the yellow sun. The red touched the yellow and made orange. Real orange, bright like a leaf in autumn.

"Magic!" whispered Zoe.

Tommy at the next seat was frowning. His yellow had turned muddy too. Zoe leaned over. "Wash your brush first," she said, polite and quiet. Tommy rinsed his brush. His yellow came out bright and clean.

Zoe painted a green frog with her rinsed brush. "Look," she said. "My sun is orange and my frog says hello."

Ivy ran to the swings. It was summer and the sun was warm. "One swing, two swings, three swings," she said. She wanted Saturday to come. On Saturday, Dad would bring her best friend Mia to the playground.

"Is Saturday tomorrow?" she asked Mom. Mom smiled and shook her head. "Count the days with me," Mom said. Ivy held up her little hand. Mom touched each finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven days in a week. Ivy wiggled all seven fingers.

Then Ivy saw a boy drop his juice cup. It began to spill on the sand. "Careful!" said his mama, wiping it up. Ivy ran to get the boy a paper cup from the water fountain. "Thank you," the boy said. He gave her a big smile. Then he helped count petals on a flower. "Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ivy laughed. She looked at her fingers again. Seven more sleeps until Saturday. She swung high in the sky. "One, two, three!" she called to the clouds.

Eliana wanted the big book on Grandma's shelf. It had a purple cover. Grandma took it down and opened it.

"Read it, Grandma!" said Eliana.

Grandma read the first page. "The little bear crawled under the blanket." Then she turned the page. Eliana saw the little black marks. The marks sat on the page like tiny ants.

Later, Grandpa sat down. "My turn," he said. He opened the book from the front. He read page one. "The little bear crawled under the blanket."

Eliana's eyes went wide. "Same words!"

"Same words," said Grandpa.

Eliana looked at the page. A map was on the next page. The bear was looking for his honey.

"I read it," said Eliana. She pointed at the ants. "Little bear crawls under!"

Grandma clapped. "You read it, Eliana!"

Isaac sat in the waiting room with his father. He held his favorite teddy bear tight. Today he would get a shot, and that made him worry.

Then the doctor came in. A funny tube hung around her neck. "What is that?" Isaac asked. The doctor smiled. "It is for listening." She put the little ends in her ears. She held the other end on Isaac's chest.

Thump, thump. Thump, thump. Isaac heard his own heart beating inside him. "I hear it!" he said. He listened to his teddy bear too, but the bear was quiet.

Then it was time for the shot. Isaac sat on his father's lap and hugged his bear. The doctor said, "One, two, three." It was done, quick as that. She put a small bandage on his arm.

"You were so brave," his father said. Isaac looked at the tube around the doctor's neck. "Can I hear my heart one more time?" he asked.

The doctor put the ends in his ears again. Thump, thump. Thump, thump. "Still going," said Isaac.

Matteo put on his red shoes. One shoe went on his left foot. One shoe went on his right foot. Today was his first day of school. His tummy felt funny. He hid behind Mama's leg.

"Ready?" Mama asked. Matteo shook his head. A lady in a yellow sweater opened the big door. "Hello," she said. "I am Miss Jo." Matteo peeked out. He did not know her name before. Now he knew it. Miss Jo. Miss Jo held out her hand. Matteo put his small hand in it.

They walked to the toy corner. Miss Jo got him a truck. Then she got him a block. Matteo pushed the truck on the dark green rug. It rolled far. He pushed it again. It rolled again. Then Matteo turned to Miss Jo. "Hello," he said. "Hello, Matteo," said Miss Jo. He smiled and pushed the truck one more time.

William wanted a turn on the red trike. Three friends were in line by the door. William ran fast to the front. "No, William," said Mia. "I am first. You are last." William looked at the line. Mia was in front. Then Ben. Then Sam. Then William.

William walked back to his spot. He put his hands in his pockets. He waited. Mia rode the trike around the rug. She pedaled past the blocks. Then she got off. "Your turn, Ben," said Mia. Ben rode the trike. He rang the little bell. Then Ben got off too.

Sam had a turn. Then Sam got off. Now it was William's turn. William sat on the red trike. He gripped the handles. He pedaled past the shelf and past the toy barn. The bell went clink, clink. Mia clapped her hands. "Nice riding, William," she said. William rode one big loop, then stopped. "Your turn again, Mia," he said. He stood at the back of the line and waited.

Elena woke up and saw white. Snow! Lots and lots of snow. "No school today!" said Mama. "It is a snow day!" Elena jumped out of bed. She put on her boots and her red coat. She ran outside fast, fast, fast. Then her boot slid. Whoosh! Elena fell down on the icy sidewalk. "Ouch," she said. She felt a little grumpy. Why did she fall? The ice was slippery. That was why.

Elena stood up slowly. She tried small steps. Slip, no. Slow steps. Careful steps. "Slow like a turtle," she said. It worked! She did not fall. Next came her friend Sam. Sam ran. Sam slipped too. "Walk slow!" Elena called. "Slow like a turtle!" Sam took small, slow steps. Sam did not fall. "Yay!" they both shouted.

They found a big stick. Elena let Sam hold the stick. They tapped the snow. Tap, tap, tap. The snow popped off the bushes. "Do it again!" said Sam. Tap, tap, tap. Then Mama called from the door, "Hot cocoa time!" Elena and Sam walked home, slow like a turtle, all the way to the warm house.

Connor ran to the swings at the playground. The big swing was taken. A girl was on it, going high. Connor stopped and watched. "Can I have a turn?" he asked. "You can come next," the girl said. "I will count to ten, then stop."

Connor waited. He counted with her. One, two, three. The swing went slow. Four, five, six. The swing went lower. Ten! The girl jumped off. "Your turn now," she said. Connor got on the swing. It was hard to start at first. He pumped his legs again and again. Then he went up, up, up.

A small boy came to the swings too. He had no turn. He stood and watched Connor. Connor saw him there. So Connor counted to ten, just like the girl. Then he stopped the swing. "Your turn now," he said.

The small boy got on. Connor gave him a push. "Is this a present for me?" the boy asked. "No," said Connor. "It is just my turn, given to you." The boy laughed and swung high.

Florence stood in the backyard with her dad. "Let's play the senses game," said Dad. "One, eyes to see. Two, ears to hear. Three, nose to smell. Four, tongue to taste. Five, hands to touch." Florence clapped. "I can guess them all!"

"I see the sky," said Florence. "I use my eyes." Then she wanted to see the sun up close. She looked up. The sun was too bright. Her eyes blinked and blinked. Dad held up his hand like a hat over her eyes. "Never look straight at the sun," he said. "It can hurt your eyes." Florence looked at Dad's pink sneaker instead. "I see your pink shoe," she said. "My eyes are safe."

Next came ears. Florence heard a bee buzz. "Buzz, buzz, my ears hear it!" Then her nose smelled the flowers. Then her hands touched the warm grass. "I can touch the grass, but not the sun," said Florence. Dad laughed. "That's right, clever girl." Florence patted the grass again. "Five senses, all done. That was fun!"

Sophie put on her red team shirt. Her grandpa tied her shoes. The sky was big and gray. The park had green grass.

The game began. Sophie ran to the ball. She kicked it hard. The ball rolled and rolled. It went toward the big net. Sophie clapped and cheered.

Then the coach waved her hands. "Sophie, that net is not ours," she said. Sophie looked around. "Which net is mine?" she asked. Her friend Ben pointed to the other side. "Kick the ball that way," he said.

Sophie picked up the ball. She set it down again. She turned her whole body. Then she kicked the ball to the far net. The ball went in. The team all shouted for joy. Ben did not cry. He laughed and hugged Sophie.

Sophie waved to her grandpa. He waved back from the bench. "Again, again!" Sophie said. She ran to get the ball.

Jasper lost his special red car. He looked on the swing. He looked by the sand. "One, two, three, look," said Jasper. No car.

Miss Jo came to help. "Where did it go?" she asked. Jasper shrugged his little shoulders. Then he saw the playhouse. It had a little green couch inside. Jasper gasped. The couch was low. Small toys could roll right under it.

"One, two, three, look," said Jasper. He got down on his knees. He peeked under the couch. There it was! The red car sat in the dark, by a small brown leaf. "Miss Jo! My car rolled under here!"

Jasper reached in and pulled the car out. He held it tight. Miss Jo smiled. Then Jasper pushed the car down the little slide. "Whee!" said Jasper. "Go, car, go!"

Hannah stood in the big school gym. A small beanbag sat in her hand. She wanted to throw it into the hoop on the floor. She threw it. It flew past the hoop. "Oh no," said Hannah. "Can I try again?" she asked. "Yes," said Teacher Jo. "Try again."

Hannah threw the beanbag. This time it landed in the hoop. "I did it!" she said. Teacher Jo clapped.

Then Teacher Jo rolled a big ball to Hannah. Hannah's hands were in her pockets. The ball rolled right past her. Hannah pulled her hands out. She held her arms out wide. Her hands were open. Teacher Jo rolled the ball again. The ball came and Hannah caught it with both hands. "I caught it!" she said. Teacher Jo smiled and rolled the ball once more.

Olivier was at the doctor's office. He was not late. He sat on a big chair with his mom.

Olivier saw fish in a tank. He used his eyes to see the blue fish swim. He heard a loud noise. It was the doctor's paper cutter. It went "Whirr!" Olivier did not like the loud sound.

He put his hands over his ears. "Hmm," he thought. The sound got quiet. He took his hands off. The whirr was loud again. He put his hands back on. Quiet again! Olivier smiled.

The doctor came in. "Hello, Olivier," she said. "Open your mouth so I can see inside." Olivier opened his mouth. "Say ahh," said the doctor. "Ahh," said Olivier. She looked with a little light.

Then the doctor gave him a sticker. It was a plane. Olivier touched it. It felt smooth. He sniffed it. It smelled like nothing much. "Can I keep it?" he asked. "Yes," said the doctor.

Olivier drew a picture while mom talked. He drew the fish, the plane, and his two hands on his ears. "That is me," he said. He held the picture up so his mom could see it with her eyes.

Asher went to the library with his dad. Today was craft day. Asher wanted to make a butterfly. The librarian gave him paper and paint.

Asher painted one wing. It was red and blue, like a little rainbow. Then his tummy felt hungry. "Snack first," said Dad. Asher set his paper down. It closed in half while he ate his crackers.

When Asher came back, he opened the paper. He scratched his head. There were two wings now! Both sides looked the same. The wet paint had copied itself.

Asher tried it again. He painted one wing green. He folded the paper. He pressed it with his hands. He opened it. Two green wings, both the same!

"I made a butterfly," said Asher. He showed it to the librarian. "Two wings, just alike," she said. A little girl next to him had no paint left. Asher shared his green. "Fold it," he told her. She folded her paper and opened it. "Two wings!" she said. Asher held his butterfly up high.

Evelyn went to the park with Dad. She carried her blue bunny under one arm. Bunny had one ear that flopped down.

Evelyn ran to the slide. She climbed up. She slid down. Then she looked for bunny. Bunny was gone.

Evelyn wanted to run and look all alone. She stopped. She ran to Dad instead. "Bunny is lost!" she said. "Help me look."

Dad took her hand. They looked at the slide first. One slide, no bunny. They looked at the swings next. Two swings, no bunny. They looked at the big rock. One rock, and there sat bunny!

A boy had set bunny on the rock. "I found it on the grass," he said. "I put it here so someone would see it."

Evelyn hugged her blue bunny tight. "Thank you," she said. Dad smiled. "Good job telling me first," he said.

Evelyn slid down the slide one more time. She held bunny up high. "Wheee!" said Evelyn.

Zayn stood on the big ferry with his mama and baba. The boat went chug, chug across the water. Zayn held his small blue bag. Inside were his socks, his cap, and a snack.

"Where is my red car?" Zayn asked. He looked in the bag. No car. His tummy felt wobbly, like jelly. He wanted his car for the trip.

Baba knelt down beside him. "Let's look together," Baba said. They searched the bag, sock by sock. Then Zayn felt something hard in his shoe. He pulled off his shoe and shook it. Out fell the red car, and one little seed from the park.

"My car!" Zayn said. He laughed and hugged it. The seed had come from a stinky fruit tree they sat under yesterday. Now it sat in his hand, small and round.

When the ferry reached the other side, the family walked to their little room. Then they got home after the trip, and it was time to unpack. Zayn put his socks in the drawer. He put his cap on the hook. He put his red car on the shelf, right next to the seed.

Mama helped him stir the pot for dinner, safe and slow. Zayn put the seed into a cup of dirt by the window. "Grow, little seed," he whispered.

Rehmat woke up and saw white. Snow was on the grass. Snow was on the car. Snow was on the path. "No school today," said Mama. "It is a snow day." Rehmat was hungry, so Mama made warm toast.

Then they heard a sound. Beep, beep. "The mail is coming," said Rehmat. But the path was deep in snow. The mail carrier might slip. Papa got the big shovel. Rehmat got her little red shovel. She pushed one pile, then two piles, then three piles of snow. It was slow work. She kept going.

The mail carrier walked up the clean path. No slipping. "Thank you," she said, and put a letter in the box. Rehmat looked at her mittens. The snow on them began to melt into little wet spots. "One shovel, one path, one letter," said Rehmat. Papa laughed and scooped her up.

William sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump. "Look at the bag, William," said Mom. William looked in the toy bag next to him.

He saw cars. One car, two cars, three cars. They were all small and round. Then he saw something long and yellow. It was not a car. It was a banana! "Mom, a banana is in with my cars!" Mom laughed softly. "That is the odd one out," she said. "It does not belong."

William held the banana up. "You do not belong with the cars," he said. "You belong with the food." Mom said they would put it in the lunch bag at the next stop.

The car went on and on. William played a game. He looked at his snack box. He saw grapes, crackers, and one little toy duck. "Duck, you are the odd one out! You are a toy, not a snack." The duck fell onto the floor. "Quack," said William, in a small duck voice.

At the stop, Mom put the banana in the lunch bag. "Good job, William." William patted the banana. "Bye bye, odd one out." Then he hugged his toy duck tight. The car door closed with a soft click, and off they went again.

Noah ran onto the green field. Coach Mia was there with a big smile. All the kids sat in a line.

Coach Mia put one red ball on the grass. Noah wanted it first. He ran fast and grabbed it. He held it tight with both hands.

Sam started to cry. "My turn," Sam said. Noah felt mad inside. He wanted the ball so much. Coach Mia knelt down next to them. "Sam can play with the ball too," she said softly. She held up her clipboard. "I will write your names on my list. Then we know whose turn is next."

Noah looked at the ball. He looked at Sam. Sam had no ball at all. Noah took a big breath. He rolled the ball to Sam. Sam stopped crying. Sam kicked the ball back. Then Noah kicked it again.

"Nice pass, Noah," said Coach Mia. Noah laughed. Sam laughed too. The ball went back and forth like a little boat on the ocean.

At the end, Coach Mia gave them both a drink of water. "Same time next week," she said. Noah waved to Sam. "See you, Sam," he said. Then he held his dad's hand all the way home.

Charles sat at the dinner table. He saw a bowl of peas. He did not want peas.

"Can we have pasta?" he asked. "We had it tomorrow."

Dad smiled and put a hand on his shoulder. "We had pasta yesterday," said Dad. "Yesterday is the day before today. You ate it before this day."

Charles looked down. He wiggled his tiny toe inside his sock under the table. He thought hard. "So yesterday is done?" he asked. "It already went by?"

"Yes," said Dad. "It went by."

"And today is now?"

"Today is now," said Dad. "Later we can have pasta."

Charles picked up his spoon. He took one small bite of peas. "Then I will eat some now," he said. "Pasta comes later."

Mom brought warm bread from the kitchen. She tore a piece for Charles. He dipped it in the peas.

"Now peas," he said. "Later pasta."

Dad laughed. "That is right, Charles. Tomorrow we can have pasta too."

Charles grinned and took another bite.

Raphael was at daycare. Mia was crying. She had dropped her doll on the floor. "Baby fell down," Mia said.

Raphael looked at the doll. It was on the mat. It did not move. It did not cry. Hmm, thought Raphael. Do dolls cry? He picked the doll up. He gave it a big hug. "There, there," he said softly. Mia stopped crying. She looked at the doll. "Is baby okay?" she asked.

"Baby is okay," said Raphael. "She wants a sock. A thick one, for her cold toes." Mia laughed. She found a tiny sock in the toy box. She put it on the doll's foot. "Baby says thank you," said Raphael, in a small baby voice. Mia hugged the doll too.

Then Mia fed the doll a pretend bottle. Raphael patted the doll's back. The doll made a pretend burp. Both children laughed out loud. Teacher Sam smiled and came to sit with them. "Can baby have one more sock?" he asked.

Raphael held up the doll's bare little foot. "Yes," he said. "This one is cold too."

David woke up. Snow was everywhere. No school today. "Snow day!" said Mom.

David looked out the window. The road was white. The road was all covered up. "How will we go sledding?" he asked.

Then David heard a big noise. A huge truck came down the street. It had a big blade in front. The blade pushed the snow off the road. David watched. The road turned black again. The snow piled up on the side.

"The truck cleaned the road!" said David.

"Yes," said Mom. "Get your boots."

At the sledding hill, David climbed up. He sat on his sled. "Be careful," said Mom. David went down, down, down. Snow flew up like little fish jumping in the sky.

"Again!" said David. He climbed up the hill one more time.

Emily sat in her car seat. She held her little bag of things. The car went bump, bump, down the road.

"I want my teddy," said Emily. She looked in her bag. She pulled out a sock. "That is not a teddy!" she said. She laughed. She pulled out a shirt. "Not a teddy either!" Then she found a hat. "Silly hat," she said, and she put it on the teddy. A sock, a shirt and a hat were all in the bag together. "Are you all clothes?" Emily asked the bag. She looked again. "Yes! Clothes, clothes, clothes." Then her hand found something soft at the bottom. It was the teddy! "There you are," she said, and she hugged him tight.

A little spider crawled up the window outside. Tap, tap. It looked like it wanted to knock and come in. "No, spider," said Emily. "This car is for teddies and clothes." Daddy laughed from the front seat. "Safe and sound," he said. Emily gave the teddy one more hug. Then the car went bump, bump, all the way home.

Elizabeth ran to the slide at the park. Her friend Mia was already there. So was a boy named Sam. "Let's take turns," said Mia. "We go one at a time."

Elizabeth went first. Then Mia went. Then it was Sam's turn. Sam slid down fast. Then he ran back to the ladder. "My turn again!" he said. "You changed the rules," said Mia. "The rule is we take turns. One, two, three." Sam grabbed the ladder and would not move.

Mia sat down on the grass. Elizabeth sat down too. Nobody was on the slide. Sam looked at his friends. They were not playing. Sam let go of the ladder. "Okay," he said. "I will wait my turn." He stood at the end of the line.

Elizabeth slid down. Mia slid down. Then Sam had his turn. He waited for his next turn all by himself. "Good waiting," said Mia. She shared her round ball with Sam. They rolled it back and forth on the grass. Elizabeth's mom sat on a bench nearby. She waved. Elizabeth waved back. "Same time tomorrow?" asked Sam. "Yes," said Elizabeth. "Same rules, too."

Ayla ran into the school cafeteria. It was her first day! She looked at one long table, two long tables, three long tables. So many chairs. So many kids.

Then her tummy made a sound. Grrrumble! Ayla was hungry. She wanted lunch right now. "Can I eat now?" she asked Miss Jo. Miss Jo shook her head and smiled. "Not yet. First we go to our room." Ayla did not know about school days yet.

So Ayla waited. She sang a song. She stacked blocks. She drew a cat, a dog, and a smelly sock, because that made her laugh. Then Miss Jo clapped her hands. "Snack time!" The whole class walked to the cafeteria. Ayla sat down and opened her little bag. One apple, two crackers, three berries. She bit the apple. Crunch! A surprise jumped out of her bag. It was her winter mitten, hiding all along!

"Snack time comes every day," said her new friend Ben. Ayla laughed and held up her mitten like a flag.

Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. Bennett wanted Grandpa to sleep in his room. But there was no bed for Grandpa yet. That was a problem.

Bennett went with Mama to the market. They pushed a little cart. "I want a soft pillow," Bennett said. He touched one pillow. Too bumpy. He touched another. Too big. Then he found a small blue one. "This one is soft!" He put it in the cart. Next to it sat a fresh loaf of bread for Grandpa's breakfast.

At home, Mama set up the small guest bed. Bennett put the blue pillow at the top. He ran and got his blanket with turtles on it. He spread it flat. He tried to make it smooth. It looked cozy.

The doorbell rang. Grandpa came in with his bag. He saw the little bed. He saw the turtle blanket. He sat down and patted the pillow. "A bed all ready for me," said Grandpa. Bennett climbed up for a hug. Grandpa said, "Best pillow at the whole market."

Maeve rides the city bus with Grandma. Maeve holds her little bunny. The bus bumps and bounces. Now Maeve looks down. Bunny is gone.

"Oh no," says Maeve. "Where is bunny?"

Grandma holds her hand. "Let's look," says Grandma. Maeve checks under the seat. No bunny. Maeve checks her bag. No bunny. She looks at the floor by the door. No bunny.

Maeve thinks hard. "I had bunny on my lap," she says. "I gave him a pretend crumb from my snack." Grandma smiles. "Then let's look right there," she says. Maeve lifts her sweater, which had slipped down in a big heap. There sits bunny, tucked straight under it. "I catch you!" Maeve says, and hugs him tight.

The bus stops. Grandma picks up the bags. Maeve sits back with bunny on her lap, both hands around him all the way home.

Ryan wore his gray sweater to daycare. Snow was falling outside the window. Miss Jo held up a big card. It had a 5 on it. Ryan did not know that sign.

The class sang the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." Ryan looked at his hand. He counted his fingers. One, two, three, four, five. Then he looked at the card again. The 5 was the same as his five fingers.

Now the class went to play. Miss Jo said, "Find the door with five." Ryan saw doors with 2 and 3. He held up one hand. He counted all five fingers. Then he saw it. A door with a big 5.

"That one," said Ryan. He opened the door. Inside were five little trucks, waiting on the shelf.

Billie stood at the bus stop with her mother. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. Billie wore her sun hat. "Where is the bus?" she asked. "It is coming soon," said her mother.

Then the wind came. The trees began to sway. Big sway, little sway, sway, sway, sway. Leaves blew all around the bus stop. One red leaf blew right past Billie's nose. "I will catch it!" she said. She ran after the leaf. The leaf blew left. Billie ran left. The leaf blew right. Billie ran right.

The leaf stopped by a thick bush. Billie grabbed it. "I caught you!" she said. She held the leaf up high. The wind blew again and her hat flew off. The hat rolled down the sidewalk. Billie chased her hat too. Her mother laughed and picked it up. "Wind, you are silly," said Billie.

Then rain began to fall. Plip, plip, plip. Her mother opened a big umbrella. "Where is the sun now?" asked Billie. "Hiding behind the clouds," said her mother. The bus came at last. Billie climbed on with her leaf and her hat. "Next time, I want snow," said Billie.

Charlotte was painting at the big table. Mama sat next to her. Charlotte painted a fat yellow bee with black stripes.

The doorbell rang. Grandma came in with a small red bag. Inside was a new blue hat for Charlotte. Charlotte put it on right away. She ran to the mirror. The hat looked just right.

Grandma sat down and waited. She looked at the door. Then she looked at the floor. Charlotte stopped. She took off the hat. She ran back to Grandma. "Thank you, Grandma!" she said. Grandma smiled a big smile. She gave Charlotte a hug.

Charlotte went back to her paint. She painted Grandma a bee hat too. Grandma laughed. "My turn to say thank you," she said.

Madison went to the library with her brother Sam. Sam was little. He wanted to count the toy ducks. He touched each duck. "One, two, four," said Sam.

Madison tilted her head. Was that right? She sang the counting song in her head. "One, two, three, four," she sang out loud. Sam pushed a duck toward her. "Say it with me," said Madison. "One, two, three, four." Sam tried. "One, two, three, four!" Now four ducks had names.

Then Sam got stuck again. He counted the library chairs. "One, two, three, four, five, seven," he said. Madison thought hard. What came after five? She sang the song again, slower. "Five, six." Sam tapped the next chair. "Six!" he said. Then he kept going. "Seven, eight, nine, ten."

After the library, they walked to the park. Sam counted the swings. The words came out in the right order, all the way to three. Madison slid down the slippery slide and laughed. "How high can you count tomorrow?" she asked Sam. Sam held up his hands and grinned. "Ten!"

Gabriel wanted to make a toy car. He found a small box in the toy basket. The box had four sides, like a square. "Good car body," said Papa.

Now Gabriel needed wheels. He took some cardboard. Papa helped him cut four little squares. Gabriel taped them on. Square wheels, one, two, three, four. He pushed the car on the floor. The car went thump, thump, thump. It did not roll. "Silly car!" said Gabriel. He laughed his loud laugh.

Papa held the scissors. He cut the squares into circles. Round wheels, one, two, three, four. Gabriel pushed the car again. It rolled fast, fast, fast. It rolled under the chair. Gabriel got down on his arm and tummy to catch it. "My car rolls!" he said. "Go, circle wheels, go!"

Sarah sat at the big table. Mom gave her paper and paint. Sarah dipped her brush in the yellow cup. She painted a big round sun. She painted green grass too. The paint smelled like rain in a garden.

Sarah wanted to hold her picture up. She grabbed it with her hand. Her thumb pressed on the sun. The yellow paint smeared. The sun now had a yucky smudge on it. Sarah's lip went wobbly. "My sun is messy," she said.

Mom sat down next to her. "Let's look at it," Mom said. Mom touched the paper with one finger. "Still wet," she said. "Wet paint makes smudges." Mom got a new sheet of paper. "This time we can wait."

Sarah painted a new sun. It was big and round and yellow. She put her brush down. Then she put her hands under her legs. She sat very still. She watched the paint shine. It looked wet and shiny, like a puddle.

Sarah waited and waited. She ate some crackers while she waited. She glued a cotton ball cloud onto the paper. Then Mom touched the corner. "All dry now," Mom said. Sarah picked up her picture with two careful hands. The sun stayed round and bright. No smudge at all. "I did it!" Sarah said. Mom clapped, and Sarah held her sun up to the window.

Lily was at school. It was time to sleep on her little mat. The room was dark. Lily closed her eyes. One, two, three, she counted sheep. Then she slept.

Lily woke up. She saw dark. She thought, "It is morning!" She sat up fast. "Time to play!" she began to shout. The teacher came over. "Shh," she said. "Look out the window." Lily looked. The sky was dark. The moon was up. It was still night, not day. Night and day were not the same. Lily lay back down. One, two, three, she counted sheep again.

Later the sun came up. The room turned light. Day was here now. Lily got up slow, not fast. She put on her shoes. One shoe, two shoes. On the table there was a letter for each child. Lily found her letter. It had a big L on it. Her friend Tom's letter had a small t.

At snack time, Lily touched a wet cup. "Slimy," she said, and wiped her hands. The teacher gave out warm bread. She poured cold milk. Lily took a big bite. Then a small sip. Outside the window, a bird flew fast. A snail went slow, slow, slow on a leaf. Lily watched the snail all the way to the edge. "Bye, snail," she said.

Elijah sat in the big waiting room. He was waiting for his first haircut. He did not want one. "My hair will fall off," he said. "It will be gone forever."

Mom held his hand. A man with long dark hair walked by. "Look," Mom said. "His hair grew long."

Elijah peeked at the barber's chair. The scissors made a snip, snip sound. A little girl sat very tall in the seat. Clippings fell on the floor. Then she jumped down and smiled. "It works," she said. "The chair goes up and down!"

Elijah sat very still in the chair. The barber snipped and snipped. Hair fell like little dark pieces of string. Elijah watched them drop.

At home, Elijah looked in the mirror. His hair was short. He touched his head. It felt soft. "Grow back fast, hair," he whispered.

Mom laughed. "You will see it grow." Elijah smiled and patted his head two times.

Emilia ate her toast in the kitchen. Crumbs fell on the floor. "I can sweep them," she said. She got the little brush and swept. The crumbs went into the dustpan.

Then Mama said, "Bath time." Emilia ran to the tub. She wanted to jump right in. But she stopped. Mama put her hand in the water first. "Too hot," said Mama. She added some cool water. She put her hand in again. "Now it is just right."

Emilia put one toe in. The water felt warm and nice. She climbed in with Mama's help. She splashed and played with the yellow duck.

After the bath, Mama helped her get dressed in soft pajamas. Emilia yawned. She hugged her bear. Soon her eyes closed and she fell fast asleep while Mama sang a quiet song. The phone rang, but Mama let it ring and kept singing softly.

Zoey wanted to make a special picture for Grandma. She drew one sun. She drew two clouds. She drew three red apples, and she wanted to eat every one. She counted the apples out loud. "One, two, three." Then she drew more. Four flowers, five birds, six shoes, seven cups, eight hats, nine cats. She wrote the numbers on her picture, too. Each number had one shape.

Now Zoey wanted to draw ten cats. She sang her counting song. "Eight, nine, ten." Ten! She tried to write ten. She made one shape. It did not look right. She looked at her brother's book. There it was. Ten used two shapes, a 1 and then a 0. Zoey wrote them. A 1 and then a 0. She looked and looked. Ten! She drew one more cat.

"Ten cats for Grandma," said Zoey.

Sarah was in the bathroom. She wanted to wash her hands all by herself. Dad turned the tap for her. "This side is cold," Dad said. "The red side makes hot water. I will turn it for you." Sarah felt the cold water on her hands. It felt nice and fresh. She rubbed the soap and made white bubbles. Dad waited by the door.

After her bath, Sarah put on her socks. Then she heard something. "Do you hear that?" she asked. Dad said, "Yes! The ice cream truck." Sarah wanted ice cream. The truck was across the street. She looked out the window. Cars went by, fast and slow.

"Can we go?" Sarah asked. "Yes," said Dad. "But first, what do we need?" Sarah looked at the street. Then she looked at her hand. She held it up to Dad. Dad took her hand in his big old hand. They stopped at the curb. They looked left. They looked right. The cars stopped. Then they walked across together.

Sarah got a pink ice cream. She licked it and smiled at Dad. "We held hands," she said. Dad gave her a big hug right there on the park grass.

Abigail looked out the window. The park was white with snow. "Snow day!" said Mama. Abigail put on her warm coat. She put on her boots and her hat. Her mittens were still on the shelf.

Abigail ran to the park. She patted the snow. It was soft and cold. She made a big snowball with wide, red hands. Then her fingers began to hurt. They felt like ice. "Ow," said Abigail. She ran back home.

"My hands are cold," she said. Mama helped her put on her mittens. Then Abigail clapped her mittens together. Back at the park, she made a snow frog. It had round snow eyes. Her fingers stayed warm and cozy. "Hop, hop, little frog," said Abigail.

Milan went to the park with his dad. Milan saw a bird with his eyes. He heard it sing with his ears. He smelled flowers with his nose. Then they sat on the grass. Dad opened the picnic bag.

"Strawberries!" said Milan. He touched one with his fingers. It felt bumpy and cold. He took a big bite. "Mmm, so sweet!"

Then Milan pinched his nose closed. He took another bite. The strawberry tasted plain, like nothing much. He let go of his nose. He took one more bite. The sweet taste came back! "Dad, the taste went away when I held my nose!"

Dad laughed. "Try the apple too," he said. Milan held his nose and bit the apple. Plain again! Then he let go. Crunch, sweet, yum.

An elephant statue stood by the swings. "That elephant is lucky," said Milan. "It has a big nose." He ran to touch the cool gray stone. "Can the elephant smell strawberries?" he asked. Dad smiled and handed him one more.

Grace stood in the school hallway. It was her first day. Her tummy felt like butterflies.

Grace had ridden the school bus. She had seen a big cat on the street. She wanted to wave at it. She stood up on her seat. The driver said, "Please sit down." So Grace sat down fast. The bus bumped and wiggled. Grace held on tight. Then she waved from her seat instead. The cat did not wave back. Silly cat!

In the hallway, Grace saw a boy. He was crying big tears. Grace wanted to help. She waved at him. He did not wave back. So Grace made a funny face. The boy froze. Then he giggled. He made a funny face back. Grace laughed too.

Then Grace's teacher called, "Time for class!" Grace took the boy's hand. They walked together. Grace let him go through the door first. "You can be last," the boy said. "No," said Grace. "You go first." And they both laughed all the way in.

Maria went to Miss Kim's music room. She was learning to play the drum. First she would build a tall tower of sounds. Boom, boom, boom went her hands.

"Play it for me," said Miss Kim. "I am your audience today." Maria played her drum. Boom, boom, boom. The room felt hot from all her jumping. She played loud like a lion, then soft like a little cat. Miss Kim clapped and clapped. "Clap, clap, clap!" Maria stopped. She looked at Miss Kim's hands. They clapped more.

Maria remembered what she saw at the big concert. The man played his violin. Then he bent down low. Maria bent down low too. She bowed. Miss Kim clapped even louder now. "Again!" said Maria. She stood up. She played boom, boom, boom. Miss Kim clapped. Maria bowed down low, and her hair swung near her knees. "Yay!" said Miss Kim, and she clapped and clapped.

Kayden ran to the big green field. The sun was warm on his face. Today the weather was good for a game. Mom held his hand. Dad carried a red blanket.

"Kick the ball!" Kayden shouted. The players ran fast. One team kicked. One team blocked. The crowd clapped and stomped. Kayden stomped his little feet too.

Then the whistle blew. The game was over. Everyone looked at the big board. Kayden pointed up. "Who won, Mom?"

Mom looked at the numbers. Both teams had two points. "The score is a tie," she said. Kayden frowned. He wanted a winner. He stamped his shoe on the grass.

Then both teams got a big shiny cup. They held it up together. The crowd cheered loud. Kayden clapped and clapped.

"Both teams win?" he asked.

"Both teams tie," said Dad, laughing.

Kayden spun in a circle. He did not dream of one winner anymore. He waved at the players. "Good game!" he called. The players waved back at him.

Luke ran into the storytime room. Today he would get his first library card! The librarian smiled. "Pick any book you like," she said. Luke found a book about a round pumpkin. Inside was a tiny black seed. He loved it.

A girl named Mia put her book back on the shelf. But it did not fit. The books next to it were big. Hers was small. Luke watched the librarian slide it out. She tapped the white label on the book's spine. Then she found the right spot. The book slid in just right.

Luke looked at his pumpkin book. It had a white label too! He matched it to the shelf. The book fit like a puzzle piece.

"You get to wear this on your backpack," said the librarian. She clipped on his new card. Luke held his book up high. "Let's go home and read about the seed!"

Isaac wanted to cook soup for his family. He ran to the backyard garden with his red bucket. He pulled up two fat carrots. Pop! One came out fast. The carrots were covered in dirt.

Isaac held up a carrot. "Yuck," he said. "Can we eat dirty carrots?"

Mom looked at the carrot. "Let's find out," she said.

At the sink, Isaac turned on the cold water. He scrubbed the carrots with his hands. The dirt washed away. The water turned brown. The carrots turned bright orange.

"Look, Mom! The dirt went down the drain!" Isaac said. "The carrots are clean now!"

Mom chopped the carrots with her big knife. Isaac watched from his stool. Mom boiled the soup on the hot stove. Soon the soup was ready.

Dad and Grandma came to the table. Everyone took a big slurp.

"Who made this soup?" Grandma asked.

"Me!" said Isaac. "I washed the carrots all by myself!"

Grandma held up her spoon. "More soup, please!"

Ivy went to the doctor with her teddy. The nurse said, "Time to check your ears." Ivy put teddy on a chair.

The doctor looked in Ivy's ears. "You hear with these," he said. Ivy heard a little beep. Then she saw a picture of a duck on the wall. She touched the cold stethoscope. She smelled soap on the doctor's hands. At the end, the nurse gave her a sweet sticker. Ivy stuck out her tongue. "I can taste the grape!" she said.

Then Ivy looked for teddy. Teddy was gone! The coat room door was open. The room was dark. Ivy could not see teddy anywhere. She felt sad and a bit grumpy. "I will look again," she said. She went slow. She patted the soft coats. No teddy. The nurse came in. "Let me help," she said. She turned on the light. Now the room was bright. There was teddy, under a red hat! Ivy held him tight. "The light helped me see," said Ivy. The nurse smiled and said, "Teddy and you make a good team."

Everly went to the big library with her dad. She wanted her very own library card. The lady at the desk said, "First, tell me your name." Everly said, "Everly! Like ever so much!" The lady laughed and made the card.

Then Everly heard a loud voice in the next room. "What is that?" she asked. Dad said, "Let's go see." A librarian sat in a circle of chairs. She opened a book about a cow who blew a trumpet. All the children laughed.
