Everly hid behind dad's legs. Then the librarian turned a page. The cow blew the trumpet even louder. "MOO!" said the librarian. Everly giggled and sat right down.

After storytime, she picked the cow book. "My card," she said, and held it out. The lady beeped the book. Everly hugged it all the way home.

Zayn ran onto the baseball diamond. "Play ball!" he shouted. He wanted to swing his bat right away.

Coach Maya blew her whistle. "First we warm up," she said. "Teams warm up by running or stretching before a game."

Zayn made a silly face. "Do bats warm up too?" he asked.

"Maybe they do," said Coach Maya. "Take yours for a little run."

Zayn ran around the bases. He held his bat up high. Then he stretched his arms way down deep, like a tall tree bending in the wind. His friend Ana copied him. "I'm a floppy noodle!" she said. Zayn laughed so hard he fell in the grass.

The game began. Zayn took a big swing. Crack! The ball flew far. "My legs feel fast!" he called to Ana.

"Told you," Ana said, and stuck out her tongue. Zayn chased her past first base.

Violet was on the swim team. Her little team was called the Blue Fish. Today was a big, hot day at the pool.

Violet jumped in the water. She kicked her legs. She splashed to the other side. The coach blew the whistle. "Break time!" he called.

All the Blue Fish climbed out. They sat on the warm bench. Every player grabbed a water bottle. Everyone drank and drank. Violet looked in her bag. She looked again. Her water bottle was at home!

Violet began to wonder what to do. Then Coach Ben came over. He held out a little blue cup. "Here you go," he said. "Players drink water during breaks, especially on hot days."

Violet drank the cool water. It felt good in her throat. Her tummy felt happy too.

Then the whistle blew again. "Back in the pool!" said Coach Ben. Violet jumped up. She splashed into the water. She kicked her legs fast.

"Go, Violet!" her friend Mia called.

Violet swam and swam. The cool water washed over her arms. She reached the wall first. "I did it!" she said with a big smile.

Coach Ben laughed. "That was fast," he said. "Same time tomorrow?"

"Yes!" said Violet. "And I will bring my water bottle."

Mackenzie turned four today. Her party was at the bowling alley. She wore shiny red shoes with wheels on the bottom. Her dad helped her put them on. "These are my party shoes," she said.

The whole family came. Grandma came. Her friend Lily came too. There were bowling shoes to borrow. Mackenzie picked blue ones. "Blue like my birthday cake," she said.

Dad blew up a big yellow balloon. He gave it to Mackenzie to hold. She held it tight. Lily had a balloon too. It was pink. Lily let go of her balloon. It did not fly up. It went down, down, down to the floor. Mackenzie watched it land.

"Let me try," said Mackenzie. She let go of her balloon. It went down, down, down too. It landed right by her blue shoe. "Again!" she said. She picked it up and let go again. Down it went, right onto Lily's pink balloon.

Then came a small surprise. The yellow balloon landed on the cake table. It touched a bowl of salty pretzels. "My balloon wants a snack," said Mackenzie. Grandma laughed and laughed. Lily picked up both balloons. "Let's do it together," she said. They let go at the same time. Down, down, down, side by side. "Happy birthday to me," said Mackenzie, and she hugged the yellow balloon tight.

Emily wanted her bunny book at bedtime. She could not find it in the pile. She looked under her bed. She looked in her toy box. "Not there," she said. Daddy helped her look. He found the book under a chair. "Here it is," he said.

Emily sat on the bed with Daddy. She opened the book from the front. The first page had words on it. "Read the words," she said. Daddy read them out loud. "This book was painted by Mr. Lee," he read. Emily touched the curly letters in his name. "Mr. Lee made my bunnies?" she asked. "Yes," said Daddy. "He is the person who paints the pictures for books."

Emily turned the pages one by one. She found a bunny with curly fur. "Mr. Lee painted this one too," she said. She smelled the pages. The air smelled like paper. Daddy read the whole book, front to back. On the last page was a small bunny sleeping. Emily smiled and whispered, "Goodnight, Mr. Lee."

Beatrice woke up and saw white. Snow! No school today. Mama said, "Snow day!" Beatrice put on her boots and her red hat.

They went to the sledding hill. Beatrice slid down, down, down. Then she fell off in the soft snow. She lay there and swept her arms. She swept her legs. She stood up and looked. There was an angel in the snow! But oh no. Her boot made a big smudge on it.

"Wait," said Beatrice. She found a different spot. She lay down carefully. She swept her arms. She swept her legs. Then she rolled to the side and stood up far away. The angel was perfect! "Two angels," she laughed. "One is sleepy."

On the way home, they saw a bird hopping in the snow. "He wants us to feed him," said Mama. They sprinkled seeds on a stump. The bird pecked one up fast. Beatrice waved. "Bye, bird! Make a snow angel too!"

Livia could not find her spotted bunny. She looked under the table. She looked behind the blocks. "Where can bunnies hide?" she asked. Miss Jo smiled. "Let us look some more," she said.

Livia looked in the toy box. No bunny. Then she saw her coat on the hook. The coat had a big pocket. Things could end up inside other things. She put her hand in the pocket. Something soft was in there. Out came the spotted bunny! "You were in my pocket all along," Livia said. She hugged bunny tight.

Then the pocket wiggled again. Livia pulled out a toy car too. It was Tim's little red car, lost last week. "I can speak to Tim at snack time," Livia said. She put bunny on her lap and drove the little car round and round.

Everly sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She did not like shots. So she covered her eyes with her hands. "Now the doctor cannot see me," she thought. The nurse said, "Hello, Everly!" The doctor could still see her! Her hands hid only her own eyes.

The nurse held up a chart. "Can you read this line for me?" Everly looked with her eyes. She said the letters out loud. Then the nurse rang a little bell. Everly heard it with her ears. Ding, ding! "Where is it?" asked the nurse. Everly pointed. She had heard it just right.

The doctor gave her a round sticker. Everly touched it with her fingers. It was smooth. The room smelled like soap. Everly sniffed with her nose. "I smell it!" she said. At the end, the nurse gave her a cookie. Everly tasted it with her tongue. Yum. It was sweet.

Everly was not angry anymore. On the way out, she covered her eyes again. Then she peeked. The door was still there. The chairs were still there. "When I close my eyes, I can't see them," she said. She opened her eyes wide and waved. "Bye, doctor! Bye, bell!"

Anna went to the band room after her cookie snack. She picked up a little drum. Her teacher, Mr. Pip, showed her a song.

Anna hit the drum. Bong, bong, boom. She made a mistake. "Too hard!" said Anna. "I am afraid I will never get it."

"Try again tomorrow," said Mr. Pip. "And the next day too."

So Anna came back. She played a little bit. Then she played a little more. Each day she came back after snack time.

On Friday, Anna sat at the drum. Bong, bong, boom, bing! She played the whole song. No mistakes!

"Mr. Pip, listen!" she said.

He clapped his hands. "Now that is a song!"

Anna played it again, even louder.

Rowan was in the backyard with his dad. He wanted his animal book. It had a bear on the cover. But the book was not in his toy box.

"Where is my bear book?" Rowan asked. Dad said, "Let's look inside." Rowan was worried. What if the book was lost?

Dad said, "We can go to the library. They have lots of books." Rowan put on his shoes. Dad got a cold frozen popsicle from the freezer for later.

At the library, a librarian took Rowan's hand. She walked to a big shelf. All the books on that shelf were about animals. Rowan saw a bird book, a dog book, and a fish book. And there was a bear book! The animal books sat together in one spot.

Rowan held the bear book tight. At home, he sat in the backyard. He made a stack of books by his chair. The animal books went in one stack. The truck books went in another stack. Dad brought the frozen popsicle and cut it in half.

Rowan licked his popsicle. He turned a page. The bear on the cover smiled at him.

Peyton ran to the park with Dad. "Look, a juice stand!" she said. Dad bought her a cold juice with ice cubes in it.

Peyton poked an ice cube with her finger. "Ooh! Cold, cold, cold!" she cried. She pulled her hand back fast. Then she picked up the ice cube with her whole hand. It was so cold! She dropped it into her cup. Plink! It splashed. "It went in the water!" said Peyton.

Then she heard a loud sound. Honk, honk! A big black bird was by the fence. Peyton saw it flap its wings. She smelled popcorn. "I smell popcorn!" she said. Dad bought a bag. Peyton touched a bumpy kernel. It felt warm. She tasted one. "Yummy!" she said. Dad smiled. "Your hands are busy today!" Peyton held up her cold juice. "My hands, my eyes, my nose, my mouth!" she said. Then she took another big sip.

Maeva went to the store with Dad. She wanted a book about fish. Fish swim in the blue water, and Maeva loved that. On the shelf she saw a birthday card. It had letters on it. "M-A-E-V-A," said Maeva. "That is my name!" The letters were red and shiny.

Near the card there was a sticker. It had letters too. "M-A-E-V-A," said Maeva again. One, two, three, four, five letters. The same letters. The same order. Her name looked just the same both times. Maeva put her finger on each letter. M, A, E, V, A.

Then she found the fish book. Dad helped her hold it. They opened the front cover first. On the first page, deep down in the sea, a big fish smiled at her. "Look, Dad," said Maeva. "The fish sees me too!"

Jayden was at the park. It was his birthday party. Mom put a big cake on the table. The wind blew the napkins. Dad held them down. Everyone sang the birthday song. It was the same song as last year.

Jayden looked at his cake. He counted the candles. "One, two, three, four." Then he counted again. "One, two, three, four."

"How many candles should I have?" he asked Mom.

"Count how old you are," said Mom.

Jayden counted on his fingers. "I am one, two, three, four, five!"

"One candle for each year," said Mom. She took a small candle from her pocket. It was a red one. She pushed it into the cake.

"A red candle!" said Jayden. "That is my surprise!"

Dad lit the candles with a match. Jayden stood back, way back. The flames flickered in the wind. Everyone clapped.

"Make a wish," said Mom.

Jayden closed his eyes. The sun came out for a warm little spell. He blew out the candles, one, two, three, four, five.

Athena lost her bunny at daycare. Bunny had soft white ears. Athena looked in the toy box. No bunny there. She looked under the art table. She found a red crayon, but no bunny. Athena felt like crying a little. It was cold outside, almost winter. Bunny could not stay lost.

Her big sister came to pick her up. "I lost Bunny," Athena said. Her sister knelt down. "I will help you look," she said. Then their dad came in too. "I can help too," he said. Now three people were looking.

Dad looked by the coat hooks. Sister looked in the play kitchen. Athena looked near the book shelf. Dad lifted a big green coat. The coat had been hiding something. Bunny was under the coat!

"Bunny!" Athena hugged her tight. Bunny's ear was a little crunchy from a left-over cracker. "We can wash that off at home," said Dad. On the way out, Athena held sister's hand. "Thank you for helping," she said. "More eyes found Bunny," said sister, and she smiled. Athena waved to her teacher. "Bye! See you tomorrow!" she called.

Isaiah went to the big store with Mama. "Let's find our juice," said Mama. Isaiah held her hand the whole time.

First they walked past the toys. A long train sat on a shelf. Isaiah waved at it. Then they walked past the foods. Apples, bread, and milk were all there.

Then Isaiah saw something on the floor. It was a small feather. It was soft and gray.

Isaiah picked it up. "Mama! Look!" he said.

"Where did that come from?" asked Mama.

Isaiah looked up. A bird sat on a tall shelf. The bird was picking at a big bag of seeds.

"Birds have feathers," said Isaiah. "The bird lost one!"

Mama laughed. "You are right!"

They got the juice. They did not forget the feather. At home, Isaiah put it in his pocket, next to a toy car.

"Feather, meet car," said Isaiah.

Leah sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump. Her toy bunny sat next to her. One, two, three bumps, and the car turned a corner. Bunny fell on the floor. "Oh no," said Leah. "Sorry, Bunny. Are you okay?" She reached down, but her arms were too short. The seat was deep and she could not reach. "Mom, can you help me, please?" she asked. Mom could not reach either. Dad stopped the car at the red light. He turned around and picked up Bunny. "Thank you, Dad," said Leah. She gave Bunny a big hug. "Bunny makes a joke," she said. "She fell on purpose!" Dad laughed. Then the light turned green, and the car went on. Leah waved Bunny's paw out the window, just a little swing, swing, swing.

Owen wanted to tell Miss Lily something big. It was about his birthday cake. It had a blue truck on it. He ran to her at the paint table. Miss Lily was talking to Ben. "Owen," said Miss Lily, "please wait one minute." Owen opened his mouth. Then he closed it. He put his hand on her arm and waited.

Ben told about his windy walk to daycare. The leaves had blown all around. Then Ben stopped talking. Miss Lily looked at Owen. "Now I can listen," she said. Owen took a big breath. "My cake had a blue truck!" he said. "I want to paint a truck." Miss Lily smiled. "Thank you for waiting," she said. "Here is the blue paint."

Owen painted a big blue truck. Ben leaned over. "Can I add a road?" he asked. "Yes, please," said Owen. Ben painted a grey road under the wheels. Owen looked at his picture. "I want to show my mom," he whispered to Miss Lily. "She will hang it up." Miss Lily nodded. "At pickup time," she said. Owen watched the door and waited.

Amira ran into the backyard. "Grandma comes today!" she said. Dad said, "We will keep her bag safe in the house." They got in the car. They drove to the train station.

At the station, people stood on the platform. There was a yellow line on the floor. Dad stood behind it. Amira stood behind it too. Then she heard a sound. Choo, choo! She wanted to lean out to see the train. Dad held her hand. "Stand here with me," he said. So Amira stepped back behind the line. The train came in. It went whoosh, whoosh, whoosh. Then it stopped. Only then did the doors open. And there was Grandma!

"One grandma, one big bag, one warm hug," said Amira, counting on her fingers. Grandma laughed. At home, Amira showed Grandma the backyard. "One swing, one sandbox, two sheep in the next yard," said Amira. The sheep said baa. Grandma sat down on the swing. Amira pushed her gently, back and forth, back and forth.

The next day they went back to the station, just to watch. They stood on the platform, behind the yellow line. "Is a train coming soon?" Amira wondered. She heard choo, choo far away. She watched the train stop, all by itself. Then the doors opened. "Again!" said Amira.

Ryan ran into the music studio. A big guitar sat on a stand. "Can I play it?" he asked.

His teacher, Miss Kim, smiled. "You can try."

Ryan tapped the guitar like a drum. Tap, tap, tap. But the guitar stayed quiet. Only a small thump came out. Ryan frowned. "Why won't it sing?" he asked.

Miss Kim passed him a little pick. "Try brushing the strings," she said.

Ryan held the pick. He brushed it across the strings. Strum! A big, warm sound filled the room.

"Again!" said Ryan. He strummed fast. Then he strummed slow. His tummy felt jumpy with joy.

"Can I show Mom?" he asked.

"Yes," said Miss Kim. "You are ready."

Ryan stood tall and proud. He strummed one more time, loud and happy, all the way to the door.

Zayn was a little boy in a big hotel room. He jumped on the squishy bed. "We fly home today!" said Mama. Zayn slid his small suitcase across the floor. Vroom!

At the airport, Zayn found his seat near the window. The plane began to rumble. Zayn wanted to stand up. He wanted to see out the window now!

"Click, click, click," went the seat belts all around him. Everyone buckled up. Papa buckled Zayn's belt too. "But I want to see!" said Zayn.

The plane went faster and faster. Then it lifted up, up into the sky. Zayn stayed in his seat. He could still see the clouds. "Wow," said Zayn. "I can see from here!"

Mama laughed. "Silly boy, the window came to you." Zayn watched a cloud shaped like a bunny hop past the window.

Mya stood at the school gate. The gate was huge. Behind it was her very first day of school.

"Hold my hand," said Mama. "We wait for the teacher."

Mya waited. She counted the gate bars. One, two, three, four. The teacher came and opened the gate. "Hello, Mya! Come in."

Inside, the teacher read a paper out loud. "Our class rules. One, we walk inside. Two, we hang our coats. Three, we sit for stories."

At play time, Mya wanted to ride the toy horse. It was a huge horse, red and shiny. She began to run to it.

A boy named Sam held up his hand. "Stop! We walk inside," he said. Mya stopped walking fast. She walked slow, slow, slow to the horse. Sam laughed. "Slow like a turtle!" Mya laughed too.

At story time, Mya hung her coat on her hook. Then she sat down on the mat.

"Sam," she whispered, "did I do all the rules?" Sam counted on his fingers. "Walk, coat, sit. Yes! All three."

Mya clapped her hands. "I did it!" Then she patted the space next to her. "Sit here, Sam."

Sam sat down, and the teacher opened the book.

Arnaud did not want to sleep. He wanted his favorite toy, a soft brown cow. He looked under his bed. The cow was not there. Arnaud's mouth turned down. His face felt sad. He showed his face to Mama. "I see a sad face," she said. "Let us look together."

They looked in the toy box. They looked behind the chair. Then Arnaud heard a sound. "Moo," said the cow, from inside the closet! Arnaud ran to the closet. He hugged his cow. His mouth turned up into a big smile. "I see a happy face now," said Mama.

Then the lamp made a click and went off. The room went dark. Arnaud held his cow tight. His eyes grew wide. "I feel scared," he said. Mama turned on her small light. The room was not dark anymore. Arnaud's eyes got small again. His face felt calm.

Mama held up a little mirror. "Make a face," she said. Arnaud made a happy face. The boy in the mirror smiled too. Arnaud made a grumpy face, like when he was angry at nap time. The boy in the mirror scowled too. Arnaud laughed. The mirror boy laughed.

He put his cow under his arm. He got into bed. Mama kissed his head. "Good night, cow," said Arnaud. "Good night, mirror boy." Then he closed his eyes to sleep.

Jules ran to the community garden with his dad. He had little pea seeds in his hand. He wanted to grow big plants, fast!

Jules dug a small hole. He dropped the seeds in. He patted the dirt down. Then he watered the soil. Every day he came back to look.

But nothing grew. Jules looked and looked. Just dirt! His dad said, "Wait, Jules. Watch." So Jules waited. A red ladybug sat on the dirt. A frog hopped near the fence. Then one day, Jules saw something new. A tiny green sprout!

The sprout grew tall. It grew leaves. It grew more and more. Soon there were fat green pods on the plant. Jules picked one pod. He squeezed it. Pop! The pod opened. Inside was a row of little round peas! "Dad, come see! The peas were hiding in here!" Jules picked more pods. He filled his whole bucket. That night, snow peas from Jules's plant sat on his plate. He ate them all up and said, "I grew these myself!"

Beatrice sat in a big chair at the mall. It was her first haircut. Mama stood close by her side.

The hairdresser cut with scissors. Snip, snip. Beatrice felt something stick to her sleeve. It was a little piece of hair. She brushed it off, and it fell down.

"Now you look so neat," the hairdresser said. Beatrice wanted to see. She turned her head left. She turned her head right. "I can't see the back," she said. "That is not bad. We can fix it," said the hairdresser.

The hairdresser picked up a small mirror. She held it up behind Beatrice. Beatrice looked in the big mirror. There was the back of her hair! "I see it!" said Beatrice. "Short and neat."

Mama smiled and held out her hand. Beatrice jumped down and took it.

Evelyn went to the park with Dad. Today the ice cream cart was not there. "Where is the ice cream man?" she asked. "He came yesterday," said Dad. "He comes once a week. Tomorrow he will still be far away."

Evelyn wanted ice cream now. "How long is a week?" she asked. Dad held up one hand. "Count the days on your fingers." Evelyn counted. One, two, three, four, five. Then she ran out of fingers. "A week is too big for one hand!" she said. Dad helped her count on his hand too. Six, seven. "A week has seven days," said Dad. "That is a lot of days."

Evelyn played while she waited. She went down the slide. Now it was sunny. Later the sun moved and made a wide shadow by the bench. Evelyn sat in the shadow. "The shadow is big now," she said.

Each day she counted one finger. One day the ice cream man came. He gave her a present, a little spoon with a star on it. Evelyn held it up high. "Seven days are done!" she said. "Can we count them again tomorrow?"

Elijah went to the store with Mama. He wanted a book about trucks. "We can find one," said Mama.

At the door, Elijah saw a big red sign. "What do those words say?" he asked. Mama held his hand. "They say Open," she said. "Words tell us things." A man read the sign too. Then he walked in. The words made him come inside!

Elijah skipped to the book shelf. He found a truck book with a cute dog on the cover. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one, front to back. Each page had words and big trucks.

At the counter, the lady read the box of stickers. The words said Blue. The stickers were blue, just like the words said. Elijah hugged his book. "Trucks," he read on the cover. "That word says Trucks," said Mama. Elijah smiled. His dream truck book was his.

Abigail was sleeping at Grandma's house. At bedtime she pulled open the sock drawer. The room was very dark. She felt two socks that seemed the same. She put them on and went to sleep.

In the morning, Grandma opened the curtains. Sunlight filled the room. Abigail looked down at her feet. One sock was red. One sock was green. "Grandma, look!" she said. "They looked the same last night!" Grandma laughed a friendly laugh.

"Try again tonight," said Grandma. Abigail picked new socks in the light. One was blue. One was yellow. She held them up to the window to be sure. Then she laid them by her bed. After her bath, she put them on in the dark. In the morning she peeked under the blanket. Two blue toes. Two yellow toes. "It worked!" said Abigail.

Henry was at Grandma's house. He had a little cold. His nose was red and his cough came back and back.

Grandma sat with him by the window. The sky was cloudy. Henry looked at the birds. Then he felt a big sneeze coming. "Ah... ah... achoo!" The sneeze went right into his hand.

Grandma brought a towel and wiped his hand. "Try this," she said. She lifted her arm and made a little cave with her elbow. "Sneeze in here."

Henry wanted to try. He lifted his arm. He made a little cave too. He waited. The sneeze came. "Achoo!" It went into his elbow, not his hand. His hand stayed clean. Grandma clapped softly.

Henry sneezed two more times that day. Each time, up went his arm. Each time, his elbow caught the sneeze. "I did it," he said. Grandma gave him a warm hug and a glass of juice. Henry smiled and took a big sip.

Layla woke up at Grandma's house in the morning. She smelled something warm. "Grandma, what is that smell?" she asked. "Cinnamon rolls," said Grandma. "My nose smelled them!" said Layla.

Grandma laughed. "Your nose is one sense. Smelling." Layla held up one finger. "One, smelling," she said. Then she touched the soft kitchen towel. "Two, touching with my hands!" She heard the kettle sing. "Three, hearing with my ears!" She saw the pink flowers on the table. "Four, seeing with my eyes!"

Grandma put a small piece of roll on Layla's plate. Layla tasted the sweet cinnamon. "Five, tasting with my mouth!" She counted all five fingers on her hand. "One nose, two hands, two ears, two eyes, one mouth. Five senses!" Grandma clapped. Layla took a big bite of her favorite roll and smiled.

Harper ran to the farm gate. "I know my five senses!" she said. Grandpa smiled. "Show me," he said.

"First, my eyes!" said Harper. She peeked over the fence. She saw beautiful white sheep. "My eyes see the sheep!" Next, she touched a soft lamb. "My hands feel soft fur," she said. Then she heard a loud moo. "My ears hear the cow!" A sweet smell floated by. It came from the kitchen. Cookies! "My nose smells cookies!" said Harper.

Harper pinched her nose shut. She sniffed and sniffed. She could not smell the cookies at all! She let go of her nose. Sniff, sniff. The sweet smell came back! Harper laughed and laughed. "Grandpa! My nose was off!" she said. "One cookie for my tongue to taste, please." Grandpa handed her a warm cookie. Harper took a big bite. "Mmm! My tongue wins!"

Jules had a cold. His nose was red. His throat felt scratchy.

He sat at the big kitchen table. Mama gave him warm soup. The bowl was too hot. Mama held the spoon herself. Jules blew on the soup. Then he took a tiny sip.

Mama went to the sink. She began to dig in the drawer for a spoon. Jules felt his throat hurt more. He wanted to hide it. But he thought of Grandma's words. Grandma had told him once, "When you feel sick, you tell a grown-up."

"Mama," said Jules. "My throat hurts."

Mama came right away. She touched his head with her hand. "You told me," she said. "That was good." She gave him a little cup of honey. The honey went down slow and sweet.

Jules closed his eyes and rested. Then he heard a tap, tap at the window. A small red bird sat there, looking in at him.

"Hello," said Jules. The bird tapped again.

Leah stood by the alphabet chart. Her teacher, Miss Po, pointed at a big red letter.

"This is A," said Miss Po. "A says ah, like apple."

"Ah, ah, apple," said Leah. Then she saw something. Each letter had a picture. B had a ball. C had a cat.

"I want to count them," said Leah.

She tapped each letter with her finger. "One, two, three." Her friend Tom came to help.

"Count with me," said Leah. Tom tapped too. They went all the way down the chart. "Twenty-four, twenty-five, twenty-six!"

Leah jumped up. "Twenty-six letters! That is a lot!"

"Yes it is," said Tom. "Almost as many as my toy cars."

Miss Po laughed. "Now find the letter for your name."

Leah looked hard. "L!" she said. "L says lll, like lion."

"And what does M say?" asked Miss Po. "For Miss Po, my name."

Leah slid her shoe on the floor. "It goes mmm," she said, "like my foot going mmm down the hall."

The bell rang. The door opened. The kids ran out to play.

"Wait!" called Leah. "P! P says puh, like play!"

Tom giggled. "You found it fast."

"Twenty-six letters," said Leah. "I know them all. Almost."

Elena was at Grandma's house. She wanted the cookies on the high shelf. "Please, Grandma, may I have one?" she asked. Grandma smiled and gave her a warm cookie. It smelled like sugar and butter.

Then a boy named Mateo came to play. He lived next door. Grandma gave him a cookie too. "Gracias," said Mateo. Elena stopped chewing. That was a new word! "What did you say?" she asked. "Gracias," said Mateo again. "It means thank you." Elena practiced it in her mouth. "Gra-cias," she said slowly. Mateo laughed, so she said it again.

They ran outside into the cool air. Elena tried to jump over the hose and slipped. She fell in the wet grass. "Sorry," said Mateo, "I moved the hose." Elena felt her knee. "Grandma!" she called. Grandma came fast and washed the little scrape. It did not even hurt much.

They played until the sun went down and it got late. "Say bye to Mateo," said Grandma. Elena waved. "Bye, Mateo! Gracias for playing with me!" Mateo grinned. "De nada," he called back. Elena giggled. A brand new word, again!

Kinsley sat in her car seat. Today they were going to Grandma's house. Yesterday they had stayed home. Tomorrow they would go to the park.

"Are we there now?" Kinsley asked.
"Not now," said Mom. "Later, when the clock says two."
The clock sat on the car dash. Its little hands moved, tick by tick.

Kinsley watched the clock. She held her book on her lap. The hands moved some more. "Is it later yet?" she asked.
Mom looked. "Look at the clock," she said.
The big hand was at the two now. Right then, the car turned a big corner. There was Grandma's house!

Kinsley climbed down from her seat. Grandma held out a red apple. "A juicy one for you," Grandma said. Kinsley took a big bite. Crunch!

"Can we have pie later?" Kinsley asked.
"Yes," said Grandma. "Later, after lunch."
Kinsley smiled and looked back at the door. The car clock was still ticking away inside.

Matthew wanted to give his bear a drink. But the water table was empty. There was no water for tea today.

Miss Ana saw Matthew looking sad. She gave him three little cups. The cups were empty too. "Hmm," said Matthew.

Mia sat down next to him. She picked up a cup. She tipped it over her bunny. "Tea for you," said Mia. "Careful, it's pretend hot!" The bunny drank nothing at all. But Mia patted her softly anyway.

Matthew tipped his cup over his bear. Nothing came out. But he made a loud pour sound. "Glug, glug." Bear drank it all up. "More tea?" asked Matthew. He poured again and again.

Soon the cups were stacked up tall. Bear was full of pretend tea. Matthew remembered the shiny coin in his pocket. He put it under a cup. "You pay for tea now," he told Mia. Mia giggled and paid with a pretend coin from the air.

Miss Ana smiled at the quiet tea party. "May I have some tea too?" she asked. Matthew poured her a big pretend cup. "Careful," he said. "It's pretend hot."

Oliver was at Grandpa's house. It was the day of the big game. Everyone was coming to watch. Grandpa put on his red shirt. Uncle Ben put on his red shirt too. Aunt Mia wore a red hat.

Oliver looked down at his blue shirt. He wanted red, like everyone else. "Grandpa, I need red," he said. Grandpa looked in the closet. He found a little red shirt. "This was mine when I was small," said Grandpa.

Oliver put it on. It was a bit big, but he wore it anyway. He walked to the couch and sat by Grandpa. Then the doorbell rang. It was their neighbor, Sam. Sam was wearing blue! "Oh no," said Oliver. "Sam cheers for the other team!" Sam laughed and sat on the far side of the room. Grandpa handed out popcorn. The game was just about to start. "Go red team!" Oliver shouted. Sam shouted back, "Go blue!"

Arthur had a sniffly nose. He sat on the big couch with his red sock on one foot. His other sock was lost under a pillow.

Arthur wanted to run outside. He slid off the couch. "I want to play ball," he said. Mama picked him up. "Not today," she said. She tucked him in with his bear and his favourite book.

Arthur felt grumpy. His tummy felt sour and his nose was red. He looked out the window. A bird hopped on the grass. Arthur snuggled his bear closer. He read his book, page by page. Soon his eyes felt heavy. He slept for a long, long time.

When Arthur woke up, he sniffed. His nose was better! "I can breathe again," he said. Mama smiled. "Rest helped you," she said. Arthur bounced a little on the couch cushions. He found his lost sock under the pillow. He put it on his foot. Then he hugged his bear and said, "You rest too, bear. Then we both play."

Victor woke up on his birthday. "Today is my party!" he shouted. Grandma was there. Aunt Lily was there. Ben from next door was there too. On the table sat a big box. It was covered in blue paper with stars. "Is it for me?" asked Victor. "Yes," said Grandma. "But you must wait."

Victor could not wait. He shook the box. He heard something go thump. He squeezed it. Something soft touched his fingers through the paper. "Is it a bear?" he asked. Ben leaned in close. "Maybe it is a truck," said Ben. "What can it be?" They shook it again. Thump, thump. Nobody could see inside.

Then Dad helped Victor open it. The paper came off. The box came open. Inside was a big red bear! "A bear! A bear!" Victor hugged it tight. Ben laughed. Grandma clapped. "Now we know," said Victor. "The paper was hiding him!" The bear wore a little blue hat. Victor put the hat on his own head. "Happy birthday, Victor!" everyone sang.

Brielle stood in the grass at school. Miss Patty, a kind woman with white shoes, held a big red ball. "Now we throw the beanbag in the hoop," she said.

Brielle threw her beanbag. It went to the side. It did not go in the hoop. Tom threw his beanbag. It went in! Tom clapped. Brielle picked up her beanbag. She looked at the hoop. She looked and looked. She threw it again. This time it went in. She had watched the hoop, and the beanbag went in. "I did it!" she said.

Then it was time for the big ball. Miss Patty rolled it to Brielle. Brielle shut her eyes tight. The ball bumped her arm. It rolled away. Tom ran after the ball and brought it back. "Here you go," he said.

Miss Patty rolled the ball again. This time Brielle kept her eyes open. She watched the ball all the way to her hands. She held it with both hands. She caught it!

"Again!" said Brielle. Miss Patty rolled the ball. Brielle watched it all the way. She held it tight. Tom held out his hands too. "My turn!" he said. Brielle rolled the big ball to her friend.

Natalie put on her red shirt. It was her soccer team shirt. She liked to wear it on game days. Today the team played at the big park.

Natalie kicked the ball to Ben. Ben kicked it back. The ball went into the net. The team cheered. One small kick made a big cheer happen.

After the game, Dad sat on the grass with her. Natalie watched a shy ant crawl on her shoe. She shook her shoe and the ant ran off fast.

"When does soccer stop?" Natalie asked. Dad opened the team paper. It had all the games on it. They counted together. One, two, three games were left. "Then the season is done," said Dad. Natalie looked at the paper. So a season was all those games, from the first one to the last one. She had played some already. Three more were still coming.

The next game, it rained. Natalie slipped in the mud. She got up and kept running. She kicked the ball with her muddy foot. It went to Ben. Ben kicked it in. "Good pass!" Ben said.

On the last game day, the coach gave everyone a ribbon. Natalie held hers up high. "We played the whole season," she said. Dad hugged her. "All the practices and all the games," he said. Natalie spun around with her ribbon in the sun.

Maya stood in the school hallway. It was her very first day. She held her teacher's hand.

"Where do we go?" Maya asked.

"We walk to the music room," said Miss Kim. "Watch. Everyone makes a line."

The children stood one behind the other. Maya did not know where to put herself. She ran ahead to the front door.

Miss Kim shook her head. "Not yet, Maya. Find your spot."

Maya looked back. There was an empty space. It was between Ben and the tall girl with red shoes. Maya stepped into the space. Now she had a spot.

The line started to walk. Maya walked in her spot. Ben walked in front of her. The tall girl walked behind her. Maya could see everyone.

"Like a train," said Maya.

"Yes," said Miss Kim. "You catch on fast."

The line went down the hallway. Maya held her spot all the way. The music room door was open. Inside there was a big rug.

Miss Kim said, "Sand buckets are for play time later. For now, come sit on the rug."

Maya sat down next to Ben. She smiled. School was a good place to be.

Natalie was at daycare. It was clean-up time. The block corner was very messy. The sun did shine on the blocks through the window. Natalie made piles. All the red blocks went in one pile. All the blue blocks went in another pile. All the yellow blocks went in a third pile. Then she made a green pile too.

Natalie counted her piles. "Where is my big red block?" she asked. She looked in the red pile. It was not there. She looked at the blue pile. There it was, hiding with the blue blocks. The red block was in the wrong pile. Natalie picked it up. She put it with the red blocks. Now all the red blocks sat together.

Ben played with his toy doctor kit next to her. "My patient needs a red block," he said. Natalie gave him one from the red pile. "All better," said Ben.

Jack stood at the airport with Dad. He waited for Grandma to come. "Her plane will land soon," said Dad. Jack watched the big doors. People came out, one, two, three. Grandma came out last, and she waved.

Grandma had a big red suitcase. "What is inside?" Jack asked. "My clothes and my things," said Grandma. "I will stay with you for one week." Jack helped pull the suitcase. It was heavy. It went bump, bump, bump across the floor.

At home, Grandma opened the suitcase. Out came a shirt, a sweater, and warm socks. Out came a small ant toy for Jack. He laughed and held it tight. Then Grandma put her clothes in the drawer, one, two, three. "Now I am all moved in," she said. Jack hugged her leg and smiled up at her.

Wesley stood by a tall cage at the pet store. A small brown puppy looked at him. "That one," said Wesley. "I want that one." Mom smiled and nodded.

At home, the puppy sniffed every corner. Then Mom set down a bowl of food. Wesley wanted to pat the puppy now. He reached out his hand. The puppy growled a tiny growl and kept eating. Wesley stepped back. He watched the puppy eat. He waited and waited. Soon the bowl was empty. "All done," said Wesley. Now the puppy ran to him. It licked his hand and spun in a circle. Wesley laughed. Mom found a soft ball, and they played together on the rug.

Later the puppy curled up in its bed and closed its eyes. Wesley whispered, "Sleepy puppy. I will pat you later." He sat nearby and watched. The puppy's tail wagged once, even in its sleep.

Mateo went to the library with his mama. He wanted to find the letter A. On the wall, he saw a big A. "There it is!" he said. He patted the wall. The big A felt smooth and cool.

Then he opened a thick book. He looked at the page. He saw a small round letter. "That is not A," he said. He turned the page. He saw it again. "Where is A?" His mama sat down next to him. "Take your time," she said.

A girl at the next table leaned over. "That little one is A too," she said. Mateo looked. He looked again. The small a did not look the same as the big A. But it was the same letter. "Big A, small a," he said softly.

He found B, big and small. He found C, big and small. His finger traced the small c on the page. "Same letter," he said. His mama smiled. "Can we read this one now?" Mateo asked, patting the thick book.

Violet went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about a boat. She looked on the shelf where the boats might hide. She pulled out a big blue book. It felt smooth and cool in her hands.

Violet sat down on the soft rug. She opened the book. The boat was there, but it looked funny. The boat was upside down. The sail pointed down. The words looked upside down too. They hung from the top of the page like little bats.

Violet felt worried. "This book is broken," she told her dad. Her dad sat down next to her. He was warm and smelled like outside. He said nothing. He just smiled and waited.

Violet looked at the book again. She turned it around in her hands. Now the boat sat up straight. The sail pointed up. The words sat on the lines, quiet and neat. Violet laughed. She had been holding the book upside down!

Violet turned one page, then the next. The boat sailed through the whole book. The last page was empty, just blue water and sky. "The end," said Violet. Dad said, "Time to check it out." Violet held the book the right way up all the way to the desk.

Wesley came to school early. He smelled something warm and sweet. "What is that smell?" he asked. Miss Pam smiled. "Bread is baking. Come and see." Wesley used his eyes to look. He saw the big oven. A grown-up was the only one near the hot oven, so Wesley stood back with Miss Pam.

"I smell it with my nose," Wesley said. Miss Pam held up a little mirror. "Look at your nose," she said. Wesley looked. He saw two little holes. He counted them. "One, two! My nose has two holes!" Miss Pam laughed. "Those are your nostrils." Wesley touched his nose with his fingers. The holes tickled.

Then Miss Pan clapped her hands and shouted, "The bread is ready!" She took it out with big mitts. The bread sat on a wood board. Wesley touched the board. It was smooth. Miss Pam gave him a small warm piece. He tasted it with his tongue. "Yum!" said Wesley. Then he heard a happy sound. It was his own tummy, rumbling. Everyone laughed.

Stella woke up and saw white. Snow! Lots of snow. School was closed, and it was a snow day. She put on her boots and ran to the backyard. Dad made a little hill out of snow. It was small, but Stella loved it.

"I will go down like a penguin!" she said. She lay down on her tummy, head first at the top of the hill. Dad shook his head. "Watch me," he said. Dad sat on the sled. He sat up. He faced forward. He held on with both hands. Then he slid down. "Wheee!"

Stella tried it his way. She sat up. She faced forward. She held on tight. Down she went, fast and smooth. She laughed so hard she fell over in the snow. "Again!" she said. Dad pulled the sled back up the hill. Stella touched the cold snow with her mittens and grinned. "Wheee!" said Dad, and down they went together.

Thomas stood by the big door. The hall was full of people. Music played and everyone danced.

Thomas did not dance. He held Grandma's hand. His feet stayed very still. "I wish I could dance," he said softly. But his shoes did not move one bit.

Then Uncle Sam walked by. He was dancing like a wobbly duck. He flapped his arms and spun around. Thomas laughed and laughed. His feet began to tap. Tap, tap, tap. They went all by themselves!

Grandma smiled. "Our feet like the music," she said. She took his hand and they stepped out onto the floor. Step, step, turn. The music was fast now. Thomas spun like Uncle Sam. He wobbled like a duck too.

Outside, the street was dark. It was getting late. But inside, the music played on. Thomas danced and danced. Then he shouted, "Look at me, Uncle Duck!" Uncle Sam quacked back at him.

Axel sat at the big table. He wanted to paint a picture. Mom put the paint cups out. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was green paint. There was gray paint too.

Axel began to paint a house. He used red for the roof. He used green for the grass. Then he wanted to paint the sky. He picked up the gray brush. He made one gray line at the top.

Then Axel looked out the window. The sun was shining bright. The sky outside was not gray. The sky was blue. Axel put the gray brush down. "We need blue," he said.

Mom found a blue paint cup. It was a different cup, just for blue. Axel dipped his brush in it. He painted over the gray line. Now his sky was blue, like outside.

Axel held up his picture. "Look, Mom! My sky is sunny day blue!" Mom smiled and hung it on the wall.

Sienna sat in the family car. She held her brown bag. But her toy bunny was gone.

"Where is Bunny?" she asked. Her tummy felt tight.

Mama said, "Let us think. Where did we go today?" Sienna thought hard. "We went to the swings. Then we went to the slide. Then we got in the car."

"Then we go back," said Mama. "Swings first. Slide next. The same way, one stop at a time." Sienna buckled her seat belt. The car started to move.

First stop: the swings. Sienna looked under the swing seat. No bunny. Just sand and a brown leaf.

Next stop: the slide. Sienna ran to the slide. She looked at the top. She looked at the bottom. There, in the grass by the ladder, was Bunny! "Bunny!" Sienna hugged her tight. "Thank you, Mama. Going back the same way found her."

At home, Sienna sat by the warm lamp. Bunny sat in her lap. Mama put a soft blanket over them both.

"Bunny can sleep with me," said Sienna. She gave Bunny one more squeeze.

Theodore stood in the gym with his teacher, Ms. Rose. He wanted to throw the red beanbag into the big hoop. He aimed and threw. The beanbag hit the floor. "Oh no," said Theodore. Ms. Rose smiled. "Try again," she said. Theodore looked at his hands. He moved his hands down low. He threw the beanbag up and out. It sailed through the hoop. "I did it!" said Theodore.

Then Ms. Rose rolled him a big blue ball. He held out his arms. The ball came fast. It hit his hands and bounced away. He tried again. The ball bounced away again. Theodore frowned and pulled his hat down over his eyes. Then the ball came once more. Theodore caught it and pulled it right to his chest. He hugged it tight. The ball stayed!

"Now we can play," said Ms. Rose. She gave him a crunchy cracker for a snack. Theodore hugged the ball again, just because. "My turn," he said. He spun around and laughed. Ms. Rose clapped her hands. The ball stayed snug against his chest all the way to the snack table.

Chloe went to the store with Dad. She wanted a red apple. Outside the store, they had to cross the road. Dad held her hand tight.

"Look, Dad, a light!" said Chloe. It was up high on a pole. The light turned red. All the cars stopped. Then the light turned green. All the cars started to go. "Red means stop. Green means go!" said Chloe. Dad laughed. "Yes, let's go now." The light was green, so they walked.

Inside the store, Chloe saw yellow bananas and green grapes. She picked one big red apple. It felt heavy in her hands. On the way out, a little boy was crying by the toy pig. Chloe gave him a wave. He smiled at her. At the crossing, the light turned red again. "Stop!" said Chloe. Dad squeezed her hand. The cars stopped, and they waited for green.

Nathan went to the park with his dad. They were bringing home a new pet. It was a small guinea pig named Pip. Nathan wanted to carry Pip all around.

"I can hold him while I run," said Nathan.

Dad shook his head. "Let us sit on the grass first," he said. They sat down. Dad showed Nathan how to use two hands. "Hold him gently," said Dad. "Not too tight."

Nathan held Pip with two hands. Pip was soft and warm. Pip wiggled a little. Nathan sat very still. Pip did not fall at all.

Then a baby bird hopped near them. Pip made a happy squeak. What a small surprise!

"Again!" said Nathan. He held Pip gently, gently, with two hands. Then they walked home, slow and happy, Pip squeaking all the way.

Elijah went to the vet with his mom. A small puppy sat in a crate. "Can he be my pet?" Elijah asked. "Yes," said Mom. "He is ours now."

The vet clipped a leash to the puppy's collar. The leash went from the collar to Mom's hand. "I will walk him," said Mom. Outside, a bird hopped on the grass. The puppy wanted to chase it. He pulled and pulled. But the leash kept him close to Mom. He could not run away. "The leash holds him!" said Elijah. "Is that what it does?" "Yes," said Mom. "It keeps him near us."

At home, the puppy's tummy made a big growl. Was he grumpy? No, he was hungry. Mom poured food in his bowl. The puppy ate it all up. Then he curled up on Elijah's lap. "I will walk you every day," Elijah whispered. The puppy licked his hand.

Charles was at school. Today was a big day. He was going to write his own name!

Ms. Amy gave him a chunky pencil. She gave him a paper with the letters C-H-A-R-L-E-S.

Charles picked up the pencil. He began to trace the C. But the paper slid away! His line went crooked. "Oh no," said Charles.

He tried again. He took off his shoe and tried to hold the paper with his foot. That did not work at all. The paper still slipped. Everyone giggled.

Then Charles had an idea. He put his shoe back on. He pressed his other hand flat on the paper. The paper stopped sliding!

He traced the C. It came out round and neat. He traced the H. Then the A. His letters went up and up, all the way to the S.

"I did it!" said Charles. Ms. Amy put his paper on the wall. Charles stood in his cozy sweater and clapped his hands.

Austin went to the store with Mom. He wanted one big orange carrot. He was a bunny today, and bunnies need carrots.

The carrot aisle was busy. A tall man stood in the way. Austin squeezed and squeezed. He could not get past. "Mom, I'm stuck," he said.

"Try the magic words," Mom said. Austin thought hard. Then he looked up at the man. "Excuse me, please," he said. The man smiled and stepped aside. "Thank you!" said Austin. He zoomed past like a little bunny.

Austin found the biggest carrot of all. It looked like a magic wand. He put it in the cart, next to the frozen peas. At the checkout, he bumped the cart into a shelf. A can fell down. "Sorry," said Austin. He picked up the can and put it back.

At home, Mom washed the carrot. Austin held it up high. "Abracadabra!" he said. "Now we are bunny wizards." Mom laughed and took a big crunchy bite.

Rosalie ran up the steps to Grandma's house. The door opened fast. "Happy Hanukkah!" said Grandma. Inside, the house smelled like warm potato pancakes. Cousin Ben was already at the table. Rosalie had not seen Ben for a long, long time.

"Ben!" she called. "You got so big!" Ben laughed and showed her his new truck. It had a black wheel that spun around. Rosalie spun it too. It went whir, whir, whir.

Then Daddy came in with the menorah. He lit the candles with a match. Rosalie stood back and watched the little flames. "One, two, three candles," she counted. The candles made the room glow. "Why so many candles tonight?" she wondered. Grandma smiled and patted the big chair. "Everyone sit close," she said. "The family is all here now."

Ben handed Rosalie a small gift. It was a dreidel with short sides. "Spin it," said Ben. Rosalie spun it on the table. Round and round it went, and then it fell with a tap. "My turn," said Ben. He spun it back to her.

Olivia wanted to paint a big sky. She had red, yellow and blue paint. She knew their names now. "Red like a strawberry," she said. "Yellow like the sun. Blue like my cup."

She set up her wooden easel. She dipped her brush in the blue. She painted a big blue sky. Then she stepped back to look. "Oh no," she said. "My sky is too dark. It looks like night!"

She wanted a morning sky. A light blue sky. She looked at her paints. Then she had a question. "What if I add white?"

She found the white paint. She stirred it into the blue. Round and round went the brush. The blue began to change. It got lighter and lighter. "Look, look!" she shouted. "My sky is getting soft!"

She painted the light blue over the dark blue. Now it looked like morning. Dad came to see. "Did you paint that?" he asked. Olivia grinned. "I did! White made my blue light!" Then she dipped her brush again. "Now I will paint a yellow sun."

Blake's teddy bear, Boo, was sick. He had a big cough. "Ah-choo!" said Blake for him. She put Boo in a small box. The box was his bed. "You need medicine," Blake told him.

She ran to the kitchen. Mom was there. "Can I have pretend medicine?" Blake asked. Mom gave her a spoon of water. "Only pretend," said Mom. Blake held the spoon near Boo's mouth. Boo drank it all up. Then Blake wrapped Boo in her old blue blanket. She tucked him in. She gave him a kiss on his nose.

Boo opened one eye. He felt better already! Blake said, "Your job is to sleep now." She turned off the light. From the dark came a tiny sound. "Ah-choo!" Blake ran back. "Boo! You need a hat too."

Sophia sat at the dinner table. The lamp glowed warm and yellow. Her plate had peas, bread, and milk.

"Papa, story now," said Sophia.

"A story is not now," said Papa. "Now we eat dinner. The story comes later, after dinner."

Sophia looked at her plate. She ate one pea. Then she ate two peas. "One pea, two peas, three peas," she counted. The peas went into her tummy, one by one.

She took a big drink of milk. Oops. The cup tipped. Milk ran across the table. "Messy," said Sophia.

Papa brought a towel. He helped her wipe the table. "The milk spilled now," said Papa. "Now we clean it up." They wiped and wiped until the table was dry again.

Sophia shook her napkin open. She put it on her lap, all by herself. She ate her bread. She ate more peas. Her plate was empty at last.

"Dinner is done," said Papa. "Now it is story time."

Sophia clapped her hands. "Now? Now the story?"

"Yes, now," said Papa. He sat down next to her. He opened the big story book.

Sophia snuggled close. "Yesterday we read the bear book," she said.

"That's right," said Papa. "Today we read this one. Tomorrow we can pick a new book."

Sophia smiled. "Today is story day." Papa turned the first page, and he began, "Once there was a little duck."

Mya sat on the playroom rug. She had five toy monkeys. She wanted to sing their song. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed," she sang. "One fell off and bumped his head!" She made one monkey fall down. It rolled under the chair. She counted the monkeys left on the rug. "One, two, three, four," she said.

She sang the next part. "Mama called the doctor and the doctor said..." She made her voice deep like Daddy's. "No more monkeys jumping on the bed!" Then she sang again. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed. One fell off and bumped his head!" Another monkey fell. This one landed on her foot. She giggled and put it with the first monkey. "One, two, three," she counted.

Mya went on singing. Each time the song said a monkey fell, she took one away. Three monkeys, then two, then one. The last monkey had a big job. It jumped all alone. "One little monkey jumping on the bed!" Mya sang loud. Then it fell too, right into her lap.

Mya looked at her empty rug. All the monkeys were in her lap now. "Zero monkeys," she said. Her little brother crawled over. He wanted a monkey too. "You are lucky," Mya said. "I have five!" She handed him one. Then she counted what she had left. "One, two, three, four." She hugged the monkeys and started the song again.

Jake was at school. He wanted to play outside on the slide. Then the sky got dark. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap.

"No park," said his teacher, Miss Kim. Jake felt sad. His lip went down. He sat on the rug and looked at the wet window.

Then Mia came over. "Let's make a blanket house," she said. They put a big blanket on two chairs. It made a soft little cave. Jake crawled inside. It smelled clean, like fresh towels. He smiled a big smile.

"I feel happy now," said Jake. Miss Kim laughed softly. "The rain gave us a surprise," she said.

Jake heard the rain tap again. It sounded like a song. "Rain, rain, spell your name," sang Mia. Jake sang too, inside their cozy blanket house.

Jacob ran to the playground. The big slide waited for him. The small slide waited too. "Which one should I ride?" he asked. "The big one!" said his friend Mia.

The sun was hot. The water fountain was cold. Jacob drank and drank.

Then it was quiet time. Baby Ben was sleeping on a blanket. Jacob wanted to bang his drum. Boom! Boom! So loud! Mama put her finger to her lips. "Shh. The drum woke the baby."

"Can a drum be quiet?" Jacob asked himself. He tried a little tap. Tap. Tap. So quiet! Baby Ben kept sleeping.

After nap, Jacob tapped fast. Then he tapped slow. Ben laughed and clapped.

"Your drum is a good gift," said Mia. She sniffed her shoe. "My sock is smelly!" Everybody laughed. Jacob tapped one more quiet tap. "Shh," he whispered, grinning.

Edouard saw a big blue truck at the park. It was full of books. A man inside gave books to kids. Edouard wanted a book too. But the man said, "You need a card."

Edouard patted his pockets. He had no card. He ran to his grandma. "Can you help me get one?" he begged. Grandma smiled and took his hand. They went to the little desk in the truck. The man gave them a paper to write on. Grandma wrote her name. Then Edouard wrote his name, all wobbly. The man gave Edouard a small blue card. "This card is yours," he said.

Edouard picked a book about a sleepy bear. The bear fell asleep in a cave. Edouard held the book tight all the way home. At bedtime he read it two times. Then he put the card under his pillow.

Sara ran to the park with her bunny. She squeezed him tight. But at the swings, her hands let go. Bunny was gone!

Sara looked and looked. One swing, two swings, no bunny. One slide, two slides, no bunny. A dog barked near the bench. No bunny there either.

Then Sara saw a little house. It had a sign with a hat and a shoe on it. A kind man opened the door. Inside were lost things. A thin scarf hung on a hook. A red cup sat on a shelf. One box, two boxes, three boxes of hats!

"Things people find go in here," the man said. "Look inside this basket." Sara peeked in. Soft gray ears popped up at her. Bunny!

Sara hugged him all the way home. "One swing, two swings," she sang, "and one bunny, found!"

Mia wanted cold milk. She was so thirsty after helping Papa shop for big oranges and small plums. "One bag, two bags, three bags," she had counted at the store.

She opened the fridge door. The milk was cold inside. Then Mama called, "Mia, come see the tea!" Mia ran fast to the table. Mama poured hot tea from the pot. "Blow on it," said Mama. "It is hot. Your milk is cold."

Mia blew. The steam went up, up, up. Then she heard a humming sound. She looked back at the fridge. The door was open! Cold air was puffing out. Mia walked slow and careful. She pushed the door shut. The humming stopped. "All closed," said Mia. "Now the milk stays cold, and I can drink it." She took a big sip.

Zoe rode in the car with Daddy. They drove down the long road to the hospital. The sky was cloudy and gray. Mommy was at the hospital with a new baby.

Zoe held Daddy's hand in the hall. They found Mommy's room. Mommy was in the big bed. Next to her was a small basket. Inside was a tiny baby. "This is your brother," Mommy said.

The baby began to cry. The nurse said, "He needs a clean diaper." Daddy looked in the bag. He could not find one. Zoe saw something under the blanket. "I will look," she said. She lifted the soft blanket. A clean diaper was hiding there. She gave it to the nurse.

The nurse changed the baby. He stopped crying. He looked at Zoe. Mommy smiled. "You helped him," she said.

Zoe patted the baby's small hand. The baby held her finger. Daddy brought a warm blanket. Zoe helped tuck it in around him. "Hello, baby brother," Zoe whispered. "I will help you every day."

Elena sat on her soft rug. The sun made a warm spot by her bed. Her toy bunny, Boo, sat in a little boat made of a shoebox. The boat was a boat on a pretend pond.

Elena pushed the boat gently. Then she pushed too hard. The boat tipped over. Boo fell out and bumped the floor. Elena felt scared. She held her breath.

She picked Boo up and looked at his face. "Are you okay?" she asked. Boo stayed quiet. Elena hugged him soft and close. She patted his ears. Then she felt happy again. Her tummy felt warm.

Elena set Boo back in the boat. "I will send you across the pond," she said. She blew a little puff of air. It was like a windy day for Boo. The boat moved slow across the rug. Boo did not fall this time. Elena clapped her hands. "You did it!" she said. She gave Boo one more gentle push and watched him float.

Scarlett sat on the red rug at school. Miss Ana held up a big blue bag. "Let's play the feely-bag game," she said. "Put your hand in. Don't peek. Guess the toy!"

Tom went first. He put his hand in the bag. "It is a ball," he said. He pulled it out. The ball was yellow. "I thought it was red," said Tom. "The bag tricked me!"

Now it was Scarlett's turn. She closed her eyes and pushed her hand in. She felt something round and smooth. She squeezed it. She pat pat patted it. "Is it a ball?" she asked. "Yes!" said Miss Ana. "But what color is it?" Scarlett felt and felt. "I can't tell," she said. "My fingers can't see." She pulled out the ball. It was green, her favorite color! Everyone clapped.

Scarlett had an idea. "Let me try one more," she said. She felt inside the bag. Something small and bumpy. "A car!" she said. "But I must look for the color." Out came a blue car. "Blue!" she shouted. Tom laughed. "The game is tricky," he said. "My fingers know the shape. Only my eyes know the color."

At play time, Scarlett made a sign for the bag. She drew a big eye on it. Tom drew a hand next to it. "Eye for colors," said Scarlett. "Hand for shapes." They hung the sign on the wall. "Next time, I will guess better," said Tom. Scarlett smiled and patted the green ball. "Me too," she said. "But green is still my favorite."

Mason sat at Grandma's big table. He held a fat yellow pencil. "I want to write my name," he said. "Can I?" Grandma smiled. "Yes. Let me show you how to hold it." She put his fingers on the pencil. Three fingers, just like that.

Mason made an M. It looked wobbly, like a cat had walked across the paper. He laughed. "Silly M!" He tried again. Still wobbly. "Why is it so hard?" he asked. Grandma said, "Try it lots of times." So Mason wrote M, M, M. Then A, S, O, N. He was not afraid of the wiggly letters anymore.

Every day at Grandma's house, Mason wrote his name. One, two, three letters, then four, then five. Soon the M stood up straight. The O turned into a nice round circle. "Look, Grandma!" said Mason. Grandma clapped. "That says Mason!" Mason held up his paper high and said, "That's me!"

Owen came to the playground early. The sun felt warm on his face. He heard kids laughing on the swings.

Owen ran to the slide. But a big boy was there. The big boy pushed in front of Owen. Owen felt angry. His face got hot. He wanted to stomp his feet. He sat on a bench instead. The bench felt cool and smooth.

His teacher Miss Ana sat down next to him. "Owen, how are you feeling?" she asked. Owen looked at his shoes. "I feel sad," he said. "I feel angry too. That boy pushed ahead of me." Miss Ana nodded. "Thank you for telling me," she said. "Let's go talk to him together." The big boy said sorry. Then he slid down and clapped for Owen's turn.

Owen slid down fast. The wind whooshed by his ears. He felt excited and happy. He ran to tell Miss Ana. "My tummy tickled!" he said. She smiled and held his hand. It was soft like his pillow at home. They walked to the swings, nice and slow. Owen pumped his legs higher and higher. "I feel so happy!" he shouted. Miss Ana clapped and said, "I can tell!"

Matteo ran to the pool in his thick swim shorts. He was ready to jump in. "Stop right there," a lifeguard called out. "Shower first, then swim."

Matteo looked at the pool. The water looked big and shiny. He looked at the shower. The water there was small and warm. Matteo did not want the small water. He wanted the big water.

"Shower first, then swim," Mom said with a smile. Matteo stood under the shower. The warm water ran over his hair. It ran over his arms. "Shower first, then swim," Matteo said this time, all by himself.

Then he walked to the pool steps. Splash! His feet went in. The water was cool. "I showered first!" Matteo shouted. Then something surprising happened. Another boy ran past him, straight toward the pool. The lifeguard said the same words. "Shower first, then swim."

The boy stopped. He looked at Matteo. Matteo pointed at the shower. "Warm water," he said. "It is nice." The boy stood under it too.

Then the two boys sat on the pool step together. Splash went Matteo's hands. Splash went the boy's hands. "Shower first, then swim," they both said, and in they went.

Layla woke up with funny hair. It stood up on one side. It flopped over the other side.

She hopped out of bed. She looked in the little mirror. "My hair looks like a bird nest!" she said. Her socks peeked out of the covers like two sleepy mice. Layla laughed and put them on her feet.

"I want to look nice today," Layla said. Mommy was awake too. "Ask me for the brush," said Mommy. Layla asked. Mommy gave her the soft blue brush.

Layla brushed the top. That part was easy. Then she came to a tangle. Ouch! It pulled. "Go slow," said Mommy. "Little bits at a time." Layla brushed one little bit. Then another little bit. The tangle got smaller and smaller. Then it was gone! Layla smiled big. Her hair was smooth and shiny.

After that, Layla had a bath with bubbles. She got dressed all by herself. She ate eggs for breakfast. Her heart felt happy and bouncy. She ran to show Daddy her hair.

"Look at my smooth hair!" said Layla. Daddy patted it gently. "Very nice," he said. "Can I borrow your brush? My hair looks like a bird nest too!"

Layla giggled and handed him the blue brush.

Wyatt ran to the slide at school. The ladder went up, up, up. Wyatt climbed to the top. Then he slid down, down, down. "Again!" he said. He went up and down many times.

His friend Milo was little. Milo's legs felt weak at the bottom of the ladder. He could not climb up. Wyatt saw Milo's sad face. He held Milo's hand. "One step," said Wyatt. "Then one more." Up they went, slow and slow. Then they slid down, fast and fast. Milo laughed out loud.

After the slide, they went inside. Miss Jo had a big cup of tea. The tea was hot. She held it with both hands. "Careful," she said. She gave the boys small cups of cold water. Wyatt drank his cold water fast. Milo drank his slow. Then Wyatt and Milo sat at the table. They used blocks to build a big tower. It went up tall. "Push it!" said Milo. Wyatt tapped one block. Down came the tower, block by block. Wyatt put out his cup. "More water, please," he said.

Evan ran to the sandbox. He wanted the big yellow digger. It was his turn now. Ben had it last.

But the door was open. The little babies were sleeping inside on soft mats. Evan did not know yet.

"I WANT THE DIGGER!" Evan shouted very loud. A baby inside woke up and began to cry. Miss Amy came out fast. She put her finger by her lips. "The babies are sleeping," she said in a small, small voice. "Come with me."

Evan stood still. He heard the baby cry. Then the baby stopped. Miss Amy rocked her gently. Evan watched. When someone sleeps, you need a quiet voice, he thought. Would a whisper work?

Evan leaned close to Ben. "Can I have the digger next?" he whispered. Ben nodded. He dug one more scoop of sand. Then he gave Evan the digger.

Evan dug a big hole. He put a stick in the hole like a tree. "Look at my tree," he whispered. The babies kept sleeping. Miss Amy smiled and gave them both a cracker.

"Quiet voices all morning?" Evan whispered to Ben. Ben held his cracker up high. "Yes," he whispered back.

Nathan stood on the ferry with his big brother Sam. The wind was cold. The water below was dark and wavy. "One suitcase, one backpack, one bear," Nathan counted. He hugged his bear tight.

Before the trip, Nathan had packed his blue swimsuit. "For swimming!" he had said. But Dad opened the suitcase and smiled. He held up Nathan's mittens and his warm red coat. "We are going to the snow," said Dad. "Snow needs mittens." Nathan put on the mittens. His hands felt cozy at once.

Now the ferry horn went honk, honk. Nathan looked out the window. White flakes began to fall on the black water. "Sam, look! Snow!" said Nathan. He waved his mittened hand at the sky, and one soft flake landed right on his brother's nose.

Leon dumped out his big basket of picture cards. Cards went everywhere! He wanted to make a town with them. But the cards were all mixed up. He could not find what he needed.

Leon looked at a card with a cow. "You are an animal," he said. He made an animal pile. Cow, duck, and dog went there. Then he found a ball and a drum. "You are toys," he said. He made a toy pile. Then came apple, bread, and egg. "You are foods," he said. He made a food pile. Now the town had a farm, a toy shop, and a food store.

Leon lined the animals in a row. He followed them with his toy truck. The truck was carrying fresh apples to the store. Then a card fell from the pile. Leon picked it up. It was a little cat wearing a tiny hat! Leon laughed out loud. "You go with the animals," he said. "But you can keep the hat."

Lea sat on the city bus with Mama. She held a little card with her name on it. It was her first library card. On her lap was a big red book about a snowy day.

Lea opened the book. There was a cat in the snow. The cat had soft white fur. Lea put her finger on the page. She wanted to draw a hat on the cat. She took out her purple crayon. The crayon came closer and closer.

Then she saw small marks on the page corner. Other kids had held this book too. Lea looked at Mama. "This book is not mine," she said. Mama smiled and nodded.

Lea put the crayon away. She pulled a paper from her bag. On the paper, she drew a snowy hill. She drew a cat with a big purple hat. "There," said Lea. She closed the big red book very gently. The bus went beep, and Lea felt happy all the way home.

Alice wanted to make soup for dinner. "I can help," she said. Dad said, "Yes, you can."

First, Alice put the carrots in the pot. Then she counted three potatoes. Dad dropped them in. Plop, plop, plop.

"Now we need an onion," said Dad. He picked up the knife. Alice stood back, way back.

Dad cut the onion into small squares. Then his eyes went drip, drip, drip. Big tears ran down his face.

"Dad, you are crying!" said Alice. "Are you sad about the soup?" She patted his arm.

Dad laughed. "Look at the onion, not me." Alice looked. The onion sat on the board, cut into squares. Dad blinked and blinked.

"It is the onion," he said. "Silly onion. It makes my eyes water."

Alice giggled. "Onion, you are a trickster!" she said.

They added the onion to the pot. Dad's eyes stopped dripping. Alice stirred with a big spoon, and the soup went round and round.

Then Mom came in. She sniffed the pot. "Mmm," she said. "Who cut the onion?"

Alice pointed at Dad. Dad made a funny crying face. Everyone laughed.

After dinner, Alice helped wash up. Then she yawned a big yawn. "Bath time," said Mom. Alice jumped in the tub. The water was warm. Her toes made little splashes.

"Dad," she called. "No onions in my bath!"

Rose wanted Grandpa to read her book about puppies. But Grandpa sat down and said, "One moment, Rose." He reached for his glasses. He put them on his nose.

Rose looked at the glasses with her eyes. "Why do you wear those?" she asked.

Grandpa opened the book. "Watch," he said. He read the first page slowly. Rose listened with her ears. She heard every word clearly.

Then Grandpa lifted the glasses off. He looked at the page. His eyes got wide. He turned the book toward Rose. The letters looked small and cloudy to him.

Rose touched the glasses gently with her fingers. They felt smooth and cool.

"I smell cookies," she said, sniffing with her nose. Grandpa laughed and put his glasses back on.

"Let's read, then eat," he said. "Mama made them sweet."

Rose tasted a warm cookie after the story. "Yum," she said, and Grandpa read the puppy book one more time.

Felix went to the library with his mama. He wanted a book about dogs. He found a big red book with a black dog on the front. He showed it to a girl named Mia.

"That is a dog," said Mia. "Dogs are animals. My book has a cow. Cows are animals too."

Felix found a little blue book. A fish was on the cover. "Is a fish an animal?" he asked. "It has no legs."

"Let's look," said Mia. She put her book next to his. The fish book sat on the shelf under a sign. The sign said animals. The dog book was there. The cow book was there too.

"The fish is with them!" said Felix. He put his head close to the shelf. He tapped the fish book. "Fish, dog, cow. All animals."

The librarian smiled. "Would you like to take that one home?"

"Yes, please," said Felix. He hugged the blue book to his chest and walked to the desk, holding mama's hand.

Hunter ran into the backyard. The sun felt warm on his face. Daddy was cooking at the grill. "Hot," said Daddy. "Stay back, please." Hunter stopped and watched. He could smell the food cooking. It smelled good.

Then Hunter saw his little slide. He wanted to slide down fast. He climbed up and sat down. He began to lie down on his tummy. His head went first. That felt wobbly. Hunter slid just a bit and stopped. He sat up and turned himself around. Now his feet went first. Down he went, whee, all the way to the grass.

Hunter ran to get his blocks. He stacked one block, then two, then three. The tower fell over into a messy pile. Hunter laughed. "Again!" he said. He put the first block down on the soft green grass.

Charlie got a new pet today. It was a little gray bunny. He carried the cage to the backyard. "Hello, bunny!" he said.

Charlie opened the cage door. But the bunny did not hop out. It hid in the corner. It stayed very still.

Charlie frowned. He wanted to pet the bunny. He reached in fast. The bunny moved back more.

"Mom, the bunny won't come!" said Charlie.

Mom came outside. "Let's sit on the grass," she said. "We can fill this bowl with bunny food and wait."

Charlie sat down on the warm grass. He put the food bowl near the cage. He sat very still, like a rock. It was hard to be so still.

Then Charlie heard a sound. Plop! The bunny hopped out! It sniffed the bowl. It nibbled the food. Charlie giggled softly.

"It feels safe now," Mom whispered.

Charlie smiled big. The bunny hopped one tiny hop closer.

"Hi, friend," said Charlie.

Sienna sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. Her tummy felt stormy. "I will get a shot today," she said quietly. Mom held her hand. "I will stay right here," said Mom.

Nurse Amy came in with a small tray. Sienna saw the tiny needle. "Can I hold it?" she asked. "Only I touch the needle," said Nurse Amy kindly. "But you can hold my sticker sheet." Sienna took the sticker sheet. It had a flower on every sticker. She looked at the flowers while Nurse Amy gave the shot. It was done fast, like a little pinch. "All done!" said Nurse Amy. Sienna picked a pink flower sticker for her arm.

"Let's go get ice cream," said Mom. Sienna did not have to wait long. She got a cone with two scoops. She licked it and smiled. "My flower sticker matches my pink ice cream," she said.

James ran into writing club with his pet rabbit, Benny. "Today I write my name!" he said. His teacher, Miss Kim, smiled. She gave him a chunky pencil and a name card.

James held the pencil tight. He wrote J, then A, then S. Then he wrote a big M and another A. He looked at his paper. Something was wrong! Two letters had popped into the wrong spots. "Miss Kim, my name looks funny!" he said. She held up his name card. James looked. Then he looked again. The M came before the A, not after. He erased and fixed the letters, one by one.

He wrote his name once more, top to bottom. Same letters, same order, every time. "Benny, look!" he said. "My name is all full of letters, and they stay put!" He hugged the soft rabbit and wrote it again.

Kayden ran to the kitchen. Lunch was on the table. Warm bread and apple slices. Yum!

"Wash your hands first," said Mama.

Kayden stood at the sink. He pumped the soap. Bubbles grew on his hands. Mama helped him count. "One, two, three." They counted all the way to twenty. Bubbles, bubbles, bubbles!

Then the water went off. Kayden's hands were wet. He shook them. Drip, drip! Water fell on his shirt. Water fell on the floor. Little drops everywhere!

Where did the water go? Would it ever stop?

Then Kayden saw it. A blue towel hung on the hook. He reached up and took it. He rubbed one hand. Then the other. His hands went from wet to dry. All clean and dry!

He planted his dry hands on the bread. He held it tight. No slips, no drops. Kayden took a big bite.

"Mmm," he said. "Dry hands, yummy bread."

Wyatt dug a little hole in the dirt. He dropped a carrot seed inside. He patted the dirt down with his hands. "Grow, little seed," he said.

Every day Wyatt looked at his garden. One morning, tiny green leaves popped up. "Hello, leaves!" he said. But then he saw something else. Little green leaves were growing in the wrong spot too. Wyatt frowned. Were those his carrots? He reached down to pull one up.

Mom came outside with a spoon. "Wait, Wyatt," she said. "Let's look first." She knelt in the grass. "These leaves are in your seed line, straight in a row," she said. "Those other ones are not. Those are weeds. Weeds grow where we don't want them." Wyatt touched the weed leaf. "Not my carrot?" he asked. "Not your carrot," said Mom.

Wyatt pulled the weeds and put them in a bucket. His carrots got sun and water. Soon tall green tops stood in a straight row. Mom pulled one up. A fat orange carrot hung from the leaves. Wyatt took a bite and began to chew. "It grew!" he said. Mom smiled and held up the watering can. "More water for the others?"

Leo ran to the play corner at school. His friend Mia was there. She put cushions on the floor.

"Watch out!" said Mia. "The floor is a river!"

Leo looked down. The floor did not look like a river. It was just brown and flat.

Mia hopped on a cushion. "Pretend it is a river," she said. "Pretend the cushions are rocks!"

Leo wanted to cross too. He wanted to get to the toy kitchen on the other side. He held his baby doll tight. He wanted to cook dinner for her.

Leo took a big jump. One rock! Then another jump. Two rocks! Then one more. Three rocks!

"You made it!" said Mia. "Now you are home."

Leo smiled. He sat at the toy kitchen. He turned the pretend knob. He stirred a pretend pot.

"Time to eat, baby," said Leo. He held the doll close. He patted her back, just like his mom did for his little sister.

Then Mia called, "The baby is cold!"

Leo looked around. He found a small blanket. He wrapped the doll up. "Nice and warm," he said.

"You are so kind to your baby," said Mia.

Just then a boy named Sam ran by. He stepped right on the floor river!

"Splash!" shouted Mia. "You fell in!"

Sam laughed and laughed. "I am a fish!" he said. He wiggled on the floor.

"Fish can come to dinner too," said Leo. He handed Sam a pretend cup.

Sam sat down. Mia sat down. The baby sat in Leo's lap.

"One soup, one cup, one warm baby," said Leo.

Mia clapped her hands. "Best dinner ever!"

Amira ran to the dress-up corner at school. She was so excited to wear the red cape. But Ben was there first. He had the cape on already. Amira felt angry. Her face got hot and her hands made fists. She wanted to grab the cape.

Then Amira heard a small sound. Drip. Drip. It was Leo, sitting close to the toy nest on the rug. Tears ran down his cheeks. Leo was sad. He was crying because his block tower had fallen down. Amira forgot all about the cape. She went to the rug and got her teddy bear. She put the teddy in Leo's hands.

Leo hugged the teddy tight. His tears stopped. Then he smiled a big smile. "Thank you, Amira," he said. Amira felt happy inside, warmer than any cape. Ben saw them and took off the red cape. "Your turn," he said. Amira put it on and twirled around the nest of soft toys. "Teddy helps sad friends," she told Leo. Leo nodded and clapped.

Owen sat in the big waiting room chair. His feet did not touch the floor. He held his toy truck in both hands. Dad sat next to him and smiled.
