"Owen," the nurse called. Owen stood up slow. He took one step, then one more. The nurse had a nice voice. She pointed to a little chair. Owen sat and held his truck tight.

"Will it hurt?" Owen asked.

"Just a quick pinch," said the nurse.

Owen felt the pinch. He blinked. Then it was done. Dad gave him a big hug. "All done," said Dad.

In the car, Owen rubbed his arm. "Ow," he said. "Why does my arm hurt?"

"That can happen after a shot," said Dad. "It will feel better soon."

Owen waited. He looked out the window. A red truck went by. He waved at it. Then he rubbed his arm again.

"Better now," said Owen. He held his truck up high. "Beep, beep!"

Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She had blocks of every shape. She picked a round one first. It rolled away! "Come back!" she laughed. The circle block would not stay still.

So she tried a square block. It sat nice and flat. She stacked another square on top. Then her friend Max came in. "Look!" he said. "That one is a new shape. It has a point at the top!" Lillian looked. She had turned one square sideways on the rug. "Is it a square?" she asked.

She turned the block back. Flat side down, it looked the same as before. She tilted it again. The point went up. "Silly block," she giggled. "You are still a square!" She stacked it back on the house. The snake slid in through the triangle roof and curled up on a rectangle block. "Perfect house," said Lillian.

Lena stood in her bedroom. She wanted her red boots. They were not here yet. "Yesterday we went to the store," said Mom. "You tried on the red boots. Do you remember?" Lena nodded. The store was loud and bright. Mom had said, "We will buy them tomorrow." Now it was today. But where were the boots? "The boots come soon," said Mom. "Soon?" asked Lena. What did soon mean? Was it a long, long wait? Lena looked at her old shoes. They were small. Her toes felt squished. She sat on her bed to wait. Mom read her one book. Then Mom brushed her hair. Then Lena heard the doorbell. It was Grandma! Grandma held a big bag. "Something is in here for you," she said. Lena peeked inside. The red boots! So that was soon. Soon was not long at all. Lena hugged Grandma. "Thank you, Grandma!" she said. She slipped the boots on, one, two. "Look at me!" said Lena. "Now let me stomp."

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She had one big spoon. She had two little cups. Daddy put three peas on her plate. Aubrey poked them with her spoon. "Peas are round," she said.

Then her big brother Ben came in. He was smiling big. "I am seven today!" he said. He held up his fingers to show Daddy. Aubrey peeked at his hands. Seven was lots of fingers.

"How old are you, Aubrey?" Mommy asked. Aubrey looked at her own hand. She held up some fingers. "I am five!" she said. Ben laughed so hard his milk went slosh. "No, silly. Five is me, next year. You are three." Aubrey put down some fingers. Three fingers stayed up. "I am three," she said. Her voice felt upset for a minute, but then she grinned.

"Three peas for a three-year-old," said Daddy. He counted them out. "One, two, three." Aubrey ate them one by one. Then she held up her three little fingers again. "Three!" she said, and banged her spoon like a drum.

Athena put on her red boots. It was snowy at the park. Snow fell on her brown mittens. "Snow, snow, snow," she said.

"I want to keep some snow," said Athena. She rolled a little snowball. It was round and white. "I will put it in my glass cup."

The wind blew. It was windy, and her hat flew off. "I will hold my hat," she said. Papa picked it up.

At home, the house was warm. Athena put the snowball in her glass cup. "Now it is safe," she said.

She played with her blocks. She looked at the cup. The snowball was small. Then it was gone. A little puddle sat in the cup. "My snow turned to water," said Athena. Papa smiled. "Snow melts inside where it is warm," said Athena. "Next time I will keep it outside."

Papa hugged her. "Let's look out the window," he said. Outside, the snow would grow deep all night. Athena waved at the white park. "Bye bye, snow," she said. "See you tomorrow."

Ava and her family were going on a long drive. They were going to the beach to see Grandma. Ava sat in her car seat. She looked out the window.

After a while, Ava said, "I need the potty." Mom said, "Don't worry. We can stop soon." The car turned off the big road. It stopped at a rest stop. Ava asked, "Can we potty here?" Dad said, "Yes, that is what it is for." Ava held Mom's hand. They walked inside. Ava used the potty. Then she stretched her arms up high. Dad stretched too. They got back in the car.

Soon they saw the blue sea. Grandma waved from the sand. Ava dropped her short pink bucket by the water. The water came up. The bucket floated! Ava laughed and held Grandma's hand.

Raphael held his daddy's hand. They walked into the pool changing room. The floor was wet and shiny. Raphael could smell the water. He could hear kids splashing far away.

Raphael let go and started to run. His feet slid. He sat down with a bump. "Ouch," he said. Daddy helped him up fast. "The floor is wet," said Daddy. "Let's walk."

Raphael looked at his feet. He took one slow step. Then another. No sliding now. "Daddy, can I run to the pool?" he asked. "No," said Daddy. "We walk to the pool. Then we can play."

They walked all the way. Raphael held his towel tight. At the door, a big splash went boom. Water jumped over the edge. Raphael laughed. "A swimming game!" he said. Daddy held his hand. "Ready," said Daddy. "One, two, three, splash."

Charlie sat in her reading nook. She had letter cards all over the soft rug. Her cat, Socks, lay near her like a gray feather pillow. Charlie wanted to put the cards in a row. But she did not know where M went.

Dad sat close by with a warm mug. He did not pour tea on her cards, so she was not worried about spills. Charlie held the M card. "I am stuck," she said. Dad said, "Try your song."

Charlie sang the alphabet song. She sang slowly. A, B, C, D, E, F, G. She kept going. L came, and then M. M went after L. She put the card down in its spot. "It fits," she said. Socks woke up and yawned a stinky yawn. Charlie laughed and sang the song again.

Ivy got a new library card. It had her name on it. She held it with both hands.

At the library, Ivy picked a book. It was about a worm in a garden. The worm dug in the dry dirt. "I want to keep this forever," Ivy said.

The librarian put a white paper in the book. "Bring the book back on this day," she said. She pointed to the white paper. That day was the due date.

At home, Ivy read the worm book. She read it in the morning. She read it after her nap. She read it three more times.

Then the due day came. Mom said, "Time to take the book back." Ivy hugged the book tight. "I don't want it to hurt to say goodbye," she said.

At the library, Ivy set the book on the desk. Then she saw a boy. He took her worm book. He sat down to read it. His smile grew big.

Ivy picked a new book to take home. The librarian stamped the white paper. "See you on the due date," she said.

Ivy grinned and held her card up high.

Sofia sat at the big table. She had a bag of letter cards. Mama sat next to her.

Sofia put the cards in a line. "A," she said. "B, C, D." She went on and on. "L, M, N, O, P." Then she stopped. "That is all," she said. "P is the last letter."

Mama smiled. "Let's sing the song," she said. They sang it slowly. They sang it again. After P came more sounds. Q, R, S, T. Sofia clapped. "Keep going," said Mama.

They sang to the end. "X, Y, Z," sang Sofia. "Now I know my A B Cs." She looked at her line of cards. P was not last. Z was last. She found the Z card in the bag. She put it at the end of the line.

Sofia touched each card. "A first," she said. "Z last." She picked up the bag. "Let's do it again," she said. Mama laughed and sang.

Aaron stood in the pool changing room with his dad. He pulled on his swim pants. Then he sat on the big bench to wait. "Will the water be too big for me?" he asked. "The teacher will help you," said Dad.

The pool room had a painting on the wall. It was a huge picture of a blue sea. Aaron looked at it while they walked to the water. Miss Kim the teacher smiled at him.

"Now we float on our backs," she said. Aaron felt scared. The water looked so wide. Miss Kim put her hands under his back. Aaron lay down on top of the water. Her hands held him up. "I'm floating!" said Aaron. "My tummy goes up and down with the waves." He kicked one foot and a splash hit Dad's nose. Dad laughed and said, "You are a real swimmer now."

Emilia went to the library with Dad. She wanted a book about a sleepy bear. She found a book with a bear on it. She opened it at the back. The pages went the wrong way. The bear was already in bed.

"No, no, sleepy bear," said Emilia. She turned the book around. She found the front. The bear woke up on page one. She patted the floor. "Sit here, book," she said.

"Who made up this bear?" she asked the librarian. The librarian pointed to the cover. "This name is the author," she said. "The author wrote the words."

Emilia looked at the name. She read the letters out loud, one by one. The author wrote the words. The words made the story.

She hugged the book. "You made my bear," she said to the name.

Sara ran to the pretend kitchen at the playground. It had a little orange pot and a little orange spoon. "I will make soup," she said. She stirred one potato, two carrots, three beans. A boy named Ben came to play too. "I am the baby," he said, and he sat in a small chair.

Sara fed the baby soup. "More, please," said Ben. The sun began to go down. Sara's mom called, "Time to go home soon."

Sara looked at the kitchen. It was a big mess. The pot was on the floor. The cup was under the bench. "We can't leave it like this," said Ben. Sara picked up the pot. Ben found the cup. They put back the spoon, the potato, the carrots, the beans. One, two, three, all done.

"Now the kitchen looks tidy," said Sara. She took one last look at the clean little kitchen. "Good night, kitchen," she whispered. Then she ran to her mom and held her hand.

Liam looked out the window. The sun was gone. The sky was gray. "Rain," said Mom. Big drops hit the glass. Tap, tap, tap.

"I want to go to the park," said Liam. "Not in the rain. My hair will get wet." Mom held up something red. It was the umbrella. She pushed it open. It went pop. "Put on your boots," said Mom. Liam pulled them on. They had ducks on them.

Outside, the wind blew. The tree waved its leaves. Mom held the umbrella over them both. Liam listened. The rain went tap, tap on the red top. But his hair stayed dry. He put out one hand. That hand got wet. He pulled it back under. "Dry again," he said.

"Is it snowy today?" Liam asked. "No," said Mom. "Snow is white and soft. Today is just rainy." They walked to the end of the street and back. At the door, Mom shook the umbrella. Drops fell off. Liam drank his juice by the window. The rain kept tapping. His hair was dry and straight, all the way home.

Amelia ran to the play kitchen at daycare. Her friend Ben was there too. He held a big red pot. "Soup!" he said. "Pinecone soup!"

Amelia peeked into the pot. She saw pinecones and paper leaves. She stirred with a big wooden spoon. Round and round the spoon went. "It's ready!" said Ben.

Amelia lifted the spoon to her mouth. She wanted to taste it. "Stop," said Miss Kim. "That soup is pretend." Amelia looked at the pinecones. Pinecones were not real food. Real soup came from the real kitchen. This soup was for pretending.

So Amelia opened her mouth wide. She made a big slurpy sound. "Sluuurp!" she said. She did not eat anything at all. Ben laughed and slurped too. The baby doll got a pretend spoon next. Amelia patted the doll's arm. "All gone," she said. "More soup tomorrow."

Ben clapped his hands. "Best soup ever!" he said.

Logan had a small violin. It was in a black case. He wanted to play it very much.

He opened the case. He took out the bow. He held it in his fist like a stick. He poked the violin with the tip. The violin made a squeak. "Oh no," said Logan. That sound was not pretty.

His big sister Mia came in. The cat ran to see too. "Can you help me?" asked Logan. "It is hard," said Mia. She sat down by him. She put the bow in his hand the soft way. "Now pull it across the strings," she said.

Logan pulled the bow across the strings. The violin sang. It went, "Looo!" Logan laughed. The cat's ears went up. "Again!" said Logan. He pulled the bow again. "Looo!" sang the violin.

Mia read her book while Logan played. He played to the cat. He played to Mia. The cat sat very still and listened.

"Play one more," said Mia. Logan pulled the bow, slow and smooth. "Looo," sang the violin, all the way to the end.

Clara was at school. It was cold outside. "Brrr," said Clara. Everyone put on mittens.

Miss Kim gave out scarves. Clara got a red scarf. It was long. It went down to her shoes. Sam got a blue scarf. His scarf was short. It sat on his shoulders.

Clara tried to walk in her long scarf. She stepped on it. Plop! She fell down softly on the mat. "My scarf is too long," said Clara. Sam laughed. "That is a silly joke, scarf," he said. Clara laughed too.

Then Clara had an idea. She wrapped the scarf around and around her neck. Now it was short, just like Sam's. "Look, Miss Kim!" said Clara. "Now we match." Miss Kim smiled. "Good thinking, Clara," she said.

It was time to go outside. Clara ran fast to the door. Sam walked slow. Outside, the wind blew. Clara's scarf flapped like a red wing. Sam's scarf stayed snug. Miss Kim swept the snow off the steps with a big broom. Clara helped push the snow with her boot. A naughty gust of wind tugged at Sam's hat. Sam grabbed it just in time.

"Ready?" said Sam. "Ready," said Clara. They stepped out into the snow together.

Leon was at Grandma's house. It was a snowy day. Snow fell past the big window. Leon wanted to bake bread for the whole family.

Grandma helped him mix flour and water. The dough felt sticky. It stuck to his fingers. "Oh no," said Leon. "Is it ruined?"

"Watch me," said Grandma. "Cooks push the dough and fold it." She pushed and folded. Then Leon tried it. He pushed the dough with his hands. He folded it over. The sticky bits came off his fingers. The dough turned smooth and soft.

"Did I do that?" asked Leon. "Yes, you did," said Grandma. She laughed at his happy noise.

Grandma put the bread in the hot oven. Leon stayed back and waited. Soon the bread was warm and golden. The family ate it together. Leon said, "I made this bread!"

Isabella painted a sun at school. It was high in the sky. She wanted to show it to her friend Mia. But Mia was not at school today. Mia was sick yesterday, too. Isabella felt sad. "I want to go now," she said. Her teacher said, "Mia is at her home. She lives near the park." Isabella put the painting in her bag. She would take it home after dinner. She would sleep in her bed. Then it would be tomorrow. Tomorrow is the day after today. So tomorrow, Isabella would wake up. She would get dressed. She would run to school with her painting. The next morning, Mia was there. Isabella held up the sun. Mia smiled big. "I love it," said Mia. "Let's paint one together now."

Aurora went to the dentist for the first time. The chair went up and down like a little ride. "Can I make it go?" she asked. The dentist smiled and said, "I will let you press the button." Aurora pressed it. The chair rose. She pressed it again. The chair came down.

Then a girl named Mia came in. She was young too. Mia picked up a toothbrush. "Oops," said Mia. "That one is Aurora's." Mia had grabbed the wrong one. Mia put it back and took her own toothbrush instead. Aurora looked at the two brushes. One was green. One was blue. Each brush had its own person.

"Where is my brush?" Aurora asked. The nurse pointed to the cup. "There it is, the green one." Aurora held it up. "Mine!" she said. The dentist laughed. "Yes, all yours." Aurora sat in the chair, opened her mouth wide, and let the little wheel spin and tickle her teeth.

Lucy wanted to sort her crayons by color. She made a red pile, a yellow pile and a green pile. Then she held up a dark blue crayon. "Where do you go?" she asked it. She put it in the blue pile.

Then she found a light blue crayon, the color of the sky. "Are you blue too?" she asked. "You look so pale!" She put it next to the dark blue one. They did not match. But they were both still blue. "Two blues," said Lucy. "Hello, blue family!"

She ran to get her doll. "Look, Dolly, light blue socks," said Lucy. She pointed at the doll's dark blue dress. "And this is dark blue. You wear two blues, Dolly!" Her big brother Sam peeked in. "That one is navy," he said, pointing at the dress. "Navy is dark blue," said Lucy. Sam laughed. "Okay, okay. You win."

They lined up all the blue crayons on the rug. Lightest first, darkest last. One, two, three, four, five, six. "It goes from sky to deep sea water," said Sam. Lucy clapped her hands. "Blue can be light. Blue can be dark. Blue is blue!" She picked up the lightest blue crayon and drew a big snow cloud, all white and pale. Sam drew deep dark waves under it. "Snow on top, deep blue below," he said. Lucy held up her drawing to show the doll. "Dolly, look! Our blue day!"

Gabriel went to the park with his dad. There was a little pond near the trees. Gabriel saw a fish swim by in the water. He waved at it. The fish swam away.

Dad brought two beanbags and a big red ball. "Let's play," said Dad. Gabriel wanted to toss a beanbag into the hoop. He threw it too low. It landed on the grass. He tried again, higher this time. The beanbag went in. "I did it!" said Gabriel.

Then Dad rolled the ball fast. Gabriel tried to catch it. It bumped his hands and fell. Dad said, "Let's try again." He tossed the ball slow and soft. Gabriel held out both hands. The ball came down gently. He caught it! Gabriel laughed. "Again!" he said.

A little girl came to play too. Gabriel rolled the ball to her, very softly. She caught it with both arms. "Silly ball," she said, and giggled. The sun went behind a cloud. They played until Dad called, "Time to go home." Gabriel waved to the fish in the pond.

Wyatt wanted a snack. Mom said, "You can have three grapes." Wyatt looked at the bowl. There were big grapes and small grapes. He picked three small ones. Then he saw the big grapes. Maybe big grapes counted less? He put the small grapes back. He took one big grape. That was only one grape on his plate. He took two more. One, two, three. He counted them with his finger. Three grapes sat on the plate. The big ones did not make more. Three still meant three.

Wyatt ate his grapes. They were sweet and cold. Then he saw a small bug on the window. "Mom, a bug!" he said. Mom came to look. Wyatt started to count the bug's legs. "One, two, three," he said. The bug crawled up. "Four, five, six." It went higher. "Seven, eight." Mom laughed. "Keep going," she said. "Nine, ten!" said Wyatt.

The bug found a little hole and went outside. "Bye, bug," said Wyatt. He waved at the window. "One bug," he said. "Ten legs." Mom gave him a kiss on his head. "One kiss," she said. Wyatt giggled. "Two!" he said, and kissed her back.

Alexander walked into the music classroom. A big guitar sat on a little red chair. "Can I play it?" he asked. Miss Rosa smiled. "Yes, you may try."

Alexander pulled the strings with his fingers. Plunk, plunk. He made a face. "It sounds funny," he said. "It does not sound like your guitar." Miss Rosa had a guitar too. Her strings made a nice sound.

Miss Rosa sat next to him. She turned the little pegs at the top of the guitar. She turned one, then another. "Now try again," she said. Alexander pulled the strings once more. The sound came out sweet and clear.

"It sounds good now!" said Alexander. He played a slow song. Miss Rosa tapped her foot along. On the wall, a poster showed a pig playing a violin. Alexander laughed. "Pigs can't play violins," he said. "But if one did, it would have to tune it too." He pulled the strings one more time.

Elizabeth wanted to help sort the shopping. Mama put the bags on the floor. "Can I help?" asked Elizabeth. "Yes," said Mama. "You can sort."

Elizabeth made a pile of toys. She put the teddy bear in the pile. She put the ball in the pile. Then she held up a carrot. She put the carrot with the toys too.

Elizabeth looked at the carrot. She looked at the teddy bear. The teddy bear was soft. The carrot was hard and orange. Then she looked at the table. There sat an apple. There sat the bread. Mama was eating the apple. Papa was cutting the bread with a safe knife.

Elizabeth picked up the carrot. She carried it to the table. She set it down next to the apple. "Is this right?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "Good sorting, Elizabeth."

"Snack time," said Papa. He gave Elizabeth a small piece of apple. Elizabeth took a gentle bite. Then she gave the carrot a little kiss, just to say hello. Outside, a truck rolled down the street. Elizabeth waved at it and took another bite.

Aurora sat on the big clean rug. Everyone was watching the game on TV. Dad was there. Grandma was there. Mr. Lee from next door was there too.

A man on TV threw a ball at a hoop. The ball went through the hoop. The crowd made a big happy sound. Aurora clapped her hands. "The ball went in the hoop," she said. She wanted to try that.

She ran to her toy bin. She found her soft red ball. She could not reach the real hoop. So she found something else. Her laundry bag hung on the door hook. It had a round open top, like a hoop.

Aurora stood back. She threw the ball. It hit the wall. She picked it up and tried again. The ball went into the bag. Dad clapped. Grandma clapped. Mr. Lee laughed a happy laugh.

Aurora bowed. Then she stirred her arms in a big circle like a slow wave. "More popcorn, please," she said.

Jake stood in the backyard. The sun was warm on his face. He wanted to play hide and seek with Mama.

"Close your eyes," said Mama. Jake covered his eyes with his hands. "I see nothing," he said.

Jake peeked through his fingers. "I see the tree! I see the ball!" He opened his hands wide. Now he saw the flowers too.

"Eyes are for seeing," said Jake. "That is one sense!"

Then he heard a bird. "Ears are for hearing," he said. He sniffed the flowers. "My nose smells them!"

Jake touched the grass. "Fingers feel soft things," he said. Then he ate a nice snack. "My mouth tastes the apple!" He wiped his hands on a towel.

"Five senses," said Jake. "I said them all!"

"Yes you did," said Mama. She clapped her hands. "Now count to ten and find me!"

Jake closed his eyes and began. "One, two, three..."

Elijah sat in his reading nook. He held a big letter card. The letter was S. It looked like a little snake.

"Can you find the S sound?" Mama asked. "It goes sss, like a hiss." Elijah listened. Sss. The sound tickled his ears a little.

He looked around the nook. Sun came in the window. "Sun!" he said. "Sss-un!" Mama smiled and nodded. Elijah put the card next to the sunny spot on the floor.

Next he saw his sock on the rug. He picked it up. "Sock starts with sss too!" The sock was sticky from his snack. He wiped his hands on his shirt and laughed.

Then he saw his sand pail by the door. "Sand! Sss-and!" He held up the card again. Sun, sock, sand. All three began the same way. All three made the hissing sound.

Elijah looked for more. He found a spoon in his toy box. "Sss-poon!" he said. Mama clapped her hands. Elijah hugged his letter card and whispered, "Sss."

Matthew went to the store with Mama. He wanted to buy apples for snack time. Mama said, "We need four apples." Matthew counted, "One, two..." Then he stopped. What came next? He could not remember.

A girl walked by with her daddy. She was singing a song. "One, two, buckle my shoe." Matthew listened. The song went on. "Three, four, shut the door." Matthew tapped his toes. The words felt bouncy in his ears. Did the song help him count?

He tried it himself. "One, two, buckle my shoe," he sang. Then he said, "Three! Four!" He looked up at Mama. "Mama, I know what comes after two!" Mama smiled. "Let's hear you count, Matthew."

He put apples in the bag. "One, two, three, four." The apples went plunk, plunk, plunk, plunk. The bag felt heavy and warm from his hands. The store lamp made a bright circle on the floor. Matthew stepped into the light. "Five, six, seven," he sang. What if he kept going?

"Eight, nine, ten," said the singing girl, passing by again. Matthew waved. "Ten! Big hen!" The girl laughed. At home, Mama cut the apples at the counter. Matthew sat safe at his little table. He sang his new song to the apples. "One, two, buckle my shoe." Then he took a big, crunchy bite.

Ellie went to the library with Dad. There was a big game on the rug. "Put things in piles," said the librarian. "Animals here. Toys here. Foods here."

Ellie found a stuffed dog. It was soft and brown. She put it in the animal pile. Then she stopped. She looked at the dog. She patted its fur. It did not wag. It did not bark. It was not alive. So it was a toy! Ellie moved it to the toy pile. "Good try," said the librarian. "You fixed it all by yourself."

Next Ellie found a cat, a ball, and an apple. "One cat, two toys, three foods," she said. The cat went in the animal pile. The ball went in the toy pile. The apple went in the food pile. She counted again. "One, two, three!"

Then Ellie found a little pillow. It was soft like the dog. She put it in the toy pile too. Now the dog sat on the pillow. It looked cozy. Ellie yawned. She was getting sleepy. "Close your eyes for one minute," said Dad with a smile. Ellie gave the sleepy toy dog one more pat. "Night night, little dog."

Ella wanted to read her new book all by herself. She sat on her bed and held it up. But she had it the wrong way round. The pictures looked funny. The bear came before the honey. The rain came before the clouds. "That is all mixed up," said Ella.

She turned the book over. Now the bear was on the front. She opened the front cover. She turned one page. Then another page. The bear found the honey at last. The cloudy sky came first, and then came the rain. "Is this the right way?" asked Ella. "Yes, it is," she said.

Some words sat under the pictures. Ella did not know them yet. She put her finger on them. She moved her finger, slow and careful, from left to right. Then she brushed her hand over the page, soft like paint on paper. "Words say something," said Ella. She turned the page to see what came next.

Luka ran to the park with Dad. Dad had a picnic basket. "Let's play a game," said Dad. "We will find our five senses." Luka clapped his hands.

First, Luka closed his eyes. He heard a tiny bird. "I used my ears!" said Luka. Then he saw a big rainbow over the trees. "I used my eyes!" Next, he touched the warm slide. "I used my hands!" Then he sniffed an apple. "I used my nose!"

"Now the last one," said Dad. He held up a lemon slice. Luka licked it with his tongue. "Sour!" said Luka. His whole face scrunched up. Dad laughed. Then Luka chewed a sweet strawberry. "Yum! Sweet!" said Luka. "My tongue did that!"

"So what is the fifth sense?" asked Dad. "Tasting!" said Luka. "And my tongue does it!" Dad gave him a thumbs up. Luka licked the strawberry juice off his fingers and ran to the swings.

Maeva went to the big Diwali festival with Mama and Papa. The street was full of colors. There were flowers and drums and sweet smells. Maeva carried a basket of small clay lamps called diyas.

"I want to help," she said. So she set the diyas in a slow, careful row along the step. But the lamps looked dark and plain. "Why don't they shine?" she asked. Mama smiled. "Watch Papa."

Papa had a spoon of oil. He poured a little into each lamp. Then he touched a match to the wick. One lamp glowed. Then the next one glowed. Then the whole row glowed! Maeva clapped her hands. The oil had made the lamps light up.

A tiny flame flickered near Maeva's fingers. "Careful, it's hot," Papa said. He moved the lamp a safe bit away. Maeva watched the little lights dance. The whole street began to shine, one lamp at a time.

"More lights!" Maeva said, pointing down the step. She slipped another diya into place. Papa filled it with oil. It glowed too. "Now it's bright," Maeva whispered, and she and Mama counted all the little flames together.

Athena sat under a big tree at the park. She had a bag of blocks with her snack. She tipped the blocks onto the grass. "I will sort them," she said. She put all the red blocks in one pile. Then she put all the blue blocks in another pile. Soon every block was in a pile by color.

Her friend Milo came to play. "Can I sort too?" he asked. Milo put the big blocks in one pile. Then he put the small blocks in another pile. Athena looked and looked. Same blocks, different piles! "They can go both ways," she said. She laughed and clapped her hands.

Milo found something round in the grass. It was a pinecone. Athena put it with the small pile. "It fits here," she said. Then she opened her snack bag. Apple slices and crackers came out. She gave some crackers to Milo. A leaf fell from the tree and landed on the big pile. Athena smiled and let it float down onto her knee. "Snack time," said Milo, munching happily.

Abigail wanted to draw a cat on the tablet. The screen was dark. She tapped it. Nothing happened. She tapped again and again.

Her teacher, Miss Kim, came over. "Press the round button on the side," said Miss Kim. Abigail pressed it. The screen lit up. It was bright and ready.

Abigail opened the drawing app. She drew a cat with a long tail. Then she drew wings so the cat could fly over a tree. "Look, Miss Kim! My cat can fly!" she said.

The bell rang. It was time for snacks. Abigail pressed the round button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf, all by itself, next to a book about a tree with one big root.

"Thank you, Abigail," said Miss Kim. Abigail smiled and ran to the snack table.

Penelope loved water day at daycare. Teacher Mia let everyone splash in the little tub. First the kids took off their shoes and socks. Then they rolled up their pants. Penelope splashed and splashed until her arms were all wet.

Tommy jumped out of the tub and ran away. Drip, drip, drip went his feet on the floor. "Slip, slip!" he laughed. But then he got cold. He came running back for the big blue towel. He rubbed his arms and his legs. The towel made him dry and warm.

Penelope wanted to try that too. She stepped out of the tub, all drippy. "Towel, please!" she said. Teacher Mia gave her a soft yellow one. Penelope rubbed her arms. The drips went away. After that, everyone got dressed again. It was snack time. "Wet feet, dry feet, apple feet!" said Tommy. Penelope giggled and took a big bite.

Charlie stood by the big red gate. It was her first day of school. She held her mama's hand tight. The playground had swings and a slide. A boy ran past her fast. A girl laughed on the swings. Charlie looked around. Her tummy felt funny. She needed to find the bathroom. She did not know where it was.

She looked at the tall teacher. The teacher had yellow shoes. Charlie took one step. Then she took one more step. "Excuse me," she said. "Where is the bathroom?" The teacher smiled big. "Come with me," she said. "It is right inside." The teacher held out her hand.

Charlie took it. They walked past a poster of a silly worm wearing a hat. "The sun would melt that worm," Charlie said. The teacher laughed. They found the bathroom door. It had a blue sign. Charlie washed her hands after. Then she ran out to the slide. The teacher waved from the door.

Felix sat at the paint table at school. He wanted to make a card for Grandma. On the card he would paint a pink flower, big and round. But there was no pink paint on the table.

He looked and looked. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was green paint. There was white paint too. No pink anywhere. Felix felt like crying. "No pink, no pink," he said.

His teacher sat down next to him. "You can mix paints here," she said. Felix dipped his brush in the red. He made a red dot on his paper. Then he dipped his brush in the white. He stirred the white into the red dot. Round and round the brush went. He was a little scared to look. Then he peeked. The dot was pink! "Pink!" shouted Felix. "I made pink!"

He painted one big pink flower. Then he painted a yellow sun. He painted green grass and a blue sky. He held the card up high. "This is for Grandma," he said. "I hope she loves pink." He ran to show his teacher the pink flower first.

Madelyn had a party dress. It was red and shiny. "I wish to wear it all night," she said. She twirled in front of the mirror.

But the dress was scratchy at bedtime. It poked her arms. It rode up when she sat. "Hmm," said Madelyn. "Can a dress sleep?" She looked at her bed. She looked at her dress. What could she wear to sleep?

Then she saw her pajamas. They were soft and warm. They had wild bears on them. She touched the pajamas. So cozy! Madelyn put on the pajamas all by herself. Off went the dress. On went the bears.

Madelyn climbed into bed. She snuggled down. The pajamas were warm. Her teddy was warm too. "Good night, bears," she said. The bears did not answer. They were sleeping, just like her.

Elizabeth put on her new coat. It had no zipper. It had five red buttons.

She pulled the coat shut. The sides fell open again. She pulled them shut. They fell open again. Her friend Tom began to laugh. Elizabeth laughed too.

Teacher Mia sat down next to her. She held the coat still. Elizabeth looked at the little holes. She pushed a button through a hole. Pop. The button went in. The coat stayed shut on that side. Elizabeth's eyes got big. She pushed the next button through its hole. Pop. Two sides closed now.

She pushed and pushed. One button slipped away. She tried again, slow this time. Pop. At last all five buttons were in. The coat was closed and warm.

Tom showed his big tooth in a smile. "Let's go out," he said. Elizabeth ran to the door. She was fast in her red coat.

Gianna stood at the airport. She held a big sign. It said "Grandpa!" People walked and walked. Then she saw him. "Grandpa!" she yelled. He gave her a hug.

At home, Grandpa took out a card game. "My turn first," said Gianna. She put down a card. Then she put down another. "My turn again!" Grandpa smiled. "Now it is my turn," he said. He put down one card. Then he pointed to her. "Now you." Gianna put down one card. Then Grandpa put down one. One for her, one for him, one for her, one for him. The cards made a funny long line. The line grew and grew!

"Grandpa, the cards make a train," said Gianna. "Choo choo!" Grandpa laughed. He turned over the last card. It had a red fish on it. "Oh no," said Gianna. "The fish ate the caboose!" Grandpa clapped his hands. "Good one," he said. "Same game tomorrow?" Gianna jumped up and down. "First turn is mine, then yours!"

Paisley wanted to play shop at school. Ben had set out little pots on a table. "Welcome to my shop," said Ben. "I am the shopkeeper."

Paisley picked up a tiny red pot. "I want this one," she said. She gave Ben a bottle cap for money. "Thank you, shopper," said Ben. He put the cap in his shoe.

Then Ben wanted to buy too. He waited behind a block wall like a shopper on a road to town. Paisley sat in the shopkeeper chair. She held up a tiny sock. "This sock is not stinky," she said. "It smells like flowers." Ben laughed and paid two caps.

After shop time, they dug in the sand tray outside. Paisley buried the red pot and dug it up again. "Let's play shop tomorrow," said Ben. "Yes," said Paisley. "I will be the shopkeeper next."

Mateo sat at the art table. He had a big purple crayon. He wanted to draw a house with a window.

"First I need a square," said Mateo. He drew four lines. But one line was too short. The square looked crooked. "Oh no," said Mateo.

His teacher gave him a cracker. "Look," she said. "This cracker is a square." Mateo was not sure. He took a piece of string from the craft box. He laid the string on one side. Then he laid it on the next side. Then the next one. Then the last one. All four sides took the same string! The cracker was a square.

Mateo smiled. He drew four lines again. He made each line the same length. Now he had a real square. He drew a triangle on top for the roof. He drew a little round circle for the doorknob. Then he drew a baby sleeping inside, and a rectangle for the door.

"I did it!" said Mateo. His teacher poured him a tiny cup of juice. Mateo munched his square cracker, crunch, crunch, crunch.

Ava sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Are we almost there?" she asked. "Almost," said Dad. "We are going to see your cousin Ben."

Ava had a job to do. She had a box on her lap. It was for Ben's new toy box. Ava looked inside. She found her red ball. She found her doll named Lucy. She found her blue blocks. "Ball, you go in," said Ava. She dropped it in the box. "Doll, you go in too." The doll went in. Then the blocks went in, one by one. They made a little click sound.

Ava saw the box was getting full. The ball made room for the doll. The doll made room for the blocks. When all the toys were in, the box was just right. Ava gave the box a pat. Then she saw her sock at the bottom of her bag. She held it up. "A sock is not a toy," said Ava. She put the sock back. Outside the window, a cow stood by a fence. "Moo," said Ava. The cow looked at her. Dad laughed. "A cow is not a toy either," said Ava. The car turned into Ben's street. Ben was waiting at the door, waving. Ava hugged the box tight. "I brought toys," she said. "So many toys."

Henri ran up the steps to Grandma's house. Today he would meet the new baby. Grandma opened the door fast. "She is here," Grandma said. "She is so small."

Henri tiptoed to the basket. The baby was tiny. She had little hands. She was sleeping. Henri wanted her to wake up. He wanted her to look at him.

"Can I touch her hand?" Henri asked. Grandma nodded. Henri put one finger near the baby. The baby's hand opened. Then it closed. She held his finger tight! Henri laughed. He pulled his arm a little. The baby still held on. "Grandma, look!" Henri said. "She likes me!" The baby opened her eyes. She looked right at Henri. Grandma smiled and got the camera. "Say worm," said Grandma, because the baby was small and pink. But Henri stood frozen, so happy. The baby kept his finger. She would not let go. "I will follow you everywhere," Henri told her. Then the baby let out a big yawn. At last she let go. Henri waved. "Bye, little hand," he said.

Harrison stood at the bus stop with Mama. It was a sunny morning. The sun made his toes feel warm in his sandals. Then a big cloud came. The sun went away. "Where did the sun go?" Harrison asked. "The cloud is hiding it," said Mama. Harrison looked up. He could not see the sun at all.

Then the wind began to blow. It blew Mama's scarf. It ruffled Harrison's hair. The cloud turned gray. Rain fell down, tap tap tap. "Brr," said Harrison. His toes were cold now. Mama opened a little umbrella. They stood under it together. The rain made dots on the ground.

They waited and waited. Harrison watched the sky. The gray cloud moved away, slow and soft. The sun came out again. "Hello, sun!" said Harrison. His toes got warm once more. Mama put the umbrella down. The wet road turned shiny and sweet in the sun.

The bus came round the corner. Harrison held Mama's hand. They climbed up the steps together. "I saw the cloud hide the sun," said Harrison. Mama smiled at him. The bus door closed with a soft little whoosh.

Henri sat in the big waiting chair. He hugged his doll tight. Today he would get his very first haircut. He did not want the scissors to come near his doll.

"Mama will hold her," said Mama. She set the doll on her lap. Henri climbed up into the salon chair all by himself. The lady picked up her scissors. Snip, snip went a little curl. The curl fell down. It landed on the cape like a soft brown ring.

Mama picked up the curl. She put it in a small envelope. "Why?" asked Henri. "To keep," said Mama. She tucked the envelope in her bag. Henri looked in the mirror. His hair was short now, and the curl was safe too. He gave the mirror a big silly grin. "Home now," he said. Mama laughed and took his hand.

Leah turned three today. The party was in the backyard. A big cake sat on the picnic table. Mom had put three candles on top. Leah held a little match in her hand.

Dad knelt down near her. He took the match gently. "I light the candles," he said. "You can help after." Dad touched the match to each candle. One, two, three little flames. Leah hopped up and down on one foot. The flames made little warm lights on the cake.

Everyone came close to the table. "Now you," Dad said. Leah took a big breath. She blew and blew. The flames went out. Smoke curled up like a soft gray ribbon. Grandma clapped. The friends clapped too. Leah looked at the candles. "Again tomorrow?" she asked. Dad laughed and cut the cake.

Beatrice went to the store with Dad. She wanted a big red ball. On the shelf were big balls and small balls. Beatrice picked a big one. It was too big for her hands. So she picked a small one instead. "This one fits," she said.

Near the bread, the oven door was open. Dad said, "That oven is hot. Stay back." Beatrice stayed back. Then she touched the cold milk box. "Brrr," she said. "Cold!" Dad smiled.

At the toy bin, a baby kept taking toys out. Beatrice put a toy in. The baby took it out. Beatrice put it in again. Out it came again. The baby giggled. "You like out," said Beatrice. "I like in. In and out are not the same!" She put a toy in fast. The baby pulled it out slow. Dad laughed. "What a silly game," he said. "Can I play too?" Beatrice handed him a toy. "Put it in, Dad," she said.

Wren sat at the dinner table. She wore her big red hat. Dad said the hat would not work at the table. It fell into the soup. So she took it off.

Wren wanted more potatoes. She reached far across the table. Her cup tipped over. Milk went everywhere. Wren felt her face go hot. "Sorry," she said softly. "That is okay," said Dad. He wiped the milk with a cloth. Mom brought a towel too. "Can you help me?" Wren asked. Mom helped her wipe her chair.

Then Wren tried again. "More potatoes, please," she said. Dad smiled and gave her some. Wren ate a bite. They were warm and good. She was not a lazy eater tonight. She looked up at Dad. "Thank you," she said. Dad passed her the bread too. "Thank you," Wren said again, and took a big bite.

Grayson ran to the window at daycare. "Look, look!" he shouted. Big white snow was falling down. It fell on the slide. It fell on the swings.

Miss Ana held up a sign. It had a snowflake on it. "Snowy day!" she said. "Time for snow pants and boots!"

Grayson zipped his puffy coat. He pulled his hat on. Everyone ran outside. The snow crunched under his boots. It was cold and soft.

"I will make the biggest snowball!" said Grayson. He scooped and patted. His ball grew big and round.

His friend Milo made a snowball too. But Milo's hands turned red. "Ow, ow," said Milo. He had no mittens. His hands were cold. Grayson had fuzzy blue mittens. His hands stayed warm inside them.

"Here," said Grayson. He shared one mitten with Milo. Milo put it on one hand. Then Miss Ana found a spare pair in the big basket.

"Miss Ana!" yelled Milo. "My hands feel warm now!" He held up his mittened hands like they won a prize.

Grayson smiled a shy smile. Then he pushed his big snowball down the hill. It rolled and rolled and got even bigger. "Come on!" he called. "Let's build a snow man!"

Livia lost her bunny. Bunny was soft and pink. Livia looked under her bed. No bunny there.

She peeked in the toy box. She saw a small red car. The car was not hers. The car was her brother Sam's car. Sam had looked for it yesterday. "When you find something that belongs to someone else, you give it back to them." Livia ran to Sam. "I found your car!" she said. Sam smiled big. "Thank you, Livia!"

Sam wanted to help her too. They looked in the hall. They looked by the big chair. No bunny. "Maybe bunny is far away," said Sam. They peeked behind the couch. It was dark back there. Livia reached in her hand.

Something soft touched her fingers. She pulled it out. It was bunny! Livia hugged bunny tight. Sam clapped his hands. "Yay!" he said. Livia put the red car in Sam's hand. Sam put bunny in Livia's arms.

Then they sat together on the rug. Sam pushed the car. "Vroom," he said. Livia made bunny hop. "Hop, hop, bunny," she said.

Sofia wanted to be a big kid. Big kids know five whole senses. Sofia knew only one. That felt like a problem.

Mama had an idea. She put a soft sock over Sofia's eyes. "Now we play a guessing game," said Mama. She put things in Sofia's hands, one at a time.

Sofia held a cold spoon. She held a fuzzy peach. She held a bumpy rock. She did not peek. She used her fingertips. The fingertips told her things. "The peach is soft!" said Sofia. "The rock is bumpy!" Her fingertips felt it all. Sofia smiled big. Touching was a sense too.

Then Mama held up her hand. "Can you turn around fast?" she asked. Sofia spun around. The sock slipped off. On the table was a cookie, warm from the oven. Sofia could smell it with her nose. She could see it with her eyes. "Three senses!" said Sofia. "I can hear you munch." Mama laughed.

Soon it would be the moon's turn to come up. Sofia ate her cookie slowly. "Tomorrow I will learn the last one," she said. Mama kissed her head. "That one is easy," said Mama. "You will love it." Sofia held Mama's hand. Her fingertips felt warm.

Emilia sat at the big table. Mom put warm toast on her plate. "I want to do it myself," Emilia said. Mom gave her a small knife with a round edge. Mom held the butter dish close.

Emilia poked the toast with the pointy tip of the knife. The toast got a hole in it. Butter fell off in little lumps. An ant crawled near the plate, looking for crumbs. "Hmm," said Emilia.

Mom turned the knife over. The flat side shined in the light. Emilia took some butter on the flat side. She pushed it across the bread, slow and slow. The butter went smooth all over. No holes. No lumps. Just smooth, shiny toast.

Next came the milk. Emilia held the little cup with both hands. She poured, drip by drip. One small drop ran down the side. She wiped it with her finger. She tried again. This time nothing spilled at all.

Emilia bit her toast. "I did it," she said. Mom sat down beside her and poured her own milk.

Anthony rode the bus with his mama. He held his little blue bunny. The bus went bump, bump, bump. Bunny jumped out of his hands! Anthony looked down. Where did bunny go? He peeked under the seat. He saw a shoe. He saw a gum wrapper. No bunny. Then mama lifted the seat flap. There was bunny! The bus went bump, and bunny had slid under. Anthony hugged bunny tight. "Was bunny hiding?" he asked. At home, Anthony found a clean box. He put a soft sock inside. "This is bunny's nest," he said. Every night, bunny slept in the same nest by his bed. One morning Anthony could not see bunny. He looked at the nest. There sat bunny, waiting. "It's true," said Anthony. "The nest keeps bunny easy to find." He smiled and gave bunny a kiss.

Florence held Mama's hand on the bus. They were going to the dentist. It was her first time.

"I want to be brave," said Florence.

"We can go slow," said Mama.

At the dentist, a kind lady looked in Florence's mouth. "Open big," she said. Florence opened. The lady counted her teeth. "All done," she said. Florence got a sticker shaped like a fish. It was blue and shiny.

On the bus home, a boy sat near them. His mama gave him an apple slice. The boy bit it with his front teeth. Then he moved it to his back teeth and chomped. The apple got small. Then it was gone.

Florence watched. She had a biscuit in her bag. She took it out. She bit it with her front teeth. The biscuit made a crunch. Then she moved it to her back teeth. She chomped and chomped. The biscuit got small. It tasted sweet.

"Look, Mama," said Florence. "Front bites, back chomps."

Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Sienna held her hand at the market. The stalls smelled like bread and peaches.

"Can we buy apples?" Sienna asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "Your mom loved apples when she was little."

Sienna stopped walking. "You know my mom when she was little?"

Grandma smiled. "I am her mom too."

Sienna looked up. "You are a mom? But you are a grandma!"

"Both," said Grandma.

Sienna thought hard. So Grandma was Mom's mom. Just like Mom was her mom. She squeezed Grandma's hand.

Then Sienna saw a paint stand. Bright paints in little jars. Red, blue, and yellow.

"Can we paint together?" she asked.

"We can paint a clock for your room," said Grandma.

At home, Mom helped set out the paper. Sienna painted a big round face. Grandma painted the numbers. Mom painted the hands.

The paint dried by the window. It took a long time, but Sienna waited.

At bedtime, the clock hung far above her bed. Mom, Grandma, and Sienna stood back to look.

"We all made it," said Sienna.

Grandma kissed the top of her head. "Moms and grandmas and girls," she said. "That is how it goes."

Leah ran to the big slide at the playground. She wanted to be a rocket ship today. Her friend Sam was already at the top. "I am a rocket," he said. "But I need help. I forgot how rockets start."

Leah thought hard. She had heard counting at home. Mommy counted apples at the store, one, two, three. At school they sang a number song, all the way to ten. But rockets did not go up that way.

"I know," Leah said. "We count the other way. Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one." Sam held the line of the slide with both hands. "Then what?" he asked. "Then blast off!" Leah said.

Sam counted with her. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Sam zoomed down the slide and jumped up at the end. He was so happy. "You did it!" he said.

A small boy stood by the ladder. He looked sad. "I want a rocket too," he said. "I don't know the numbers." Leah took his hand. "Come with me," she said. "We will count together."

They stood in a line at the ladder. Leah helped the little boy climb up. Then he called out, "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Down he came, fast and laughing. Leah clapped and said, "One more rocket is ready."

Penelope wanted to paint a cat at school. Yesterday she had painted a dog. Today she wanted a cat with a long tail. But the paint shelf was empty. "No more orange," said her teacher. "Come back tomorrow."

Penelope frowned. "Where did today go?" she asked her dad at bedtime. He tucked her in. "After you sleep tonight and wake up, today will be called yesterday," he said. Penelope closed her eyes.

She slept. The sun came in low through the window. She woke up and put on her shoes. "Yesterday is done," she said. At school, she walked to the paint shelf. New orange paint sat on the top. Penelope painted her cat with a long tail. "Now it is today," she said, and held it up. "A cat!"

Arthur dug in Grandpa's garden. He planted little seeds with his hands. Grandpa helped him pat the soil. "Where did we put the tomatoes?" Arthur asked. He could not remember. He looked at the dirt. All the rows looked the same. Arthur scratched his head.

Then Grandpa held up a stick. A paper picture was on it. It showed a red tomato. Grandpa pushed the stick into the soil. "Now this spot has a name," he said. Arthur clapped his hands. He ran inside for more paper. He drew a long orange carrot. He drew a round yellow squash. He put a stick in the middle of every row.

Day by day, green shoots popped up. Arthur froze when he saw a tiny sprout. "Which one is it?" he gasped. He ran to look at the labels. The sprout was by the carrot picture. "Carrots! Carrots are growing!" he shouted. Grandpa laughed. Arthur counted the labels. "One, two, three rows!" Every row knew its own name. Arthur watered them all and said, "Grow big, little labels!"

Owen ran to the park with his dad. He felt so excited. The slide was tall and red.

Near the slide, a girl was crying. She looked sad. Her kite was stuck in a tree. "I want my kite," she said.

Then a big dog ran by. It barked very loud. Owen felt scared. He ran to his dad. "Dad, the dog scared me," he said. His dad held his hand. "I will help you," said Dad. They walked to the bench together. Owen watched the dog from far away. The dog was only playing with a smelly old ball. Owen began to feel a little better.

His dad asked the dog's owner for help. The tall man got the kite down from the tree. The girl smiled big. Now she looked happy. She ran with her kite, and it flew up high.

Owen clapped. He felt happy too. "Can we come back tomorrow?" he asked. His dad laughed. "Yes," he said. "And if you ever feel scared, just tell me." Owen nodded. He took one more ride down the big red slide.

Grandpa came to stay at Juliette's house. He wore a big blue hat. Juliette gave him a hug. Then Mommy took them to the market.

At the market, Juliette saw apples. She saw bread. She saw a dog with a waggy tail. Grandpa said, "I can stay for a week." Juliette did not know how long a week was. She asked, "When do you go home?" Grandpa said, "We will count the days."

At home, Mommy showed Juliette the calendar. Juliette drew a red circle on one day. That was day one. The next morning, she drew another circle. Day two! Each morning, she drew one more circle. Day three, day four, day five, day six.

Juliette counted her circles. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Only six circles. She was sorry. She thought the week was over. "Is today your last day?" she asked. Grandpa said, "Count again with me." Juliette pointed at each circle. Then she drew one more. Seven circles!

"A week has seven days!" said Juliette. Grandpa laughed and clapped. On the seventh day, he put on his big blue hat. Juliette waved and waved at the door. "Come back for seven more circles!" she called. Grandpa waved his hat in the air.

Max saw the big red truck at school. Ben had it first. Max wanted it so much. He reached out his hand to grab it. Then he stopped. He put his hands in his pockets instead.

"Can I have a turn?" Max asked. Ben looked at him. "You can have it after this," said Ben. Max sat on the pillow to wait. His sweater was itchy, so he tugged his sleeve while he waited. It was hard to wait. He watched Ben push the truck up the ramp.

Then Ben held out the truck. "Your turn," said Ben. Max took it with both hands. "Thank you," he said. Ben smiled a big smile. Then Ben sat on the pillow to wait, just like Max did.

Max pushed the truck fast. It rolled under the table. A little kitten was hiding there! The kitten batted the truck with one paw. Ben laughed and laughed. Max got down on his knees to look. "Truck for the kitty too," said Max.

Henry sat at the paint table. He wanted to paint a big pumpkin. But there was no orange paint.

He looked and looked. He saw red paint. He saw yellow paint. "One, two, no orange," said Henry.

His teacher Miss Jo sat down next to him. "What do you need, Henry?" she asked.

"I need orange for my pumpkin," said Henry.

Miss Jo gave him a white paper cup. Henry put in some red paint. Drip, drip. He put in some yellow paint. Drip, drip. He mixed it round and round with his brush.

The paint turned orange!

Henry stared at the cup. He dipped his brush. He painted the big pumpkin. Red and yellow made orange, all by mixing.

His friend Milo came over. Milo had a sad face. "I want orange too," said Milo.

Henry gave Milo his white cup. "Here," he said. "You can mix with me."

They painted together. Milo tickled the paper with his brush. One pumpkin, two pumpkins, three pumpkins.

"Happy Halloween!" said Henry, and he held up his orange pumpkin for everyone to see.

Jasmine wanted her book about the rainbow. She looked at her shelf. So many books! She pulled one out. She looked at the front cover. The words said "Sleepy Bunny". That was not it.

Jasmine asked, "Where is my rainbow book?"
Mama said, "Look for its name."
"But books don't talk," said Jasmine.
"The name is written there," said Mama. She pointed to the big words at the top.

Jasmine put "Sleepy Bunny" back on the shelf. She pulled out another book. She looked at the big words. They said "Rainbow Moon". She held it up. "This one!" she said.

"That's the one," said Mama.

Jasmine opened the front cover. Page one came first. Mama read it to her. Jasmine turned each page, one by one, all the way to the end. The last page had a big orange moon.

"Again," said Jasmine.

David waited by the gate at school. He saw his grandma come walking up. She had his green hat in her bag.

"Time to go home," said Grandma. "You can help me today."

At home, David ate his snack. He ate apple slices that Grandma cut into small pieces. Then he had a nap on his little bed.

When he woke up, Grandma said, "Bath time." David took off his socks and his shirt. He left them on the floor.

Then he looked at the laundry basket. He picked up a sock. He threw it. It went in the basket. He picked up the other sock. It went in too. "Basket!" said David. He threw his shirt. It landed on the edge. He pushed it in with his hand.

After his bath, David put on soft pajamas. The dirty clothes stayed in the basket. "They will get washed," said Grandma.

David pointed at the basket. "More socks tomorrow," he said.

Sadie sat at the dinner table. She wanted the big strawberry on her plate. "Can I eat the strawberry now?" she asked. Mom said, "Eat your peas first. You can have the strawberry later." Sadie looked at the strawberry. It was red, her favorite color. "Is it later yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mom. Sadie ate one pea. "Is it later yet?" "Not yet." Sadie ate another pea, and another. "Is it later yet?" Mom smiled. "Now it is later." Sadie was happy. She picked up the strawberry and took a big bite.

Then Dad said, "Yesterday we had bananas. Today we have strawberries. Tomorrow we will have apples." Sadie counted on her fingers. Yesterday, today, tomorrow. "Can we talk about tomorrow now?" she asked. Dad laughed. "We can talk about it now, and eat it later." Sadie looked at her plate. Later was after now. She had made later come, all by eating her peas. She held up the last strawberry piece. "This is now!" she said.

Jayden sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin on his paper plate. But he had no orange paint. His jars held red, blue, yellow and green. "No orange," said Jayden. "That is bad."

Grandma set the jars in a row. "One red, two blue, three yellow, four green," she said. Jayden dipped his brush in the red. He made a red dot on his plate. Then he dipped in the yellow. He stirred the two dots together. The paint turned orange! "Look, Grandma!" said Jayden. "Red and yellow make orange!"

He painted his pumpkin round and bright. Then he added a green leaf and a blue sky. "My pumpkin looks real," said Jayden. Grandma held it up to the sunny window. "One pumpkin, one leaf, one happy boy," she said, and hung it on the wall.

Riley sat at the little blue table. She had a crayon in her hand. Miss Ana gave her a paper with letters on it.

"Find the R," said Miss Ana. Riley looked. She looked some more. She pointed at a small r. "That one!" she said. "Yes," said Miss Ana. "That is r. It says rrr." Riley made the sound too. "Rrr," she said, and laughed.

Then Miss Ana wrote Riley's name. "Riley starts with R," she said. Riley took the crayon. She wrote her name all by herself. But her first letter was small. She looked at Miss Ana's writing. That first letter was big. It stood tall.

Riley tapped her small r with her finger. She looked again. Then she drew a big R on top. The big R stood up tall, just like the big girl letter in Miss Ana's writing. "Look!" said Riley. She held up the paper. "My name! Big R!"

"Good work," said Miss Ana. "Time to go wash hands for dinner." Riley carried her paper with her, holding it high.

Charlie ran to the writing table. Today he would write his name! Miss Amy gave him a fat pencil. "Grip it like this," she said. Charlie held it tight. He pushed the pencil down the road of paper. The letters came out wobbly.

"C, H, A..." Charlie stopped. The C looked like a squiggle. "Yucky C!" he said. He looked at Ben's name. Ben was sorting letter cards. "Look," said Ben. "L is all straight lines. O is all curves." Charlie picked up his card. L had straight sticks. O was round like a ball.

Charlie tried again. He drew two straight sticks for his H. One, two! Then he made a big round curve for his C. It looked good! "I did it!" he shouted. He lifted his paper up high. "C for Charlie! C with a curve!" Miss Amy clapped. Charlie grinned and wrote his whole name, one letter at a time.

Aurora sat down at the dinner table. She saw a big bowl in the middle. Steam rose up from it. "What is that?" she asked. "Soup," said Mama. "You will see."

Aurora sniffed with her nose. Mmm, it smelled like carrots. Then she heard a funny sound. Pop, pop, went the bread in the toaster. Her ears heard it first!

Mama put three little things by Aurora's plate. "Close your eyes," said Mama. "Now touch." Aurora felt one thing. It was soft. "Feather!" she said. She felt the next one. It was rough and bumpy. "Pinecone!" She felt the last one. It was smooth and cool. "My stone!" She opened her eyes. She was right, right, right.

Aurora took a small sip of soup. Her tongue tasted carrots. "More bread, please," she said. The toaster popped again. Aurora laughed. "The bread jumps when it is hot!" She painted a picture of the jumping bread with her carrot on her plate, and the bowl of soup sat grumpy and steamy in the middle, waiting.

Amira wanted to wear her new socks. She opened her sock drawer. She pulled out one red sock. Then she looked and looked. Where was the other sock?

"One sock," said Amira. "I need two." She put the sock on her foot. Her other foot was still bare. She counted her toes. "One, two, three, four, five. Toes need socks too."

Amira searched the laundry basket. She counted the socks she found. "One, two, three." None of them were red. She looked under her bed. Dust made her nose scratch. No red sock there.

Then she saw something behind the door. It was small and red. It was the other sock! "A pair!" said Amira. She put it on her bare foot. Now both feet were warm.

Amira ran to show Mama. "Mama, look! Two socks!" Mama smiled. She held up her own feet. She was wearing one blue sock and one yellow sock. "Oh no," said Mama. "Now I need a match."

"I will help you," said Amira. She took Mama's hand. Together they went to the sock drawer. "Let's count them all," said Amira. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten socks in a big pile, waiting to make pairs.

Camille put on her warm mittens. Today was hockey rink day! The ice was far away, and the smooth floor by the rink was for games. Camille saw a red hoop on the floor and a small beanbag in her hand.

"Can I get it in?" she asked her dad.

"You can try," he said.

Camille threw the beanbag. It fell far from the hoop. She threw again. It missed again. Camille frowned. Then she took three little steps closer to the hoop. She threw the beanbag. It went in! The beanbag sank right down in the middle of the hoop.

"I did it!" she shouted. Dad clapped his hands. Camille jumped up and down.

Next came the big blue ball. Dad rolled it to her. Camille held out both hands. The ball bumped her tummy and fell. Dad rolled it again, slow and easy. Camille opened her arms wide. The ball came right into her hands.

"I caught it! Can I throw the beanbag one more time?"

"Yes, one more big throw," said Dad.

Camille stood close to the hoop. She threw the beanbag high. It sank in again.

"That was pretty great," said Dad. He wrapped Camille in her soft blanket. "Time for warm cocoa."

Camille hugged the ball all the way home.

Quinn went to the pet store with Dad. She saw fish and birds and one small kitten. The kitten was in a box with soft blankets. "This one," said Quinn. "She is coming home with us," said Dad.

At home, the kitten drank and drank. Then she played. Then she slept. In the morning, Quinn ran to see her. The water bowl was empty! The kitten sat by it and looked sad. "She wants more water," said Quinn.

Quinn tried to reach the sink, but it was too high. "I will help," said Dad. Dad turned on the tap. Quinn held the bowl under the cool water. It filled up, splash by splash. "Fresh water for you," said Quinn.

She set the bowl down by the kitten's food. The kitten ran over right away. She lapped and lapped until the bowl was half empty. Quinn patted her soft head. The kitten purred. "Every day I will fill your bowl," said Quinn. The kitten blinked at her, then curled up to sleep.

Jasmine wanted to fill her cup at the little sink in the playroom. The cup was empty. It had nothing inside. She turned the tap fast. Water splashed out fast and sploshed over the top. "Oh no," said Jasmine. She mopped it up with a towel. She tried again. This time she made the water go slow. Slow, slow, drip. The cup began to fill. It got full to the top. Then she turned the tap off. Not one drop spilled. "I did it!" she said. Daddy clapped from the big chair. Then he brought her a small cup of cocoa. It was hot, so Daddy held it. Jasmine waited and waited. Then she took a tiny lick. It was warm and sweet, not sour like the lemon she once tried. Her toy duck on a string sat beside her. It was small, and the water cup was big. Jasmine smiled and drank it all, slow sip by slow sip.

Felix sat in his car seat. The road was bumpy. Bump, bump, bump went the wheels. "I want my apple," said Felix. Mama reached into the bag. She gave him a red apple. It felt cool and smooth in his hands.

Then Felix saw his picture cards on the seat. One card showed fruits. Bananas, grapes, and oranges. One card showed foods. Bread, cheese, and milk. Felix held up his apple to the fruit card. "Apple goes here," he said. Then he held it by the food card. "No, apple goes here." He looked and looked. His sister Maya leaned over. "Apple is a fruit," she said. "Apple is a food," said Felix.

Mama smiled in the mirror. "Let's see," she said. Felix put the apple on the fruit card. Then he put it on the food card too. It sat on both cards at once. "Two spots!" said Felix. Maya clapped. Bump, bump went the wheels. Felix took one big bite. Crunch! "My apple is a food and a fruit," he said. Maya laughed and gave him a napkin. "Surprise!" said Felix, juice dripping down his chin. "One apple, two cards." The car drove on and on.

Hayden went to the library with his mom. The sky was cloudy, so it was a good day to stay inside. He wanted one special book, a book with a cat on the cover.

At the story table, a girl named Mia had cookies. She held the box out to Hayden. "Want one?" she asked. Hayden looked at the cookie. It had raisins in it. He did not like raisins. "Yuck!" he said loudly. The library lady put her finger to her lips. "Shh," she said softly. Hayden felt his face get warm.

Mom knelt down next to him. "Try again," she whispered. Mia held out the box one more time. Hayden took a big breath. "No, thank you," he said. Mia smiled. "Okay!" she said. Then she found a plain cookie in her bag and gave it to him. "This one has no raisins," she said. "Thank you," said Hayden. He munched his cookie while the library lady found the cat book, hiding behind three big books. It was the last one on the shelf, and it was his.

Brooks was getting over his cold. His nose still ran a little. His cough came at night. So Mama took him to the pharmacy.

The pharmacy had bright lights. There were big shelves full of boxes. A lady in a white coat waved at Brooks. He waved back from Mama's side.

Mama picked out a small bottle. She put it on the counter. The bottle had a purple cap. Brooks looked at it. He wanted to open it himself. He reached up his hand.

Mama shook her head. She held the bottle high. "Only a grown-up gives a child medicine," she said. She showed him the little cup. It had lines on it. Mama poured the medicine slowly. The liquid went up to one line. Then she stopped.

At home, Mama sat by Brooks. She gave him the little cup. He drank it all down. It tasted like grapes.

The last thing before bed, Brooks looked at the bottle on the high shelf. He pointed at it and said, "That's Mama's job." Mama smiled and turned off the light.

Alice went to the playground with her friends. "Let's play hide-and-seek," said Ben. "You seek, Alice. Close your eyes and count to ten." Alice closed her eyes. She counted very fast. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" She turned around. Nobody was hiding yet. Mia stood in the open. Ben ran to the slide too late. "Alice, count slowly," said Mia. "Then we can hide." "Why slowly?" asked Alice. "Because we need time to hide," said Mia. Alice nodded. She closed her eyes again. This time she counted slowly. "One, two, three, four..." Mia hid behind the bush. "Five, six, seven..." Ben climbed under the bridge, careful not to bump his head. "Eight, nine, ten." Alice opened her eyes. The playground was quiet. Where did they go? She looked by the swing. She looked at the sandbox. Then she saw Mia's shoe stick out by the bush. "I see you, Mia!" Mia laughed and came out. They looked for Ben together. Alice found a slimy snail on a leaf. She did not touch it. She just looked. Then she heard a giggle. Ben was under the bridge! "Found you," said Alice. "That was fun," said Ben. "Let's play again. I had a dream about this game last night, and we all won." They all held hands and skipped to the swings.

Louis stood at the little table. Toast sat on his plate. So did a cup of milk.

"Watch me," said Miss Ana. She took her knife. She spread butter on her toast. The butter slid from edge to edge. Louis picked up his own knife. He spread slowly. The butter made soft waves. "I did it!" said Louis. Then he lifted the milk jug with both hands. He poured a little bit. Then a little bit more. Not one drop fell. His heart felt big and happy.

Miss Ana clapped. Louis drank some milk. Then he ran off to play. The milk stayed on the table. He saw it sitting there. "Oh no! You go back in the fridge," he said. He carried the milk to Miss Ana. She opened the fridge door. Louis set the milk inside, where it was far from the warm room. "Good job, Louis," said Miss Ana. Louis smiled and went to chase his friend Sam across the room.

Connor wanted to build a big tower in his playroom. He saw a heavy box of blocks under the shelf. He pulled it. It did not move. He pulled again. Still no move!

"Why is this so hard?" he asked.

His teddy sat on top of a light feather pillow. Connor picked up the pillow with one hand. Up it went, so easy! He wondered, "Can the pillow help me?" He put the dirty pillow on the floor and sat on it. Then he pushed the box with his feet, slow and steady. The box slid a little. He pushed fast. It slid more!

Mama heard him and came in. "Let's carry the blocks together," she said. "You take the light bag. I'll take the heavy box."

Connor filled his small red bag. It was light in his hands. Soon he had a big, tall tower. He put the teddy on top, soft and slow. "Hello up there!" said Connor.

Raphael sat in the big chair at the dentist. The dentist had a friendly smile. She showed Raphael her tiny mirror. She wanted to look at his teeth.

"I want to see clean teeth," she said. Raphael had eaten lunch before he came. He had used the toilet too. Then he had skipped straight to the toys. His hands were still sticky.

The dentist looked at his hands. Raphael looked too. He saw the sticky fingers. He jumped down from the chair. He ran to the sink. He pumped the soap. He rubbed and rubbed. The bubbles grew big. He counted to twenty with the nurse. The water washed the bubbles away. His hands were clean now.

Raphael skipped back to the big chair. He held up his hands. The dentist looked at his shiny fingers and his shiny teeth. "All clean," she said. She gave him a sticker with a star on it. Raphael stuck it right in the middle of his shirt. "Next time, I will wash first," he told the nurse. She laughed and gave him a high five.

Isaiah sat in his car seat. "Let's play the shout game," said Dad. "I say a word. You shout the opposite."

Dad said, "Big." Isaiah shouted, "Small!" A big truck went by. Then a small car went by. "Look, small!" said Isaiah.

Dad said, "Hot." Isaiah touched the warm vent near his feet. "Ooh, hot," he said. Then he touched his cold cup. There was ice inside. "Cold!" he shouted. "I win!" said Isaiah.

Dad said, "Fast." The car zoomed down the big road. Then the car stopped at a light. A little turtle crossed in front of them. It was so slow. "Slow!" laughed Isaiah. "The turtle is slow!"

Then Dad said, "Up." Isaiah thought and thought. He pointed at his shoe. "Down!" he said.

Just then the light turned green. The turtle was safe on the grass. Dad drove on. "One more," said Isaiah. "Say night."

"Night," said Dad.

"Day!" Isaiah shouted, and the sun peeked out from a cloud.

Arlo sat at the big table. He had paper and markers. He wanted to make a garden. First he drew one green stem. Then two green stems. Then three green stems.

Arlo grabbed the red marker. He pressed too hard. The marker jumped! It made a red line on his hand. Arlo looked at his hand. "Oh no," he said. The red mark would not rub off on the dry paper.

Mom came over. "Let's go to the sink," she said. She turned on the water. It was warm, not hot. She gave Arlo the soap. The soap felt slippery. Arlo rubbed and rubbed. The red mark began to fade. Then it was gone! His hand was clean again.

Arlo went back to the table. He drew his garden again. Red flowers, yellow flowers, blue flowers. He held up his hand and smiled. "All clean," he said. Then he drew one more flower, just for Mom.

The school bus was big and yellow. Eva held her mama's hand. She climbed the steps all by herself. She sat by the window. She saw a pink backpack on the seat across from her. A boy rubbed his nose. He looked a little sleepy.

The bus went bump, bump, bump. Eva counted the seats. One, two, three, four. Then the bus stopped. It was school.

The teacher took the class outside. There was a slide. Eva ran to it fast. She went down once. "Again!" she said. She ran to the front. But other children stood in a line. Eva stood at the back. One child went down. Then one more. Then it was Eva's turn. She slid down and laughed. The line moved like that, one by one. At story time, Eva got to write her own name on a paper. Then the boy from the bus sat next to her. "You kept going down," he said. "You waited so well," said the teacher. Eva smiled and got back in line.

Avery sat at the little table at school. It was snow day. Big flakes fell past the window. "Look, the snow!" said her friend Milo. Avery wanted to paint the snow. She got white paper. She got white paint. She made a stroke. It did not show. White on white was hard to see. Avery tipped her cup. Paint began to spill. "Be careful," said Teacher Jo. She helped Avery wipe it up with a towel. Then Avery looked at the paper shelf. She saw blue paper. She took it. She painted with her white paint. The snow showed up bright on the blue. "I see the snow!" said Avery. Milo leaned close. "It looks soft like my pet bunny," he said. Avery painted one more soft white hill.

Asher ran to the park with his mom. He wanted to go down the big slide. He touched the slide with one finger. The slide was hot. The sun had made it hot. Asher pulled his hand back fast.

"Too hot," said Mom. She put her hand on it too. "Let's find the shady slide." They found a small slide under a tree. Asher touched it. This slide was cool. He went down, down, down. "Again!" he said. Mom laughed. Asher was happy. He drank his juice in the shade. Then it was time to bring his trucks home and get ready for bath.

At home, the tub filled with water. Asher wanted to jump right in. He remembered the hot slide. He stopped his feet. "Mom, check it first," he said. Mom put her hand in the water. "It is warm, not hot," she said. Asher put in one toe. The water felt nice. His little toy duck was already floating there. "Quack!" said Asher, and he climbed in slow.

Beau sat in his car seat. He was going to Grandma's house. "I can't wait!" said Beau. Daddy said, "Look out the window." The trees bent and shook. "It is windy today," said Daddy.

Beau had a little bag of toys. He looked inside. He saw toy cars. One, two, three cars. Then he saw something yellow. It was long and bendy. "A banana!" said Beau. The banana was hiding with the toy cars. Beau held it up. "You do not go with cars," he said. "You are the odd one out!" He put the banana in the lunch box. It sat by the apple and the crackers.

Then Beau found his book under the seat. "Look, Daddy!" he said. "A book about animals!" Daddy said, "Read it to Grandma when we get there." The car went zoom. Beau hugged his book and smiled.

Elizabeth stood at the classroom door. Her tummy felt fluttery, like little birds inside. She held her mommy's hand very tight.

"Your tummy feels funny?" Mommy asked. Elizabeth nodded. "My tummy felt that way on my first day too," said Mommy. "It is okay to feel this way." Elizabeth looked up. Mommy had felt fluttery too? She took a big breath. Then she let go of Mommy's hand and stepped inside.

A boy sat at a table. He was pulling on his coat zipper. It was stuck. His face looked worried. Elizabeth knew stuck zippers. She walked over and held the coat flat. The zipper slid down easy. The boy smiled. "Thank you," he said.

The teacher brought a box. Inside was a green toy frog. It felt slimy and fun. Elizabeth laughed and laughed. Her tummy did not feel fluttery anymore. The boy sat next to her. He held the frog too.

"Look, he jumps!" said the boy. The frog hopped across the table. Elizabeth clapped her hands. "Let's make him jump again," she said.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Myles took him to the park. It was spring, and the flowers were open. The gate was closed, so Grandpa pushed it, and it swung wide.

Myles rode his bike on the path. "My dad rides a big bike," said Myles. "Was Dad always big?"

Grandpa laughed. "No, no. Dad was little once. I know a story about his first bike." Myles stopped pedaling. "Dad was little? Tell me!"

"Dad fell off. Then Dad got up. Then Dad fell off again!" Grandpa said. Myles laughed and laughed.

"I can't see it," said Myles. "Tell it again!"

Grandpa told it again. Dad fell off. Dad got up. This time Myles could see it. Little Dad, on a little bike, wobble, wobble, bump.

"Look at me, Grandpa!" said Myles. He pedaled fast. "I am like little Dad!"

Nora was at her friend Mia's house. Mia had a tablet on the table. Nora wanted to draw a cat, but she did not know how to make the tablet work. "Can I try?" she asked. Mia's mom said yes.

Mia showed Nora the small button. Nora pressed it once. The screen lit up. Then Mia tapped the little paint picture. A white page opened. Nora put her finger on the screen. She slid it across. A blue line followed her finger. Nora gasped. Her finger moved, and the line moved too. The line went all squiggly. "It looks like a snake," said Nora. She gave it a red tongue and two eyes.
