Then it was time for snacks. Nora pressed the button again, and the screen went dark. She put the tablet away in the box, just like Mia's mom showed her. "My snake is in there," said Nora. "Sleeping."

Paisley saw a big blue bus at the park. It was a bookmobile, full of books! She held her mama's hand and they began to walk toward it.

Inside, the shelves went up and up. Paisley ran her fingers over the books. One cover felt rough and bumpy. It was red, with a bear on the front. "This one," said Paisley. "I love this bear."

A kind lady at the desk smiled. "Would you like your own library card?" Paisley stood very tall. The lady typed, and out came a little card with Paisley's name on it. Paisley jumped up and down.

Then the lady scanned the red bear book. Beep! "Now this book is yours to take home," she said. Paisley looked at the card in her hand. The card made the book hers! She hugged the book tight.

"Can I read it at home?" asked Paisley. "All the bear pages?" Mama laughed. "Yes, all of them. Tonight, we will read every page."

Paisley waved to the bookmobile. "Goodbye, books! Goodbye, blue bus!"

She skipped to the car, book under her arm, card in her fist.

Lucy put on her red hat. "Sunny day," said Mom. "Wear your hat."

At the park, the wind began to whoosh. The trees went swish, swish. Lucy's hat jumped right off her head. "My hat!" she cried. It rolled over the grass. Lucy ran after it, but the wind pushed it again. "It keeps flying away!" she said.

Mom held Lucy's hand. They chased the hat together. The wind blew it near the big tree. Mom picked it up and brushed off the dirt. "This wind is strong," said Mom. "It can blow a hat right off your head." She tucked the hat snug under Lucy's chin. "Hold it with your hand, too."

The wind slowed down. The sun came out warm and bright. Lucy sat on the bench with Mom. She kept her hat on tight. "Nice hat," said a kind old man on the next bench. Lucy smiled. "The wind gave it back," she said.

Lily wanted to draw a cat on the big tablet. The tablet sat on the shelf in the computer lab. Lily took it with one hand. The tablet slipped. It wobbled and tipped. "Whoa," said Lily. She caught it just in time.

She tried again. This time she used two hands. One hand on each side. The tablet did not wobble at all. Lily carried it to the table. She walked slow, like an ant carrying a stick.

Now she had to turn it on. She pressed the round button. One, two, three. The screen lit up. She tapped the blue square with her finger. The drawing app opened. Lily made a cat with straight ears and a long tail. Then she made a sun. Then she made a red ball.

Teacher Mia clapped. "Time to put it away," she said. Lily pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She stood up tall. Two hands on the tablet, one on each side. She walked to the shelf. One, two, three, place it down. "All done," said Lily.

Lennon held Mama's hand at the big hall. Little lamps glowed on every table. They looked like tiny stars. Lennon wanted to light one all by herself.

She reached for a match. "No, no," said Auntie Rosa. "Fire is for grown-ups." Lennon's face felt hot. That was the wrong thing to do. She wanted to help anyway.

Mama knelt down beside her. "Pick a lamp for me," said Mama. Lennon looked at the box of lamps. She picked the blue one. It felt smooth in her hands. She gave it to Mama, and Mama lit it with one little match. The flame popped up, small and warm. Lennon clapped her hands.

Auntie Rosa gave the lamp a place on the table. "You sent the blue lamp here," said Mama. "And it glows because of you." Lennon smiled and watched the little flame dance.

Now, everyone needed more lamps. Lennon picked a yellow one for Papa. She picked a green one for Auntie Rosa. Each time, a grown-up did the lighting. Lennon did the picking.

At the end of the night, the whole room was full of light. Lennon looked at her blue lamp. It was still glowing. "That one is mine," she said. "I chose it."

Sarah went to the store with Grandma. Sarah wanted pancakes on Saturday. "How many days until Saturday?" she asked. "Guess," said Grandma. Sarah held up her little hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven," she said. Seven fingers. Seven days. Sarah giggled. At the store, they saw one big red apple. Then two yellow bananas. Then three cute little oranges in a bag. Sarah put them in the cart one at a time. "Four, five, six," she counted. The cart rolled when she pushed it. Push, roll. That made her laugh. Grandma held up a box. "How many pancakes will we make?" Sarah guessed. "Ten!" she said. "Ten, nine, eight, seven," she counted down. At home they would mix the batter. Grandma would cook. Sarah would watch. "Seven days is a long time," said Sarah. "Yes," said Grandma, "but Saturday always comes." Sarah hugged the apple bag all the way to the car.

Hailey sat in the cafe with her mama. She had a paper and a pencil. She wanted to write her name.

She held the pencil in her fist. She pressed hard. The H came out all wiggly. "That looks ugly," she said, and her lip went down.

Mama put her hand over Hailey's hand. She set the pencil on Hailey's middle finger. "Now pinch it," said Mama. Hailey pinched with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil felt light, like a little bird.

She wrote H. Then A. Then I. Then L. Then E. And then Y. "HAILEY!" she said so loud that a man at the next table looked up and smiled.

Mama kissed the top of her head. Hailey wrote her name again. Pinch, rest, write. Pinch, rest, write. Each letter stood up straight, like little trees.

The waiter brought mama's cup, and a cookie for Hailey. On the napkin, Hailey wrote her name one more time. She drew a heart under it and painted the heart red with her pencil.

"Can we take this home?" she asked, holding up the napkin.

"We can," said Mama. "Right after one more HAILEY."

Ibrahim sat in his car seat. The car went over a bridge. Below them was a wide river. The water sparkled in the sun.

"I want my juice," said Ibrahim. He reached for the cup. It was far away. His little hand could not get it. He pushed and stretched. His face went hot and cross.

Then he remembered his words. "Daddy, can you help me, please?" he asked. Daddy smiled at him in the mirror. "Of course," said Daddy. He reached back with one hand. He passed the cup to Ibrahim.

"Thank you, Daddy," said Ibrahim. He took a big sip. The juice was cold and sweet. "Sorry I made a grumpy sound," he said. "That's okay," said Daddy.

The car went over another bridge. The river slid under it. Ibrahim waved at the water. "See you, river," he said. He held his cup with both hands. "Can we go to the park early tomorrow?" he asked. "Yes," said Daddy. "Early it is."

Lydia stood at the big baseball diamond. Daddy put a purple hoop on the ground. "Throw the beanbag in," said Daddy.

Lydia threw the beanbag high. She thought it would bounce. She thought it would bounce right into the hoop. But the beanbag came down. Flop. It just sat in the grass. It did not bounce at all. Lydia walked over and picked it up.

"Again," said Lydia. She threw it again, up and up. Flop. It landed in the grass again. Then she threw it low and soft. Flop. It fell right into the hoop. "It went in!" said Lydia. "Good throw," said Daddy. "Bring me the beanbag, please."

Lydia ran and brought it back. Then Daddy rolled her a big ball. "Catch it with both hands," he said. Lydia held out one hand. The ball bumped her fingers and fell. She tried again with one hand. It fell again.

"Both hands," said Daddy. He rolled the ball slowly. Lydia held out both hands. She waited. She waited. The ball came and came. Both hands closed around it. "I caught it!" said Lydia. She hugged the big ball and laughed. "One more time," said Daddy. He rolled the ball again.

James sat at the paint table at school. He wanted to paint green grass. But the green paint pot was empty. James looked in the pot. He tipped it upside down. Nothing came out.

"I need green," said James. His teacher, Miss Anne, sat down next to him. "Let me see," she said. She put out a pot of blue paint. Then she put out a pot of yellow paint. "You can try," she said.

James put his brush in the blue paint. He made a blue spot on his paper. Then he put the same brush in the yellow paint. He made a yellow spot on top. James waited. He looked very close. The spot turned green! James smiled big. He dipped his brush again and again. Blue, then yellow. Green, green, green. He painted tall grass all over his paper. "Look, Miss Anne!" he said. "My grass is so green!"

Charlie ran to the table with muddy hands. She wanted her supper right now!

"Stop!" said Mommy with a laugh. "Look at those paws."

Charlie looked. Her hands were brown and dirty. "Am I a puppy?" she asked.

"A muddy puppy," said Daddy. "Puppies eat from bowls. Do you want a bowl on the floor?"

Charlie giggled. "No! I want a chair."

"Then off to the sink," said Mommy. "We wash our hands before we eat."

Charlie stomped to the sink. Mommy turned on the water. Charlie rubbed and rubbed. The mud went down the drain. Now her hands were pink and clean.

She held them up. "Look, Daddy! No more puppy paws!"

"Smart girl," said Daddy. "Now come and eat."

After supper, Charlie had her bath. The water was warm and bubbly. She washed her tummy and her toes. Then Mommy helped her put on her soft pajamas. They had stars on them.

"I washed my hands before supper," Charlie told her teddy. "And now I am clean all over!"

She climbed into bed. Mommy tucked her in and kissed her nose.

"Tomorrow I will bake cookies with Daddy," Charlie said, "and I will wash my hands first."

"Good plan," said Mommy, turning off the light.

Charlie yugged teddy close. "Night night, muddy puppy," she whispered.

Athena had curly hair and a small red chair. She sat in the kitchen with her family. Papa was making soup in the big pot. The soup was hot, so Papa stirred it, not Athena. Athena had her own little cup of cold water. "Cold for me," she said. "Hot for the soup."

Athena wanted to help. Papa said, "You can carry the napkins." The napkins were light. Athena ran fast to the table. Then she walked slow and careful, like a turtle. She put the napkins down, one by one. "I helped!" she said.

Then Athena saw a puddle on the floor. A tiny puddle by the sink. She stomped in it. Splash! Her socks got all wet. "Oh no," said Mama. "Wet socks are cold. You need dry ones." Mama peeled off the wet socks. Athena touched them with one finger. Wet. Then Mama gave her fluffy new socks. Athena squeezed them. Dry and warm.

"Wet socks go here," said Mama. She hung them on the rack. Athena watched the water drip, drip, drip into a bowl. "The socks are crying," Athena whispered. She waved at them. "Bye bye, little tears." The dry fluffy socks waited on her feet, and Athena jumped up and down, soft as a bunny.

Lillian had a cold. She caught it from her big brother. Now she was resting at home on the soft couch.

Grandma came over with a big smile. "Would you like some water?" she asked. Lillian shook her head. She did not feel thirsty at all. Her throat was scratchy and her tummy felt funny.

Then Grandma held up a tiny blue cup. It had a plane painted on the side. "This cup is for brave pilots," Grandma said. "Little sips only." Lillian sat up and held the cup. She took one small sip. Then another. The water was cool and fresh.

Soon Lillian felt a bit better. She sat up tall. She wanted to draw a plane just like her cup. Grandma found the crayons and paper. Lillian drew a big plane in the sky. She sipped more water while she drew. "Look, Grandma!" she said. "My plane is flying to the sun." Grandma gave her a gentle hug and one more sip of water in the little blue cup.

Beatrice stood by the blocks at school. She wanted to play with Leo and Mia. But they were busy feeding a teddy bear. Beatrice did not know how to start. She looked at her shoes. She looked at her hands.

Then she took a big breath. "Let's pretend I am the bear's mama," she said. Leo looked up fast. Mia clapped her hands. "Yes! You came home!" said Leo. Just like that, the game began. Beatrice picked up the teddy and hugged him. "My baby," she said softly. "Time for soup."

Mia bent a paper cup and made it a tiny pot. "One spoon, two spoops, three spoons," she counted. Leo wrapped the bear in a red scarf. "Warm blanket, warm baby," he said. Beatrice was happy. She rocked the teddy side to side.

"Let's pretend the bear is sleepy," said Leo. "Let's pretend I sing a song," said Beatrice. She sang a small hum, one note, two notes, three. The teddy closed his button eyes. All the friends whispered, "Shh." Mia set one blanket, then two, then three on top. Then they all tiptoed in a circle around the sleeping bear, hands on lips, giggling like tiny pirates sneaking past a whale.

James went to the bank with his dad. It was cold outside. James held his little blue coat in his hands.

"Time to put your coat on," said Dad.

James pushed one arm into one sleeve. Then he looked for the other sleeve. The sleeve was hiding behind his back. James turned around and around. "I can't find it," he said.

A girl named Mia was waiting with her mom. She saw James spinning. "Watch me," said Mia. She laid her coat on the floor. She put her arms in the sleeves. Then she flipped it over her head. The coat was on!

James wondered, could his coat do that too? He laid his coat on the floor. He put his arms in the sleeves. He touched the soft fabric with his fingers. He flipped it over his head. The coat landed on him just right.

"Now the zipper," said Dad. James pulled it up, up, up. Click, it stopped at the top.

"You look good," said Mia. "Your coat has a picture of a bear on it."

James looked down at the bear. "My coat did a flip," he said. "Zip it again, Dad?"

Mohamed went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought a big round loaf of bread. They bought fresh butter in a little dish. A bee tried to fly near the bread. "Go away, bee," said Mohamed. The bee buzzed off to the flowers.

At home, Mohamed wanted to make lunch. "I will spread the butter," he said. He tried. The butter was hard. It would not spread. It made a hole in the bread. "Oh no," said Mohamed. "My bread has a big hole!"

Dad smiled. "Let's put the butter on the counter," he said. They set it down. They washed apples. They sang a silly song about a hammer that went tap, tap, tap. Mohamed's tooth felt a little loose, so he wiggled it with his tongue.

Then Mohamed touched the butter. It was soft now! He spread it, slow and smooth. The bread was all gold and shiny.

"Mohamed made lunch!" said Dad, and he took a big, big bite.

Addison went to the library for story time. She sat on a round rug. It was a big circle.

Miss Jane held up a square book. "Time for a story and a craft," she said. The craft was paper pizza. Addison got red paper and green paper. Then Miss Jane gave her a yellow circle.

Addison wanted to cut the circle. She looked for a corner to start. She turned the paper over. She peeked at the edge. She scratched her head. "Where is the corner?" she said.

Benji next to her laughed. "It ran away," he said. "It did not run," said Addison. "It is not there." She ran her finger all around the paper. Round and round and round. No corner anywhere. "Silly circle," she said. "You have no corners at all."

Miss Jane helped with the scissors, because scissors are for grown-up hands. She cut a red square for cheese and a green triangle for a pepper. Addison glued them on. Benji glued a rectangle for a crust.

"Your pizza looks yummy," said Benji. "Do not eat it," said Addison. "That would be a mean trick on my tummy." Benji giggled so hard he fell over on the round, round rug.

Rosalie was going on a trip. It was winter, so she wore her red coat. The airport was very busy. So many feet! So many bags!

Then Rosalie saw them. Big planes out the big window! One plane went up, up into the sky. "Look, Mama!" she called. Rosalie wanted to run to the window. She took one step. The crowd was big and fast. Where was Mama's hand? Rosalie reached up and found it. She held on tight.

Mama squeezed her hand. They walked to the window together. The planes were giant, but Rosalie felt tiny next to them. A truck pushed a plane slowly along the ground. "It goes so slow," said Rosalie. A man in a vest waved two big sticks. The plane turned and followed him.

"Where do the planes sleep?" Rosalie asked. Mama smiled and pointed out at the sky. Another plane came down, down, down, soft as a bird.

Jake went to the library with his mom. He saw a big toy train on the rug. A girl named Mia was already there. She was holding the engine.

"I want the engine," said Jake.

"Me first," said Mia.

They both pulled. The train cars went crash. Blocks fell down. It looked messy on the rug.

Then Mia had an idea. "You can go first," she said. "Then I get a go."

Jake drove the engine around the rug. "Choo choo!" he said. "It's a bee train, going fast!"

Then he stopped. "Your turn now, Mia."

Mia drove the train too. Jake made a tunnel with his arms. The train zoomed through it. They took turns again and again.

The librarian smiled at them. "Time for story time," she said. "Everyone sits in a circle."

Jake sat down next to Mia. She let him hold half of her book.

"I like the bee train," said Jake.

Jaxon woke up at Grandma's house. The sun made a warm line on his blanket. He wanted to go outside and play in the leaves. But first he had to get dressed.

Grandma laid out his clothes. Jaxon pulled on his shirt. He pulled on his pants. Then he sat down with his shoes. He pushed and pushed. His toes felt squished and bumpy inside.

Jaxon knocked on the wall to call Grandma. She came in and smiled. "Try again, sweet boy," she said softly. Jaxon took the shoes off. He looked at his bare feet. He looked at his socks. Then he put the socks on first. His toes felt cozy and warm.

Now the shoes slid right on. Jaxon laughed. He stomped his feet. "Ready!" he said.

He ate his oatmeal by the window. A shy brown rabbit sat near the fence. Grandma filled the tub for a warm bath later. But now it was leaf time.

Jaxon ran outside. He jumped in the leaves with his socks on first, then his shoes. The rabbit hopped away through the golden pile.

Brooklyn went to the library with her mama. She wanted to write her name. She found a basket of bumpy letter cards. Each card had a big letter on it. Brooklyn picked up the letter B. "B says buh," she said. The letter A said "ah." The letter K said "kuh."

Brooklyn got a crayon and paper. She tried to write K. She made the lines go the wrong way. "Oh no," she said. "That looks bad." She tried again. The K was still wrong. Her mouth turned down.

Then Mama sat close by her. "Try the bumpy card," Mama said softly. Brooklyn put her finger on the bumpy K. She traced the shape. Down the tall line. Then the little arm. Then the other arm. The bumps tickled her finger. She traced it again and again.

Now Brooklyn picked up her crayon. She drew the K. The tall line went down. The arms went out. The K was right! Brooklyn held the paper up high. The lamp made her letters shine. "Look, Mama! Brooklyn!" She traced the K one more time, just to feel the bumps. "Kuh, kuh, Brooklyn," she said.

Emile wants to read a book all by himself. He finds a thick red book on the rug. He opens it near the cover, like always. He turns the pages from front to back. "Am I doing it right?" he asks. Miss Ada smiles. "Look at the pictures. Do they tell you a story?"

Then his friend Noa comes over. She has a little blue flag on her bag. She holds up her own book. "This one opens the other way," she says. Emile looks. The book opens from the left side. The pages turn the other way. "Why does it do that?" he asks. "It is in Hebrew," Noa says. "We read it from right to left."

Emile tries it. He opens her book the new way. He turns the pages with care. The pictures flow like a little river. Then he takes his red book again. He finds the first page. He puts his finger under a word. The word says "cat", and the picture shows a cat. Emile laughs and turns to Noa. "Your book is a book too, just turned around," he says.

Mason was at Grandma's house. He could not find his monkey. "Where did you go, monkey?" he asked.

Mason looked under the big chair. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. One car, two blocks, three balls. No monkey. Grandpa said, "Let's look in the garden."

They looked by the flowers. They looked by the swing. No monkey. Then Mason saw something. "Spotted fur!" he said. The monkey was in the green bush.

"Grandma, who found him?" asked Mason.

"The bus driver did," said Grandma. "He knocked on the door. He saw the tag on the monkey."

Mason looked at the tag. It had his name. M-A-S-O-N. The bus driver read the name. Then he brought the monkey to Mason.

"What a good tag," said Mason. "It says my name!"

Later, Mason took a sticker and a pen. He asked Grandma to help. She wrote his name on the tag. Mason held the tag up high.

"Now everyone knows," said Mason. "This monkey is mine!"

He hugged the monkey tight. "Hello, monkey. Hello, tag."

Blake ran into Mia's house. Music was playing in the big room!

"Listen!" said Mia. "We will sing a song. My mom will count first."

Blake was so excited. She opened her mouth to sing. "Twinkle, twin..."

"Wait," said Mia. "Not yet! You will lose your place. Wait for the count."

Blake closed her mouth. She waited. Her hands sat still.

Mia's mom stood up tall. "One, two, three, four!" she said.

"Now!" cried Mia. Both girls sang at the same time. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star!"

Blake clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps fit right on the beat, just like the song!

"You did it!" said Mia.

Then came the small surprise. Mia's mom clapped too. Clap, clap, clap! Even the dog barked, woof, woof, woof.

"This is easy!" said Blake. She sang it again. "One, two, three, four," she counted all by herself.

"Twinkle, twinkle, little star!"

Kai sat on Grandpa's big red rug. Grandpa had a gift for him. It was a little drum with a happy face.

"Let's sing," said Grandpa. "Clap with me." Grandpa clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Kai clapped too. But Kai did not know the star song words yet. He stopped. His mouth made no sound. That felt like a problem.

Kai waited. He tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. Then he tried a song he knew. "A, B, C, D," he sang. Grandpa's eyes went wide. Grandpa clapped along. Clap, clap, clap. The tune fit! It was the same tune as the star song!

"Now the star words," said Grandpa. He sang. "Twinkle, twinkle." Kai sang too. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." He sang it all by himself.

After the song, Kai patted the drum face. "Was it a naughty drum?" he asked. Grandpa laughed. "It was a good drum. It kept the beat."

Kai clapped and sang again. The goldfish swam in its bowl by the window. Clap, clap, clap went the little drum.

Ava sat at the dinner table. She drank warm milk from her cup. "Milk comes from a cow," said Daddy. Ava giggled. A big cow! Moo!

After dinner, Ava begged, "Can I stay up late? Please, please?" Outside, the sky was stormy and dark. "No, sweet pea," said Mommy. "It is bedtime." Ava got a warm bath. The water smelled like soap. She put on her soft pajamas. She got kisses and went to sleep.

In the morning, Ava woke up with stretchy arms. "I feel big!" she said. She ran to her blocks. She stacked them tall, so tall. She danced with her bear. "Wow," said Ava. "I slept, and now I can play!" She clapped her hands. "Bedtime again tonight?" she asked Mommy. Mommy smiled and nodded.

Felix wanted to write Grandpa a note. He took a pencil and wrote his letters. He wrote big and small, all in a row. "This says come play with me," he said.

Grandpa looked at the note. He shook his head. "I see letters," he said. "But the words are all squished." Felix looked at his paper. All his letters were holding hands in one long line. Then Grandpa held up a book. He turned the pages from the front to the back. Felix looked close. The words had little gaps between them. Was that why Grandpa could read them?

Felix tapped his pencil. He drew a small space after each word. "Now can you read it?" he asked. Grandpa smiled big. "Come play with me," he read out loud. Felix clapped. "The spaces did it!" he said.

Florence went to the library with Dad. She wanted a book about a mouse. She found one with a tiny gray mouse on the cover.

"Please read it," she said. Dad opened the front of the book. He read the first page. Then the next page. He pointed at the little black marks under the picture. "I read these words," he said. Florence touched the marks with her finger. Dad's voice had come from them!

One page had only a picture. The mouse looked at a big cheese. "Read this one!" said Florence. Dad turned the page slowly. "There are no words here," he said. "Nothing to read." Florence looked hard. The page was empty of marks.

She turned back to a page with words. Dad read them. The mouse began to move to the cheese. Florence laughed.

She held the book herself. She started at the front. She turned each page one by one. "This is a special book," she said. Dad smiled and read the words again.

Hudson sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. He had paper and a brush. But the orange paint jar was empty. Hudson looked and looked. No orange anywhere.

He found red paint. He found yellow paint. Hudson sighed. Then he dipped his brush in red. He put red on the paper. He dipped his brush in yellow. He put yellow on top of the red. He swirled it around. The paint turned orange! Hudson gasped. His pumpkin was orange now.

Mom set a snack beside him. It was salty crackers. Hudson munched one. He painted a big pumpkin. Then he painted a little bear next to it. "The bear can sleep by the pumpkin," Hudson said. He put down his brush and smiled.

Isla went to the pharmacy with Mama. There was a little sink by the counter. It had pink soap and a paper towel holder. A sign showed a fox washing its paws. Isla wanted to wash her hands there too.

Mama bought some medicine. Then she said, "Isla, it is almost snack time." Isla held up her hands. "My hands aren't dirty!" she said. They looked clean and smooth. Mama turned on the water anyway. It felt cool and bubbly. Isla pumped the pink soap. It smelled like flowers.

"Now we sing," said Mama. They sang a little song about a fox. Isla rubbed the soap hard between her fingers. Bubbles went pop, pop, pop. She counted to twenty with Mama. Then she dried her hands on the paper towel. At home, Isla ate her crackers. "Good washing," said Mama. Isla looked at her clean hands and smiled.

Eleanor turned four today. There were balloons on the door. Grandma was baking bread. Dad was stirring something sweet.

Then the door opened. Friends came in with presents. Big ones and small ones!

Eleanor grabbed the first box. She pulled off the paper fast. Inside was a red truck with a strong wheel that spun round and round. Leo had brought it.

She dropped it and ran to the next box. That one had a pretend kitchen with tiny pots. She hugged the pots to her chest.

Then she stopped. Leo was standing quietly by the wall. He looked down at his shoes.

Eleanor ran back to him. She held up the red truck. "Thank you, Leo!" she said.

Leo smiled a big smile. "You can spin the wheel again," he said. "Watch me!"

He pushed the truck across the floor. The wheel spun fast, all the way to the cake.

Leah held her doll tight. "Daddy, look! Big cart!" Daddy pushed the big cart. Leah walked slow, slow, slow. Then she saw the bakery, and she ran fast, fast, fast.

Daddy picked up bread with a big glove. "Hot," he said. Leah felt the warm air with her hand. Then they went to the freezer. Leah touched the cold glass. "Frozen peas!" she whispered. The peas were cold, cold, cold.

Leah found a little doll. A small doll for her big doll! Daddy said yes. Outside, the sky was dark. "Is it morning?" Leah asked. Daddy shook his head. "It is night. Night is the opposite of day." Leah looked up. The dark sky was full of stars. She hugged both dolls. "Night night, stars," she whispered. The car door went click.

Eli sat on his bed. He had a big red book. He wanted to know what the dog in the picture was doing. But the pages had little black marks too. They were words.

Eli put his finger at the right side of the page. He moved it that way. The words felt like a big jumble. He tried again. His finger ran into the edge of the book. "Hmm," said Eli.

Mom came in and sat down. "Read with me," she said. She opened the book at the front. "This part comes first," she said. Then she put her finger at the left side of the page. Her finger slid to the right. The words flowed out like a little river. "The dog can jump," Mom read.

Eli looked. Yes! The dog was jumping over a pot in the picture. Eli put his finger on the left side. He slid it to the right. "The pot fell down," he said. Mom smiled and clapped.

Eli turned the page himself. He started on the left again. "Read it to me," he said, and patted the bed.

Xavier lost Bunny at the grocery store. Bunny was soft and gray. Xavier ran to the fruit area. No Bunny there. He ran to the bread area. No Bunny there. He ran past the milk. He ran past the eggs. "I looked everywhere!" he said.

Mama held his hand. "Let's go slow," she said. "We look at one aisle at a time." Xavier walked down aisle one. He looked up. He looked down. He looked under the apples. No Bunny. Aisle two. He looked behind the big boxes. No Bunny. Aisle three. He looked and looked.

There! Bunny sat by the soup cans. "You were hiding!" said Xavier. He hugged Bunny tight. "Bunny wants lunch," said Mama with a smile. "Bunny speaks soup language," said Xavier. Mama laughed. They put Bunny and three soup cans in the cart.

Miles sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a big apple. Apples are red, he thought. "I need the red paint," he said.

The paint jars lived in the art closet. The closet was very dark. Miles reached in. He felt a jar. He carried it to his table.

Uh oh. The jar was green, not red. Green paint made a green apple. "That is not right," said Miles.

He went back to the dark closet. He felt another jar. It was blue. Blue paint made a blue apple. Outside, a dog barked. The dog pushed its nose on the window. Miles laughed so much he felt dizzy.

Then Miss Kay came. She opened the curtains. Sun lit up the closet. Now Miles could see every jar. He found the red one all by himself. He painted one red apple, one green apple, and one blue one too.

Nova loved art class. Today she painted a cow. She made the cow brown with big black spots. Her paper was high up on the easel. She dipped her brush in red, blue and yellow paint. Red made her think of apples. Blue made her think of the sky.

Then the teacher said, "Clean-up time!" Nova put the caps on the paint. Sam made piles of blocks on the rug. He made a red pile, a blue pile and a yellow pile. Nova looked at the red pile. One block there was yellow. It was hiding in the wrong spot! Nova picked it out. She set it down with the other yellow blocks.

Sam looked at his piles. He smiled big. "Yellow goes with yellow," he said. Nova smiled too. She could hear the paint brushes drip drip in the water cups. Someday she dreamed she would paint a purple cow. For now she picked up the last blue block and put it with its friends.

Kinsley went to Mia's house. Mia had a big toy box. "Let's play house," said Mia.

Mia put a blanket over a chair. It made a little house. Kinsley picked up a teddy bear. "The baby is sleepy," she said. She patted the bear's back. The bear did not wake up.

Then the bear began to cry. Mia made a crying sound. "The baby needs a doctor!" said Kinsley. But Kinsley did not feel like a doctor. She was just Kinsley in her play clothes.

Mia ran to the dress-up box. She pulled out a white coat. "Put this on," she said. Kinsley slid her arms in. Now she looked like a doctor. She stood up tall. "I will help the baby," she said.

Kinsley checked the bear with a toy spoon. "The baby needs a hat," she said. Mia found a tiny sock and put it on the bear's head. The crying stopped. "All better," said Kinsley. Then the two doctors cleaned up the little house. Kinsley left the white coat on.

At the door, Mia waved. "Bye, Doctor Kinsley."

Charles sat at the book club with his friend Mila. Miss Jo held up a big card. It had the word dog on it. Charles looked and looked. Then he laughed. "That says bog!" he said.

Mila laughed too. "Silly! A bog is not an animal." Charles looked again. He made a b with his finger. Then he made a d. The round parts did not face the same way. "Oh!" he said. He turned his b around. Now it was a d. "D, d, dog!" he said.

Miss Jo clapped. "Try one more, Charles." The card said bed. Charles checked the round parts. He counted, "One round this way, one round that way." He said, "B, e, d. Bed!" His itchy sock needed a scratch, but he kept reading. "Dog, bed, dog, bed," said Charles, and everyone cheered.

Raphael took his old truck to the doctor's office. He could not wait to show it to Doctor Maya. "Today we check your eyes," she said. Raphael looked with his eyes. He saw a red chart on the wall. "I see an A!" he shouted.

Then Doctor Maya held up a small yellow lemon slice. "Open wide," she said. Raphael thought lemons taste like orange juice, sweet and good. He opened his mouth. His tongue touched the lemon. WOW! His whole face scrunched up. "Sour!" he cried. "So sour!" Doctor Maya laughed. "Your tongue can taste that," she said.

Next, Raphael heard a beep with his ears. He sniffed a sticker with his nose. It smelled like strawberries. He touched his truck with his fingers. It felt bumpy. At last he stuck out his tongue for one more tiny taste. "Sour again!" he said, and he giggled and giggled.

Julia stood in the kitchen. Her baby brother Sam was asleep. Mama was at the stove. The stove was hot, so Julia stayed back.

Julia wanted to play her drum. She hit it. BANG! BANG! It was loud. The loud sound woke Sam up. He cried and cried.

Mama held Sam. Julia felt bad. She looked at her drum. Then she tapped it. Tap. Tap. It was quiet. Sam stopped crying. His eyes closed. Mama put him down softly.

Julia tapped her drum again. Tap. Tap. The kitchen stayed quiet. The big drum could be loud. The big drum could be quiet too. Julia liked quiet better right now.

Then Julia saw something small and gray by the window. A little bird sat there. It sang one soft note. Julia tapped her drum slow, so slow. The bird sang back fast, so fast. Julia giggled. She played quiet and slow, all the way to the end.

Mama smiled. "Snack time," she said. Julia got a cold cup of milk. The milk was cold, and her warm cookie smelled good. She sat next to Sam. Everyone was happy.

Amelia woke up and saw white. Snow had come in the night. "A snow day!" said Mom. "No school today."

Amelia put on her boots and her red mittens. She went out to the backyard. She patted the snow. She made a small snowman with a stick for an arm. From the fence she could see the train go by, all covered in white. "Pretty," said Amelia.

Then Mom called her in for warm milk. Amelia pulled off her boots. Water dripped on the floor. Her mittens were soaked too.

"I want to go back out," said Amelia. She picked up her mittens. They were cold and wet. "Yuck," said Amelia.

"Let's put them here," said Mom. They hung the mittens on the chair by the warm vent. The boots went under it. Mom held the warm milk, and Amelia drank it all up.

Later Amelia touched her mittens. They were dry! She slid them on. She put on her boots. They were dry too.

"Back to the snowman," said Amelia. Mom smiled and opened the door.

Kai stood in the garage with Dad. Dad turned on a song. It had a big, steady beat. Boom, boom, boom.

Kai wanted to clap along. He clapped too fast. "Slow down, silly!" Dad laughed. Kai chased the beat with his hands. He clapped again. This time his claps landed just right. Clap, clap, clap. The song went boom and his hands went clap. They matched!

"Now let's sing the spider song," said Dad. Kai loved that song. It had hand actions. He made his fingers climb up, up, up the spout. Then he made the spider climb down. Dad froze like a statue. "Wait! Where is your spider going?" Kai giggled. He had mixed it up! The rain comes down, but the spider climbs up. He tried again. His fingers went up, up, up. Then down came the rain, and his fingers swooshed low.

Mom came into the garage. She clapped along with them. Kai sang the whole song all by himself. His fingers climbed and the beat went boom. Mom gave him a big hug. "One more time!" said Kai. His spider climbed up, up, up again.

Luke went to the mall with his dad. Luke was getting his very first haircut. The salon had a big fish tank. The fish were orange and blue.

A lady named May put a low stool by her chair. "Hop up," she said. Luke sat down. May sprayed warm water on his hair. It felt like soft rain.

Luke saw a fish swim by. He turned his head to look. Snip went the scissors. May had to fix the same spot twice. "Hmm," said Luke. "What happens if I sit very still?" He tried it. He sat like a statue. He watched only the mirror. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell down like soft snow. It tickled his nose.

"Can I bring the fish a magnet?" Luke asked his dad. Dad laughed. "Fish don't want magnets," he said. "They want fish food." May turned the chair around. Luke looked in the mirror. His hair was neat and short. All even, all around. "I look like a big boy," said Luke. He held the mirror himself and smiled.

Matteo wanted to find the best spot at the park. He looked with his eyes. He saw a big tree and a red slide. He heard a dog bark with his ears. He smelled flowers with his nose. "The flowers smell sweet," he said.

Then Matteo saw a berry bush. "Can I taste one?" he asked. Mama said, "No, those are not for eating. Here, take this apple instead." Matteo took a bite. "Sweet!" he said. He touched the apple with his hands. It was smooth and cool.

Near the tree, Matteo saw soft green grass. He sat down and took off his shoes. He wiggled his toes. The grass tickled his feet! "My feet can feel it too," he said. He laughed and stomped. "Tickle, tickle, tickle!" Mama came to sit by him. "This is the best spot," said Matteo. He put his careful hands in the grass and wiggled his toes again.

Levi ran to the shape table at school. A big red clock sat there. It was round like a ball.

"My button is small," said Mia. "It can't be a circle like the big clock."

Levi held up his tiny button. He spun it on the table. It rolled and rolled. The big clock was round too. He put the button next to the clock. Both were round! Levi clapped his hands.

"They are both circles!" said Mia.

Levi looked for more circles. He found a little round cracker. He found a big round hoop outside. The cracker fit in his hand. Levi had to stand inside the hoop. Big circle, tiny circle. They were still circles!

Then Levi found square blocks and a triangle roof. He stacked them fast. A rectangle door went at the bottom.

"Look at my new animal house!" he said.

A toy cat walked in. "The cat can stay here," said Levi. He drew a tiny round door for a mouse, too.

Ava sat at the big table in writing club. Her paper was yellow like a bee. Miss Jo gave her a pencil. "Now we write your name," said Miss Jo. Ava wanted to write AVA all by herself.

Ava held the pencil tight. She pressed down very hard. She made a big A. Then she made a V. Then the pencil tip went SNAP. The little black point fell onto the paper. "Oh no!" said Ava. "My pencil broke!"

Tommy laughed, but not in a mean way. "That happened to me too," he said. Miss Jo gave Ava a new pencil. "Try again," she said. Ava held it soft this time. She pressed gently, gently. She made a A. She made a V. She made another A. No snap! The letters stayed on the paper.

"Look, look!" said Ava. "A V A! That is me!" She jumped up so fast her chair went wobble. "Careful," said Miss Jo with a smile, "or you will lock that chair under the table." Ava giggled. She sat back down and wrote her name one more time, soft as a bee landing on a flower. "I can write all day," said Ava, "if I press like this."

Harper held Mama's hand at the big blue door. "This is the dentist," said Mama. Inside there was a soft chair, and a small gray toy mouse sat on the counter.

A kind dentist came in. "Hello, Harper," she said. "One, two, three fingers up. Now I will count your teeth." Harper saw the dentist's hands were blue. "Your hands are blue!" said Harper.

The dentist pulled at her fingers. Snap went one glove. Snap went the other. Underneath, her hands were not blue at all. She slid the gloves back on, one by one, and they were smooth and clean.

"Now open wide," said the dentist. Harper opened her mouth like a little mouse opening for cheese. The dentist counted, "One tooth, two teeth, ten teeth!" Her gloved fingers tapped each one, so soft and gentle.

Harper squeezed the gray mouse toy. "All done," said the dentist. "You were so brave."

"Can I wear blue gloves too?" asked Harper.

Mateo was going to the car. "My blue dinosaur!" he shouted. "He is lost!" Mateo loved that dinosaur. He could not leave it alone at home.

He looked on the car floor. He looked by his feet. "I see dust," said Mateo. "I see one old cookie. No dinosaur." He looked under the seat. It was too dark. He could not see anything at all.

"I can't see!" said Mateo. "The dark spot is too dark!" Mom smiled. She reached into her bag. She took out a flashlight. Mom clicked it on. The light was bright. "Here you go," she said.

Mateo pointed the flashlight under the seat. The dark spot was not dark anymore. He saw his dinosaur! "I see his tail! I see his hair!" Mateo laughed. He reached in and pulled. Out came the dinosaur, all dusty and happy.

Mateo hugged him tight. "You were under the seat! The light found you!" He held the flashlight up high. "Mom, can we look for more things?" Mom laughed too. "Maybe we can sell cookies at the big sale," she said. "But first, let's buckle the dinosaur in." Mateo clicked the seat belt over the dinosaur. "There," said Mateo. "Now you ride with me."

Thomas put on his red coat. He pulled the zipper up. It stuck near his tummy. He tried again. It stuck again.

"Let's practice at the store," said Mom. "It is cold by the freezers."

They walk to the grocery store. First they pick apples. Then they walk down the milk line of the store. The freezer aisle was very cold. Thomas pulled his zipper again. It went up a tiny bit. Then it stopped. "Keep trying," said Mom. Thomas pulled it again. Up it went, a little more. Then it stopped at his chin. He tugged hard. The zipper closed all the way. His coat was warm and neat.

"Look, Mom! I did it!" said Thomas. Mom clapped. They walked to the cold freezer. Thomas got to pick the ice cream. He held the cold box in his warm hands.

On the way home, Thomas zipped his coat all by himself again. "Zip," he said. "Zip, zip."

Elizabeth went to the park with Grandma. She saw a big black grill near the picnic table. Smoke came up from it. "Who made the smoke?" she wondered.

A man came to cook on the grill. Elizabeth wanted to see close. Grandma held her hand. "Stay with me," Grandma said. Elizabeth stood by Grandma and looked from far away.

The man put a hot dog on the grill. It went sizzle, sizzle. Elizabeth clapped her hands. The hot dog began to turn brown. She saw that the fire made the hot dog hot. Then the man turned a knob. The fire went away. "Is it cold now?" Elizabeth wondered. She did not touch. She asked the man instead. The man shook his head. "Only I touch it," he said. He waved his hand over the top. He kept his hand high, not on it.

The hot dog was ready. The man put it in a bun. He gave it time to cool. Then he handed it to Grandma. Grandma broke a little piece for Elizabeth. It was warm and soft now. Elizabeth took a gentle little bite.

Some ducks walked by in a line. "They look like a class going to school," said Elizabeth. Grandma laughed. Elizabeth waved at the ducks. "Hello, class!" she said.

Ella was at daycare. She wanted to play pretend with Leo. Leo had a big toy dragon.

Ella hugged the dragon. "The dragon is nice," she said.

Leo shook his head. "The dragon is scary," he said.

Ella made a sad face. "Can we both be right?" she asked.

Leo thought. "Maybe," he said. "The dragon is scary to bad guys. But he is nice to us."

Ella smiled. "Yes! A friendly dragon." The dragon gave Leo a pretend scratch on his arm. Leo laughed.

Then the dragon got an owie. Ella put a bandage on it. Leo used pretend glue to stick a paper wing back on. Ella patted the dragon. "There, there," she said. "All better."

The friendly dragon flew them both home to the playhouse for a snack.

Nora looked out the window. "It is rainy today!" she said. Big drops went plip, plip, plip.

Nora wanted to jump in puddles. She grabbed her orange rain boots. But one boot was missing! She looked under her bed. She looked behind the turtle tank. No boot.

Nora wore her sneakers instead. She ran outside. The wind blew her hat off. She splashed in a big puddle. Splash! Her socks got soggy. Water squished in her shoes. "Oh no," said Nora. "My feet are all wet."

She ran back inside. There was the boot, under the table! Nora pulled it on. She put on the other boot too. She ran out again. Splash! This time her feet stayed dry. "Dry feet, dry feet!" she shouted. Then she painted a picture of the rainy day.

Aubrey wanted the bunny book at daycare. But Ben had it first. Ben sat on the rug and held the book upside down.

"Can I read it too?" Aubrey asked.

"Okay," said Ben. "But I can't read the words yet."

Miss Jo came over. "I can read it," she said. She turned the book around. She opened the front cover first. Then she began.

"One little bunny hopped down the road," Miss Jo read.

Aubrey peeked at the page. She saw the little black words. Then Ben's big sister came in to help. She read the same book to them later.

"One little bunny hopped down the road," she read.

Aubrey sat up fast. "You said the same words!" she said. "The same as Miss Jo!"

The big sister smiled. "The words stay on the page," she said.

Aubrey turned to the next page. She pointed at the words. "Now say this part," she said.

So the big sister read it. Aubrey listened and looked. Then she held the book herself. She turned one page, then the next, all the way to the back.

"Again!" said Ben.

"The end," Aubrey read, pointing at the last page.

Avery went to the store with Dad. She wanted the big red apples by the window. She saw them right away.

Dad was talking to the fruit man. "Avery waited. But she wanted to talk so much. She pulled Dad's sleeve. Dad held up one finger. So Avery waited some more. The fruit man stopped talking. Then Dad said, "Yes, Avery?" She said, "Can we get apples?" Dad smiled. "Yes, we can."

At the meat counter, a man had a sharp knife. The man cut the ham. Dad kept Avery back a safe step. She watched the knife go up and down. The man gave Dad the ham. Then it was their turn. Avery said, "Thank you," all by herself.

In the checkout line, a phone rang. The lady at the register answered it. "Why is she talking on the phone?" Avery asked. Dad said, "Someone called her. We wait." So they waited. The lady finished, and she said, "Your turn now." Avery put the apples on the belt. They went round and round. Outside, the wind made the bags dance. Avery held Dad's hand all the way home.

Isaiah sat on the big couch. His dad sat next to him. Auntie May was there too. The TV showed a game with running people.

Isaiah pointed at the TV. "Who has the ball now?" he asked. He could not tell. All the people looked mixed up to him. He squeezed his dad's arm.

"Look at the shirts," Dad said. "One team wears red. One team wears blue." Isaiah looked hard. A red shirt spun around with the ball. A blue shirt ran after him. Now Isaiah could see them apart. "Red has it!" he shouted. His smile grew wide.

Auntie May clapped. "Good eyes, Isaiah!" she said. Isaiah watched the red shirts and blue shirts run up and down. He lost a tooth last week, and he showed everyone his new gap when he laughed.

Then a blue shirt took the ball and kicked it far. The net moved. Everyone jumped up. Isaiah jumped too, right on the soft rug. Dad caught his hand so he would not fall.

"Red can still score," said Dad. Isaiah sat close to him. He knew just who to watch now. "Go red team!" he called.

Max sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to play the senses game. Grandma said, "Ears hear. What do ears hear?"

Just then a big truck went by. It rumbled loud. Max put his hands over his ears. The rumble got quieter. He took his hands off. The rumble got loud again. He put his hands back on. Quiet again.

"Grandma!" said Max. "My hands make it quiet!"

Grandma smiled. "Yes, your ears were covered. Can your nose cover too?"

Max shook his head. "Noses smell," he said. "My nose smells your cookies!" His tummy felt happy.

Grandma put a warm cookie on his plate. Max looked at it with his eyes. "Eyes see the cookie," he said. Then he touched the plate. It was smooth. "Hands feel it!"

He took a little bite. "Tongue tastes it! That's all five!"

Grandma clapped. "You didn't miss one."

Max felt brave and proud. "Tomorrow can we play again?" he asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "And maybe next time, the ocean sounds on my radio."

Max giggled and covered his ears, then peeked out with a smile.

Jacob sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. The doctor smiled at him. "Let's check your eyes," she said. Jacob used his eyes to see a picture of a river on the wall. The water looked blue and cold.

"Now your ears." Jacob used his ears to hear the doctor's bell. Ding! Then she looked in his nose. "Sniff like a puppy," she said. Jacob sniffed. Then he opened his mouth, and she peeked at his tongue.

At home, Jacob played with his blocks. He sniffed the air. "Soup!" he said. "I smell soup!" He ran to the kitchen. There it was, bubbling on the stove, where Dad stood. "You smelled it before you saw it," said Dad. Jacob laughed. "My nose remembers soup." Dad gave him a soft piece of bread. Jacob touched it with his fingers. It was warm. "I will get you a blanket," Dad said, "because you look tired and a little weak." Jacob ate his bread and smiled. "Good nose," he said to himself, and he patted his own nose.

Ali sat on the big back step. Mom sat next to him with a bundle. Inside was his new baby sister. Her name was Nia. Ali wanted to pat her head. He patted her, but too hard. Nia's face scrunched up. She began to cry. Ali felt like he might lose his happy day.

Mom took Ali's hand. "Try like this," she said. She moved his hand slow and soft. Ali stroked Nia's tiny fingers. He used one finger, very gently. Nia stopped crying. Her eyes found Ali's face.

Mom smiled. "She likes that," Mom said. Ali stroked again, soft as a feather. Nia's little hand wrapped around his finger. Ali grinned. "She is holding me," he said. Mom kissed the top of his head.

Arya went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about ducks. The duck books were not on their shelf. "Hmm," said Arya. "Where did they go?"

She saw a sign with a big 5 on it. Arya held up her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. The sign said five too. "The five on the sign is my five!" she said. Her dad laughed. "You found it," he said.

Arya counted her steps to the room with the 5. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven," she said. She walked in. There were the duck books on the top shelf. A boy was singing a counting song. "Five little ducks went out one day," he sang. Arya sang along. She picked a duck book and let dad carry it. "Ten little duck toes," said Arya. "Salty duck feet?" said Dad. "No, silly," said Arya. "Ducks are not salty."

Ivy walked home with Dad. She held the little box with two hands. Inside was her new puppy, Pip.

Pip had a soft collar. Ivy did not like it. "It is ugly," she said. The collar was old and gray. Dad smiled. "We can get a new one at the shop." At the shop, Ivy picked a red collar. Then Dad showed her a small tag. Ivy held the tag in her hand. It had words on it. It had their phone number too.

"Why the number?" Ivy asked. Dad said, "Put it on and see." So they did. The tag went click on the red collar.

The next day, Pip wriggled out the door. He ran down the street! Ivy called and called. Then a kind woman walked up with Pip in her arms. "I saw the tag," she said. "I called the number. It is your puppy!" Ivy hugged Pip tight. She patted the little tag. It went click, click on the red collar.

Rosalie stood by the big blue pool. Her swim team was called the Little Fish. She put on her flat pink flippers. The water smelled like sunshine and chlorine.

Coach Dana blew her whistle. "Fish, line up on the wall!" All the kids found a spot. But Rosalie did not know where to stand. She stood in the middle, all alone.

"Rosalie, come stand next to me," said Coach Dana. She pointed to the wall. Rosalie walked over and put her hand on the warm tiles. "Now kick like this," said Coach Dana. She splashed her legs in the light water. Rosalie kicked too. Splish, splash! Her feet made white bubbles.

"Look at that!" said Rosalie. "You kick, and you go forward!" Coach Dana clapped her hands. "Kick, kick, kick!" said Coach Dana. Rosalie kicked all the way to the rope.

"Did you see me swim?" Rosalie called to her mom. Mom waved from her chair. Rosalie turned around and kicked back to the wall. The water went swish, swish, swish behind her.

Riley held the little dog's leash. The vet smiled and said, "His name is Biscuit." Riley wanted to give Biscuit a treat right away. She dug in her pocket. She found her chocolate coin. "Here, Biscuit," she said.

The vet shook her head. "Not that one. Chocolate can make dogs very sick." She handed Riley a small dog treat instead. "Try this." Riley held it out flat on her hand. Biscuit sniffed it. He sniffed it again. Riley waited. She waited some more, watching the cloudy sky out the window.

At last Biscuit took the treat. His tail wagged and wagged. "Good boy," said Riley. In the corner, a green snake sat in a glass tank. Riley waved at it too. Then she and Biscuit walked home together, one slow step at a time.

Anthony sat in the car. "We will meet Miss Kim today," said Mom. "She cuts hair." Anthony held his hat down tight. "Scissors are sharp," he said. "Will they hurt my head?" "Let's go and see," said Mom.

At the salon, Anthony sat in a big chair. It went up and up. Miss Kim picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. Anthony squeezed his eyes shut. Then he waited. But he did not feel anything at all. He opened one eye. A little piece of hair fell down. It floated like a tiny feather. Snip, snip, more hair fell. Still no hurt! Anthony laughed.

"Look," said Miss Kim. She held up a mirror. Anthony saw a short, pretty haircut. "It tickles," he said. "Can we keep the hair?" Mom put some in her pocket. Then Anthony waved and ran to the car.

Jasmine ran to the playground with her toy rabbit. Her friend Mia was already there. Mia had a small teddy bear and a big toy pot.

"Let's play house," said Mia. Jasmine smiled big. "I will be the mama," said Jasmine. "No, I want to be the mama," said Mia. Both girls held their toys tight. Nobody moved. The house had no mama at all.

Then Jasmine had an idea. "You be the mama now," she said. "I can be the baby later." Mia nodded. "Okay! We can switch." Mia stirred leaves in the pot. She mixed them with a stick. "Time to eat, little rabbit," she said in a mama voice. Jasmine made her rabbit hop to the pot. "Yum, yum," said the rabbit.

Mia patted the teddy bear's head. "Sleep now, baby bear," she sang. The friendly sun went behind a cloud, like a blanket for the sky. "Switch time!" said Jasmine. Jasmine became the mama. She rocked the rabbit and sang a soft song. "My turn to mix the soup," she said. She stirred and stirred. "More, please," said Mia in a tiny baby voice. Jasmine gave her a leaf cookie. "All gone," said the baby.

Elena went to the park with Dad. She had a new juice box in the cooler. She wanted it cold. Dad opened the cooler. Then a big dog ran by, fast. Elena watched the dog. The cooler stayed open. The sun was hot. It shone right in.

Later Elena drank her juice. It was warm now. Warm, not cold. She made a sad face. "It got warm in the sun," she said. Dad nodded. "The lid was open."

They got one more juice box from home. Elena held it. It felt so cold in her hands. Dad put it in the cooler. Elena pushed the lid. Click. It was closed. She pulled it open. She pushed it shut again. Open, shut, open, shut.

"You can draw the lid on paper," said Dad. "What will you name your picture?" Elena smiled. "Cold juice." She sat down by the little tree. She waited. Slow waiting, then a sip. The juice was still cold. "Yum," said Elena, and she gave the lid one more click.

Emile sat at the little table at daycare. He was making a house from paper shapes. He had a red circle for the sun. He had a blue square for the house. He had a green triangle for the roof. But he needed a door. A door is a rectangle. He looked in the shape box. There was no rectangle left. "I wish I had a door," said Emile. Then he saw a white square napkin. He picked it up. He folded it in half, edge to edge. He pressed it flat with his hand. He opened his fingers. The square was gone. Now he held a rectangle! "Look at my door," said Emile. He glued it on the house. Mia clapped. "A door," she said. Emile got another napkin. He folded it in half, edge to edge. Another rectangle! He made a mailbox too. Then he put on his shoe and went outside to play.

Billie went to the playground with Dad. The sun was warm on the slide. The metal slide felt hot under her hand, so she slid down fast and kept her hands up.

Near the fence, Billie saw a shiny can in the grass. She reached out. Dad came quickly and picked it up. "Not for little hands," he said. He put it in the bin. Billie waved bye-bye to the can.

Then Billie saw the big red ball. It rolled far, far away. It went past the trees to the far end of the playground. Billie ran after it. She ran and ran. Then she stopped. She looked back. She could not see Dad. The trees were big. Dad was not there.

Billie stood very still. Then she walked back the way she came. She walked past the trees. She walked past the swings. And there was Dad, waving by the slide. Billie ran to him and held his hand. Dad gave her the red ball. It had rolled all the way back, lazy and slow, in the wind.

"Again!" said Billie.

Matteo sat in his car seat. He wanted to count the red cars going by. "One, two, four," he said.

His big sister Rosa turned around. "Try again," she said. "Say it with me."

They said it together, slow and loud. "One, two, three, four, five."

A red car zoomed past. "Six, seven!" shouted Matteo.

"Good counting," said Rosa. "Keep going. The words stay in the same line."

Matteo watched the road. A truck. A bus. Three red cars! "Eight, nine, ten!" he yelled.

Mama laughed from the front seat. "Ten red cars! What a big day."

"Now count the blue ones," said Rosa.

Matteo looked out the window. He took a big breath. "One, two, three!"

Eloise sat with her dad in the big stadium. Her cousin Mia sat on the other side. The green field below was clean and bright. The players ran and ran after one ball. Eloise pointed. "That team is blue. That team is red. My favorite shirt is red too," she said.

Then a loud sound came. Tweet! Tweet! All the players stopped running. They stood still. Eloise tugged her dad's sleeve. "Why did they stop?" she asked. Mia cupped her hands by her ears. "The whistle did it," she said. Eloise watched the man in black. He put the small whistle to his mouth again. Tweet! The players stopped once more.

Eloise counted on her fingers. "One whistle, they stop. One nod, they go," she said. The game began again. The crowd clapped and roared. Eloise clapped too. "Maybe I will blow a whistle one day," she said. Mia laughed and held her hand.

Declan wanted to wash his hands all by himself. He stood at the sink and looked up. The faucet was high, high up. "Can I do it, Mama?" he asked. "I will stay right here with you," said Mama.

Mama turned the faucet. First came cold water. Declan touched the stream. Brrr, it was cold like ice! Then Mama turned it a tiny bit the other way. The water got warm. Declan felt the warm water on his hands. One turn made cold. Another turn made warm. How did that happen? He turned his head to see the pipes.

Then he saw something on the wall. It was a small white face with two little holes. It looked shy, hiding near the sink. What was it? Declan pointed at it. "Mama, what is that?"

"That is an outlet," said Mama. "Fingers never go in there. Only plugs go in." Declan looked at his wet fingers. He kept them far, far away. He put them in the warm water instead.

"I build with my fingers," said Declan. "And I paint with my fingers too."

"Yes," said Mama. "So we keep them safe." She gave him a soft towel. Declan dried each finger, one by one. Then he waved at the little white face on the wall.

"Bye bye, outlet," he said.

Wyatt was at the grocery store with Mom. The big doors opened. Cold air rushed in. Wyatt bounced on his toes. Brrr!

"Time for your coat," said Mom. Wyatt wanted to do it himself. He pushed one arm in. Wrong hole! He tried again. Yes! Arm one, arm two. Now the zipper. He pulled it up, up, up. It stuck. He tugged hard. Zip! It went all the way to his chin.

"I did it!" said Wyatt. The cold air touched his cheeks. But his body stayed warm inside the coat. He felt like a cozy feather.

Outside, snowflakes started to fall. Wyatt ran to the window. "Look, Mom! Snow!" His zipper was still up. His coat was still warm. "Zip me again tomorrow!" he said.

Maeve went to the big field with Mama and Pop. There were many people there. They all sat on a blanket in the grass. Maeve could see two nets, one at each end.

A big game started. People ran and kicked a ball. Maeve watched the ball go up high. She thought the ball had to go over the net. "Up, up!" she said. She pointed at the sky.

Then a player kicked the ball low. It rolled on the grass. It went right into the net. The net moved and the ball stayed inside. Everyone clapped and cheered. Maeve jumped up. Her tummy felt funny and happy.

Later, Maeve skipped over to a small ball by the fence. She kicked it toward a cone. The ball rolled in behind the cone and stopped. "It went in!" said Maeve. Mama laughed and clapped too. "Again," said Maeve, and she ran to get her ball.

Michael ran to the cookie jar. Grandma had just put out warm cookies. Michael reached out his hand. Then he stopped.

He looked down at his fingers. They had dirt on them. He had planted seeds in the garden that morning.

Michael ran to the sink. He pushed the soap pump. The soap felt smooth and slippery. He rubbed his hands together. He counted slowly to twenty. "One, two, three," he said. Bubbles grew big and white. They smelled like lemons.

He rinsed the bubbles away. He dried his hands on the soft towel. Then he ran back to Grandma. He picked up a cookie and took a big bite.

Grandma smiled and gave him a second cookie. "Crunchy one for you," she said.

Michael looked at his clean pink fingers. He took another happy bite.

Madelyn went to the library in the morning. She wanted to make her very own counting book. One kitten, two shoes, three red apples, and more, all the way to ten.

She drew and drew. Then she got to the ten page. Ten needed a number, but Madelyn felt stuck. All the other numbers had one shape. She wrote a big 1. It did not look right all alone. Her tummy felt funny.

The librarian came close. "Can I help?" she asked. Madelyn showed her page. The librarian smiled and wrote on her own paper. Madelyn watched. First a 1, then a 0, side by side. Madelyn tried it. A 1 and then a 0. Ten! It looked just right.

Madelyn read her book out loud. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. The librarian clapped. Madelyn hugged her book. "Can we take it home?" she asked. "Yes," said Mommy. Madelyn smiled and held it tight.

Miles was four years old today. His family was at the park for his birthday. There was a big table with cake and juice. Balloons bobbed on the chairs.

A boy named Sam came over. Sam had curly hair and a red shirt. "How old are you?" Sam asked.

Miles looked at his hand. He held up three fingers. Sam counted them. "Three?" Sam said. Miles shook his head. That was not right. He thought hard.

Miles put one more finger up. Now he had four fingers in the air. "Four!" said Sam. "I am four too." Sam held up four fingers too. They both laughed. Two hands, four fingers each, side by side.

"Look, Mom," said Miles. "Four!" His mom smiled and gave him a glass of cold juice. It was sweet and cold on his tongue. Sam sat next to him on the bench. Dad lit the birthday candles, way over at the grill table, and everyone sang.

Miles blew out the candles with one big breath. Smoke curled up like a little ribbon. Sam clapped. "Happy birthday, Miles," he said. Miles grinned and held up four fingers one more time.

Sadie sat in her car seat. She had a little bag of crackers. "Crackers, please," said her brother, Ben. Sadie did not know what to say. Then she said, "Yes, please wait." She gave Ben a cracker, slowly, one at a time.

Ben ate the cracker. "Thank you, Sadie," he said. Sadie was quiet. What could she say back? She looked out the window. She saw a cow by a fence. She heard the cow go moo. Then she heard Mom say, "You're welcome, Ben." Mom had given Ben a puzzle book. Ben had said thank you to Mom first.

Sadie saw it. Someone says thank you. Then someone says you're welcome. The words went back and forth, like a ball. Ben held out his hand. "Another cracker, please?" he asked. Sadie gave him one. "Thank you, Sadie," said Ben. "You're welcome," said Sadie. Mom smiled in the mirror. "Cool words," said Sadie, and she read the cover of Ben's puzzle book all the way home.

Charlotte went to the store with Mama. She held the shopping bag with both hands. Charlotte wanted a new crayon. She wanted to draw the sky.

First she found the crayon bin. She saw a red crayon. Red like a big apple. She saw a yellow crayon. Yellow like the sun. She saw a green crayon. Green like the grass. Then she found a gray crayon. "This one is for the sky," Charlotte said.

Mama needed a hot pizza for dinner. The store lady used big gloves. She put the hot pizza in a box. Mama carried the box, because it was hot. Charlotte did not touch it.

Charlotte held her gray crayon. Then she looked out the big window. The sun was out. It was a clear, sunny day. The sky was not gray. The sky was blue! Charlotte put the gray crayon back. She took a blue crayon instead.

At home, Charlotte sat at the little table. Mama opened the pizza box. The pizza was still hot, so Mama cut it into small pieces. Charlotte waited, then took a bite. Then she tried to draw her picture. Blue went on top, all across the sky. Green went on the bottom, for the grass. Yellow went in the corner, for the sun.

"Look, Mama," said Charlotte. "Blue sky, sunny day."

Snack time was coming. Ruby wanted to set the big table. Her teacher, Miss Ana, gave her a basket of cups.

"Count them," said Miss Ana. Ruby touched each cup. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." Eight cups. Then she counted the chairs. Eight chairs.

"Which has more?" Miss Ana asked. Ruby looked and looked. The cups were in a jumble. The chairs were in a row. She could not tell. "I don't know," she said. "How can I find out?"

Then Ruby had an idea. She put one cup in front of one chair. One cup, one chair. She went all the way around the table. One cup, one chair. One cup, one chair. Her friend Ben watched and handed her a shiny spoon for each cup, too.

At the last chair, Ruby put down the last cup. Her basket was empty. Every chair had a cup. Every cup had a chair. Nothing was left over. "They match!" said Ruby. "Same number!"

Ben picked up his cup and took a big drink of water. "Good counting, Ruby," he said. Ruby lifted her cup, and it went click against Ben's, like a little cheer.

Lea packed her little red bag. "We are going to the beach!" she sang. The car ride was long. Lea counted three cows, then five cows, then she fell asleep.

At the beach, the water went splash, splash, splash. Lea found a shell with a hole in it. "Dad, take my picture!" she said. Dad held the camera. Click! "Now hold the shell up," said Dad. Click! Click!

Mom took a photo of the sand castle. Lea put seaweed on top. "It has hair!" she laughed. Mom laughed too. Click!

Then it was time to go home. The beach was far away now. Lea missed the waves. She missed the splash, splash, splash.

"Look," said Mom. She opened the photos on the big chair. There was Lea with her shell! There was the castle with seaweed hair! There was Dad with sand on his nose.

"Grandpa wants to see the beach too," said Dad.

"Then he can look at my pictures!" said Lea. "Click!"

Nolan ran to the garden with his small red watering can. "Can I plant lettuce today?" he asked. His grandma smiled. "Yes, we can plant it together." They patted the smooth brown dirt. Nolan dropped tiny seeds into the hole. He covered them up, pat, pat, pat. Then he gave them a drink of water.

Every day Nolan came back. The sun was hot. The lettuce grew small and green. But one morning the leaves were drooping. They hung down low. "Are you sleepy?" Nolan asked. He touched a leaf. It felt soft and sad. "Maybe you need water!" he said.

Nolan filled his can at the pond nearby. He poured water all over the leaves. Drip, drip, drip. The next day the lettuce stood up tall. "Look, Grandma!" Nolan shouted. "It's not droopy anymore!" Grandma clapped her hands. Nolan watered the plants every single day after that.

Lucy woke up and saw white outside. No school today! It was a snow day. She put on her red hat and her warm boots. Then she ran to the sledding hill with Dad.

Lucy went down the hill on her sled. Whee! She rolled off into the soft snow. A little leaf was stuck to her mitten. That was funny. Lucy wanted to keep some snow too. She made a small snowball. She put it in her pocket and zipped it up tight, like a lock.

At home, Lucy reached into her pocket. She felt something wet. The snowball was gone! There was just a puddle in her pocket. Lucy held up her wet mitten. "Dad, look! My snow turned into water!" Dad helped her hang the wet mitten by the fire. Lucy laughed and patted her pocket dry.

Athena went to Miss Kim's music room. Big drums sat in a circle. Athena picked a small red drum. Her friend Leo picked a blue one.

Outside the window the sky looked stormy. Big gray clouds moved by.

"Now we play together," said Miss Kim. Athena tapped fast. Leo tapped fast too. Their drums went boom-boom-boom. It was too fast. They bumped sticks and stopped.

"Why did we stop?" asked Athena.

"We did not go the same speed," said Leo.

Miss Kim clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. It was slow and even. Athena clapped too. Leo clapped too. Then they tapped their drums just like the claps. Tap, tap, tap. Slow and even. The two drums sounded like one big drum.

Then came the surprise. Athena tapped her drum, and Leo's drum made the same sound back. "It is like a picture in a mirror!" Athena said.

"Thank you, Miss Kim," Athena said. She tapped some more, slow and even, all the way to the end.

Theodore went to the farmers' market with Dad. He held the basket with both hands. They needed eggs, milk and butter. Theodore picked the eggs one by one. He did not let them knock together. "Good job," said Dad.

At home, Theodore had big news. "I will bake Papa's birthday cake!" he said. Dad helped him crack the eggs. Theodore poured in the milk. He stirred and stirred. The batter was thin and runny. It went slosh in the bowl.

Theodore looked worried. "This is not a cake," he said. "It is just wet soup. Papa will have birthday soup." He stuck his finger in the bowl. The batter dripped off, drip drip drip. "A cake is big and round. This is not round at all!"

Dad poured the batter into a pan. He put the pan in the hot oven. Theodore watched from his stool, far away. The kitchen began to smell sweet. Theodore waited and waited.

Then Dad opened the oven. Out came a real cake! It was big and golden. Dad turned it out of the pan. Then he cut it, and each slice came out soft and neat. "Papa gets a lion on top," said Theodore. "With a frozen strawberry for its nose!"

Brielle ran into the sunny backyard. Daddy held up a big red hoop. "Throw the beanbag in!" he said.

Brielle had a yellow beanbag. She squeezed it. Then she saw her friend Milo at the fence. "Hi, Milo!" she called. She waved and threw the beanbag. It landed in the grass. It missed the hoop. "Oh no," said Brielle.

Daddy held the hoop up again. "One, two, three, throw!" This time Brielle looked at the hoop. She looked and looked. Then she let the beanbag go. It flew through the hoop. It hit the ground with a little sound, pat!

"I did it!" said Brielle. She jumped up and down. "Again! Again!" Daddy tossed her a big blue ball. "Catch it with both hands," he said. The wind began to blow. The ball wobbled in the air. Brielle held out both hands. She held on tight. She caught it!

Milo clapped at the fence. Brielle held the ball up high. "Look, Milo, I caught it!" she said.

Maverick sat at the little red table. He had one sheet of paper. He had one fat crayon. He drew a cat with a long tail. One cat, one tail, one happy smile.

Next to him, his friend Nina drew too. She made a cat as well. Her cat had a long tail too. Then the teacher said, "Put your papers on the big shelf." Maverick put his paper down. Nina put her paper down. Then two papers sat side by side. They looked the same.

"Which one is mine?" Maverick asked. He looked and looked. He could not tell. Nina could not tell either. Her lip began to wobble. Maverick wanted to help her. He was kind to his friend.

Then he had an idea. "I can write my name," he said. He picked up the crayon. M for Maverick. A for Maverick. He wrote it on his cat. "This one is mine!" The other one had to be Nina's. Nina hugged her paper. "Thank you, Maverick," she said.

"Now we both know," said Nina. She wrote her name too. One name, two names, two cats, two smiles. Maverick tapped his paper. "Hello, Maverick's cat," he said.

Layla ran to the toy corner fast. A little blue truck sat on the rug. She wanted it so much.

Ben grabbed the truck too. They pulled. The truck went back and forth. It nearly fell.

Layla let go. She looked at Teacher May. "We both need the truck," she said.

Teacher May smiled. "Let's take turns," she said. "Ben first. Then Layla."

Layla sat on the rug. She watched Ben drive the truck. It went zoom, zoom, zoom.

Then Teacher May said, "Layla's turn." Ben gave her the truck. Layla drove it to the block tower.

"My turn," said Ben. Layla gave the truck back. He drove it under the table.

Layla waited again. She clapped when Ben zoomed by. Soon it was her turn once more.

"Your turn is fast," said Layla. She pushed the truck all the way to the door. Ben laughed and held out his hands.

Claire stood at the front door. She wanted to play outside. But which clothes should she wear?

She looked out the window. The wind blew the big tree. Leaves flew all around. "It is windy today," said Mom. "Wear your jacket." Claire put on her jacket. The jacket flapped like a flag.

Then the sky grew dark. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. Puddles formed on the path. "It is rainy now," said Mom. "Where are your boots?" Claire found her yellow boots. She stepped in a puddle. Splash! She sailed a leaf like a little boat on the water.

Next the rain turned to snow. White flakes fell on the grass. The snow did not melt. It stayed on the ground. "Snowy days need mittens," said Mom. Claire pulled on her red mittens.

At last the sun came out. It was sunny and bright. Claire ran to the swing. The sun shone in her eyes. She squinted and squeezed her eyes shut. She could not see her swing at all.

Mom came out with a hat. "Try this, Claire." Claire put on the sun hat. The hat shaded her face. Now she could open her eyes wide. She swung high and laughed.

"Best hat ever!" she said.

Theo went to the community center with his dad. There was a music room with small chairs. On a table lay some recorders.

Theo picked up a blue recorder. He wanted to play his favorite song, the duck song. He blew into the recorder. It made a loud squeak. Theo tried again. Squeak, squeak.

A girl named Maya sat next to him. She put her fingers flat on the holes. Then she blew. A nice low note came out. Theo looked at her fingers.

Theo pressed his finger on one hole. He blew. The sound was low. He lifted his finger off the hole. He blew again. The sound was high. Theo tried another hole. He got a new note.

Soon Theo played a tune. Maya clapped. Theo played some more. "Quack, quack," he sang, and the recorder went low, low.

Ibrahim went to the park with Mama. He brought his little blue car. It was his favorite toy. The grass was wet from last night's rain. The air smelled like winter was coming.

Ibrahim set his car on the bench. Then he ran to pet a small brown dog. When he came back, the car was gone. He looked at the bench seat. He looked at the ground by his shoes. No car anywhere.

"I will try one more spot," he said. He got down on his knees. He peeked under the bench. The blue car sat there in the shade. It had rolled off the seat and slid underneath. A tiny ladybug sat on top of it.

Ibrahim reached in and pulled the car out. The ladybug flew away on red wings. "Hello again," Ibrahim said to his car. He held it tight in both hands all the way home.

Leah sat on the big rug in the living room. She wanted to draw a red sun. "Where is the red?" she asked. Mom helped her hold the tablet and press the little button. The screen lit up. Leah tapped the drawing app with one finger. It opened!

At the bottom of the screen there were small round colours. Leah tapped the blue one. Her finger made a blue line. Then she tapped the red one. Her finger made a red line. "I tapped red, and now I draw red!" she said. She drew a big red sun with soft yellow rays. "Is the sun too hot?" she asked herself. "No, it is a paper sun. It cannot be hot at all."

Leah drew a green hill under the sun. She drew a small brown dog on the hill. When she was done, she looked at her picture. "All finished," she said. Mom showed her how to press the button once more. The screen went dark and quiet. "I will put it away now," Leah said. She carried the tablet with two hands. She set it in its safe spot on the shelf. Then she ran to tell Mom, "I turned it on, I drew a sun, and I put it away all by myself!"

Eva went to the library with Mama. She found a book with a bear on the front. The bear wore a red hat. Eva loved the pictures. "Who drew this bear?" she asked.

Mama said, "Let's look inside." Eva grabbed the book. She opened the front cover first. There was a page with names on it. Mama pointed to one name. "That name is the artist," Mama said. "An illustrator made these pictures." Eva put her finger on the name. "The illustrator made my bear," she said.

Eva turned the pages one by one. The story went from the first page to the last page. The bear found his red hat at the very end. "Again!" said Eva. Mama laughed and turned back to the front. Eva hugged the book tight and whispered, "Hello, bear."
