David stood at the big table in the cooking classroom. He was making muffins for his family. He stirred the batter round and round. His teacher, Miss Ana, put the pan in the oven. She turned a little knob. "Now we set the timer," she said.

The timer ticked and ticked. David drew a fox on paper while he waited. Then he and his dad began to play a game with red cards. David got busy matching the cards. He forgot all about the muffins.

Beep! Beep! The timer rang out loud. David jumped up. "The muffins!" he said. Miss Ana put on big mitts and took out the pan. The muffins were round and golden. "Smell them," said Dad. David sniffed. They smelled sweet. "The timer told us," said David, and he clapped his hands.

Florence sat in a big chair by the window. Mom held a tiny baby in her arms. "This is your new sister," Mom said. Florence looked and looked. The baby was small like a little mouse. Florence wanted to hold her. "Not yet," said Dad. "She is too tiny." Florence's face felt hot. "No fair," she said. "Everyone looks at the baby. No one looks at me." She hid behind the curtain. The curtain was soft and cool.

Mom called, "Florence, come here." Florence came slowly. Mom patted the chair. "Sit close to me." Florence sat. Mom gave her a kiss. "You can miss me. That is okay. I still love you big." Dad got paper. Florence began to draw. She drew the baby. She drew Mom. She drew herself. The wrong color went on the baby's face. Florence laughed. "She is green!" Mom laughed too. Florence drew one more picture. "This one is for the baby," she said.

Ali ran into the big kitchen. "I want to help!" he said. Miss Rosa smiled. "Wash your hands," she said. "Then you can make toast." Ali washed his hands. The toast was ready. Miss Rosa had made it on the hot stove. Now it sat on the cool table. Ali held the butter knife. He spread the butter. Slow, slow, slow. The butter went soft and smooth. "Look at my toast!" he said. "So smooth!" "Very nice," said Miss Rosa. "You are a cute little helper. Now pour some milk." Ali got the little jug of milk. He poured and poured. The cup filled up to the very top. Ali picked up the cup. He took one step. Milk spilled over the edge. It ran down his hand and onto the floor. Ali got a cloth. He wiped the spill. Then he poured again. This time he stopped before the cup was full to the top. Ali picked up the cup. He walked across the kitchen. Not one drop spilled! Outside the window, snow was starting to fall. "Look, Ali!" said Miss Rosa. Ali sat down with his toast and his milk. He took a big bite and a big sip. "Mmm," he said. "I did it all by myself."

Leah saw a big cardboard box at school. She wanted it to be a house. She put her teddy bear inside. "This is teddy's house," she said.

Then Ben came. He wanted the box too. "It's a car," said Ben. "Beep beep!" Leah held the box hard. Ben pulled the other side. Teddy fell out. His hat fell in the bucket of toys.

Miss Rosa came over. "You can take turns," she said. Ben went first. He drove the box car around the rug. Leah waited. She picked up teddy and his hat.

Then it was Leah's turn. The same box became a house again! She tucked teddy in with a small blanket. Ben knocked on the wall. "May teddy come out to play?" he asked. Leah smiled. "Yes! Bring your car. Teddy needs a ride."

Isabelle held Mama's hand at the cultural center. It was a big Lunar New Year party. There were red lanterns and paper flowers everywhere. Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! Boom! Isabelle covered her ears. "Too loud!" she said. She hid behind Mama's coat. "Will the loud noise hurt me?" she asked. "No," said Mama. "Just listen. Watch the lion." Isabelle peeked out. The big lion dance was starting. The drums went boom, and the lion jumped. The drums went boom again, and the lion shook its head. Isabelle watched and watched. "The lion jumps when the drum goes boom!" she said. Mama smiled and nodded. Isabelle let go of her ears. She clapped along with the drums. The lion jumped and spun. Isabelle laughed and clapped louder. "It is not a rainy day," said Mama, "so we can stay outside as long as we like." After the party, Mama said, "Then we will go home, and I will bathe you in warm, soapy water." Isabelle clapped her hands one more time. "Boom!" she said.

Nova was at daycare. It was show and tell day. She had a small toy tooth from her dentist kit. She wanted to show it to everyone. But her tummy felt jumpy. She felt afraid to talk in front of the class. Her hands hid the tooth behind her back.

Then Nova saw her teacher, Miss Kim. Miss Kim's hands were shaking too. "I always feel nervous on show and tell day," Miss Kim said. Nova looked up. Grown-ups feel like this too? That made her feel less alone. Miss Kim took a big breath. So Nova took a big breath too. Miss Kim smiled. Nova smiled.

Nova walked to the front. She held up the tooth. "This is a tooth," she said. Her voice was small but it stayed strong. The class clapped. Nova felt a big, warm, happy feeling. Miss Kim clapped loudest of all.

Everly was at Grandma's house. Baby Jack was sleeping in a soft basket. Everly wanted to give him a present.

She found a cracker in her pocket. It was a good cracker. She held it out to the baby. "Jack, look! A cracker for you!"

Jack woke up. He opened his tiny mouth. He made a little cry. Everly put the cracker close, but Grandma came over fast. "Babies can't eat crackers yet," Grandma said. "Baby Jack only drinks milk."

Everly looked at the cracker. Then she looked at Jack. He was still crying. His tummy was rumbling loud.

Everly followed Grandma to the table. Grandma picked up a small bottle. The milk inside was warm, not hot. Grandma held the bottle, and Jack grabbed it with both tiny hands. He drank and drank. His eyes got sleepy and cool and calm. The crying stopped.

"More milk?" Everly asked.

"Maybe later," Grandma said.

Everly sat down beside the basket. She ate her cracker, bite by bite. Jack watched her with big eyes. "When you are big," Everly said, "I will give you one."

Jack made a small milk smile.

"Shh," said Everly. "Sleep now, Jack."

Violet zipped up her red coat. Dad held her hand. They walked to the playground.

Violet wanted to go on the swing. But a big kid was on it. "Can I have a turn, please?" asked Violet. The big kid slid down. "Thank you!" said Violet. She pumped her legs. The swing went high.

Then a boy came by. He had a truck. He hid behind his dad. He peeked out at Violet. Violet smiled. "Hello!" she said. The boy peeked out more. "Hello," he said back, very small. Then he rolled his truck to her feet.

"I can push it to you," said Violet. She pushed too hard. The truck bumped his toe. "Sorry," said Violet. "It's okay," said the boy.

Dad called, "Snack time!" Violet held the boy's hand. They ran to the bench together.

Mason wanted his toy lion. It was up on a big shelf. He reached and reached. His fingers could not touch it.

He tried to shake the shelf a little. The lion did not move. Mom came into the room. "Mason, what do you need?" she asked.

Mason said, "Help, please." Mom smiled. "May I have the lion?" Mason asked. Mom said, "Yes, you may." She took the lion down and put it in his hands.

"Thank you," said Mason. He hugged the lion tight. Then his sister Mia walked in. She looked at the lion. She wanted a turn too.

"May I have a turn?" Mia asked. Mason thought for a minute. Then he said, "Yes, you may." Mia held the lion gently. She made it roar, "Roar!" Mason laughed.

Later Mason bumped into Mia's tower of blocks. The blocks fell down. "Sorry," said Mason. Mia patted his arm. "It is okay," she said. They built the tower again, tall and strong.

Mom brought two cups of milk. "Thank you," said Mason and Mia together. Mom sat on the couch with them. The lion sat on Mason's lap, all warm and safe.

Weston ran to the dress-up corner at daycare. He wanted to be a firefighter today. But the dress-up box looked all mixed up. There was a truck on top. There was a banana toy under a hat. His friend Pip had already taken the red firefighter coat.

Weston found one red sock. He put the sock in the toy bin. Then he laughed. A sock was not a toy. A sock was a hat for your foot. He moved the sock to the pile of shirts and hats. Shirts, socks and hats all went together. Now the pile looked neat.

Miss Joy came over to help. "You made a sorting place," she said. Weston put the truck with the toys. He put the play bananas and apples with the foods. The dress-up box was easy to open now. Pip hung the red coat on a hook, but the hat shelf was empty.

Weston looked and looked. Where was a firefighter hat? He felt worried. Then he saw something sticky on the shape table. It was a triangle hat made of paper! Miss Joy had made it just for him. Weston put it on his head. "I am the firefighter!" he said. Pip handed him a toy hose.

Willow sat in the car with her teddy bear. She was going to the dentist for the first time. "Open wide," she said to teddy. Teddy did not open. "You try it," said Mom. Willow opened her own mouth wide. "Very good," said Mom.

At the dentist's office there was a big chair. Willow was scared of the big chair. She held her teddy tight. "You can sit on my lap," said Mom. So Willow sat with Mom, and the chair went up with them too.

Then the chair began to tip back. It leaned and leaned, like a slow ride. Willow giggled. She was lying down, and teddy sat on her tummy. "I fall back like a leaf," she laughed. The dentist looked in her mouth. "Smart girl," said the dentist. "Open wide." And Willow opened wide, just like she had practiced.

Sienna sat on the train with Mama and Papa. She was going on a family trip, far from home. "One bag, one bear, one hat," she counted. "One little Sienna!" said Papa with a smile.

After the train, they got in the car. Papa drove and drove. "Oh dear," said Papa. "I do not know this road." He stopped the car. The windows were down, and the air smelled fresh like grass.

Sienna looked at her book. It was not a storybook. It had lines and little pictures. Roads and towns and rivers. It was a map. She put her finger on a line. "Our train went here," she said. Then she slid her finger along. "And the road goes this way!"

Papa leaned over and looked. "You found it, Sienna!" He drove where her finger pointed. One bend, two bends, three. Then a small white house appeared. A cow stood by the fence. It mooed at them.

Grandma opened the door. "My sweet friend!" she said, hugging Sienna. Inside, there was ice cream in little bowls. Sienna ate hers slowly and watched it melt. "The map got us here," she whispered to her bear. "All the way here."

Aaron was at Grandma's house. He wanted his favorite book. But which one was it? Grandma had so many books on the shelf.

"Can you find the one that is yours?" Grandma asked. Aaron looked and looked. Then he saw something. His school bag sat by the door. It had a little card on it. The card said AARON. Grandma handed him a birthday card. It said AARON too.

"Look, Grandma, it is the same!" Aaron said. The letters were the same. The letters were in the same order. He traced them with his finger. A, A, R, O, N. Then he traced them again on his bag. A, A, R, O, N.

"Now hurry," said Grandma. "Find a book with your name." Aaron picked up a big book. He opened the front cover. There it was. AARON, written right inside. "This one is mine!" he said. "It is my favorite book!"

He sat on Grandma's soft lap. Grandma turned the pages one by one, front to back. "My name, then the story," Aaron said. He snuggled close. Grandma read to him until bedtime.

Joshua sat at the picnic table. Summer camp was loud today. Birds sang high in the trees. His sun hat sat next to his paper. He was painting a big park.

He painted a slide. He painted a blue sky. Then he wanted grass. He looked in his paint box. There was no green paint. He looked again. Only blue and yellow.

"I need green," he said. His friend Mia looked over. "Try mixing two colors," she said. Joshua put blue on his brush. He put yellow on top. He swirled them on the paper. The paint turned green!

Joshua clapped his hands. He painted green grass all along the bottom. He painted a green tree too. The teacher hung his picture on the fence. "Look at my park!" said Joshua.

Gabriella went to Mia's house to play. Mia had a big spotted doll named Bob. Bob had a cloth swimming pool on the floor.

Mia dropped Bob on the rug. Mia began to cry. "Bob fell! He is sad!"

Mia's mom came over. She picked up Bob. "Bob is fine," she said. "Dolls cannot really feel. But you can pretend he does."

Mia stopped crying. She gave Bob a hug. Then she kissed his soft spotted head.

Gabriella watched. Then she held up a toy duck. "My duck fell too," she said. She dropped the duck on purpose. Then she picked it up and hugged it. "All better, little duck."

The girls put bandages on all the toys. Bob got the biggest bandage. Then they laid the toys on a towel. "The toys swam all day," said Gabriella. "Now they need a nap."

Mia covered Bob with a small blanket. "Shh," she said. "Bob is sleeping."

Gabriella put her finger to her lips. "He is a sleepy spotted swimmer," she whispered.

Asher went to the store with Mama. He wanted apple juice. "Find the juice, Asher," said Mama. Asher looked and looked. The boxes were tall, tall, tall. He could not find any juice.

Then Asher saw little marks on a box. "Mama, what are these?" he asked. "Those are words," said Mama. "Words hide on boxes and tell us things." Asher looked at another box. "Words!" he said. Another box. "More words!" He counted them out loud. "One box, two boxes, three boxes, all full of words."

Mama pointed to a red box. "These words say apple juice." Asher hugged the box. It was soft and squishy on top. He carried it to the cart. At home, Mama opened a book. She read from the front page first. Asher turned the pages, one by one, all by himself. "Again!" he said.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Eleanor skipped around the backyard with him. They looked at the tiny ants on the step. "Where do they go?" she wondered.

On the second night, Grandpa took a bath. Then he called out, "Where are the towels?" Eleanor ran down the hall. She opened the tall cupboard. The towels were stacked in the middle, right where Mom always put them. She pulled one out and gave it to Grandpa. "Here you go!" she said.

The next morning, Grandpa wanted to wash his hands. "Where is the bathroom?" he asked. Eleanor laughed. She took his big hand and led him down the hall. "This door," she said. Grandpa smiled and patted his hands dry. Eleanor puffed up her chest like a proud little host. "I know where everything is," she whispered.

Cooper ran to the art room. He loved paint day. He sat down at the big table. His friend Mia put on her apron. Cooper did not put one on. He wanted to start right away.

Cooper dipped his brush in blue paint. He made a big swoosh. A dot of paint fell on his shirt. It was his favorite shirt. Another dot fell. Oh no. Blue spots everywhere.

The teacher brought Cooper an old shirt. "Put this on," she said. Cooper put it over his favorite shirt. Then he painted a happy dog. Paint splashed on the old shirt. He looked down. His favorite shirt was still clean under it.

At the sink, Cooper washed his hands in the glass window's bright light. The room was noisy with happy painters. "Next time, apron first," Cooper said to Mia. He smiled and held up his painting for his mom.

Eliana sat on the soft rug in the living room. The big game was on TV. Grandpa sat in his big chair. Mom and Aunt Jo sat on the couch. Everyone was cheering.

"Who is winning?" Eliana asked. She could not remember the score. She asked again. "Who has more points?"

"Look up high," said Grandpa. He pointed to the TV.

Eliana looked. There it was. A big bright board at the top of the screen. It had numbers on it. One side had a red four. The other side had a blue six.

"Blue is winning!" Eliana said. She clapped her hands.

The blue team ran fast. They kicked the ball. The net moved. The crowd on TV got loud. The big board changed to a blue seven.

"It went up!" Eliana said. She pulled her teddy bear close and hugged it.

Later the buzzer went off. The game was over. The curtains were closed and the room felt cozy. Grandpa picked Eliana up.

"Who won?" he asked her.

"Blue," said Eliana. "I looked at the board."

Nolan went to Grandpa's house for a fun day. "We are going somewhere special," said Grandpa. "You get your first haircut!" Nolan patted his hair. "My hair is getting long," he said.

They walked to the salon. It was bright and shiny inside. There was a big chair that went up and down. Nolan jumped on. But he was too small. The hairdresser could not reach the top of his head. "Hmm," she said with a smile.

The hairdresser brought a booster seat. It was like the one at the playground, small and strong. She set it on the big chair. Nolan climbed up and sat on it. Now he was tall! "I can see the mirror," said Nolan. The hairdresser could reach all his hair now.

Snip, snip, snip. Little pieces of hair fell down. They landed on the clean white cape. Nolan watched each piece fall. He wiggled his toes. The booster seat held him just right.

Grandpa gave him a big thumbs up. Then the hairdresser brushed him off, and Nolan hopped down. "All done!" he said. "Look at my short, clean hair, Grandpa!" Grandpa laughed and took his hand.

Emile was at Grandma's house. It was time for lunch. Grandma set the big bowl on the table. She poured warm soup into the cups.

"Emile, would you like to say grace?" asked Grandma.

Emile looked at the soup. Emile looked at his shoes. He did not know what to say. He hid his face in his hat.

"That's okay," said Grandma. "Everyone holds hands. We say thank you."

Emile peeked out from the hat. Grandma held out her hand. Emile took it.

"Thank you for the soup," Emile said, very small.

"Yay!" said Grandma. She clapped.

Emile sat up tall. "Thank you for the soup!" he said again, very big.

Grandma laughed. "Now we eat."

Emile drank his warm soup. He was still holding the hat.

Raphael ran to the block corner at the community centre. The sun came in through the big window. His friend Mia was there too. They both grabbed blocks.

"I have more," said Mia. "No, I have more," said Raphael. He asked himself, how can we know? He looked at his blocks. He counted, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Mia counted hers. "One, two, three, four, five, six." But which pile was more? The piles looked the same.

Raphael had an idea. "Let's line them up," he said. He put his blocks in a row. Mia put hers in a row right across from his. One block faced one block. Then another faced another. At the end, Raphael had one block with no friend facing it. "My row is longer," said Raphael. "So I have one more."

Mia's lip began to melt into a sad face. Raphael counted his blocks again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." He picked up the last block, the one with no friend. "Here," he said. "Now we both have six." Then they built one big tower together. But it wobbled, and it fell. The tower was broken! They laughed and counted the fallen blocks all over again.

Kai sat at the art table. The sun felt warm, like summer coming in the window. He had red, blue, yellow and green paint. He wanted to make a traffic light for the toy cars.

But which color goes on top? Kai tapped the brush. He thought about walking to the park with Grandma. At the corner, the light turned red. The cars stopped. Then it turned green. The cars got to zip past.

"Red means stop," Kai said to himself. "Green means go." So he painted red on top. He painted green on the bottom. He painted yellow in the middle, just like the real one.

Then Mia drove a toy car across the table. Kai held up his paper. "Red!" he called. Mia stopped her car fast. "Green!" Kai said. The little car zipped down the table and around the paint cups. "Again!" said Mia. Kai smiled and turned his paper back to red.

"One more time," said Mia, "then a blue car too."

Asher sat in the big barber chair. It went up, up, up! "My first haircut!" he said. The barber, Mr. Sam, picked up his scissors. Snip, snip, snip.

Then Asher wiggled. He wiggled some more. "My neck itches!" he said. Tiny bits of cut hair sat on his neck. Mr. Sam got a soft brush. He brushed, brushed, brushed the hairs away. The itch was gone! Asher stopped wiggling. He sat very still.

Then Mr. Sam held up a mirror. Asher saw his new short hair. "I look big!" he said. He clapped his hands. He did not miss his long hair one bit. On the way out, Asher waved his hand. "Bye, Mr. Sam! Bye, big chair!" He was one happy boy with his nice new hair.

Sienna ran to the big dog. She patted his soft fur. "Hello, dog!" she said. The dog wagged his tail. His ears went up and down. Then Mom called, "Lunch time!"

Sienna looked at her hands. They had dog fur on them. Yucky hands. She ran to the sink. The sink was not far from the table. Mom turned on the water.

Sienna pumped the soap. "Bubbles!" she said. She rubbed her hands. Then she counted. "One, two, three, four, five." Mom counted too. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Sienna kept going. "Eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen." Her hands were slippery. "Sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty!"

Sienna looked at her hands. The fur was gone. The bubbles lifted away down the drain. Clean hands! Mom gave her a warm sandwich. Sienna took a bite. Then she held up her hand to high five Mom. A tiny bubble was still on her thumb. "Look, Mom! One bubble missed the drain!" said Sienna. Mom laughed. "That one wants to stay for lunch," said Mom. Sienna popped it with one finger.

Everett ran to the feely-bag game at daycare. Teacher Mia held up a big blue bag. "Put your hand in," she said. "Don't peek!"

Everett reached in. He felt something round. Something smooth. Something bouncy. "A ball!" he shouted. "A red ball!"

"Open your hand and look," said Teacher Mia. Everett pulled it out. It was a yellow ball! He laughed. His friend Poppy peeked in next. She felt something soft and small. "A green sock?" she asked. It was a white sock with a cute cat on it. Everyone giggled.

Then Teacher Mia pulled out paints. Everett dipped his brush. He painted a green ball for Poppy. He painted a blue sock for himself. He held them up high. "Look! My eyes know!"

Beatrice ran to the block corner. She wanted to build a big robot. There was one box of blocks left. Her friend Tom grabbed it first. Tom gave all the blocks to his friend Mia. Mia hugged the box to her chest. Beatrice had no blocks at all. She could not build her robot.

Beatrice stood very still. Then she had an idea. She held up her hands and showed five fingers. "Five for you," she said to Mia. "Five for Tom. Five for me." She counted out the blocks, one by one. Mia watched the pile grow on the floor. Tom watched too. Soon each friend had a small stack.

Then they all got to build. Mia made a tall tower. Tom made a robot with big arms. Beatrice made a nice robot with square feet. When Tom ran out of red blocks, Mia gave him two of hers. He smiled and waved a block at her like a little flag.

At circle time, the teacher rang the bell. Everyone sat down fast. Beatrice sat next to Mia and Tom. "Tomorrow, can we build together?" asked Mia. "Yes," said Beatrice. "A robot for three." Tom clapped his hands. "With square feet and big arms!"

Avery went to the store with Mama. She saw a big bin of apples. The apples were red and bright. Avery wanted an apple.

Another girl stood by the bin too. Avery reached out fast. Her hand bumped the girl's hand. The girl stepped back. Avery looked at her hand. Then she looked at the girl.

Avery put her hand down. "You can go first," she said. The girl took one apple. Then Avery took one apple. Mama smiled.

At the counter, Avery held her apple up. She grabbed at it, but the man did not hand it over. Avery remembered. She tried again. "Apple, please," she said. The man gave her the apple. "Apple, please," Avery said again. She hugged it.

The girl came back with her apple. "Want to sit?" she asked. Two chairs stood by the window. They each took one chair. They each ate one apple. Outside, the sun was warm and bright. "More apples next time," said Avery, and the girl laughed.

Mia was ready for bed. But her toy horse was missing. She looked under the bed. No horse. She looked in the toy box. No horse. Mia's face went hot. She stamped her foot. "My horse is gone!" she said. She felt angry.

Outside the window, soft snow was falling. Mama came in and sat down. "Let's take big slow breaths," said Mama. "Like this." Mama breathed in slowly. Mia breathed in slowly too. Then she let the breath out, slow and long. They did it again. Mia's tummy felt soft now. Her feet felt still. "Where could he be?" asked Mia. Mama said, "Look by the pillow." There was the horse, tucked under the blanket, all cozy.

Mia hugged him tight. She felt happy. Mama turned off the light. The snow kept falling outside. "Night-night, horse," whispered Mia.

Sarah sat at a big table in the restaurant. A big screen glowed on the wall. Mom and Dad and Uncle Ben were there too. Everyone was watching the game.

The red team ran with the ball. Sarah clapped her hands. "Go, go!" she shouted. The blue team scored a goal. Everyone at the table jumped up. They cheered and clapped for the blue team. Sarah looked around. She had clapped for the red team! She laughed and laughed. "Oops," she said. "I clapped for the wrong team."

Sarah watched the screen some more. Now the blue team ran fast. A player kicked the ball. It went in! Sarah jumped up with everyone. She clapped and cheered too. "Blue team!" she called. Uncle Ben gave her a high five. A waiter brought fries, and Sarah shared them with her cousin. "Sorry, I ate the big one," her cousin said. Sarah giggled and took the next one.

Grandma was coming on a plane. She would stay at Harrison's house for a whole week. Harrison packed his toy truck. He packed his big red ball. "Grandma can play with me," he said.

Dad drove them to the airport. They stood by the doors where people come off the plane. Harrison watched the doors very hard. A man came out. "Grandma!" cried Harrison. "No," said Dad. "Look again." A lady came out with a big coat. "Grandma!" cried Harrison. "Not yet," said Dad, and he laughed softly. "Keep watching." Then Harrison saw one shoe. Then two feet. Then a red bag. Then a face he knew. "Grandma!" Grandma opened her arms wide. Harrison ran to her. Her coat felt soft and smelled like flowers. "My big boy," said Grandma. "I heard you calling me."

At home, Grandma made tea. Dad held the hot cup. Harrison gave Grandma his red ball. She rolled it with her foot, back and forth, back and forth. "Again," said Harrison. "Again, again!" Grandma rolled the ball and laughed and laughed.

Benjamin ran to the playground. He wanted to find his friend Mia. He looked by the swings. He looked by the slide. Then he saw her in the sand. She was holding a toy farm with little cows.

Mia's mouth was turned down. Her eyebrows were scrunchy. Benjamin watched her face. She looked sad.

"What is wrong?" he asked.

"My cow is lost," said Mia. "It fell in the sand."

Benjamin dug in the sand with both hands. The sand was soft and cool. Then he felt something hard. It was the little cow!

Mia's mouth turned up into a big smile. She jumped up and down. "You found it!" she said.

Just then a big dog barked by the fence. It sounded scary. Mia hid behind Benjamin. Her eyes were wide.

Benjamin held her hand. The dog's owner called it away. The dog trotted off, wagging its tail.

"That dog is gone now," said Benjamin.

Mia laughed. She gave him a cow from the farm. "You keep this one," she said. "You are my best digger."

Benjamin put the cow in his pocket. Then they built a big red barn together in the sand.

Brielle sat in her reading nook with a big alphabet chart. She wanted to learn every letter. She pointed at A. "A says ahh," she said. She pointed at B. "B says buh." Then she got to a letter that looked like a stick and a loop. She did not know it. She felt mad and tossed her sock at the chart.

Her brother came in. "Try counting them," he said. Brielle pointed and counted. "One, two, three..." She went slowly. Some letters looked alike. She went back and tried again. She got all the way to the end. "Twenty-six!" she said. "There are twenty-six letters!"

She picked up her sock and put it away. Then she looked at the stick-and-loop letter again. "M," she read. "M says mmm, like mmmilk!" Her brother clapped. Brielle pointed to one more letter and smiled. "N. That one is next."

Kayden wanted to go to the library. "Is it library day?" he asked. Mom smiled. "Yes, it is today." Kayden jumped up and down. "Today means now?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Today is the day that is happening right now."

But first they had to wait. Mom had to wash the dishes. Kayden watched the water splash. He heard a plane fly over the house. It made a big sound in the sky. Then the plane was gone. "Later we go," said Mom. "After the dishes."

Kayden felt shy about waiting. He wanted to cry a little. Yesterday he had waited too. Yesterday, Grandma had read him a book. That was yesterday, not now. Mom finished the dishes. "Now we go!" she said.

At the library, Kayden picked three books. "Can we come again?" he asked. "Tomorrow," said Mom. "Tomorrow is after today." Kayden held her hand tight. They walked home with the books. "Tonight I will read them," he said. Mom laughed and kissed his head.

Sadie ran to the sink at summer camp. It was snack time. She wanted to wash her hands first. She turned the tap on. Then she stopped and waited.

Miss Jo came over. She put her own hand under the water. "Too hot right now," she said. She turned the tap a little. She put her hand under again. "Warm now. You can wash."

Sadie put her hands in the water. It felt warm and nice. She picked up the soap. She rubbed her hands together. Miss Jo sang a small song. Sadie sang too. The song was twenty seconds long. Bubbles ran down the sink.

Then the water went off. Sadie's hands were clean. She dried them on the soft towel. She sat down with her crackers. "All done," she said, and took a big bite.

Elizabeth was at the farm with Grandpa. The pigs needed to bathe in the warm sun. "Let's play a game," said Grandpa. "Tell me your five senses." Elizabeth held up one little finger. "One! I see with my eyes!" She saw a black cow. "Two! I hear with my ears!" She heard the cow say moo.

Grandpa pointed to a rose. "Now smell this one." Elizabeth sniffed with her nose. "Mmm, sweet!" Then she sniffed a mint leaf. "Ooh, tingly!" She sniffed Grandpa's boot. "P.U.! Stinky!" Grandpa laughed and laughed. "Three!" said Elizabeth. "I smell with my nose!"

She touched a soft bunny. "Four! I touch with my hands!" Then they shared apple slices. "Five! I taste with my mouth!" Grandpa held up a flower near Elizabeth's nose. "One more sniff?" Elizabeth took a big sniff. "Sweet, sweet, sweet!" she said. Grandpa clapped his hands.

Henry went to the hospital with Dad. Mom had a new baby. The baby was Henry's little sister. She was very small.

The baby began to cry. "Why is she crying?" Henry asked. Henry thought and thought. He remembered when sand got in his shoe. He could not say "ow." So he cried too. Maybe the baby could not talk yet. Maybe crying was her way of asking.

Henry tried one thing. He gave her a soft toy. The baby kept crying. Henry tried another thing. He held her little hand. The baby still cried. Then Mom picked her up. Mom gave the baby milk. The baby stopped crying. She made a small sound. She fell asleep.

"She was hungry," said Mom. "She told us by crying." Henry gave his sister a kiss on her head. She was so young and so small. "I will listen," Henry said. "Cry, and I will come."

Ryan went to summer camp. At camp, the man who ran the lunch table said it was time to eat. But first, every child had to wash their hands. Ryan ran to the little sink. He pumped the soap onto his palms. A teacher helped him count to twenty while he rubbed the soap around. Then he held his hands under the water. The soap slipped away down the drain. His hands did not feel slippery anymore. They felt clean.

After the toilet, Ryan washed again. He rubbed the soap and counted. Then he stopped too soon. His hands still felt slippery. Soap was still on them. Ryan put his hands back under the water. He watched the water take the soap off. Now his hands felt just right.

At lunch, Ryan passed the bread basket to a small girl who could not reach it. "Thank you," she said. "You're welcome," said Ryan. Then he picked up his sandwich with his clean hands. He took a big, happy bite.

Lucas sat at the kitchen table. He had a big new pencil. He wanted to write his name!

"First letter is L," said Mom. "One line down. One line across."

Lucas held the pencil tight. He made a big L. He made a u. He made a c. He made a s. "L-U-C-A-S," he said out loud. Soon he had five letters!

Then his lines got fat and fuzzy. His last S looked like a fat fuzzy worm. "Oh no," said Lucas. He tapped the pencil tip. It was dull.

Mom took the pencil. She turned it in the sharpener. Lucas watched from his chair.

The tip was pointy again! Lucas wrote his name once more. The letters were thin and beautiful. "Look, Mom! One, two, three, four, five letters!"

"Let's tell Dad this story at dinner," said Mom. Lucas grinned and wrote his name again.

Bennett ran to the park. He wanted to slide down the big slide. But the slide was very tall.

First he climbed up the little ladder. Up, up, up he went. His feet went straight up each step. At the top he sat down. Then he slid down, down, down. Fast like a rocket!

He ran to the small slide next. It was little and slow. Bennett giggled at that.

Then he saw something odd. A tiny ant was on the slide. It crawled up. Then it slid all the way down. The ant did it again.

"Look, ant," said Bennett. "You go up too!"

Bennett climbed up once more. He held his arms out wide. The sun felt hot on his hands. The slide felt cool and smooth.

"Wee!" he called. Down he went, right past the ant.

The little ant waved its legs, as if to say hello.

Addison played at Grandma's house. She built a tall tower of blocks. She sent one block sliding across the rug to Grandpa. Grandpa smiled and sent it back.

Then Grandma called, "Snack time!" Addison jumped up and ran to the kitchen. The blocks stayed on the floor. On the table were tasty apple slices. Grandpa gave one slice to Addison and one to Grandma. Everyone got the same.

After snack, Grandma held out a basket. "The blocks go here," she said. Addison looked at the rug. She had played with those blocks. Addison ran back to the playroom. She put the blocks in the basket, one by one. Her bottom wiggled as she bent down low. Grandpa carried the basket to the shelf. Grandma clapped her hands.

"More blocks tomorrow," said Grandpa. Addison gave him a big hug.

Weston wanted to find something blue in the backyard. He looked by the big tree. He found a light blue ball. "Is this blue?" he asked himself. It looked like the sky. He put the ball in his wagon.

Then he found a dark blue sock under the tree. "This is not blue," he said. "This is too dark!" The sock was almost like night. He held them side by side. Hmm. Both were blue. One was light blue. One was dark blue. "Two blues!" said Weston.

A noisy bird flew down. It pecked at the dark blue sock. Weston laughed. The bird picked it up and put it on the grass. Now Weston had a light blue ball and a dark blue sock, sitting in a row. He lined up his blues, light to dark, and patted them both. "My blues," he said.

Jackson sat at the kitchen table. Mom gave him a big pencil. "I will write my name," said Jackson.

He held the pencil in his fist. The J looked like a little hook. He began at the right side of the paper. He wrote J, then a, then c. Now he needed k. But there was no more room! The edge of the paper was right there. "Oh no," said Jackson. "I miss a spot for my k."

Mom slid the paper over. "Try starting at the left," she said. Jackson tapped the left side with his finger. Then he began there. J, a, c, k, s, o, n. It all fit!

Then the pencil made a surprise. A wet spoon had sat on the paper. Where Jackson wrote, the letters turned dark blue! Jackson laughed. "My name is blue!" he said. He opened the door and called, "Dad, come see!"

Grandma came to stay for a whole week! "One week," said Sienna. "Seven days!" She jumped up and down. Grandma had a big bag and an itchy red scarf.

"Today we make my bread," said Grandma. "My mama made it. Her mama made it too." Sienna stood on her chair by the counter. She poured the flour. "One, two, three cups!" she counted. Grandma mixed. Sienna patted the soft dough. It felt like a pillow. "Now it must rest," said Grandma. So they waited.

Then the dough was big and puffy! Grandma put the pan in the hot oven. Sienna watched from far away. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet. Dad drove his truck to get butter. The bread came out golden. Sienna took one bite. "It tastes like a hug!" she said. Grandma laughed. Then a small surprise: the very last slice had a happy bread smile on it, just for her.

Josephine was at Mia's house. Mia had a tablet. Josephine wanted to draw on it.

Mia's mom showed her how. "Push the round button with your finger," she said. Josephine pushed it. The screen lit up. Her push made the light come on!

"Now tap the little paint pot," said Mia. Josephine tapped it. The drawing app opened. She drew a thin blue line. Then she drew a big sun.

"I win," said Josephine. "I made a sun!"

Then the screen went black. Josephine's tummy felt tight. "Did I break it?" she asked.

"No," said Mia's mom. "It is just tired." She plugged the charger into the tablet. A small battery picture showed up on the screen.

"It needs to eat," said Mia.

Josephine watched the battery picture fill up a little. Then Mia's mom put the tablet on the shelf. "It rests while it charges," she said.

"When can we draw again?" asked Josephine.

"After snack time," said Mia's mom. "Then you can push the button yourself."

They ate apple slices at the table. Josephine looked at the shelf. The tablet sat still, with its thin white cord.

After snack, Josephine pushed the button with her finger. The screen lit up again.

"It came back," she said. "Hello, sun!"

Sophie sat at the dinner table. She wanted the bread, but it was far away. She reached and reached. The basket did not move.

"Papa, we went to the park tomorrow," said Sophie.

"Tomorrow?" asked Papa. He passed her the bread.

Sophie took a bite and thought. "No, not tomorrow," she said. "It already happened. It was yesterday. Yesterday we went to the park."

"Yes," said Mama. "And today we are eating dinner. Now the bread is in your hand."

"Tomorrow I want to go again," said Sophie. "Tomorrow is not here yet."

"That is a long wait," said Mama.

Sophie looked at her cup. She looked at the flower in the middle of the table. She had picked it on their walk, the last one in the yard.

"Can we have bread again tomorrow?" she asked.

"We can," said Papa. "Bread takes time. Mama will make it later tonight."

Sophie ate slowly. Tomorrow the park would come. Tomorrow the bread would come too.

"Now I will eat my peas," said Sophie.

Matteo held his grandma's hand. They walked into the big hall with soft seats. People were quiet there. A kind man in robes smiled at them. After the quiet time, everyone went to a long table. There were bowls of warm rice.

Grandma sat down next to Matteo. "Now we say itadakimasu," she said. "We say it before we eat. It gives thanks for the food." Matteo looked at the rice. He wanted to say it just right. He tried. "Ita... daki... moose!" A boy across the table giggled. Matteo's face felt warm.

Grandma said the word slowly, one part at a time. "Ee-ta-da-kee-mas." Matteo said it with her. Once. Twice. Three times. On the third try, his mouth got it. The whole table said itadakimasu together. Then everyone picked up their chopsticks and spoons.

Matteo took a bite of rice. It tasted good. He drew a picture after lunch with a crayon. He drew the bowl and grandma and the word in wobbly letters. A boy bumped his arm and said, "Nice picture." Matteo smiled. "Want to say it with me next time?" he asked.

Arlo went to the park today. Yesterday it had rained. Today the sun was out. The slide was still wet, so Arlo had to wait.

"I want to slide now," said Arlo.

"Not yet," said Grandma. "Later, when it is dry."

Arlo waited. He watched the sun shine on the slide. Soon the slide was dry. He grabbed the rail and climbed up. Down he went, fast and happy.

Grandma sat on a bench like a desk, with her book on her lap. "Tomorrow we can come back," she said.

"Tomorrow is soon," said Arlo.

"Do you know how long a week is?" asked Grandma. "We will come back for a whole week of visits."

Arlo held up one hand. He counted his fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." He ran out of fingers. He looked at his other hand. He counted on. "Six, seven."

"A week has seven days," said Arlo. He wiggled all seven fingers.

At home, Arlo drew seven suns on his paper, one for each park day. The last one he drew snowy, with tiny dots of white. "That day will be cold," he said.

"Maybe," said Grandma, smiling.

Arlo put the paper by his bed. "Now I sleep," he said. "Tomorrow, sun number one."

Grandma tucked him in and turned out the light.

Maverick wanted his own little garden. Grandma gave him three seeds and a small spot of soil. He patted the seeds down into the dirt. "Now grow," he said.

Every morning Maverick came to look. He saw dirt. He saw a worm. He saw an old piece of wood. He did not see a plant. "Where is my plant?" he asked. "Keep looking," said Grandma. The sun felt hot on his hat. Maverick slipped his hand into the cool soil to check the seeds. Still quiet. Still brown. He looked again the next day. And the next day. And the day after that.

Then one morning, something tiny and green stood up in the dirt. It was small as his finger. "Grandma! A sprout! A sprout came up!" Grandma knelt down beside him. "Yes," she said. "That is a sprout." Maverick smiled at the little green sprout. "Grow big," he whispered. He gave it a small drink of water from his cup.

Eliana went to the store with Grandma. She held Grandma's hand. "Stay close to me," said Grandma. Elian stayed close.

In the store there was a big soup pot. Steam came up from it. Eliana felt warm air on her face. "Hot," said Grandma. "We look with our eyes. We do not touch." Eliana looked and looked. One, two, three puffs of steam went up.

Eliana saw a small box on the floor. It said "matches" on it. She did not touch it. "Grandma, look," she said. Grandma picked it up. "Good girl. Matches and lighters are for grown-ups," said Grandma. She put the box in her pocket. Then they found a kind lady in a white coat. She was a doctor buying bread. "Hello, Eliana," she said. "Would you like a taste of jam?"

Eliana tasted apple jam. It was cold and sweet. "Yum," said Eliana. Grandma smiled. At the checkout, Eliana helped put apples on the belt. One apple, two apples, three apples. The lady said, "What a clean and helpful girl." Grandma held out her hand. Eliana took it. "Home we go," said Grandma. Eliana waved to the doctor. "Bye-bye, apple jam," said Eliana.

Lydia stood in the reading corner. She held something new in her hand. It was her very first library card. It had her name on it.

"I want that dinosaur book!" she shouted. She jumped up and clapped her hands.

Then Lydia looked around. A boy sat on a big pillow. He was reading. A grandma was reading too. Their eyes went up, up to her loud voice. Lydia put her hands over her mouth. Oops.

She walked on her tippy toes. She found the dinosaur book on the shelf. She carried it to the desk very carefully. The librarian smiled and scanned her new card. Beep!

"You can keep it for next week too," the librarian whispered.

Lydia whispered back, "Next week I will get the robot book." She hugged the dinosaur book tight. Then she sat on a small red cushion. She turned page one. "Rawr," she whispered, very, very quietly. The reading boy smiled at her.

Grayson walked on the nature trail with Mama. He held a small bag of things to touch. Inside were a feather, a pinecone, and a soft purple blanket.

"I will make a puzzle," Grayson said. He put the three things on a flat rock. "Which ones are soft? Which one is rough?" He touched the feather with his finger. Soft. He touched the blanket. Soft, too. Then he touched the pinecone. It poked him a little. Rough!

"My skin can tell," Grayson said. He put the feather and the blanket on one side of the rock. He put the pinecone all by itself on the other side. Then he touched the pinecone again. Still rough. He touched the blanket again. Still soft.

A butterfly landed near the purple blanket. Grayson watched it open and close its wings. He heard a bird call from a tree. He sniffed the pine air. Then he picked up the feather and tickled his own nose.

"That tickles!" he said, and he laughed all the way down the trail.

Emilia stood at the park gate. Today was a beautiful summer day. Yesterday it had rained, and the swings were wet. Now the swings were dry.

"Can I swing now?" Emilia asked.

"Yes, now," said Mom. "But later we go home for lunch."

Emilia pumped her legs. She went high, then low. The sun made her shadow grow tall on the ground.

"When is later?" she asked. "Is it now?"

Mom held up her phone. "See this little clock? It shows what time it is. When the short hand points to the twelve, it is lunch time."

Emilia looked at the little clock. The hand was not at the twelve yet. She slid down and ran to the sandbox.

"Not twelve yet," she said. "So I can dig now."

She filled her red bucket. She tipped it over. Out came a sand cake.

"Tomorrow we come back," said Mom.

"Tomorrow," said Emilia. She waved at the sandbox. "Bye, sand cake. Bye, park."

Hannah sat on the train with Mama. The train went clickety-clack, clickety-clack. Hannah looked out the window. A cow stood in a green field. Then a little pig ran by the fence. "I see a pig!" said Hannah. "Same pig again," said Mama, laughing, because the train went around a bend.

They were going to the beach. Hannah wanted to splash in the big water. The train stopped. Daddy carried the bag. Grandma held Hannah's hand. They walked down to the sand. It was warm and soft. Hannah could hear the waves. Splash, splash, splash.

Hannah ran toward the water. Grandma called, "Wait for me!" Hannah stopped. She stood very still. The water went swish over her toes. Grandma came and stood right beside her. Then Hannah jumped. Splash! The water flew up. It got Grandma's dress all wet. Hannah laughed and jumped again. Grandma laughed too.

Mama spread out a towel. Hannah made a sand hill. Then she took Grandma's hand and went back to the water. "One more jump," said Hannah. Grandma said, "Ready?" They jumped at the very same time. Splash!

Sofia went to the library with Dad. On the craft table there was paper. There were circles, squares, and rectangles. There was a picture of a sailboat with a triangle sail.

Sofia wanted to make a sailboat. "Where is a triangle?" she asked. Dad looked in the box. There was no triangle paper. There was only a square.

Dad picked up the scissors. "Watch," he said. He cut from one corner to the opposite corner. The square fell open. Now there were two triangles! Sofia clapped her hands. "Two! One for me!"

She took one triangle. A boy named Leo got the other one. Leo smiled big. Sofia glued her triangle on her boat. It looked just like the picture in the song book. "Row, row, row your boat," she sang. Her loose tooth wiggled when she sang. Leo sang too, and their two boats sat side by side on the table.

Weston wanted a book about animals. He looked at the library shelf. The shelf was full of books. So many books! He pulled one out. It was about trucks. He put it back.

"Where are the animal books?" he asked. Miss Ana, the librarian, smiled. "Come with me," she said. "The books live in groups." They walked past a shelf of toy books. Then they walked past a shelf of food books. "Apples," said Weston. "And bread!"

Then Weston saw it. A whole shelf of animal books. "Look, look!" he said. He picked a big one. A lion was on the cover. He sat down on the floor to look. His friend Milo came over.

"I want a truck book," said Milo. Weston stood up. He knew just where to look! He took Milo's hand. They walked back to the shelf. Weston found a truck book. It had a big red truck on the cover.

Milo hugged the book. "You found it!" he said. "Listen," said Weston. "Books sit with their friends." Then he opened his lion book. The lion gave a big ROAR. Weston jumped. Then he laughed and laughed.

Eleanor sat at the dinner table. She wanted her bedtime story now. "Can we read now, Mama?" she asked.

Mama said, "Now we eat dinner. The story comes later, after bath."

Eleanor looked at her plate. She took a small bite of rice. "Is it later now?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Mama. "Now is this moment. See? You are chewing right now."

Eleanor chewed. She watched Mama fold a napkin. The napkin went from bumpy to flat. "Now I drink," said Eleanor. She took a sip.

Papa said, "Yesterday we ate soup. Today we eat rice. Tomorrow we will eat pasta."

"I like pasta," said Eleanor. She ate more rice, one spoon at a time. She waited. She was brave about waiting.

At last the plate was empty. Bath came and went. Then Eleanor sat in her soft pajamas on the big bed.

"Now?" she asked.

Mama smiled. "Yes. Now is story time."

Eleanor snuggled close. "Read it now, all of it!"

Madeline went to the park with her daddy. She wanted to paint a card for Grandma. The card needed a pink flower. But Madeline had no pink paint.

She looked around the park. One, two, three colors! She saw red paint, blue paint, yellow paint, and green paint. No pink anywhere. "I want pink," said Madeline.

She sat at the little paint table. She pushed her swing high first, then she got to work. Madeline put red paint on her brush. She painted a red flower. "Too red," she said. Grandma wanted pink.

Then Madeline had an idea. She took the white paint. She stirred white into the red. Round and round went the brush. The red turned lighter. It turned pink! Madeline looked and looked. "Pink!" she shouted. She painted the flower pink, pink, pink.

She folded the card carefully. Then she ran to show daddy. "A pink flower for Grandma!" said Madeline. Daddy said, "Grandma will love it." Madeline smiled big. Then she pointed at the grass. "Green!" she said. "Blue sky! Yellow sun!" And she danced all the way home.

Rowan ran onto the basketball court. His shoes squeaked on the long, shiny floor. He was on a team this season. His sister sat with Mom on the bench. His team had five players. Five players, one ball.

Rowan got the ball. He threw it up. It hit the rim. It did not go in. He looked down at his shoes.

Then he heard voices. "Good try, Rowan!" his teammates called. "Try again!" They clapped for him. Rowan looked up. They were still clapping. "Can they cheer if I miss?" he asked his coach. "Watch and see," said the coach. The ball came back to Rowan. He threw it again. This time it went in. Swish. His teammates cheered even louder. His sister jumped up and down. After the game, Rowan waved to his team. "Same time next week?" he asked. "Same time," they said.

Penelope wanted to make pancakes for her family. Dad said, "We need the recipe." The recipe hung on the fridge door on a big card.

Penelope read the first step. "One cup of flour!" she said. Dad helped her pour it. Then she saw the next step. "One egg," she said. She cracked it in the bowl. The egg was a little smelly, and she giggled.

Penelope got excited and skipped a step. She did not put in the baking powder. Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot pan. Penelope watched from her stool.

The pancakes came out flat. "Oh no," said Penelope. Dad said, "Let's look again."

They read the card together, one step at a time. They found the missed step. They mixed a new bowl. Dad cooked them. The pancakes came out big and fluffy.

Her little brother, a small boy named Sam, clapped his hands. "Yum!" he said. The family ate them all up.

Alexander had a new patch of dirt in the backyard. He poked little holes with his finger. He dropped a carrot seed in each hole. Then he patted the dirt down flat.

Every morning Alexander ran outside. He looked and looked. The dirt stayed brown and smooth. Nothing was happening. "Where are my carrots?" he asked.

Dad sat on the swing nearby. "Did you give the seeds a drink?" he asked. Alexander shook his head. He ran to get his little green watering can. He tipped it over the dirt. Water made dark round spots on the soil.

The next morning, something green peeked up. Then he saw a tiny worm stick out its tongue-less face, and behind it, another sprout, and another. Alexander laughed. He filled the watering can all the way to the top.

Kinsley went to the mall with her dad. They were not late. "First haircut today!" said Dad. Kinsley held his hand tight.

The hairdresser smiled. "Sit here, please." Kinsley climbed up into the big chair. The hairdresser put a cape around her shoulders. It was blue and shiny. Snip, snip, snip went the scissors. Little bits of hair fell down. They landed on the cape. They did not get on her shirt. Not on her shoes. Not one bit.

Kinsley looked down. "The hairs slide off!" she said. She puffed out her chest like a superhero. "I am Cape Girl!" The hairdresser laughed. Dad laughed too. Snip, snip, snip. More hair slid down, down, down. It slid like a pig sliding in mud. Kinsley giggled and giggled. When they were done, she jumped down. "Cape Girl needs a snack," she said. Dad said, "Cape Girl gets a snack."

Iris wanted to find her toy robot. It was lost somewhere at home. She looked under the table. She looked in her toy box. No robot there.

Then Iris went to the backyard with Dad. The grass was cool and soft. Something white lay in the grass. It was light and soft like a little fan. Iris picked it up. "A feather!" she said. Birds have feathers. So a bird must have been here. She looked up. A small bird sat on the fence. It chirped at her.

Iris wiped the feather with her fingers. She wanted to give it back. She set the feather on the bird bath. The bird hopped down near it. Then Iris heard a beep, beep. Her robot was in the flower pot by the door! She hugged it tight. "Found you," she said.

Hunter ran into the big hall. Balloons hung from the ceiling. Grandma had tied them there.

A long table stood by the window. On it was a cake with four candles. Dad used a match to light them. Hunter watched from his chair. He did not touch the matches.

"I was three yesterday," Hunter said. "Am I still three?"

"Blow out your candles," said Mom. "Then you will see."

Hunter stood up. He was careful not to lean too far. He took a big breath. He blew hard. All four candles went out. The smoke curled up like a little feather.

"Now count them," said Grandma.

Hunter touched the candles one by one. "One, two, three, four."

"You are four today," said Mom.

Hunter jumped up and down. "I got bigger!" he said. "Watch me blow again next year!"

Alexis went to the park with his drum. Bang, bang, bang! The drum was loud and fun. Alexis felt excited. He played a happy beat. He counted his hits. One, two, three!

His friend Mia came to play. Mia put her hands on her ears. "Too loud," she said. Her face looked sad and a little scared. She hid behind the big tree.

Alexis stopped drumming. He felt angry for a tiny moment. He wanted to drum more! But then he looked at Mia. She did not like the loud drum. He liked the loud drum. Same drum, different feelings. Hmm.

"Let's play quiet," said Alexis. He put the drum down. They found a cozy spot under a leafy bush. It was like a little green house. Alexis put leaves on a plate he found in the sand toys. "Leaf cake!" he said. Mia clapped softly. "Yum!" she said. Alexis patted the drum very gently. Tap, tap. Mia smiled. Alexis smiled too. "Quiet drum," said Mia. Tap, tap, tap.

Theodore ran to art class. "Today we paint shapes!" said Miss Amy. She held up a red bucket of brushes. Theodore grabbed one fast. He wanted to paint a big house.

First he painted a square. Four sides, flat like a box. Then he painted a triangle on top. Pointy like a hat! "The house needs a door," said Theodore. He looked around the room. What shape was a door?

He ran to the real door and looked. He touched one corner. Then another. "One, two, three, four," he counted. Four corners! The door was a rectangle. A rectangle has four sides and four square corners, just like this door. Theodore laughed out loud.

He ran back to his paint. He painted a rectangle door on his square house. He painted tiny circle windows too. "Look, Miss Amy!" he said. "My door is a rectangle, like the real one!" Miss Amy clapped her hands. Theodore spelled out the word D-O-O-R at the bottom. Then he held his painting up high for everyone to see.

William sat very still on the back step. His ears heard a bird singing. "What do I hear with?" he asked himself. "My ears!" Then he heard a bee buzz. Ears again.

He touched a smooth, clean stone. "I feel with my hands," he said. He sniffed a red flower. "I smell with my nose." He popped a tiny seed in his mouth. "No, no," said Grandma. "Seeds are for planting, not eating." William put the seed in the dirt instead.

A dog barked next door. William's ears heard it. He put his hands over his ears. The bark got small and quiet. He took his hands off. The bark got big again. "My ears hear the dog," said William. He listened until the dog went quiet too. Then Grandma called, "William, cookie time!" William heard her with his ears and ran.

Norah sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a big pumpkin. But there was no orange paint. "Where did the orange go?" she asked. Her teacher, Miss Kim, said, "Maybe you can find out."

Norah looked at the cups. Red paint. Blue paint. Yellow paint. Green paint. No orange at all. Sam sat next to her. He was painting a green frog. "Watch this," Sam said. He put a brush in the red cup. Then he put red in the yellow cup. He stirred it round and round.

The yellow turned orange! Norah clapped her hands. "Can I try?" she asked. "Yes," said Sam. Norah dipped her brush in the red paint. She stirred it into the yellow. Swish, swish. The paint got darker. Now it was orange, just like a real pumpkin. It smelled a little stinky, like all paints do. "Can I pay you back with my yellow?" Norah asked. Sam laughed. "You can just share it." Miss Kim came over and smiled. She stuck a magnet on the wall and hung the wet painting up high. "It will dry there," she said. Norah looked up at her orange pumpkin and smiled. "I made orange all by myself," she said.

Myles sat at the little table in the art room. He wanted to draw a big furry dog for his mom. He picked up his pencil and started to draw. He pressed down very hard. He wanted the dog to be dark and easy to see.

Then something happened. Snap! The pencil point broke off. The little piece fell onto the table. Myles picked it up and looked at it. He turned the pencil around in his hand. Would a soft press work too?

He got a new pencil from the jar. This time he pressed gently. The line was soft and gray. He pressed a little more, still gently. The line got darker. The pencil point stayed on. Myles smiled. He drew the furry dog, stroke by stroke, soft and slow.

At the end of class, the drawings hung on a string with clips. His furry dog swung a little when the teacher walked by. Myles pointed at it. "Look at my dog!" he said. "I pressed soft, so the point stayed on."

Lennon went to the library with her dad. She saw a tablet on the little table. She wanted to draw a cat on it.

The screen was dark. Dad showed her the small round button. She pushed it. The screen lit up. "I did it!" she said.

Now she wanted to draw. She looked at the screen. It had lots of small pictures. She saw a paintbrush picture. She tapped it with one finger. The drawing app opened. There was a big white page, just like a cloud.

Lennon drew a cat with a long tail. Then she drew a sun. A boy sat down next to her. He was noisy because he wanted a turn too. Lennon drew him a little dog. He smiled.

The librarian said time was up. Lennon did not cry. She pushed the button and the screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the table. "Bye bye, tablet," she said.

Athena went to the store with Mom. Today Athena wanted pink strawberries. Yesterday the store had none. "Maybe today," said Mom.

Athena looked at the fruit bins. She saw apples. She saw bananas. No strawberries yet. "The truck comes soon," said the fruit man. "Soon means a little wait," Mom said with a smile. Athena did not like waiting.

Then Athena heard a big noise outside. A bus stopped by the store. Men carried boxes off the bus. The boxes went into the store. Athena watched. One box had pink on it. The fruit man opened it. Strawberries!

"Can we get some now?" asked Athena. "Yes, now," said Mom. She let Athena pick the box. Athena held it all the way to the pay desk.

At home, Mom washed the berries. Athena ate three. They were sweet. "Can we buy more tomorrow?" she asked. "Tomorrow, yes," said Mom. Athena jumped up and down. "The truck came soon, just like the man said!" she said. Mom clapped and showed Athena one big berry. "This one is for you," said Mom.

Jake was at home with his teddy bear. Today he had to get a shot at the doctor. His tummy felt funny. "Will it hurt?" he asked Grandpa. "Just a tiny pinch," said Grandpa. "Then it is done."

In the waiting room, Jake held his teddy tight. A cute baby sat on his mom's lap nearby. Jake's feet did not stop wiggling. He did not want his turn to come.

Grandpa sat down next to him. "Smell the flower," Grandpa said. He held up his hand like a flower. Jake breathed in slow. "Now blow out the birthday candle," said Grandpa. Jake blew out slow. They did it again. One, smell the flower. Two, blow the candle. Three, smell the flower. Jake's feet stopped wiggling.

"Jake," the nurse called. Jake walked in all by himself. He smelled the flower. He blew the candle. The nurse said, "All done!" It was just a tiny pinch, and it was over.

At home, Jake got a sticker and a hug. Then he gave his teddy a pretend shot. "Smell the flower, teddy," he said. At lunch, Jake used his fork to feed himself bite by bite. He felt big. After lunch, he told teddy, "You were brave too."

Grandma came early with a big box. It was time for the family party. Inside the box were dates and honey and flour. "We make these sweets only on this day," said Grandma. Felix wanted to taste one now.

"Can I have one?" he asked. "Not yet," said Grandma. "First we mix, then we bake, then we wait." Felix helped from his chair. He poured the flour. It went poof on his nose. Grandma laughed. "Now you look like a snowy cat," she said.

The oven was hot, so Grandma put the pan in. Felix watched through the little window. The little dough balls got big and brown. When they came out, Felix was sleepy. But he woke up fast. He lifted a warm sweet from the plate. He took one big bite. "It tastes like honey and sunshine," he said. Grandma smiled and took a bite too.

Rowan sat at the dinner table. He had a warm bowl of soup. He took a big sip. Then he wiggled in his seat. "I need to go potty," he said. He ran down the hall.

Rowan used the toilet. He pulled up his pants. He washed his hands. He heard the sink go whoosh. The water felt cool on his fingers. Then he ran back to the table.

Mama was looking at him. "Did you flush?" she asked. Rowan thought hard. Had he flushed? He did not think so. He ran back down the hall. He pushed the little silver handle. Whoosh! The water swirled down. Then he washed his hands again, just to be sure. The soap smelled like flowers.

Back at the table, his soup was still warm. He patted his tummy. "All done with potty," he said. "Flush and wash. Flush and wash." Mama laughed. "That's right, Rowan." Rowan ate his soup. His toes were cozy in his red sock. Soon his eyes felt sleepy. After dinner came a bath, then pajamas. Rowan smiled. Tomorrow he would flush and wash all by himself again.

Levi stood at the running track. The sun felt warm on his arms. A big hoop lay on the ground. A box of beanbags sat next to it. Levi wanted to throw every beanbag himself.

He picked up a beanbag. He threw it. It landed in the hoop. He grabbed another one. A kid named Mia reached for the box too. "More beanbags?" Levi wondered. Then he looked at Mia's hands. She had no beanbag at all.

Levi held one out. "Your turn," he said. Mia threw it. It missed the hoop. Then it was Levi's turn again. Throw, pass, throw, pass. His hands were learning the big ball next. Coach Maya rolled it to him. Levi caught it with both hands. The ball felt real and bumpy. "Again!" he said, and passed the ball back.

Charles sat on the big couch. It was game morning at his house. Uncle Ben was there. Grandma was there. The neighbors came too. Everyone counted, "One, two, three, watch!"

The game started on TV. Charles saw a man in a striped shirt. The man ran back and forth. He kept watching the players. "Is he scary?" Charles asked. "No," said Uncle Ben. "Just watch what he does."

A player pushed another player. The striped man blew his whistle. He held up his hand. The game stopped. Then it started again.

"He watches the game," said Charles. "He made them stop!" Uncle Ben smiled. Grandma swept popcorn off the rug. The neighbors cheered. Charles waved his little flag. "One, two, three, watch!" he shouted, right along with everyone.

Iris sat in a big chair at the salon. Grandma stood right beside her. Iris wanted her hair to look pretty like Grandma's. But the hairdresser kept stopping! First she combed Iris's hair. Then she snipped once. Then she combed again. Snip. Again!

Why did she comb so much? Iris began to count. "One comb, one snip," said Iris. "Two combs, one snip." The comb made the hair lie flat and neat. Then the scissors could cut it straight. Iris watched the soft hairs fall. They floated down like little feathers.

A small piece of hair landed on a card on the counter. "Look, Grandma! A hair on my card!" Iris gave the card back to the hairdresser. Iris kicked her feet, happy in the big chair. Then she looked in the mirror. "Is that me?" she asked. Grandma smiled and said, "That is you, with your very first haircut."

Ayla went to the park with her grandma. She brought her bunny and her bear. She wanted to play tea party. But she had no real teacups.

Ayla looked in the toy box by the sandbox. There was one red cup. It was empty. No water, no tea. She felt sad. Her bunny was thirsty!

Then Ayla had an idea. She held the cup over her bear. She tipped it slowly. "More tea?" she asked. Nothing came out. She poured it again anyway.

"Drink up, bear!" she said. Bear drank and drank. "That was yummy tea," said grandma in a big bear voice. Ayla giggled. Her cup had no tea in it at all. But bear liked it anyway!

Ayla gave bunny a cup too. She poured and poured. "Careful," she said. "It is pretend hot!" Bunny sipped very slowly. Bunny blew on it. "Too hot, bunny?" asked Ayla. Bunny nodded. Ayla waited and counted to three.

Then she set the cups on a little bench. She wrapped bunny in her jacket. "Now bunny is cozy," she said. The wind came. It blew a leaf into the red cup.

"Oh no!" said Ayla. "The wind wants tea too!" Grandma laughed and clapped. Ayla tipped the leaf out. She poured one more cup, just for the wind.

"Last cup," said Ayla. She held it up high. "Tea time for everyone!" she said.

The lights went out. The TV went out too. The whole room went dark.

"Mama!" Leo called.

"I am here," said Mama. She lit a candle with a match. The flame tickled the air. Then the room had a little glow.

Leo looked out the window. The street was dark. The neighbor's house was dark. The big house at the corner was dark too.

"All dark!" said Leo. "Every house!"

"Yes," said Mama. "The power went out on our street."

Leo clapped his hands. "We are a dark team!"

Mama laughed. "A big dark team, all up and down the street."

They sat close on the rug. The candle made shadows on the wall. Leo put his hand up. The shadow got big.

"Look! My hand makes a giant!" said Leo.

Mama moved the candle. The giant grew tall. Then it got small.

Soon the lights came back on. The TV hummed. The street glowed out the window, house by house.

"It's early bedtime," said Mama. She blew out the candle. The smoke curled up like a little worm.

"Good night, candle," said Leo.

Luca sat in the family car. He was going to meet his new baby sister. "One baby, two big hands," said Daddy. "My hands will hold her," said Luca. He had been playing in the yard. His hands had mud on them. One, two, three little brown spots.

The car stopped. Mommy carried the baby in a soft blanket. Luca ran to her. "My turn!" he said. He held out his muddy hands. Mommy shook her head. She pointed to the sink.

Luca turned the faucet. The water ran over his hands. The mud washed away. One, two, three spots gone. Then he counted his clean fingers. One to ten.

Mommy put the baby in his arms. The baby had a tiny nose. She made a small sound. Luca stroked her soft blanket. "I washed," he whispered. The baby grabbed his finger. She held on tight.

Willow wanted her bunny. Bunny was not on her bed. Bunny was not in the toy box.

Willow ran for the big hall. It was full of bags from the market. She wanted to look behind all the bags. Then she stopped. She went back to the kitchen instead.

"Mama, bunny is lost," said Willow. Mama wiped her hands on a towel. "Let us look together," said Mama. They peeked in the bags. No bunny. They looked under the sofa. Willow heard a little scratch under there. Mama reached in and pulled out bunny, with a yucky bit of dust on one ear.

Mama washed the ear with a warm cloth. Willow hugged bunny tight. "We found her together," said Willow.

Asher stood by the school gate. His backpack was very big. It was full of toys.

Asher tried to walk to the door. His backpack was too heavy. He fell down on the slippery grass. His toys rolled out everywhere.

A big truck went by. It came from the farm. It honked its horn. Asher's toy cow jumped. It landed in the truck! The truck stopped.

The driver got out. She picked up the cow. "This belongs to you," she said. She put it in Asher's hand.

Asher sat on the step. He opened his backpack. He took out his toy train. He took out his robot. He took out his ball. Now the backpack was light.

He put it on his back. He could walk fast! He could even run to the door. His backpack bounced up and down.

His teacher waved at the gate. Asher waved back. Inside, he saw a surprise. The toy cow sat on the desk, waiting for him.

"How did you get here?" Asher asked. The cow just smiled.

Blake marched down the school hallway. It was her first day. She held her lunchbox tight. The hall smelled like crayons and floor wax. Her new shoes went squeak, squeak.

At lunch, a boy had a lunchbox just like hers. Red, with a dog on it. A huge mix-up! "Is this mine or yours?" Blake asked. The boy looked at his lid. "This one says Sam," he said.

Blake opened her box. Her name was inside the lid. Mom had written it there. Blake took her box and Sam took his. At home time, another kid found her dropped hat on the floor. He read the name tag. He ran it to her. Blake smiled and waved. "Thanks," she said.

Zoey put on her red sweater for school. She loved letter time. The wall had big letters. A big A hung up high.

The teacher read a book about a fish. "Look," said Zoey. "A little circle with a tail." She pointed at the small a. "That is not A. A is big."

Her friend Sam smiled. "Trace it," he said. Zoey traced the small a with her finger. Then she looked up at the big A. She traced that one too.

"Same letter!" said Zoey. "Big A. Small a. Same, same!" She clapped her hands.

The teacher read on. "The fish can swim fast." Zoey found the small f. Then she found the big F on the wall. "Same letter," she said. "F says ffff, like fish."

Sam clapped too. "You found it," he said.

Zoey turned the page. She pointed at a beautiful blue whale. "W," she said. "Big W or small w. Same letter." She smiled and read on, "Whales can swim in the sea."

Gabriel woke up at Grandma's house. He looked out the big window. Snow had fallen in the night. The snow was white. The fence was red. The bird feeder was blue.

"I want to draw the snow," said Gabriel. Grandma gave him white paper and crayons. Gabriel drew the red fence. He drew the blue bird feeder. He drew a green pine tree. Then he picked the white crayon. He drew and drew. But nothing showed up. The white snow did not show on the white paper. Gabriel made a sad face.

"Try this," said Grandma. She gave him a blue piece of paper. Gabriel drew with the white crayon again. The snow showed up! It looked soft and puffy. He drew white snow on the blue roof. He drew white snow on the green tree. Grandma clapped her hands.

"It looks like a map of the yard," she said. Gabriel smiled. He took his drawing to the window. He gave a little wave to the red fence. Then Grandma brought warm pretzels. They were a little salty. Gabriel ate one and watched the white snow fall. "More snow," he said. "More blue paper too."

Charlie was playing blocks with her friend Sam. Sam built a tall tower. It had a red block on top.

Charlie reached for a blue block. Her elbow bumped the tower. Crash! All the blocks fell down.

Sam looked at the blocks. His mouth went flat and sad. "My tower," he said.

Mom came over. She sat on the floor with them. "What can we say?" she asked softly.

Charlie thought hard. Was there a word for this? "Sorry," she said. "Sorry, Sam."

Sam's mouth went up again. "It's okay. Want to build it with me?"

Charlie nodded. She handed Sam the red block. Then she found a funny green block with a bumpy side. "Can this go on top?" she asked.

"Yes!" said Sam. "You put it on."

They took turns. Charlie placed one block. Then Sam placed one block. The new tower grew tall, taller, tallest of all.

Mom clapped her hands. "Lunch soon," she said. "First, let's put the blocks in the basket."

Charlie put in three blocks. Sam put in three blocks. The basket filled up, one handful at a time.

"Same for you, same for me," said Sam.

Charlie smiled. "Let's leave the red one out," she said. "For after lunch."

Wren put on her red coat all by herself. She pushed one arm in. She pushed the other arm in. The coat was on.

Now came the zipper. Wren held the little tab. She pushed it up, up, up. It stopped halfway. She pulled it back down. Then she pushed it up again, slowly. This time it went all the way to the top. "I did it!" said Wren.

Mama was making lunch at the stove. "Can I help?" asked Wren. "You can set the mittens by the door," said Mama. Wren ran to get her mittens. But one mitten slipped out of her hand. It slid under the chair. Wren found it again. Then she saw her coat pocket. She tucked one mitten in. She tucked the other mitten in. Both mittens sat snug and safe.

At lunch, Wren ate her sandwich. After lunch, she remembered her mittens. She opened the pocket. There they were, both together. She pulled them out and waved them. "My mittens were hiding in my pretty red coat!"

Victor went to the school library with his class. He saw a little table with paper and pencils. The teacher, Miss Ana, smiled at him.

"Today you will write your name," she said.

Victor picked up a pencil. He held it up high and waved it as he walked to his chair. Then he remembered. Miss Ana had shown them. The point goes down. He turned the pencil around. Now the point faced the floor. "Point down," he said to himself. "Point down."

He sat down and held the pencil the right way. He pressed it on the paper. A little line came out. He made a big V. Then an i, then a c, then more letters. He looked at his paper.

"I did it!" said Victor. "That is my name!"

Miss Ana clapped her hands. "It says Victor," she said.

Victor was not sad anymore. Writing was fun. He wrote his name again. Then he wrote it one more time. He carried his paper to the shelf, point down, all the way.

Addison sat with her family at the restaurant. A big screen glowed on the wall. Everyone was watching an ice hockey game. Addison wanted to see the ball. She looked and looked. "I can't find the ball," she said.

Then she saw it. The players hit a small black disc with their sticks. It slid fast on the smooth ice. The disc was not a ball at all. It was flat, like a little pancake. "That's not a ball," Addison said. Her dad smiled and nodded. "They call it a puck," he said.

Addison watched the puck zoom and spin. A player hit it hard with his stick. The puck flew into the net. The crowd on the screen cheered. The restaurant filled with happy shouts. Addison clapped her hands.

Later, the waiter brought a plate of warm bread. Addison dipped a piece in the little dish of soup. She took a bite and smiled at her root vegetable soup. Then she pointed at the screen. "Puck!" she said. The puck slid by again, fast and smooth.

Lena wanted to draw a sun at school. Teacher Sam held up a tablet. "You can draw on this," he said.

Lena pressed her whole hand on the screen. The screen stayed dark. She pressed harder. Still dark. Her friend Max slid the tablet over to her. "Try your finger," he said.

Lena lifted one finger. She tapped the screen, tap, tap. The screen lit up bright. "It works!" she said. She tapped the little yellow sun icon and the drawing app opened. She drew a big yellow sun with red rays.

Then the teacher rang the little bell. Time to clean up. Lena tapped the button and the drawing went away. She put the tablet back on the shelf, flat and neat.

Max looked for his tablet plug. Lena pointed to it on the wall. "There it is," she said. Max smiled. Then Lena tapped his screen too. It lit up for him.

John dropped his coat on the hall floor. Then he ran to see Grandpa's toy frog. The frog hopped when you pushed it. "Hop, frog, hop!" said John. The frog made a loud click every time.

Later, John wanted to go outside. "Where is my coat?" he said. He looked under the table. He looked behind the big chair. No coat. He looked at the coat pile on the floor. "That is not mine," he said. Then Grandma held up a coat. "Is this it?" It was John's coat, all dusty from the floor. "Silly coat," said John. He laughed.

The next day, John put his coat on by himself. One arm in. Other arm in. Then the zipper. Up, up, up it went. "I did it!" he said. Grandpa clapped. At the door, John saw a little hook on the wall. He hung his coat right on it. The coat stayed up, off the floor. "Look, Grandpa! My coat can stand on the wall!" said John. Grandpa laughed. "So it can," he said.

Charles went to the art studio with his mama. He wanted to draw a big sun. He looked for his crayons. "Where are my crayons?" he asked.

"We left them in the car," said Mama. "I will get them." She went out to the hot, sunny car. She came back with the box. Charles opened the box. He picked up a red crayon. It felt soft. It bent like a noodle!

Charles tried to draw. The soft crayon made a fat, shiny line. It smeared and smeared. "Oh no," said Charles. "My sun will not look right." He tried again. The red crayon bent more. It left shiny red smudges on the paper.
